0verkill.title: 0verkill
0verkill.description: A bloody 2D deathmatch drawn in ASCII: grab the shotgun, the UZI or a box of grenades and frag two bots, or your friends on the local network.
0verkill.provenance: Brainsoft (Brain, Clock and others) released 0verkill 0.16 in 2000; hackndev fixed it for newer compilers from 2008 to 2010, and ravener revived it on GitHub from 2021.
0verkill.page:
**LOAD THE BROWNING. EVERYONE ELSE ALREADY HAS.**

You start with a pistol and a bad feeling. Somewhere on the level there's a
shotgun, an UZI, a sniper rifle and a box of grenades, and everybody else in
the game wants them as much as you do. Run, jump, creep under the fire,
slide down the ladders and drop through the floors. Grab the armour, the
medikits and, if you can find it, the invisibility. When it goes wrong (and
it will) the game tells you plainly: "Bloody shrapnel killed you." Press
Space and get straight back in.

0verkill is a side-on deathmatch drawn entirely in ASCII art, and it is not
shy with the red.

- **Five weapons**: Browning, shotgun, UZI, sniper rifle and grenades. Take
  the grenades, fire and jump, and you throw them upward; the manual calls
  it playing basketball with grenades
- **Never alone**: started from Asciiverse, it opens a game on your machine
  against two bots, so there is always someone to shoot
- **Friends on your network** can join the same game, and Enter opens the
  chat for the trash talk; Tab shows who has the most frags
- **A Czech cult classic** from 2000, kept alive by the people who love it

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**: run
- **Up**: jump (with a direction, jump aside)
- **Down**: creep; **C** toggles creeping
- **D**: climb down ladders and drop through platforms
- **Ctrl** or **Z**: fire
- **1** to **5**: change weapon
- **Enter**: chat

## Playing with friends

One player starts the game; everyone else joins it with
`0verkill -i <that player's address>`.

## History

Brainsoft, a Czech group at Charles University in Prague, released 0verkill
in 2000. Its code has been kept alive since: hackndev fixed it for
newer compilers (2008 to 2010), and ravener's revival (2021 to 2026) fixed
its network checksum and a memory bug.

## Credits

- Game: Brainsoft (Brain: code, design, graphics, levels; Clock: idea, AVI
  editor, graphics)
- Fixes: hackndev (Marek Vasut, Jonathan Neuschäfer), ravener and lumidify
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0

1d-pong.title: 1D-Pong
1d-pong.description: Pong with one dimension! The whole court is a single line: wait for the ball, hit it late for a blistering return, but not too late. Starts with nothing but the line and unfolds as you play.
1d-pong.provenance: Asciiverse made 1D-Pong in Rust in 2026, after the one-dimensional Pong that hobbyists build from a strip of LEDs with a button at each end.
1d-pong.page:
**ONE LINE. ONE BUTTON. NOWHERE TO HIDE.**

Forget up and down. In 1D-Pong the whole court is a single glowing line, your paddle is the stretch of it at your end, and the ball can only come straight at you. All you decide is *when*.

Press while the ball is in your zone and it flies back. Hit it early and it goes back slow and safe. Wait, let it get deep, hit it at the very last moment and it screams back as a **SMASH!** Wait one moment too long and it's gone. Press before it arrives and your paddle goes dim, and for a heartbeat you can't hit at all.

Every rally gets faster. The ball heats from green through amber and red to white hot, the line throws sparks, and the whole game holds its breath for a split second on every hit. And whoever is ahead plays with a shorter paddle, so no lead is ever safe.

- **It unfolds as you play.** You start with nothing but the line. Sound, the score, the trail, the sparks, the menu: each one arrives the first time you earn it.
- **Four computer players,** from Easy to the King of Lineland. Beat the King and see what lies beyond the line.
- **Two players at one keyboard,** or with two gamepads: one button each, nothing else.
- **Watch** two Kings rally on their own.
- **The pure view:** press V for just the line and the score, nothing else at all.

First to seven. **ONE MORE MATCH...**

## Controls

- **Space**: hit (also A, Z, ← or Enter); you are on the left
- **Two players**: left A, right L, or one gamepad each
- **Gamepad**: any face, shoulder or d-pad button hits; Start pauses
- **P**: pause, **M**: sound on or off, **V**: the pure view
- **Esc**: back to the menu, **Q**: quit from the menu

## Options

- `--cpu easy|normal|hard|king`: straight into a match against that computer
- `--two`: straight into a two-player match
- `--watch`: the computer plays itself
- `--to N`: points to win a match (default 7)
- `--pure`: start in the pure view
- `--mute`: start with the sound off
- `--unfold all`: skip the unfolding; `--unfold 0` starts it over

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- After the one-dimensional Pong built from LED strips

2048.description: Slide, merge, double: build a 2048 tile on a 4x4 board before the new tiles bury you.
2048.provenance: Maurits van der Schee wrote 2048.c in 2014, a console version of Gabriele Cirulli's game of the same year, in one C file that draws with ANSI escape codes.
2048.page:
**TWO AND TWO MAKE FOUR. KEEP GOING UNTIL IT'S 2048.**

A 4x4 board and a couple of numbers. Every move slides every tile as far as
it will go, and when two equal numbers run into each other they merge: two
2s make a 4, two 4s make an 8, and on up through 16, 32, 64 and beyond.
After each move a fresh 2 (now and then a 4) drops into an empty square,
and the board fills up.

Keep your biggest tile in a corner. Build towards it, carefully. Then watch
a stray 2 land exactly where you didn't want it. The game ends when the
board is full and nothing can move; every merge on the way adds to your
score.

- **The puzzle that took over 2014**, in Maurits van der Schee's
  single-file C version: no libraries, nothing to set up, straight in
- **Every key you know**: arrows, WASD, vi's hjkl or the number pad
- **Colour schemes** for any terminal, and at game over the final board
  stays on screen for you to admire, or mourn

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **WASD**, **h j k l** or **4 8 6 2**: slide the tiles
- **r**: start again (asks first)
- **q**: quit (asks first)

At game over, **r** plays again and **q** quits.

## Options

- `2048 blackwhite`, `2048 whiteblack`, `2048 bluered`: other colour
  schemes for the tiles
- `2048 test`: runs the built-in tests of the sliding rules

## History

Gabriele Cirulli made 2048 in 2014 as an open-source web game, after
earlier games of the same kind. Maurits van der Schee wrote this
console version, 2048.c, the same year, in a single C file that draws
with ANSI escape codes and needs no libraries; it is packaged by Debian
and others. This edition waits at game over so the final board stays
in view, and is built for Windows as well.

## Credits

2048.c is by Maurits van der Schee, under the MIT licence.

alienwave.title: Alienwave
alienwave.description: A shoot-'em-up in the terminal: waves of zorxians swoop down at your ship, you fire lasers and drop shields to hide behind, and after 5000 points their queen Xzarna comes for you.
alienwave.provenance: Alessandro Pira wrote Alienwave in C with ncurses, a Galaga-like shooter for the terminal; it was out by 2005 and last updated in 2013.
alienwave.page:
**THEY COME IN WAVES. YOU HAVE ONE SHIP.**

The zorxians fly down in formation, peel off and dive at you. Slide left and right along the bottom of the screen, fire your lasers into the swarm, and when it gets too hot, open a shield to hide behind. Shields don't move with you, though: they stay where you put them, and they only last as long as their charge.

Survive long enough, past 5000 points, and Xzarna, the zorxian queen, comes for you herself. You have one life, and the score is printed on the way out.

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**: move your ship; **Down**: stop
- **Space** or **Enter**: fire
- **S**, **Up** or **Backspace**: open a shield (when it has charge)
- **P**: pause; **Q** or **Esc**: quit

The charge indicator for the shields is in the top left corner.

## Credits

- Alienwave: Alessandro Pira
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

all-things-devours.title: All Things Devours
all-things-devours.description: 4:17 am, six minutes, one bomb: break into your own lab and destroy the time machine before anyone can use it. Save often; this one is cruel.
all-things-devours.provenance: Toby Ord wrote All Things Devours, as half sick of shadows, for the 2004 Interactive Fiction Competition.
all-things-devours.page:
**4:17 AM. SIX MINUTES. ONE BOMB.**

"You're in. The plan now is simple: go to your lab, plant the bomb, and
run. The prototype will be destroyed. The military will have no way to
continue the experiment. No-one will die."

The guard is out securing the grounds. The building is empty, a darkened
foyer with a security desk, four CCTV screens and four buttons: 'basement',
'first', 'second' and 'alarm'. You have six minutes. Then time itself starts
to fold back on you, and every move you make has to fit with the moves you
have already made.

Be warned, in the author's own words: "it is more cruel than one might hope
for a modern piece of interactive fiction. In particular, any move you make
may put things into an unwinnable state." Save often. You will probably
start over more than once to find the best ending, and that is the fun of
it.

- **A tight clockwork puzzle**: one building, one night, six minutes
- **A familiar science-fiction idea**, explored "in what I hope is a
  rather refreshing and satisfying manner"
- **An IFComp 2004 game**, given to the public domain by its author

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/all-things-devours`.

## Credits

- All Things Devours: Toby Ord, writing as half sick of shadows; IFComp 2004
- License: Public domain, by the author's statement in the game and its source
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

alquerque.title: Alquerque and Fanorona
alquerque.description: Leap and take on the lined board of Alfonso X's Book of Games, or sweep whole lines away in Madagascar's Fanorona
alquerque.provenance: Asciiverse made Alquerque and Fanorona in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow Alfonso X's Book of Games (1283, in Sonja Musser Golladay's translation), R. C. Bell (1960), W. Montgomery's account of Fanorona (1886) and Schadd and colleagues (2008).
alquerque.page:
**LEAP AND TAKE, OR SWEEP WHOLE LINES AWAY.**

Points joined by lines along every row, column and diagonal. In alquerque, your men leap enemies like draughts pieces and can keep on leaping. In fanorona, the national game of Madagascar, you capture by moving towards an enemy or away from one, and the whole unbroken line of enemies in that direction is swept off the board at once!

Alquerque's first rules are in the Book of Games a Spanish king had made in 1283. Fanorona was being played "everywhere, in-doors and out of doors" in 1886, its lines scratched on rocks and on the paving outside the palace. Its board is two alquerque boards side by side, and in 2008 it was proved that fanorona, played perfectly, is a draw. Nobody plays perfectly.

- **Alquerque de doze, after Alfonso X**: 5 by 5, twelve men each, taking not compulsory
- **Alquerque after Bell**: the stricter game; taking compulsory, and no man steps backwards
- **Fanorona, today's rules**: 9 by 5, twenty-two men each, approach and withdrawal
- **Fanorona after Montgomery**: the rules as first written down, in 1886
- **Vela**: the game after a defeat; last game's winner must hand over seventeen men, one at a time, before taking a single one back
- **Fanoron-dimy**: fanorona on the little board of five by five

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Arrows**: move the cursor; **Enter** or **Space**: pick up a man, then put it on a lit point; a turn that takes again goes on from where the man stands; where one step could take two lines, point at the line you want swept away; **Esc**: let go of a man, or stop taking where the rules allow
- **Mouse**: click
- The men a step would take are marked ✕ when the cursor is on where it goes
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same game every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

andromeda-apocalypse.title: Andromeda Apocalypse
andromeda-apocalypse.description: It's a perfect day on the shore, just before the storm. Then Ektor Mastiff, sole survivor of a world, is adrift in space on a strange vessel.
andromeda-apocalypse.provenance: Marco Innocenti's Andromeda Apocalypse won the 2012 Interactive Fiction Competition.
andromeda-apocalypse.page:
**IT'S JUST A PERFECT DAY. THEN THE STORM COMES IN.**

"Down on the horizon, thunderstorms cloud the sky. But the sea is fresh, and
the air has taken on that orange hue. It's just a perfect day."

Korhos is setting over the shore of Monarch. Loud waves splash on the sand,
and Uncle Oren, once your mentor at the University Radiation Technology
Division, is staring at the horizon "like a bird in search of a migratory
route". "It looks like Paradise," he says. A white electric arc paints the
southern sky.

What follows takes you, Ektor Mastiff, a very long way from that beach:
"Floating in space on a strange vessel, sole survivor of a world... and
maybe of the entire human race, Ektor Mastiff must find a way through the
cosmos, on a voyage that can change the history of mankind forever."

- **Big, cinematic science fiction** from Marco Innocenti: the second part
  of his Andromeda series. You can start here, though the author recommends
  Andromeda Awakening first for the full story
- **The Extended Edition**, with achievements and a walkthrough in its own
  menus for when you are stuck
- **Plain English**: type what you want to do, and ABOUT or HELP for the
  game's own guide

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/andromeda-apocalypse`.

## Credits

- Andromeda Apocalypse: Marco Innocenti, 2012; title song by Wade Clarke
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0
- Played with Glulxe and GlkTerm by Andrew Plotkin (MIT)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

angband.title: Angband
angband.description: A hundred levels of dungeon under a little town, and Morgoth, Lord of Darkness, waiting at the bottom. Choose a race and a class, buy what you can, and go down.
angband.provenance: Alex Cutler and Andy Astrand wrote Angband at the University of Warwick in 1990 from the code of Umoria, and a line of maintainers, now the Angband Dev Team, has kept it going since.

upstream.name: Angband Dev Team, after Alex Cutler and Andy Astrand (1990)

angband.page:
**A HUNDRED LEVELS DOWN, MORGOTH IS WAITING. SO IS EVERYTHING IN BETWEEN.**

Up top there's a little town. The General Store might be kept by Bilbo the
Friendly, or by Rincewind the Chicken; there's an armoury, a weaponsmith, an
alchemist and a black market, and Farmer Maggot shuffling about in the
streets. ("He's lost his dogs. He's had his mushrooms stolen. He's not a
happy hobbit!") Underneath lie the Pits of Angband. On level 99 waits
Sauron, the Sorcerer. On level 100, Morgoth, Lord of Darkness.

Every time you take the stairs, the level is built anew: orcs and trolls,
dragons and wraiths, uniques with names out of Tolkien, traps, treasure and
artifacts like the Phial of Galadriel, the sword Ringil and the One Ring
itself. Death is permanent, and most players lose many characters before one
goes all the way down. That is the game.

- **Eleven races and nine classes**: a Hobbit Rogue, a Dwarf Priest, a
  High-Elf Mage, a Half-Troll Blackguard, a Kobold Necromancer...
- **A hundred levels**, made afresh on every visit, deeper and deadlier all
  the way to the Lord of Darkness
- **Over six hundred monsters** and a hoard of legendary artifacts, many
  straight from Middle-earth
- **The grandfather of a family**: carried on since 1990, with dozens of
  roguelikes among its variants

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or the **number keys** (1 to 9): move; walk into a
  monster to attack it
- **.** and a direction: run along a corridor
- **<** and **>**: take stairs up and down
- **g**: pick up, **i**: inventory, **e**: equipment, **w**: wear or wield
- **q** quaff a potion, **r** read a scroll, **E** eat, **a** aim a wand,
  **u** use a staff, **z** zap a rod, **f** or **v** fire or throw
- **m**: cast a spell, **b**: browse a book
- **o** and **c**: open and close doors, **R**: rest
- **C**: character sheet, **l**: look around, **M**: map of the level
- **=**: options (a roguelike keyset with hjkl is there too)
- **?**: help, **Ctrl-S**: save, **Ctrl-X**: save and quit

## Saving

Your game is saved in your data folder (`~/.local/share/angband`) when you
quit with Ctrl-X, and Angband carries on from it the next time you start.
Character dumps, options and the score list are kept there too.

## History

Angband grew out of Moria, Robert Alan Koeneke's VMS game of 1985, by way
of James E. Wilson's Umoria (1989). Alex Cutler and Andy Astrand wrote
Angband 1.0 at the University of Warwick in 1990; Ben Harrison's rewrite
from 1995, Robert Ruehlmann, Anna Sidwell and the current maintainer, Nick
McConnell, have carried it on, and dozens of other roguelikes are its
variants.

## Credits

- Game: the Angband Dev Team (maintainer Nick McConnell), after Alex
  Cutler, Andy Astrand, Ben Harrison, Robert Ruehlmann, Anna Sidwell and
  many others; based on Moria by Robert Alan Koeneke and Umoria by James
  E. Wilson
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0 (Angband is also offered under its own non-commercial
  licence)

aquest.title: AQuest
aquest.description: Mark Mackey's XQuest in the terminal: steer a drifting ship round the arena, grab every crystal, dodge the mines and leave through the gate, fifty levels deep
aquest.provenance: Mark Mackey wrote XQuest for DOS in Turbo Pascal and released it as shareware from 1994 to 1996. David ported version 1.3 to C and SDL2 as xquest-sdl, and AQuest carries that port's game logic line by line into Rust and Ratatui for the terminal.
aquest.page:
**NO INVASION FLEET. NO HIDEOUS MUCOIDS. JUST GEMS, MINES AND FIFTY LEVELS OF TROUBLE.**

"You're a jolly little ship dingus which shoots around a rather abstract
landscape collecting little gem thingies, while avoiding mines. Boring, you
say? Well, we kept the Super Kill-o-Zapper, and added LOTS of things to blow
up. Happy?" So promised Mark Mackey's XQuest manual in 1994, and he meant
every word.

Pick up every crystal on the level and the gate at the top opens; fly out through
it to the next one. Fifty levels, each with more crystals, more mines, a
narrower gate, and from level 33 a gate that won't keep still.

Every level has a par time, counting down in the corner. Beat it and
each second left is worth 500 points; overstay it and the whole game
starts to speed up. An extra ship comes every 15,000 points on the first
levels, every 100,000 later.

Your ship steers by thrust and drifts on when you let go, so brake before
the wall: on every difficulty but Wimp, the wall is as deadly as a mine.
Your shots fly the way you do, as fast as you do. Enemies come in through
the side gates, eighteen kinds of them: Grungers wander, Zippos curve,
Zingers and Snipes shoot, Miners lay mines, Meebies follow you,
Retaliators fire back when they die, Tribblers burst into five, Clusters
into fifteen shots, and the Repulsor shoves you away. Catch a Supercrystal
for a power-up (Shield, AimedFire, RapidFire, MultiFire, AssFire,
HeavyFire or Bounce; a banner says what you got and what it does, and the
status bar shows all seven, lit while they last), and keep a smart bomb
for the moment it all goes wrong.

The game is the original, rule for rule: the same physics, levels, enemies
and sounds, and Mark Mackey's sprites drawn in Braille dots and half
blocks, cell by cell, so even a small terminal shows them in fine detail
and full colour; at full size, his own status bar.

## Controls

- **Arrows**, **WASD** or the numpad: thrust
- **Space** or **Enter**: fire (hold it with RapidFire)
- **Shift**, **Z** or numpad **5**: brake
- **B** or **X**: smart bomb
- **P**: pause; **Esc**: quit the game; **V**: graphics (Mixed, Blocks
  or Braille); **M**: sound
- Mouse: move to thrust, left button fires, right bombs, middle brakes
- Gamepad: stick or d-pad to thrust, **A** fires, **B** bombs, **X** or a
  shoulder brakes, **Start** pauses

Best in a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, foot, WezTerm,
Ghostty, Alacritty, iTerm2 and others), with the mouse or with a gamepad;
elsewhere a held key stutters until the terminal's repeats start.

## Options

- `--mixed`, `--blocks`, `--braille`: how to draw
- `--demo`: watch the built-in demo
- `--record FILE`, `--play FILE`: record and play back demos in the
  original `xquest.dmo` format
- `--difficulty N`: 0 Wimp to 4 Inhuman
- `--mute`: no sound

## History

Mark Mackey wrote XQuest in Turbo Pascal for DOS, a Mode X game at
320x240, and released it as shareware from 1994 to 1996. Make it to
Inhuman, the manual promised, and he'd send you a UUencoded GIF of a
tenner.

Thirty years on, David, who played it as shareware in the mid-90s, ported
version 1.3 to C and SDL2 as xquest-sdl. AQuest
carries that port's game logic over to the terminal line by line: a demo
recorded in either one plays back in the other, frame for frame. The Hall
of Fame and the demos keep the original file formats.

## Credits

- **XQuest**: Mark Mackey, 1994 to 1996
- **xquest-sdl**: David, the C and SDL2 port this edition is built on
- **AQuest**: the terminal edition, for Asciiverse

Free to play and share, never sold.

armoured-commander-ii.title: Armoured Commander II
armoured-commander-ii.description: Command a tank and its crew through the whole war in Europe, from a Polish tankette in 1939 to a Sherman in 1945: ten campaigns, every dice roll on screen.
armoured-commander-ii.provenance: Gregory Adam Scott wrote Armoured Commander II in Python and libtcod between 2016 and 2020, and Asciiverse ported it to Rust and Ratatui for the terminal.
armoured-commander-ii.page:
**SEPTEMBER 1939. ONE TANK. ONE CREW. SIX YEARS OF WAR AHEAD.**

Climb into the commander's hatch. In front of you lies the whole war in
Europe, from the invasion of Poland to the last weeks in Germany, and a tank
that may not be up to it. Drive a Polish TKS tankette or a 7TP into the
September Campaign. Defend Finland in the Winter War with "one of the few
tanks in the Finnish armed forces". Cross into France in 1940 for Germany,
or hold the line for France or Britain in a Char B1 bis or a Cruiser. Or
roll a Sherman across Europe in Patton's Best and Canada's Best.

Each day of a campaign is a map of zones to take and hold: scout ahead, call
in the artillery and the aircraft, resupply before the ammunition runs dry.
Each battle is a hex map round your tank: spot the enemy before he spots
you, give every crewman his orders, turn the turret, choose the shell, and
watch the dice decide every hit, every penetration, every kill. Nothing is
hidden.

Your crew are people. They gain experience and skills, earn nicknames, get
wounded, spend weeks in the field hospital and come back, or don't. Refits
bring new tanks.

- **Ten campaigns, 1939 to 1945**, for Germany, Poland, the Soviet Union,
  Finland, France, the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada
- **Tanks from the TKS and the T-26** to the Char B1 bis, the Panzer IV and
  the Sherman
- **Every roll on screen**: to-hit, penetration and firepower, all shown
- **Gregory Adam Scott's art, sounds and theme tune**, laid out for the
  terminal, the maps growing with a bigger window
- **One save per campaign**, so several wars can run side by side

## Controls

- In battle: **W/S** choose a crewman, **A/D** change his order,
  **H** open or close his hatch, **F** the crewman's menu;
  **Space** ends the phase
- Moving: **W/S** forward or reverse, **A/D** pivot, **H** try for a
  hull-down position, **R** reposition
- Shooting: **W/S** choose a weapon, **A/D** choose a target, **Q/E**
  turn the turret, **C** change the shell, **R** use the ready rack,
  **F** fire; **Enter** goes on after each roll
- **Tab** in battle: your tank in full
- On the day map: **1** to **4** for Supply, Crew, Travel and Group;
  **Q E A D Z C** choose a direction, **Enter** move, **R** recon,
  **W** wait or defend, **I** abandon the tank
- On the calendar: **1** to **4** for the day's mission, crew and tank,
  journal and field hospital; **Enter** starts the day
- **Esc**: the game menu with sound, volume, message pause and keyboard
  layout (QWERTY, AZERTY, QWERTZ, Dvorak), and Save and Quit

## Options

- `--battle [campaign]`: straight into one battle with a fresh tank and
  crew, to try the battle rules (nothing is saved); campaigns are named
  as `poland_campaign`, `pattons_best`, `winter_war_finland` and so on
- `--art`: browse the game's pictures

## History

Gregory Adam Scott made Armoured Commander II in Python 3 and libtcod
between 2016 and 2020 as free software, the sequel to his Armoured
Commander; later versions went to Steam. This edition ports the free
version to Rust and Ratatui: the same rules,
campaigns, art, sounds and theme tune, with every screen laid out for a
terminal of 100x30 and the maps growing with a bigger one. Its README
lists the few places where it plays or looks different.

## Credits

- Armoured Commander II: Gregory Adam Scott, 2016 to 2020
  ([github.com/sudasana/armcom2](https://github.com/sudasana/armcom2))
- Terminal port: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

armoured-commander.title: Armoured Commander
armoured-commander.description: Command a Sherman and its five-man crew from Normandy to Germany, 1944 to 1945: give every man his orders, see every die roll, and remember the fallen.
armoured-commander.provenance: Gregory Adam Scott wrote Armoured Commander in Python and libtcod between 2015 and 2017, and Eric Normandeau maintained it from version 1.04. Asciiverse ported it to Rust and Ratatui for the terminal.
armoured-commander.page:
**FIVE MEN. ONE SHERMAN. THE ROAD TO GERMANY.**

Normandy, summer 1944. The breakout has begun, you have a Sherman and a crew
of five, and it is a long way to the Rhine. Your gunner, loader, driver and
assistant driver are waiting for your orders. Somewhere up ahead, behind a
hedge or a farmhouse wall, there's a Panther, a Tiger, or an infantry squad
with a Panzerfaust.

Fight your way across the map of the front, area by area, calling in the
artillery and air strikes. Every encounter is a battle on a hex map round
your tank: spot the enemy, give each man his order, choose the ammunition,
fire, and see every to-hit and to-kill roll on screen.

Your crew gain experience and skills. They win decorations, from the Purple
Heart and the Bronze Star to the Victoria Cross. And some of them are
killed. Every man who falls goes into the game's graveyard, and one of them
stands on a headstone beside a poppy on the title screen, each time you
start the game.

- **Two campaigns**: Patton's Best with the US 4th Armored Division from
  July 1944, and Canada's Best with the First Canadian Army from August 1944
- **Shermans of every mark**, from the M4 and M4A1 to the M4A3E2 Jumbo,
  against Panzer IVs, Panthers, Tigers, King Tigers and tank destroyers
- **Every roll shown**: nothing is hidden behind the dice
- **Gregory Adam Scott's original art and sounds**, carried over to the
  terminal

## Controls

- **W/S** or **Up/Down**: choose a crewman; **A/D** or **Left/Right**:
  change his order; **O**: the full list of orders
- **H**: open or close a hatch; **R**: the next shell to load;
  **T**: use the ready rack
- **Space**: on to the next phase
- **Enter**: fire; **Tab**: next target; **A/D**: turn the turret;
  **M**: next machine gun; **F**: area or direct fire with HE
- On the day map: **Tab** and **Enter** to pick an area and move in;
  **W/S** to scroll
- **F1** help with every key, **F2** tank, **F3** crew, **F4** settings,
  **F5** campaign stats, **F7** sound on or off; **Esc**: menu, save and
  quit

## Options

- `--encounter advance`, `battle` or `counterattack`: one encounter with
  a fresh crew, to try the battle rules

## History

Gregory Adam Scott wrote Armoured Commander in Python 2.7 and libtcod
between 2015 and 2017 as free software; Eric Normandeau maintained it
from version 1.04. Scott went on to make a sequel, Armoured Commander II.
This edition ports it to Rust and Ratatui: the same rules, art and
sounds, every screen
laid out for a terminal of 100x30 and growing with a bigger one. Its
README lists the few places where it plays differently.

## Credits

- Armoured Commander: Gregory Adam Scott, 2015 to 2017, maintained by
  Eric Normandeau
  ([github.com/sudasana/armcom](https://github.com/sudasana/armcom))
- Terminal port: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

arogue.title: Advanced Rogue 5.8
arogue.description: Fighter, magician, cleric or thief: go down into the Dungeons of Doom, take one of its unique artifacts from the monster that carries it, and bring it back. Few people ever make it out alive.
arogue.provenance: Advanced Rogue was made at AT&T Bell Labs in 1984 and 1985, by a group that seems to have included Michael Morgan and Ken Dalka, from Rogue 3.6 with parts of Super-Rogue. Nicholas J. Kisseberth restored it in the Roguelike Restoration Project.

upstream.name: Michael Morgan, Ken Dalka and AT&T (1985); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

arogue.page:
**THE DUNGEONS OF DOOM. FEW PEOPLE EVER MAKE IT OUT ALIVE.**

Rogue went to Bell Labs and came back bigger. Before you go down, choose
what you are: a fighter, strong enough to strike several times a turn; a
magic user with a growing book of spells; a cleric who prays, and turns the
undead; or a thief, who slinks past sleeping monsters, picks pockets and
stabs them in the back.

Then go after your quest. Deep in the dungeon, a few monsters carry unique
artifacts: the Wand of Orcus, the Rod of Asmodeus, the Flail of Yeenoghu,
the Horn of Geryon, the Mandolin of Brian. Bring one back and you are a
Complete Winner. Or keep going, as the manual dares you, "to match wits
with an arch-devil, demon prince, or even a deity found far down in the
dungeon."

- **Four classes**, each with powers of its own: spells, prayers, turning
  the undead, stealing and backstabbing
- **Over a hundred monsters**, many of them clever
- **Trading posts** down in the dungeon, to buy and sell
- **Experience, not gold, is your score**

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way
- **f** and a direction: move until something turns up; **t**: throw,
  **z**: zap a wand or staff
- **i**: inventory, **d**: drop, **P**: pick up
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off
- **C**: cast a spell, **p**: pray, **a**: affect the undead, **^**:
  set a trap, **D**: dip something in a pool
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start it from a
shell as `arogue -r`; a saved game is deleted once it is restored.

## History

Advanced Rogue was developed by a group at AT&T Bell Labs between 1984
and 1986, among them apparently Michael Morgan and Ken Dalka, and AT&T
distributed it for a time through its Toolchest. Version 5.8 grew from
Rogue 3.6 with parts of Super-Rogue. Nicholas J. Kisseberth (Yendor) restored
it in the Roguelike Restoration Project (5.8.1 in 2005, 5.8.2 in 2006).
This edition keeps your files in your data folder and has fixes for
64-bit machines and the score file. It is part of the Roguelike Restoration
Project in the Asciiverse catalog.

## Credits

Michael Morgan, Ken Dalka and their Bell Labs colleagues, after Rogue by
Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold and Super-Rogue by Robert D.
Kindelberger; restoration by Nicholas J. Kisseberth. BSD licence with
clauses on the names Advanced Rogue and ARogue.

ascii-fluid.title: ASCII Fluid
ascii-fluid.description: A fluid simulator that melts its own source code, then pours, sloshes and drains water in ASCII: Yusuke Endoh's prize-winning entry from the IOCCC.
ascii-fluid.provenance: Yusuke Endoh wrote this smoothed-particle fluid simulator for the International Obfuscated C Code Contest in 2012, where it won "Most complex ASCII fluid" (2012/endoh1).
ascii-fluid.page:
**THIS PROGRAM'S SOURCE CODE MELTS.**

It opens with its own C source on the screen. Then gravity switches on, and
the code slumps, slides and splashes into a puddle at the bottom of your
terminal.

That is Yusuke Endoh's ASCII Fluid: a real fluid simulation squeezed into a
few lines of C for the International Obfuscated C Code Contest. After the
source, the show goes on. A column of water collapses and sloshes, the
program "pours you a cup of tea", water runs down terraced rice fields and
through funnels, a water clock drains. Every frame is computed live and
drawn with slashes, dots and hashes, coloured by how dense the water is.

The contest judges opened their remarks with a round of Jeopardy: "A: An
obfuscated program that deals with complex numbers and produces animated
ASCII graphics. Q: What is a Mandelbrot simulator? Bzzzt!"

- **Eighteen scenes** in turn, each playing for as long as it stays lively
- **Bring your own water**: any text file is a scene, with `#` for a wall
  and anything else for water
- **Colour**, the version the author made at the judges' suggestion, or
  the original black and white

Warning: the picture changes quickly and may flicker on some terminals.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `ascii-fluid -m` shows the original black-and-white
version, `-t 20` gives every scene 20 seconds, `-l` lists the scenes, and
naming scenes plays only those (`ascii-fluid tanada clock`). A text file
of your own works as a scene too: `#` is a wall, any other character is
water.

## History

Yusuke Endoh wrote this for the International Obfuscated C Code Contest
in 2012, where it won "Most complex ASCII fluid". The whole simulator,
smoothed-particle hydrodynamics done in complex numbers, fits in 23
lines of C. The colour version came after the contest, at
the judges' suggestion. Asciiverse runs the entry as the IOCCC publishes
it, inside a small launcher that plays the scenes in turn and quits
on any key.

## Credits

- 2012/endoh1 by [Yusuke Endoh](https://github.com/mame/), from the [IOCCC](https://www.ioccc.org/2012/endoh1/index.html); clock scene by HAMANO Tsukasa, other scenes by the author and the IOCCC judges
- Copyright Landon Curt Noll, licensed under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) ([the IOCCC's summary](https://www.ioccc.org/license.html))
- Asciiverse edition: the launcher, scenes in turn, any key quits; changes listed in PATCHES.md

ascii-patrol.title: ASCII Patrol
ascii-patrol.description: Roll a moon buggy through alien country, hopping craters, blasting rocks and shooting saucers out of the sky, in a love letter to Moon Patrol
ascii-patrol.provenance: Marcin Sokalski (Gumix) wrote ASCII Patrol in C++ from 2017, after Moon Patrol, his favourite arcade game as a child; 1.7 came out in 2019.
ascii-patrol.page:
**THE GROUND IS FULL OF HOLES. THE SKY IS FULL OF SAUCERS. GOOD LUCK, CADET.**

"Be careful, they come with mega bombers fleet. Their bombs make huge
craters in the ground. Good luck cadet!"

So says the Commander, and off you roll: one cadet, one moon buggy, and
a whole planet's worth of aliens between sector @ and sector Z. The
ground never stops coming. Craters open in front of your wheels,
boulders sit in the road, saucers swing overhead dropping bombs that
punch fresh holes where the road used to be. Your cannon fires two ways
at once, straight ahead to crack the rocks and straight up to pop
whatever is hovering, and your jump has to land on all three wheels or
the suspension goes and so do you.

Marcin Sokalski grew up on Moon Patrol, his favourite arcade game as a
child, and this is his love letter to it, built in ASCII art: a parallax sky of mountains and cities, a thumping tracker
soundtrack, and between sectors a radio drama with your Commander about
minefields, missiles, alien eggs and plants that may not be as friendly
as they look. Two full missions, Mission One and The Lowering, five
sectors each. Get through the minefield, keep going, and the Commander may
even call you sergeant.

And it is your face on the radio: build an avatar from hair, eyes, nose
and chin in the Player Profile before you set off.

## Controls

- **Right** or **D**: speed up (hold)
- **Left** or **A**: brake (hold)
- **Up** or **W**: jump
- **Down** or **S**: duck (hold)
- **Enter** or **L**: fire, forward and up at once
- **Esc** or **Q**: leave the level
- **Tab**: save a screen shot to the data folder

The letters can be changed under Keyboard Input in the menu. Holding
keys needs a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, Ghostty, foot,
Alacritty, the Linux console); elsewhere the keys are sticky: tap Right
to speed up, Left to slow back down. The Control Panel sets music and
effects volume and the colour mode.

## Credits

- ASCII Patrol: Marcin Sokalski (Gumix),
  [github.com/msokalski/ascii-patrol](https://github.com/msokalski/ascii-patrol),
  2017 to 2022, C++; XM player slides and vibrato by Tom Hargreaves
  (hexwab); CMake build by Michael Hirsch
- Inspired by Moon Patrol (Irem, 1982)
- stb_vorbis by Sean Barrett (public domain); miniaudio by David Reid
  (public domain or MIT-0)
- License: GNU GPL version 3

ascii-wars.title: ASCII Wars!
ascii-wars.description: A boss rush bullet hell against ten glyphs with a grudge, from The Sentinel to The Chaos Reaper: rings, rain, walls, homing swarms and sweeping beams, and you only fire while you move.
ascii-wars.provenance: Carlos Alvarez (VikingosTeam) made ASCII Wars! in Rust and Bevy in 2025, ten bosses of glyph rings and aimed shots in a graphical window. Asciiverse brought it to the terminal and grew it into a fuller game.
ascii-wars.page:
**TEN BOSSES. EACH ONE A GLYPH WITH A GRUDGE.**

The Sentinel. The Hoarder. The Watcher. The Infernal Imp. The Spiral Beast.
The Guardian of Order. The Swarm King. The Celestial Tyrant. The Clockwork
Leviathan. And at the end of it all, The Chaos Reaper.

You fire at the boss whenever you move, and only then: standing still is
safe from nothing, so every dodge is an attack.

Each boss fights in phases, with names like Compound Interest, Thousand
Eyes, Supernova and Last Rites. It opens with its old attack, then starts to
move and brings out new ones: aimed fans, rings that turn into spirals,
shots raining from the top, walls with one gap, bullets that curve, speed
up, bounce off the edges or home in, and lasers that show as a dotted
line before they burn. Break a phase and every shot on screen turns into
points; break it without a scratch for a bonus.

Hold focus to move slowly through the tight spots, drop a bomb to clear
the shots round you, and brush past bullets to graze them for points and
the next bomb. A hit makes you blink for a moment; the sixth one ends it.

## Modes

- **Arcade**: all ten bosses in a row, with one score and your health
  carried from fight to fight
- **Practice**: any boss you have reached, with your best time
- **Classic**: the original game as it was, rule for rule
- Easy, Normal and Hard; a demo plays itself when the title is left alone

## Controls

- **Arrows** or **WASD**: move (and fire)
- **Shift**, **Z** or **J** (hold): focus
- **X**, **K** or **Space**: bomb
- **Esc** or **P**: pause; **M**: sound on and off
- **Enter**: choose; the mouse works in the menus
- Gamepad: stick or d-pad to move, **A** or a shoulder button to focus,
  **B** or **Y** to bomb, **Start** to pause

Best in a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, foot, WezTerm,
Ghostty, Alacritty, iTerm2 and others) or with a gamepad; elsewhere a
move runs on a little after the key is let go.

## Options

- `--level N`: start Arcade at boss N
- `--classic`: the original game
- `--demo`: watch the computer play
- `--mute`: no sound or music

## History

Carlos Alvarez made ASCII Wars! in Rust with the Bevy engine in January
2025: ten bosses drawn with a CP437 font in a graphical window, each
firing rings and aimed shots at a ship that fires back while it moves.
This edition brings it to the terminal and builds a fuller game around
it, with phases, moving bosses, new attacks, bombs, grazing, a score,
colour, sound and a chiptune for every boss. The original lives on
unchanged as Classic.

## Credits

- ASCII Wars!: Carlos Alvarez (VikingosTeam), 2025,
  [github.com/Alvarz/ascii-wars](https://github.com/Alvarz/ascii-wars)
- Terminal port, and the Arcade game built round the original: Asciiverse
- License: MIT

asciicker.title: Asciicker
asciicker.description: A whole 3D island drawn in characters: walk it, turn it, jump, swing a sword and fill your pack, in Gumix's ASCII action RPG
asciicker.provenance: Marcin Sokalski (Gumix), who also made ASCII Patrol, built Asciicker from 2019 to 2024 as a 3D ASCII game concept that plays in the browser at asciicker.com.
asciicker.page:
**LET'S KICK SOME ASCII.**

Asciicker is a real 3D world made of characters. Hills rise in blocks of
green and dotted grass, pines stand in dark teal stacks, a grey boulder
the size of a house sits by the path, and when you press Q or E the whole
island swings around you, mountains, lake, fences and all. Nothing is
painted on: it is a terrain and mesh renderer that happens to draw with
CP437 instead of pixels.

You wake on a forest path with two armoured companions who follow you
wherever you go. From there the island is yours: wander up the slopes,
jump the rocks, meet the bands of armed strangers, and pick up what you
find. Giant's maces and hammers, an alpha sword, a crossbow, a flail,
light and heavy armour, helmets and shields, unidentified rings in four
colours, meat, eggs and water. Equip a weapon and Enter swings it. Drink
the grey potion and you are riding a wolf; drink the gold one and it is a
giant bee.

Be warned that this is a concept, not a finished adventure: Marcin
Sokalski (Gumix, of ASCII Patrol) built it as a showcase of what ASCII 3D
can do, and the world has more to explore than to accomplish. As a piece
of terminal engineering it is astonishing.

For the curious, it is also scriptable: open the chat with Tab, start a
line with a backslash, and the rest runs as JavaScript against the game,
with `ak.getPos()` and friends.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **WASD**: walk
- **Q** / **E**: turn the view
- **Space**: jump
- **Enter**: attack (with a weapon equipped)
- **I**: open and close the inventory; **1** to **9** pick up the item
  shown under you, **0** drops the highlighted one
- **Tab**: chat; Tab again sends it (a line starting with `\` runs as
  script)
- **Esc** (or **\\**): the game menu (video, sound, controls, main
  menu, exit); Esc again closes it
- A gamepad works too (checked with an Xbox 360 pad)
- Mouse: hold the left button toward where you want to walk, right
  button to jump, drag with the right button to turn the view

In terminals with the kitty keyboard protocol (kitty, Ghostty, foot,
WezTerm) held keys walk and turn smoothly; elsewhere a held key is
followed through its key repeat, so walking starts after your keyboard's
repeat delay. **H** or **?** shows the keys in the game, and the menu's
Controls has a page for the keyboard and one for the mouse.

## Credits

- Asciicker: Marcin Sokalski (Gumix),
  [github.com/msokalski/asciicker](https://github.com/msokalski/asciicker),
  2019 to 2024, C++; [asciicker.com](https://asciicker.com)
- QuickJS-ng by Fabrice Bellard, Charlie Gordon and the QuickJS-ng
  authors (MIT); miniaudio by David Reid (public domain or MIT-0);
  stb_vorbis by Sean Barrett (public domain)
- License: MIT

asciijump.title: asciijump
asciijump.description: Ski jumping in ASCII art: ride down the in-run, take off at the lip, lean into the flight and land with a telemark. Training, a World Cup against the computer, and network games.
asciijump.provenance: Grzegorz Moskal wrote asciijump in C on S-Lang, with Michal Moskal and Przemek Niezborala, in Poland in the early 2000s; Debian has carried it since 2003.

upstream.name: Grzegorz Moskal, Michal Moskal and Przemek Niezborala

asciijump.page:
**THE IN-RUN. THE LIP. THE TELEMARK.**

A ski jumping game drawn in ASCII art. Pick a hill, push off and ride the
in-run. At the lip of the take-off you jump, then hang in the air
over the slope, leaning forward or back, while a rain of characters falls
behind you. Press **Enter** again to land in a telemark: too early or too
late and you crash. Five judges score the landing, and the longest jump on
each hill stands as its record.

- **Eight hills**, from England's K50 to the mighty Tarnica K180
- **World Cup**: you, your friends on the same keyboard and computer
  jumpers at three levels, over the hills you choose
- **Training**, to find your timing on any hill
- **Network games**: one player runs `aj-server`, invites the others, and
  everyone joins from the menu

## Controls

- **Enter**: start the run, jump at the lip, land with a telemark
- **Left** and **Right**: lean in the air
- **q**: leave the hill
- In menus: **Up**, **Down**, **Enter**, **Space** to select and **Tab**
  for the next field

Hill records are kept in `~/.asciijump/`.

## Credits

- asciijump: Grzegorz Moskal, with Michal Moskal and Przemek Niezborala
- Debian patches: Mario Iseli, Reiner Herrmann, TANIGUCHI Takaki, Adrian
  Bunk and the Debian Games Team
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

asciiportal.title: ASCIIpOrtal
asciiportal.description: A puzzle platformer with a portal gun: shoot two linked portals onto walls to cross gaps, fling yourself and move boxes onto switches, through 25 levels and 14 more map packs.
asciiportal.provenance: Joe Larson made ASCIIpOrtal at Cymon's Games in 2009, a 2D tribute to Valve's Portal with its own levels, and its players added many more map packs.
asciiportal.page:
**THINK WITH PORTALS. IN TEXT.**

You wake up somewhere you are not supposed to be, and a voice on the speaker would really rather you left. Doors need switches, switches need boxes, and the way out is always on the other side of something. Luckily you have picked up a portal gun.

ASCIIpOrtal is a side-on puzzle platformer. Shoot a blue portal and a yellow one onto the walls, step into one and out of the other. Use them to cross gaps, reach ledges, carry boxes to switches, dodge boulders and fling yourself across the room: whatever falls into a portal keeps its speed on the way out. You can't jump, so you'll need to think.

- **25 levels** in the main game, which teach every trick
- **14 more map packs** from the community, from gentle to evil
- **Doors, switches, conveyors, chain link, lasers, boulders** and companion cubes
- **Make your own levels**: they are plain text files

## Controls

- **Left** / **Right**: walk; **Up** / **Down**: climb ladders, or aim
- **Number pad**: aim in eight directions
- **Z**: blue portal; **X**: yellow portal; **Space**: the next portal; **C**: clear portals
- **R**: restart the level; **P**: pause; **Esc**: menu
- **+** / **-**: game speed

Holding a key to walk works best in a terminal with the kitty keyboard protocol (kitty, foot, WezTerm, Ghostty, Alacritty, iTerm2). Other terminals work too, with a short pause before a held key starts repeating.

Your progress and your own map packs are kept in `~/.asciiportal`.

## Credits

- ASCIIpOrtal: Joe Larson (Cymon's Games)
- Level design and testing: Joe Larson, Nicholas McGuire, Mads Lund and others (see Credits in the game)
- Map packs: their authors, including Zugz (CC BY-SA 2.0)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-3.0-only

asciiquarium.title: Asciiquarium
asciiquarium.description: An aquarium in your terminal: fish of every colour, bubbles, seaweed and a castle, visited now and then by sharks, whales, a sea monster, ships, ducks, a swan, dolphins and a fishhook.
asciiquarium.provenance: Kirk Baucom wrote Asciiquarium in Perl in 2005, with most of the art by Joan Stark; it became one of the best-known terminal toys.
asciiquarium.page:
**AN AQUARIUM. IN ASCII. THAT'S IT, AND IT'S WONDERFUL.**

Put it on a spare screen and leave it there. Fish in every colour drift by, blowing bubbles that rise to the surface. Seaweed sways in front of a little castle. Every so often something bigger comes along: a shark that will happily eat one of your fish, a whale spouting water, a sea monster rising through the waves, a sailing ship, a family of ducks, a swan, a pod of leaping dolphins, or a fishhook that comes down and catches someone.

Asciiquarium has been a favourite terminal toy since 2005.

## Controls

- **p**: pause
- **r**: redraw (the aquarium starts over)
- **q**: quit

## History

Kirk Baucom wrote Asciiquarium in Perl, on top of his own animation module. This edition is a faithful port to C: the same art, the same creatures and the same behaviour, in one small program with nothing else to install.

## Credits

- Asciiquarium: Kirk Baucom
- Most of the ASCII art: Joan Stark
- C port and Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

atc.title: ATC
atc.description: You're in the tower: type orders to jets and prop planes, launch them, land them, send them out the right exit, and never let two of them touch.
atc.provenance: Ed James wrote ATC in 1986 and 1987 and contributed it to UC Berkeley, where it became one of BSD's games; Mike Sharov later modernised it in his bsd-games.
atc.page:
**YOU'RE IN THE TOWER. THE PLANES DON'T STOP COMING.**

ATC "lets you try your hand at the nerve wracking duties of the air traffic
controller without endangering the lives of millions of travelers each
year." So says its manual, and it is right about the nerves.

Jets and prop planes appear at the edges of your radar and wait on the
runways, each with somewhere to be: out through one particular exit at 9000
feet, or down at one particular airport, facing the right way, at altitude
zero. You give every order by typing it (`atlab1`, `gtte4ab2`) while the
clock ticks and the next plane is already coming in.

Let two planes come within a square and a thousand feet of each other and
it's over. The same if one runs out of fuel, lands at the wrong airport,
leaves by the wrong exit or wanders out of your airspace. There is no
winning, only lasting: your score is the number of planes you brought home
safely.

- **Props and jets**: capital letters are props, lower case are jets, and
  the jets move twice as fast
- **Scenarios** from Easy and Novice to Killer, OHare and TicTacToe
- **A command line learned in minutes**: type `?` at any point to see
  what can come next
- **A BSD classic** by Ed James, 1986 and 1987

## Controls

A command is a plane's letter, then what it should do, then Enter. Type
`?` at any point to see what can come next, and Backspace to take back
the last part.

- **a** and a number: climb or descend to that altitude in thousands of
  feet; **a+** and **a-** (or **ac** and **ad**) change it by that much.
  At an airport, climbing means take off
- **t** and a direction: turn to that heading, with **w e d c x z a q**
  for 0, 45, 90 and so on round to 315 degrees; **tl** and **tr** turn 45
  degrees left or right, **tL** and **tR** 90
- **tta**, **ttb**, **tte** and a number: turn towards that airport,
  beacon or exit
- **c**: circle, clockwise; **cl** circles the other way
- **ab** and a number, after a turn or circle: wait until the plane
  reaches that beacon
- **m**, **u**, **i**: mark, unmark or ignore a plane on the radar
- **Enter** on its own, or **Space**: let time pass
- **Ctrl-L**: redraw the screen

From the manual: `atlab1` turns plane A left at beacon 1, `gtte4ab2`
turns plane G towards exit 4 at beacon 2, `ma+2` climbs plane M by 2000
feet, and `stq` turns plane S to 315 degrees.

## Options

Started from a shell, `atc -l` lists the scenarios (Default, Atlantis,
Killer, OHare, TicTacToe, Easy and more) and `atc Killer` plays one;
`atc -s` shows the scores.

## History

Ed James wrote ATC in 1986 and 1987 and contributed it to UC Berkeley,
where it became one of BSD's games. This edition is Mike Sharov's bsd-games, which compiled the
scenarios into the program and redrew the screen with curses.

avatar.title: AVATAR
avatar.description: Large fantasy MUD with remort classes and tiers, on heavily modified Merc code

bastet.title: Bastet
bastet.description: Falling blocks with a mean streak: Bastet looks at your stack, works out which block would hurt you most, and sends you exactly that one.
bastet.provenance: Federico Poloni wrote Bastet in C++ and ncurses; it reached Slashdot in 2005, and he rewrote it for 0.43 in 2009.
bastet.page:
**THE GAME KNOWS WHICH BLOCK YOU NEED. IT IS NOT GOING TO GIVE IT TO YOU.**

"For people who enjoy swearing at their computer," wrote Federico Poloni,
here is Bastet.

Every other falling-blocks game picks the next block at random. Bastet
doesn't. It looks at your stack, tries every block in every place it could
go, and hands you the one that does you the least good. That deep gap you
left for the long straight piece? Bastet has seen it too. Clearing even a
few lines is an achievement, and a long game is a real one.

In the normal game you see the next block, and Bastet chooses the one after
it knowing you have seen it. The harder game takes the preview away,
"thus achieving," as the README puts it, "a higher level of bastardness."

- **An opponent, not a dice roll**: a chooser that picks the worst block
  it can find
- **Two games**, normal and harder, each with its own top ten
- **Classic scoring**: 100 points for one row, up to 800 for four at once,
  and every ten rows the blocks fall faster
- **Your keys**: every one can be changed in Customize keys

## Controls

- **Left**, **Right**: move the block
- **Down**: move it down one row
- **Space**: turn it clockwise, **Up**: turn it the other way
- **Enter**: drop it straight to the bottom
- **p**: pause
- **Ctrl+C**: quit at once (high scores already made are kept)

Every key can be changed in Customize keys.

## Files

Keys and high scores are kept in the player's data folder,
`~/.local/share/bastet` (`%APPDATA%\bastet` on Windows).

## History

Federico Poloni wrote Bastet; version 0.41 reached Slashdot in April
2005, and his 0.43 rewrite of 2009 split the chooser into the two games
above. It is packaged by Debian, Fedora and
others. This edition has Debian's fix for printing names, and fixes of
our own: Enter drops the
block as the documentation always said, scores and keys follow
`XDG_DATA_HOME` instead of needing a setgid binary, and it builds for Windows.

batmud.title: BatMUD
batmud.description: More than thirty years old, with a community that meets in real life

battlestar.title: Battlestar
battlestar.description: The last battlestar is coming apart around you: get off the ship, survive the fight in space, and explore a tropical island all the way to the goddess's throne.
battlestar.provenance: David Riggle wrote Battlestar in 1979, and it became one of BSD's games; Mike Sharov modernised it in his bsd-games from 2016 to 2020.
battlestar.page:
**THE LAST BATTLESTAR IS BURNING. GET OFF IT.**

"In the days before the darkness came, when battlestars ruled the
heavens..." Now the darkness has fallen. The whole fleet is down to a single
ship, and that ship is coming apart around you.

You wake in a luxurious stateroom. The floor shudders, dull explosions
rumble through the room, and the window shows a view of darkest space. Out
in the corridors the wounded crowd the hallways and the ceilings have caved
in. Somewhere below are the hangar and the starfighters. Get to one, launch,
fight your way clear in real time, and get down to the tropical island
beneath you.

Then explore: beaches and palm groves, sea caves, a fishing village, and at
last a goddess on her throne. Win her hand, and you win the game.

- **275 rooms**, more a voyage of discovery than a puzzle box
- **A space fight in real time**, at the controls of a starfighter
- **A parser with a memory**: `take knife and sword and apple, drop all`,
  and the last thing you named stays in mind
- **Directions as you face them**: ahead, back, left and right, until you
  find a compass

## Controls

Type a command and press Enter. The parser understands simple English,
several objects at once and the word you used last:

- **take**, **drop**, **wear**, **draw**, **put on**, **take off**,
  **throw**, **eat**, **open**, **use** and many more: `take knife and
  sword, drop all`
- **ahead**, **back**, **left** and **right** (or **a**, **b**, **l**,
  **r**), **up** and **down**: move. Directions are relative to where
  you face; find a compass to know where north is
- **look**, **inven**, **score**
- **save**: save the game; it is restored the next time you start
- **quit**: leave

## History

David Riggle wrote Battlestar in 1979 "to experiment with the niceties
of the C Language", and it became one of BSD's games.
This edition is Mike Sharov's bsd-games. Between 2016 and 2020 he made
the space fight winnable within its time limit, took out the original's
sexual violence (marrying the goddess now wins the game), renamed the
parts borrowed from Battlestar Galactica, and added saving and a score
table.

beneath-a-typographic-sky.title: Beneath a Typographic Sky
beneath-a-typographic-sky.description: Revolution's Beneath a Steel Sky, the whole game, in your terminal: Union City rebuilt out of Braille dots, every word set in type, the speech and music as in 1994.
beneath-a-typographic-sky.provenance: Revolution Software made Beneath a Steel Sky in 1994 and released it as freeware in 2003. This edition brings it to the terminal through a Rust port of ScummVM's engine.
beneath-a-typographic-sky.page:
**UNION CITY. REBUILT IN TYPE.**

Robert Foster grew up in the Gap, the wasteland outside Union City, until security men came for him and his helicopter came down in the city. Now he is on the run in a vast city of soaring tower blocks, with only Joey, a talking robot circuit board, for company, and he wants to know why they took him. The answers are somewhere in the towers, and somewhere inside LINC, the computer that runs the city.

This is Revolution Software's Beneath a Steel Sky, the whole game, in your terminal. Every pixel of Dave Gibbons' art becomes a dot of a Braille character, so Union City is rebuilt out of type, and everything the game says is set in your terminal's own font. The speech, effects and AdLib music play as they did in 1994.

- **The whole game**, from the factory where Foster lands to the very end
- **Dave Gibbons' art in Braille dots**, or in half blocks or quadrants: F2
  switches
- **Full speech and the AdLib soundtrack**, as in 1994
- **Subtitles in seven languages**, picked up from your system

## Controls

- **Left click**: look at something
- **Right click**: use it, take it, talk, or walk through an exit
- **Pointer to the top edge**: the inventory; click an item to hold it, then right click it onto something
- **F5** or **q**: options, save, restore, subtitles and speech, language, restart, quit
- **Esc**: skip the intro or a cut scene; **.** skips a line of speech
- **p**: pause; **F2**: Braille, half blocks or quadrants; **Ctrl+F**: fast mode

The intro plays the first time; after that a start menu offers Continue, which picks up where you quit. Saves go to `~/.local/share/typographic-sky`.

## Options

- `--skip-intro`: start a new game at once
- `--mute`: no sound
- `--game-font`: the game's own pixel fonts instead of type, for very large terminals

The game starts in your system's language when it has it (English, German, French, Swedish, Italian, Portuguese or Spanish subtitles; the speech is English) and remembers the one you choose in F5.

## History

Revolution Software released Beneath a Steel Sky in 1994 for MS-DOS and the Amiga, and gave it away as freeware in 2003. ScummVM brought it to modern systems from Revolution's own source. This edition runs the unmodified CD version's data in a Rust port of ScummVM's engine and draws it in a terminal.

## Credits

- Beneath a Steel Sky: Revolution Software, 1994; directed by Charles Cecil; art and characters by Dave Gibbons; written and scored by Dave Cummins; programmed by David Sykes, Tony Warriner and James Long
- Game content (C) Revolution Software Ltd, freeware: free to share, never to be sold
- The sky engine: Robert Goeffringmann, Oliver Kiehl, Joost Peters and the ScummVM team (GPL-3.0-or-later)
- AdLib music: Nuked-OPL3 by Nuke.YKT, in Tony Gies' Rust port (LGPL-2.1-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse, GPL-3.0-or-later

news.notes:
- ScummVM's sky engine ported to Rust, running the original CD data
- Truecolour Braille, half blocks or quadrants (F2 cycles); game text as
  real type over the picture; the mouse through the terminal
- Speech, sound effects, AdLib music, the CD intro
- A headless walkthrough that plays the whole game, with saves at 23
  story points
- Packaging, the preview cast, the catalog entry

blackguard.title: Blackguard
blackguard.description: The deck is the dungeon: fight black-suit monsters, wield diamonds that dull with every kill, sip hearts to heal, and try to survive all 44 cards of Scoundrel
blackguard.provenance: Blackguard is Elnur Badalov's terminal version of Scoundrel, the solo card roguelike Zach Gage and Kurt Bieg designed in 2011, written in Rust and Ratatui in 2026.
blackguard.page:
**THE DECK IS THE DUNGEON.**

Forty-four cards, twenty hit points, one way out: through every card.
Each room deals four. The black cards are monsters, and they hurt as much
as they are worth. Diamonds are weapons that soak up the damage, but a
blade grows dull: once it has killed a monster, it can only kill weaker
ones after. Hearts are potions, and only the first one in a room does you
any good.

Play three cards and the fourth waits for you in the next room. Run from a
room you cannot face and it goes to the bottom of the deck for later, just
never twice in a row. Do you spend your sharp sword on the jack now, or
save it for the king still to come? Fight the queen bare-handed and hope
the next room has hearts?

Clear the whole deck to win, scored by the health you have left. Every
dungeon comes from a seed, so you can replay one, share one, or take on
the daily dungeon that everyone plays on the same day.

**Choose your fights.**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right** (or **h** and **l**): choose a card
- **Enter** or **Space**: use it: fight, equip or drink, whichever fits
- **f**: fight the chosen monster with your blade
- **b**: fight it bare-handed
- **a**: avoid the room
- **n**: a new dungeon; **r**: the same dungeon again
- **t**: switch the weapon rule and replay the same deck
- **?**: the rules; **q**, **Esc** or **Ctrl+C**: quit

## The weapon rule

Scoundrel's own rules leave open whether a dulled blade may kill a monster
of exactly the value it last killed. Blackguard starts with the strict
reading, only weaker monsters, and **t** switches to the equal reading
mid-game, on the same deck, so you can see what it changes.

## Options

From a terminal: `blackguard --seed 42` for a dungeon you can share,
`--daily` for today's dungeon, and `--rule equal` to start with the equal
reading.

## Credits

- Blackguard: [Elnur Badalov](https://github.com/ElnurBDa/blackguard)
- Scoundrel, the card game: Zach Gage and Kurt Bieg (2011),
  [rules](http://stfj.net/art/2011/Scoundrel.pdf)
- License: MIT

blightmud.title: Blightmud
blightmud.description: A modern terminal MUD client in Rust: Lua scripting for triggers, aliases and plugins, GMCP and MSDP, TLS, sound, and a screen reader mode.
blightmud.provenance: Blightmud is Linus Probert's MUD client in Rust, developed with its contributors on GitHub.
blightmud.page:
**THE MUDS ARE STILL OUT THERE. HERE'S YOUR WAY IN.**

Text worlds full of quests, guilds and other players, still running on
servers across the internet. Blightmud is a modern way to reach them from
your terminal: a MUD client written in Rust by Linus Probert, a long-time
TinyFugue user who wanted one of his own.

Connect, and everything a serious MUD player wants is there. Triggers,
aliases, timers and keybindings, a status bar you can shape and whole
plugins, all in Lua. It speaks the protocols modern MUDs use to send
structured data (GMCP, MSDP and MSSP), connects over TLS, plays a MUD's
music and sound effects, spellchecks what you type, splits the screen when
you scroll back, and has a screen reader mode.

- **Lua for everything**: triggers, aliases, timers, keybindings, the
  status bar, plugins
- **Saved servers**: `/add_server` once, then `/connect <name>`
- **Screen reader friendly**, with a mode of its own
- **The manual inside**: `/help` and its topics

## Getting started

- `blightmud --connect <host>:<port>`: connect straight away
- `/connect <host> <port>`: connect from inside Blightmud
- `/help`: the built-in manual
- `/quit`: quit

## Credits

- Blightmud: Linus Probert and contributors
- Asciiverse edition: builds and packaging, no code changes
- License: GPL-3.0

blue-chairs.title: Blue Chairs
blue-chairs.description: Twenty-three dollars for the best dream of your life: one green drink in a party attic, and the night goes a long, strange way from there.
blue-chairs.provenance: Chris Klimas wrote Blue Chairs in 2004. It came second in that year's Interactive Fiction Competition and won Best Game at the 2004 XYZZY Awards.
blue-chairs.page:
**TWENTY-THREE DOLLARS FOR THE BEST DREAM OF YOUR LIFE.**

It's ten o'clock, there's a party downstairs at the house of people you've
never met, and you're up in the attic with the guy. You know the guy: "he's
just the guy you always meet at parties thrown by people you've never met."
He's holding up a repurposed cough syrup bottle with something green
inside. "Green like candy almost never is."

All around you is junk: old sewing machines, an Easy-Bake oven, a set of
folding chairs painted carnival blue. ("The blue chairs are bad news. Best
just to leave them alone.") Downstairs, that awful trance-bop keeps playing.

You could go back down. The game will even tell you how the rest of that
night goes, and the weekend after, and the weekend after that. Or you could
say yes.

- **A strange, sad and funny night** that goes a long way from that attic
- **A voice all its own**, from Chris Klimas, written for IFComp 2004
- **Help for the jaded**: the game's menu has hints, the author's notes and
  "The Official Bootleg Blue Chairs Soundtrack"

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/blue-chairs`.

## Credits

- Blue Chairs: Chris Klimas, 2004
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 3.0
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

book-and-volume.title: Book and Volume
book-and-volume.description: Sunday night, the pager screaming, five servers down: the new sysadmin of nWare sets out across the tech-boom city of nTopia, and the night gets stranger.
book-and-volume.provenance: Nick Montfort wrote Book and Volume, a satire of the dot-com office, in 2005.
book-and-volume.page:
**SUNDAY, 9:05 PM. THE PAGER WILL NOT STOP.**

"Net extremely hoseled. Engine team being hideously masticated by this
outage. Demo rapidly approaching. Get to the cages. Reboot the servers.
Hasten. Do not rest. Please. All five of them."

That's Wilbur, your boss. You're the new system administrator for nWare.
You moved to nTopia a few days ago, and your apartment holds little more
than your nLap 500, a heap of clothes and the glowing stars on the ceiling.
It's the weekend. It doesn't matter. Out you go into the city, with the
clock in the corner running and the pager buzzing like a dental drill.

Nick Montfort's Book and Volume is a night-time wander through a gleaming
tech-boom city where everything has an n in front of it and everyone wants
something from you, right now.

- **A whole city to roam** by night, with the clock always running
- **Sharp, funny writing** about work, technology and a place that never
  quite lets you rest
- **An [auto mata] release**, with an introduction to interactive fiction
  built into its opening menu

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/book-and-volume`.

## Credits

- Book and Volume: Nick Montfort, 2005
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 2.5
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

braillestorm.title: Braillestorm
braillestorm.description: Your terminal is in a storm! Wildcard globs, rogue cursors, runaway forks and /dev/null itself swarm the screen, and you're the last prompt standing. Twin-stick fury in glorious Braille, over a grid that ripples with every blast!
braillestorm.provenance: Asciiverse made Braillestorm in Rust in 2026, inspired by Mark Incitti's freeware GridWars (2005); no code, art or sound is taken from it.
braillestorm.page:
**YOU ARE THE LAST PROMPT STANDING.**

Something has gone badly wrong in your terminal. The globs have broken loose and tumble everywhere. Block cursors blink awake and come hunting. Forks multiply: shoot one and it splits into two quick children. Spinners whirl in place, then dash straight into your line. Zombies get back up unless you shoot their bodies too. Escapes vanish and reappear right beside you. And the null device itself creeps after you, swallowing sparks, bending your shots and dragging you in. They just keep coming, wave after wave, faster every time.

You're a lone shell prompt, `❯`, with a twin stream of fire and three bombs. Move with one stick and shoot with the other, in any direction, all at once. Every shot dents the glowing grid beneath you, every burst sends it rippling, and every bomb rings the whole field like a bell.

- **Waves that never stop,** each announced in big glowing letters, each bigger and faster than the last. From the tenth, every fifth wave is a rush: cursors from every corner at once.
- **Three bombs** that blast the field clear around you when it gets too close.
- **A multiplier that climbs** with every kill you make without losing your ship, all the way to x10.
- **Pick-ups** left behind by the fallen: wide fire, rapid fire, a shield or one more bomb. Grab them before they fade!
- **Stages:** every five waves the whole grid turns a new colour.
- **Every bang made from scratch:** each enemy bursts with its own synthesised sound, pings climb the scale as your multiplier rises, and a driving soundtrack speeds up with the waves and swells as the field fills.
- **Drawn in glorious Braille:** thin, glowing vector lines of dots, sixty frames a second.
- **Gamepad, mouse or keyboard.** Clear a wave without losing your ship for a bonus, earn an extra life and bomb every 25,000 points (counted before the multiplier), and chase your own best score.
- **Toys for the grid:** drop in a drifting black hole that drinks the sparks and sucks the grid down, change the grid's colour and density, or sit back and let the autopilot play.

How long can you hold back the storm? **JUST ONE MORE WAVE...**

## Controls

- **WASD**: move
- **Arrow keys**: fire; or hold the **left mouse button** to fire at the pointer
- **Space** or **right click**: bomb
- **P** or **Enter**: pause; **Space** or **Enter**: play again after game over
- **M**: sound on or off, **N**: music on or off
- **Q** or **Esc**: quit
- **B**: a black hole on or off, **H**: hide the top line
- **F2**: glow, **F3**: grid colour, **F4** / **F5**: grid denser or sparser, **F6**: random blasts, **F7**: autopilot
- **Gamepad**: left stick to move, right stick to fire, A, a shoulder button or a trigger to bomb, Start to pause, Back to quit

Best in a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, foot, WezTerm, Ghostty, Alacritty, iTerm2 and others), or with a gamepad or the mouse. Elsewhere the arrows fire sticky: the last arrow keeps firing until you press the opposite one.

## Options

- `--demo`: watch the computer play
- `--mute`: start with the sound off
- `--no-music`: the sound effects without the music
- `--wave N`: start at wave N
- `--fps N`: draw fewer frames a second (the game still runs at 60)

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Inspired by Mark Incitti's GridWars (2005)

news.notes:
- Gamepads work on Windows: gilrs reads them through XInput, since its
  default (Windows Gaming Input) only reports to a program with a focused
  window of its own, which a terminal game never has

braincurses.title: BrainCurses
braincurses.description: Crack a secret code of four colours in ten guesses, with nothing but red and white markers to go on.
braincurses.provenance: Brian Derr wrote braincurses in 2002 and rewrote it in C++ on ncurses in 2015 and 2016.
braincurses.page:
**FOUR COLOURS. TEN GUESSES. CRACK THE CODE.**

The computer has picked a secret: four colours in a row, from red, green,
yellow, blue, magenta and white, repeats allowed. You have ten tries to name
it exactly.

Every guess gets its answer in markers: a red X for each colour in the right
place, a white X for each right colour in the wrong place. They never say
which is which. Is it the yellow in the second slot, or the blue at the
end? Work it out, narrow it down, close in.

Donald Knuth showed that this classic code can always be cracked in five
guesses or fewer. You have ten. How hard can it be?

- **Classic code-breaking**: learned in a minute, played for years
- **Longer codes** of five or six colours, and anything from one to
  fifteen guesses
- **Play again** at a keystroke

## Controls

- **r g y b m w**: type a colour (red, green, yellow, blue, magenta,
  white); the guess is scored once every place has a colour
- **Left**, **Right**, **Backspace**: move back and change a guess
- **y** or **Enter** after a game: play again; **n** stops
- **q**: quit

## Options

- `braincurses -c 5` or `-c 6`: a longer code
- `braincurses -g 12`: the number of guesses (1 to 15)

## Credits

- braincurses: [Brian Derr](https://github.com/bderrly/braincurses), under
  the GPL version 2
- Asciiverse edition: q to quit, the
  result kept on screen, fixes for 5 and 6 colour codes and incomplete
  guesses, and a Windows build

brickspire.title: Brickspire
brickspire.description: The stars are going out! The Mason has walled up the Lamplighter at the top of his tower. Five towers, fifty floors, one ball: smash your way up before the last star fades!
brickspire.provenance: Asciiverse made Brickspire in Rust in 2026: a brick breaker after the great arcade and 16-bit ones, played up a turning tower in the manner of the late-80s tower climbers.
brickspire.page:
**THE STARS ARE GOING OUT.**

Every night the Lamplighter climbs into the sky and lights the stars. But not any more. The Mason has walled the Lamplighter up at the very top of his tower, the Brickspire, and now, one by one, the stars are going dark.

Five towers stand between you and the top. Fifty floors. One ball. Smash your way up!

Clear a floor and the whole tower turns, swinging the next one round to face you. Up through the Old Keep, where a Gargoyle spits fire from its balcony and a Storm Cloud rumbles over the roof. Up through the Ivy Tower, where vines slide along their rows and a giant crow guards its twig nest. On through the Bell Tower, where clockwork bricks tick back into place and the Great Bell sends shock rings rolling across the roof. Then the Sea Tower, lashed by storms, with a serpent rising beside the balcony and the Weathercock whirling on top. And every tower you climb, there are fewer stars left in the sky...

Here's the twist: your paddle changes its path as you climb! On the floors it runs straight. On the balconies it swings along an arc. On the roofs it circles the whole arena, and every angle you thought you knew goes out of the window.

Catch the capsules as they fall: a Plank for a longer paddle, Mortar to catch the ball, Chisels to fire, an Hourglass to slow things down, a Flock of three balls, a Spare life, or a Stair straight up to the next floor.

- **Five towers, fifty floors, ten bosses,** each tower with its own look and its own trick brick.
- **Two looks:** chunky pixel art, or pipe graphics drawn in box lines. Press G to switch.
- **Keyboard, mouse or gamepad.**

At the top, the Mason is still laying bricks, as fast as you can break them. Break through, free the Lamplighter, and light up the sky again. **HURRY, BEFORE THE LAST STAR FADES!**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right** (or **A** and **D**, **H** and **L**), or the **mouse**: move the paddle
- **Space**, **Enter** or **Up**: launch the ball, fire Chisels, let go of a caught ball
- **P**: pause, **R**: restart, **Q** or **Esc**: quit
- **G**: pixel art or pipe graphics, **M**: sound on or off
- **Gamepad**: stick or d-pad moves (the stick aims round the roof), bottom or right button or right trigger fires, Start pauses

## Options

- `--floor N`: start on floor N (1 to 50)
- `--glyphs`: start in pipe graphics
- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Sound synthesised in the game

news.notes:
- Gamepads work on Windows: gilrs reads them through XInput, since its
  default (Windows Gaming Input) only reports to a program with a focused
  window of its own, which a terminal game never has

brogue.title: Brogue CE
brogue.description: A beautiful, tightly designed roguelike: 26 levels down to the Amulet of Yendor, no classes and no grinding, just what you find, what you learn and the allies you free along the way.
