brogue.provenance: Brian Walker made Brogue from 2009 to 2018; since 2019 a community team has kept it going as Brogue: Community Edition.

upstream.name: Brian Walker and the Brogue CE team

brogue.page:
**26 LEVELS. ONE AMULET. NOTHING WASTED.**

Brogue strips the roguelike down to what makes it great. There are no classes and no experience levels: you grow by what you find, enchanting the items you choose to trust. Every level is new, with lakes, chasms, bridges, traps and secret doors, and every monster has a way it wants to fight. Free a captive and it fights at your side, learning as it goes.

It is turn-based, with one life and a dungeon that is different every time, but it is also easy to pick up: the mouse-free terminal version is fully playable from the keyboard, and **x** explores for you until something interesting happens.

- **26 levels** to the Amulet of Yendor, and more below for the bold
- **No grinding**: every item and every ally is a choice
- **Allies** you can free, who learn new abilities
- **Seeded games** and recordings you can replay

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, the number pad or **h j k l y u b n**: move and attack
- **x**: explore; **>** / **<**: travel to the stairs
- **i**: inventory; **z**: rest; **s**: search
- **S**: save and quit; **Q**: give up
- **?**: every command

Your saves, recordings and high scores are kept in `~/.local/share/Brogue`.

## Credits

- Brogue: Brian Walker
- Brogue: Community Edition: the Brogue CE team
- License: AGPL-3.0-or-later

bsd-backgammon.title: BSD Backgammon
bsd-backgammon.description: Backgammon as BSD shipped it in 1980: you against the computer or a friend, with the doubling cube, saved games and Teachgammon to teach you the rules.
bsd-backgammon.provenance: Alan Char wrote backgammon and its tutorial, teachgammon, at UC Berkeley by 1980, and it shipped with BSD Unix from then on.
bsd-backgammon.page:
**ROLL THE DICE. THE COMPUTER HAS ITS EYE ON THE DOUBLING CUBE.**

Backgammon as it came with BSD Unix in 1980. You play White, the computer
plays Red, and the board is redrawn in place after every move. The computer
offers doubles and takes them, and it is watching for any man you leave on
his own. Win big enough and the game says so: "Backgammon!"

Two players can share the keyboard instead, and a game can be saved and
picked up later.

New to the game? Answer yes when it asks whether you want the rules.
Teachgammon, its built-in tutor, explains backgammon section by section and
then plays a practice game with you, move by move.

- **You against the computer**, or two players on one keyboard
- **The doubling cube**, offered and accepted by the computer
- **Teachgammon**, the tutorial that teaches the rules
- **Saved games** to come back to

## Controls

At your colour's prompt:

- **Space** or **Enter**: roll the dice
- **d**: double
- **r** or **Ctrl+L**: redraw the board
- **s**: save the game, **q**: quit

At the Move prompt, type your moves and press **Enter**:

- **8-5**: move a man from point 8 to point 5
- **13/4**: move a man on point 13 by a roll of 4
- separate moves with commas or spaces: `8-5,6-5`
- **b** is the bar and **h** is home: `b-20`, `3-h`

## Options

- `-w` or `-r`: play White or Red against the computer, skipping the
  questions; `-b`: two players
- `backgammon <name>`: pick up the game saved under that name

## History

Alan Char wrote backgammon and its tutorial at UC Berkeley (the
copyright is from 1980), and it shipped with BSD Unix from then on. This
edition keeps saved games in the player's own data folder. One fix changes
how the computer plays: when it judged whether a lone man of yours could
be hit, it looked at the wrong squares, past the end of the board. It is
part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD licence.

bsdtrek.title: BSD Trek
bsdtrek.description: Eric Allman's 1976 Trek for BSD Unix: hunt down the invading Klingons by warp, phaser and photon torpedo before the stardates run out, one typed command at a time.
bsdtrek.provenance: Eric Allman wrote Trek at UC Berkeley in 1976 and it shipped with BSD's games; Kenji Rikitake's bsdtrek later made the FreeBSD and DragonFly BSD version build on Linux.
bsdtrek.page:
**THE KLINGONS ARE INVADING. YOU HAVE ONE SHIP AND NOT MUCH TIME.**

Klingon warships are spreading across the galaxy. Starbases are calling for
help, inhabited star systems are under attack, and you have a limited number
of stardates to destroy every last invader. You command the Enterprise.

Warp between the quadrants, scan near and far, fight with phasers and photon
torpedoes, raise the shields, cloak, and dock at a starbase to refuel and
repair. Your bridge crew keep up a running commentary ("Chekov: But captain,
we are not adjacent to a starbase."), and there are novas, black holes,
tractor beams and a self-destruct sequence that asks for the password.

Get it wrong and the game has a long list of ways to tell you. "You ran into
the negative energy barrier." "You have burned up in a star." "Well, you
destroyed yourself, but it didn't do any good." Abandon ship and you are
"hereby put in charge of an antiquated but still functional ship, the Fairie
Queene." Win, and you may even be promoted.

It plays like a 1970s terminal session: type a command, read the result.
Nothing is on screen until you ask for it, so the scans are your eyes.

- **Eric Allman's original Trek**, written at Berkeley in 1976 and a BSD
  game ever since
- **Short, medium or long games**, at skill levels from novice to
  impossible
- **Every command can be shortened**, and `?` lists what each prompt
  accepts

## Controls

Type a command and press Enter. Each command can be shortened to its
first letters, and anything the game needs that you leave out, it asks
for. `?` lists what it accepts at any prompt.

- `srscan` and `lrscan`: short and long range scans
- `move`: travel under warp power, at the factor set with `warp`;
  `impulse` for short hops
- `phasers` and `torpedo`: fight
- `shield up` or `shield down`, `cloak`
- `dock` and `undock` at a starbase, `rest` to repair
- `status`, `damages`, `computer` for charts and course calculations
- `dump` saves the game; answer `restart` to "What length game" to
  continue it
- `terminate` ends the game

At the start you choose the length (`short`, `medium`, `long`) and the
skill (`novice` to `impossible`).

## History

Eric Allman wrote Trek at UC Berkeley in 1976, and it was part of BSD's
games from then on. This edition comes from Kenji Rikitake's bsdtrek,
the FreeBSD and DragonFly BSD version made to build on Linux. The
Asciiverse fixes the build for current compilers and Windows, keeps the
saved game safe from updates, and makes restoring work again: it had
been broken on every current system.

The same game, without the Star Trek names and with the whole map always
on screen, is in the catalog as Space Pirate Hunt, from BSD Games.

bugs-i.title: BUGS I
bugs-i.description: Two-letter pieces fall onto a board crawling with bugs: line up four of a letter with a bug among them and it is gone. Clear every bug for the next level, as the pieces come faster.
bugs-i.provenance: Scott Noecker wrote BUGS I in C and curses in 1991, at SUNY Utica/Rome and then UNCW, and gave it to the public domain; Ken Corey brought it to Linux in 1992, and a 2015 cleanup is the copy that survived.
bugs-i.page:
**THE BOARD IS CRAWLING WITH BUGS. SQUASH EVERY LAST ONE.**

Bugs are hiding in the board, letters in reverse video: A, L and S. Two
letters at a time come falling from the top. Steer them, turn them, and
drop them where they count: four of a letter in a line, across or down,
and they vanish, along with every bug caught among them. Whatever was
resting on top falls into the gap, and if it lines up four more, those go
too.

Clear every bug and the next level brings more of them. Every ten pieces
the fall gets a little quicker, and when the next piece has nowhere to
land, the game is over.

Scott Noecker wrote it on a university Unix machine in the summer of 1991
and gave it away, and it travelled the early Linux archives from there.

**Squash them all.**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right** (or **h** and **l**): move the piece
- **Down** (or **j**): move it down a row
- **Up**, **x** or **s**: turn it clockwise; **z** or **a**: the other way
- **Space**: drop it
- **p**: pause
- **q** or **Esc**: leave the game; **Ctrl+C** quits at once

On the title screen, choose the level (0 to 20, more bugs each) and the
speed (1 to 3) with the arrow keys, then press Enter. Your best score is
kept between games.

## Credits

- BUGS I: Scott Noecker (1991)
- Linux release: Ken Corey (1992)
- Cleanup: Grandpa's Code (2015)
- License: public domain

calvary.title: Calvary
calvary.description: An action-RTS built from Crack dot Com's unfinished Golgotha: drive the supertank yourself while your army rolls down the roads, through a forty-mission campaign from Basrah to the Arctic and back to Jerusalem in 2048.
calvary.provenance: Crack dot Com was making Golgotha when the studio closed in 1998, and gave away its source, graphics, music and levels; Patrick Grawehr's Golgotha Forever kept the code alive. Asciiverse built Calvary from them in 2026, with a campaign of its own.
calvary.page:
**2048. THEY TOLD US AN AMERICAN WAS DEAD. SHE WAS. THEY LIED ABOUT WHO KILLED HER.**

Dr. Ruth Calloway dug beneath Golgotha, the place of the skull, and found
one: human in shape, three times too large. Then she was murdered, Iraq
was blamed, and America went in. Commander John Fisher leads the
incursion. At every site on his orders his column finds her trenches, and
what she found in them.

You drive the supertank yourself: shell towers from across the water,
lock the turret on what moves, rearm at your HQ, and earn upgrades for
your next tank with every kill. Behind you the garage builds the army
and sends it down the roads to the enemy: peon tanks, rocket tanks,
electric cars, trikes, engineers that take banks and towers, bridgers
that lay themselves across a gap. Junctions decide where they go, and you
switch them. Banks fill crates of money, and planes fly them home.

**Act I, The Incursion**, seven missions through Iraq:

- **Al Basrah:** the beachhead, the supertank alone against the road north
- **Shatt al-Arab:** marsh channels, every bridge blown; bridgers first
- **Ur:** hold Calloway's first dig, under the ziggurat
- **Nakhayb:** her abandoned camp between the mesas; whoever's engineer
  gets there first takes it
- **Babylon:** the bones in the open, ringed by electric towers
- **The Euphrates line:** six trucks, two roads, a night of changing orders
- **Nineveh:** Fisher refuses to raze the site, and both armies turn on him

**Act II, The Desertion**, seven more, through the Levant and Egypt:

- **Palmyra:** five minutes of rearguard among the columns
- **The King's Highway:** trucks south past Kerak, the canyon of Wadi Mujib
- **Sinai:** four thousand in the chest; banks are taken, not owned
- **The Suez Canal:** bridgers under fire, trucks waiting at the gaps
- **Cairo:** street war in the walled town, and the first helicopters
- **Giza:** under the pyramids a third army shows itself, at war with all
- **Alexandria:** board the ships for Greece while the jets come in

**Act III, The European War**, thirteen more, from Greece to Vienna:

- **Piraeus:** Golgotha's own battle on the Greek coast
- **Delphi:** superguns on the heights above the sanctuary
- **The Ionian crossing:** an island only bombers can reach
- **Naples:** hold Herculaneum while Vesuvius wakes
- **Pompeii:** a race at night for a casket in the ash
- **Rome:** take the Palatine, with tank busters and cobras
- **Turin:** stop the truck carrying the Shroud out of the city
- **The Gotthard Pass:** trucks over the Alps, under the snow cornices
- **Zurich:** the banks of the lake, there for the taking
- **Chartres:** keep the Veil in the town for six minutes
- **The Loire:** storm the Order's chateau
- **Munich:** shut down the Order's tank factories
- **Vienna:** the race for the Holy Lance

**Act IV, The North**, eight more, from Berlin to the Arctic:

- **Berlin:** the Order's empty command, taken by an engineer
- **The Baltic crossing:** trucks over sea ice that breaks under shellfire
- **Helsinki:** the Finns join the fight for the harbour city
- **The Finnish lakes:** six narrows to bridge, the Europeans on the far shores
- **Lapland:** the polar night, and two factories hidden in the fells
- **The fjord:** one road on a ledge, and the Order's own supertank
- **Svalbard:** Calloway's last letters, in a vault under the mountain
- **The Nephilim Battle:** hold a frozen lake while the giants wake

**Act V, Golgotha**, the last five, home to Jerusalem:

- **Cyprus:** take Limassol harbour for the last voyage
- **Jaffa:** the landing, with all three armies waiting
- **The walls of Jerusalem:** hold the Old City without firing on its holy places
- **The dig:** engineers clear Calloway's trench down to her chamber
- **Beneath the place of the skull:** the keyhole, and what comes up out of it

Golgotha's own levels are on the title menu too: a battle on the Greek
coast, a skirmish in a Swiss valley, a walled town in Egypt. Play from
above, from the strategy map with its road network, from behind the
supertank in the follow view, or from its turret in first person, with
the original's music and radio voices.

## Controls

- **W**/**S** gears, **A**/**D** turn, **Q**/**E** turret, **T** turret
  lock
- **Space** main gun, **F** machine gun, **Enter** rockets; or the mouse:
  the turret follows the pointer, the left button fires
- **1** to **8** build at the garage, **V** a bridger, **9** **0** **B**
  aircraft
- **J** switches the nearest junction (or click it); click or drag to
  select units, right-click to send them; **G** rally, **X** hold, **R**
  back to the road
- **Tab** map, **M** follow view and first person, **+**/**-** zoom,
  **F1** all the keys
- A gamepad plays it too: left stick drives, right stick aims, triggers
  fire

## Options

- `calvary --no-intro`: straight to the title
- `calvary --edit maps/x.cmap`: the map editor
- `calvary --mute`: no sound

## History

Crack dot Com, the studio of Abuse, was making Golgotha, an arcade tank
game fused with real-time strategy, when it closed in 1998. It released
the source, graphics, music and levels so the work would not disappear,
and Patrick Grawehr's Golgotha Forever kept the code alive. Calvary
builds the game in the terminal from that source, its balance table, its
levels, music and sounds, and finishes the story its team had begun.

## Credits

Golgotha by Crack dot Com: Dave Taylor, Jonathan Clark, Carly Taylor, who
created the name and the plot, and the whole team. The globe is NASA's
Blue Marble. Calvary by Asciiverse, MIT licensed.

candybox2.title: Candy Box 2
candybox2.description: You have 1 candy. Eat it, throw some on the ground, ask for new features, and watch a candy counter grow into a whole ASCII world of quests, spells and lollipops
candybox2.provenance: aniwey made Candy Box in 2013 as a programming exercise; it went viral, and he promised its sequel would be free software. Candy Box 2 came out on 24 October 2013.
candybox2.page:
**YOU HAVE 1 CANDY.**

That is all you get at first: a number, ticking up once a second, and a
button to eat them. Eat them, or throw ten on the ground and see what
happens. Before long you are requesting new features from the developer
with your hard-earned sweets, and every one of them opens the world a
little wider: a status bar, a health bar, a map.

Then the map turns out to be a whole country. A village with a candy
merchant who would do anything for candies, a forge, a lonely house, a
lighthouse with questions, a desert, a bridge, a cave, a castle full of
things that want to hit you. You go questing with whatever you can carry,
cast spells from a grimoire, brew potions in a cauldron by the book, farm
lollipops, boot up a computer that runs GNU/Candies, and find out what is
really inside your box. All of it drawn in ASCII art, all of it in your
terminal.

Candy Box 2 is aniwey's sequel to his 2013 browser hit, and it is full of
jokes, secrets and surprises that are much more fun found than read
about. So this page will stop here.

## Controls

- **Mouse**: click buttons and links, hover over items for their
  descriptions, wheel to scroll (Shift+wheel sideways)
- **Tab** / **Shift+Tab**: move between buttons, lists and fields;
  **Enter** presses the highlighted one, so the game plays without a mouse
  too
- **Typing**: click a field (or Tab to it) and type; Enter sends
- **Page Up** / **Page Down**: scroll a long page; **Shift+arrows**
  sideways; on the world map the **arrows** move the view
- In quests and minigames the game has its own keys; in
  terminals with the kitty keyboard protocol (kitty, Ghostty, foot,
  WezTerm) held keys work as in the browser
- **Ctrl+C** or **Ctrl+Q**: quit. Save first, on the game's **SAVE** tab
  (it can also save every ten minutes); `candybox2 --slot 1` starts with
  slot 1

The game's own **CFG** tab changes the language (seventeen translations besides English)
and has "Invert colors?" for a black page instead of the white one.

## Credits

- Candy Box 2: aniwey (2013), ideas, game design and code;
  [github.com/candybox2/candybox2.github.io](https://github.com/candybox2/candybox2.github.io),
  kept by Andrei Kvapil
- ASCII art: Tobias Nordqvist, dixsept, Dani "Deinol" Gómez, GodsTurf and
  aniwey (CC BY-SA 3.0)
- Translations by their translators, credited in the game's CFG tab
- Terminal edition: Asciiverse, on QuickJS-ng (Fabrice Bellard, Charlie
  Gordon and the QuickJS-ng authors, MIT)
- License: GNU GPL version 3 or later for the code, CC BY-SA 3.0 for the art

canfield.title: Canfield
canfield.description: Solitaire for money: buy the deal for $13, earn $5 a card on the foundations, pay $1 a minute to think, and see whether your account is up at the end.
canfield.provenance: Steve Levine wrote Canfield at UC Berkeley by 1980; Steve Feldman moved it to curses, Kirk McKusick and Mikey Olson added card counting and McKusick the betting, with interface work by Eric Allman.
canfield.page:
**THE DEAL COSTS $13. THE CLOCK IS RUNNING.**

Canfield is solitaire with money on the table, and this one keeps the
books. The deal costs $13. A look at the game before you commit, another
$13. The rest of the game, $26 more. Every card you get onto a foundation
pays $5. Each extra run through the hand costs $5, card counting costs $1 a
card, and your think time is billed at $1 a minute. Your account carries
over from game to game, so the question is not whether you beat the hand.
It is whether you are up.

The rules are classic Canfield: thirteen cards in the stock, the first card
on the foundation setting the base rank for all four, the foundations
building up by suit and round the corner from king to ace, the tableau
building down in alternate colours and moving only as whole piles. Deal the
hand three at a time and look for the opening.

And from the manual's list of bugs: "It is impossible to cheat."

- **A running betting account**: costs, winnings, net worth and return,
  one keypress away
- **Card counting** on demand, at a price
- **A Berkeley classic** from 1980, with Kirk McKusick, Eric Allman and
  friends among its authors

## Controls

Each move is two letters or digits, typed at the Move prompt:

- **s#** and **sf**: stock to tableau pile #, or to the foundation
- **t#** and **tf**: talon to a tableau pile, or to the foundation
- **##**: tableau pile to tableau pile
- **#f**: tableau pile to the foundation
- **ht**: deal the hand to the talon
- **c**: card counting on or off
- **b**: the betting account, **i**: the instructions, **x**: hide the box
- **q**: give up this game

## History

Steve Levine wrote Canfield at UC Berkeley (the copyright is from 1980).
Steve Feldman moved it to curses and debugged it, Kirk McKusick and
Mikey Olson added card counting, McKusick the betting, and Eric Allman
and McKusick cleaned up the interface. This edition keeps the betting account
in the player's own data folder rather than a system file. It is part
of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD licence.

carrionfields.title: Carrion Fields
carrionfields.description: Roleplay-required dark fantasy MUD with cabal factions and player-versus-player conflict

cataclysm-dda.title: Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead
cataclysm-dda.description: The world has ended and you haven't, yet: scavenge, craft, build and drive through a huge open world of the dead, giant insects, killer robots and far stranger things.
cataclysm-dda.provenance: Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead began as a fork of Whales' Cataclysm (on GitHub from 2010) by Kevin Granade, TheDarklingWolf and GlyphGryph, and has been built by CleverRaven and thousands of contributors since.
cataclysm-dda.page:
**THE WORLD ENDED. YOU DIDN'T. YET.**

"The building you had chosen to reside in has suddenly caught fire! You
might want to leave."

That is one way to start. Or you "missed the evacuation and are stuck in a
city full of the risen dead." Or you made it to a government shelter, and
now the shelter is all there is. Outside: zombies, giant insects, killer
robots, "things far stranger and deadlier, and... the others like yourself,
who want what you have..."

Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead is a turn-based survival game in a huge,
persistent world made fresh for every game. Scavenge the ruins for food,
water and gear. Learn skills by using them. Craft almost anything, build a
base, and if you are lucky, find "a vehicle with a full tank of gas to get
you the hell out of Dodge." Then fix it up and drive. Death is final, and a
new world is always waiting.

- **A whole world, not a dungeon**: cities, forests, labs and the roads
  between them, and it goes on and on
- **Craft, build, cook, drive**: if you can find the parts and the know-how,
  you can probably make it
- **Dozens of ways to start**, from Evacuee to Really Bad Day: "You start
  drunk to the point of incapacitation, depressed, infected, surrounded by
  fire, and sick with the flu."
- **Pure text**, with every one of the game's translations

## Controls

- `h` `j` `k` `l` `y` `u` `b` `n`, the arrow keys or the number pad: move
  (walk into a door to open it, into a monster to attack it)
- `.` or `5`: wait a turn; `<` and `>`: go up and down stairs
- `g`: pick up; `e`: examine; `o` and `c`: open and close; `s`: smash
- `i`: inventory; `w`: wield; `W`: wear; `E`: eat or drink; `a`: use an item
- `f`: fire; `t`: throw; `r`: reload
- `&`: craft; `*`: construct; `$`: sleep
- `m`: overmap; `x` or `;`: look around; `P`: messages
- `?`: all key bindings, which can be changed
- `S`: save and quit; `Esc`: game menu

## History

Whales wrote Cataclysm, a grab-bag apocalypse roguelike, around 2010. Kevin
Granade, TheDarklingWolf and GlyphGryph forked it into Dark Days Ahead, a
grittier and more realistic survival game, and the project has grown under
CleverRaven into one of the largest open-source games, with more than a
thousand volunteers. Asciiverse builds it as is, with every file a
player has, saves and
options alike, kept in the player's data folder.

## Credits

- Original game: Whales
- Dark Days Ahead: CleverRaven and contributors, project manager Kevin
  Granade
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: CC BY-SA 3.0; the bundled fonts and libraries under their own
  licences, listed in LICENSE.txt

cataclysm2.title: Cataclysm II
cataclysm2.description: Shipwrecked fifty years after the end of the world: Whales' unfinished alpha rewrite of Cataclysm, with zombies in the towns and a world map to cross.
cataclysm2.provenance: Whales wrote Cataclysm II from 2013 to 2016 as a ground-up rewrite of Cataclysm, the roguelike Whales wrote from 2010 to 2013, and left it an early alpha. It is a separate project from Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead, the community fork of the first Cataclysm.
cataclysm2.page:
**SHIPWRECKED, FIFTY YEARS AFTER THE END OF THE WORLD.**

You were born after the cataclysm, in a coastal farming and fishing town
that kept its walls up and its people mostly safe. Then the walls broke.
You grabbed what you could, ran for the docks and put out to sea, the last
safe way out. Days adrift, no land in sight. Then a storm tore the boat
apart, and now you wake on a beach with the wreckage, and some of your
supplies, scattered around you.

Inland: fields, forests, swamps and salt marsh, and towns. Towns are where
the zombies are: fast ones, brutes, spitters and smoke zombies, and out in
the wild there are mutant rabbits, demented dogs and giant crabs. Make a
survivor from stats, traits and a profession (Survivalist, Medic, Farmer,
Mechanic, Hunter...), pick through the wreck, read the map and go.

**An unfinished alpha, and honest about it.** Cataclysm II is the rewrite
that Whales, the creator of Cataclysm, began in 2013 and stopped working on
in 2016. It plays for a while, but much is missing, things are rough, and
characters cannot be saved yet: each game is one sitting.

- **Whales' own sequel**, set fifty years after the first game
- **Small missions** to start with (eat this, read that) that pay
  experience, and experience buys skills
- **Worlds you can keep**: make one, then send new characters into it

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn** or the numpad: move, the last four diagonally; walk into a
  monster to attack it, into a door to open it
- **,**: pick up, **d**: drop, **i**: inventory
- **w**: wield, **W**: wear, **T**: take off, **e**: eat, **R**: read,
  **a**: apply
- **t**: throw, **f**: fire, **r**: reload
- **o** and **C**: open and close, **s**: smash, **x**: examine,
  **;**: look
- `<` and `>`: stairs up and down
- **:** or **M**: the world map (**q** leaves it)
- **@**: your character, **K**: skills
- **Q**: end the game

On the first screen, **H** opens the manual, with every key and how the
game works; **W** makes and chooses worlds.

## Saving

Worlds you make under **W: Manage Worlds** are kept in your data folder
and can be played again with a new character. Characters themselves are
not saved: **L: Load Character** was never finished.

## History

Whales wrote Cataclysm, a post-apocalyptic roguelike, from 2010 to 2013;
its players carried it on as Cataclysm: Dark Days Ahead, the big
community fork that is still developed today. Cataclysm II
is a different project: Whales' own start over, with new code, its own
interface layer and data files, set fifty years after the first game. It
was never finished, and its last change, in 2016, did not even compile.
This edition adds two contributors' unmerged fixes
and crash fixes of our own, keeps the game data beside the program and
your worlds in your data folder, and leaves the game as Whales left it.

## Credits

Whales, with Aninimouse, Trevmillion, superninjakiwi, WeendVidente,
Drakasin and others. GNU General Public License, version 3.

cavezofphear.title: CAVEZ of PHEAR
cavezofphear.description: Dig through the caves for every diamond while stones tumble down around you, blast a way through with bombs and crush the monsters before they catch you
cavezofphear.provenance: Tom Rune Flo wrote CAVEZ of PHEAR in C and ncurses from 2003, in the spirit of Boulder Dash; Dmitry Marakasov has maintained it since 2021.

upstream.name: Tom Rune Flo, maintained by Dmitry Marakasov

cavezofphear.page:
**YOU ARE TRAPPED IN THE CAVEZ OF PHEAR. DEATH AWAITS YOU.**

Eleven caves stand between you and freedom, and the only way out of each
one is to find every diamond hidden in it. Dig through the earth, and the
stones above you start to move: they fall into the tunnels you leave
behind, roll off each other's backs, and crush whatever is underneath,
including you.

Pick up the bombs you find, plant them where you need a door, and set
them all off at once. The bombs fall and roll like stones too, so plan
where they will land. Monsters roam the deeper caves: let them catch you
and you die, or drop a stone on them, or blow them up.

Diamonds are worth 10 points and money 100, and every thousand points
earns an extra life. Got yourself walled in? Give up the life and try the
cave again.

**Dig carefully.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** (or **8**, **2**, **4**, **6**): dig and move
- **b**: plant a bomb; **t**: set off every bomb you have planted
- **k**: give up this life, when you are stuck
- **s**: sound on and off; **w**: show where you are
- **q**: quit (it asks first); **Ctrl+C** quits at once

## The editor

From a terminal, `phear -e mycave` opens the cave editor: the number keys
place things, **l** locks drawing to the arrow keys, **s** saves and **q**
quits. Play your cave with `phear mycave`.

## Credits

- CAVEZ of PHEAR: Tom Rune Flo (2003 to 2011)
- Maintained since 2021 by [Dmitry Marakasov](https://github.com/AMDmi3/cavezofphear)
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

cbirds.title: cbirds
cbirds.description: A flock of birds wheels across the terminal in braille: Reynolds' boids, with sliders, hawks and a mouse that scatters them
cbirds.provenance: cbirds is by Alessandro Palliccia (clainstone), in C99 with nothing but the C library, from 2025.
cbirds.page:
**EIGHT HUNDRED BIRDS. THREE RULES. ONE FLOCK.**

A flock of birds in your terminal, drawn in braille: eight hundred boids
that keep their distance, match their neighbours and stay together, the
rules Craig Reynolds published in 1987. It opens by writing BOIDS in birds,
lets go, and flocks. Move the pointer into the flock and it scatters; leave
it alone for a minute and it starts moving its own sliders.

## Controls

- **q**: the flock flies off the top, and cbirds quits
- **h**: the panel of sliders: **b**/**B** boundary, **s**/**S**
  separation, **a**/**A** alignment, **t**/**T** turning, **p**/**P**
  perception, **v**/**V** speed (lowercase lowers, uppercase raises)
- **Space**: pause, **.** one frame
- **+** and **-**: more birds, fewer; **k** and **K**: a hawk more, one fewer
- **e**: tails; **Tab**: next preset; **0**: back to the defaults
- **Mouse**: the pointer scatters the flock

## Options

From a terminal: `--preset murmuration` for the starling look, `--hawks 2
--color ice`, `--flocks 3 --color ember`, `--3d` for a murmuration in three
dimensions, `--clock` or `--say "back in five"` to have the flock write,
`--matrix` for raining birds, `--render kitty` for real sprites in Kitty
or Ghostty, and `--screensaver` to quit on any key. `cbirds --help` lists
them all.

## Credits

- cbirds: [Alessandro Palliccia](https://github.com/clainstone/cbirds), after
  Craig Reynolds' boids (SIGGRAPH 1987)
- Asciiverse edition: upstream's program unchanged, built static for
  Linux and for macOS
- License: MIT

cblocks.title: cblocks
cblocks.description: Get the grand piano across the crowded room, sliding blocks only: twelve classic puzzles from 1903 to 1982, each with a known shortest solution to beat.
cblocks.provenance: Brian Raiter wrote cblocks in C for the Linux console and curses (2000, last updated 2020).
cblocks.page:
**THE PIANO HAS TO GET TO THE OTHER SIDE OF THE ROOM.**

The room is full of furniture. Nothing can be lifted. Nothing can be turned. Everything can only slide into the gap that's left. That was Dad's Puzzler, the best-known guise of a puzzle first sold in 1909, its big block a grand piano that had to cross a crowded room. Simple? Try it. And it's only puzzle number four.

cblocks is a tray of sliding blocks and a goal. Slide them until they stand where the puzzle wants them. Some ask you to march the biggest block from one end to the other; some want two identical blocks swapped; some want every block in its place. The rules take ten seconds. The solutions can take all evening.

- **Twelve classics,** from H. E. Dudeney's Motor-Car Problem (1903) and Sam Loyd's Moving Day Puzzle (1914), through L'Ane Rouge, the Red Donkey, to John Conway's Century-and-a-Half (1982), and more can be added as text files.
- **A best to beat:** every puzzle has a known shortest solution, counted in steps (a step is any number of slides of one block). The Motor-Car Problem takes 17. Conway's monster takes 148. How close can you get?
- **Your best is kept:** a new or better solution is saved, and loads back as redo when you return to the puzzle.
- **Undo and redo** slide by slide or step by step, save positions as you go, and peek at the goal whenever you need it.

**SLIDE. THINK. SLIDE AGAIN.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the selection square by square
- **h j k l**: select the next block in that direction
- **H J K L**: slide the selected block; or drag a block with the mouse
- **g**: show the goal
- **x** / **z**: undo / redo a slide; **X** / **Z**: undo / redo a step
- **R**: start again; **s** / **r**: save / restore a position
- **N** / **P**: next / previous puzzle
- **?**: help; **q**: quit

## Credits

- cblocks: Brian Raiter ([muppetlabs.com/~breadbox](https://www.muppetlabs.com/~breadbox/software/cgames.html)),
  2000 to 2020, written in C with curses; part of his cgames
- Puzzles: the classics of H. E. Dudeney, Sam Loyd, John Conway and
  others, as collected by Brian Raiter
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

cbonsai.title: cbonsai
cbonsai.description: Watch a bonsai grow in its pot, branch by branch and leaf by leaf, then another from a fresh seed, never the same twice: a calm screensaver for your terminal.
cbonsai.provenance: cbonsai is by John Allbritten and contributors, in C on ncurses, since 2020.
cbonsai.page:
**GROW A BONSAI. THEN ANOTHER. THEN ANOTHER.**

No shears, no watering can, no years of patience. Start cbonsai and a little tree grows in its pot right in front of you. The trunk climbs and twists, shoots split off left and right, and leaves gather at the tips in light and dark green.

When the tree is done it stands for a few seconds to be admired, then a new one starts from a fresh seed. Never the same tree twice. Leave it running and let the afternoon go by.

- **Live growth:** every step of the tree, as it happens.
- **Picks up where you left off:** quit halfway through a tree and it's kept; next time, that tree finishes growing before new ones follow.
- **Make it yours:** from a terminal, add a message beside the tree, or change its life, branching and leaves.

**PUT THE KETTLE ON. LET IT GROW.**

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit (the tree in progress is saved)

From a terminal, cbonsai has many more options: `cbonsai -l` grows one
tree and keeps it on screen, `cbonsai -p` prints a tree and exits,
`cbonsai -m "text"` puts a message beside the tree, and `-L`, `-M` and `-c`
change its life, branching and leaves. `cbonsai --help` lists them all.

## Credits

- cbonsai: [John Allbritten and contributors](https://gitlab.com/jallbrit/cbonsai)
- Asciiverse edition: saves in your data folder, Ctrl+C saves too, and a
  Windows build
- License: GPL-3.0-only

ceres.title: Ceres
ceres.description: Ceres Mountain: three thousand metres of ice, spikes and wind. Jump, dash and wall-kick your way to the summit, and try not to read the memorial on the way up!
ceres.provenance: Asciiverse restored Celeste Classic (Maddy Thorson and Noel Berry, PICO-8, 2015), from Noel Berry's C# port and checked against the original.
ceres.page:
**3000 METRES. ONE GIRL. ONE DASH.**

At the foot of Ceres Mountain stands a stone. *This memorial to those perished on the climb*, it says. Ceres reads it, ties her boots a little tighter, and starts up anyway.

Thirty-one screens of ice, spikes and howling wind stand between her and the summit, a hundred metres at a time. Jump! Dash through the air in any of eight directions! Cling to the rock and kick off again! When her hair turns red, the dash is spent: land, catch your breath, and go again.

Bounce off springs. Snatch a balloon for a fresh dash in midair. Race across snow that crumbles under your feet, and ride the moving platforms over the spikes. Hunt down the cherries hidden off the beaten path, though some of them flap away the moment you dash. Find the key, open the chest. And somewhere up there, past the Old Site, a golden sun-seed is waiting to give you a second dash...

You will fall. A lot. Every fall puts you straight back at the start of the screen to try again, and when you plant the flag at the summit, the mountain tells you exactly how many times.

- **Super-tight platforming, true to the frame:** 31 levels from 100 m to the summit, and every jump, dash and wall-kick plays exactly as in the original PICO-8 classic, checked frame by frame against it.
- **All-new art and an all-new soundtrack.**
- **Keyboard or gamepad,** on a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, foot, WezTerm, Ghostty, Alacritty, iTerm2 and others).

The summit is waiting. **HOW MANY TIMES WILL YOU FALL?**

## The original

In 2015, Maddy Thorson and Noel Berry made a hardcore little platformer for the PICO-8 fantasy console in just four days. They filled the cart almost to the last byte: 8186 of 8192 code tokens, the entire sprite sheet, the entire map and 63 of 64 sounds. That game was Celeste Classic, and it grew into the acclaimed Celeste (2018). Ceres restores it for the terminal, their code and their levels, with new art and new music.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **W A S D**: move
- **Z**, **C**, **N** or **Space**: jump
- **X**, **V** or **M**: dash, in any of eight directions
- **Esc** or **P**: menu, **R**: restart, **Q**: quit
- **K**: screen shake on or off, **A**: square pixels or sharp ones, **F8**: sound on or off
- **Gamepad**: stick or d-pad moves, bottom or top button jumps, the other face buttons or the triggers dash, Start opens the menu

## Options

- `--level N`: start at level N (1 to 31; 31 is the summit)
- `--no-shake`: no screen shake
- `--sharp`: exact 1:1 pixels
- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Original game: Celeste Classic by Maddy Thorson and Noel Berry (PICO-8, 2015)
- Code and levels: from Noel Berry's C# port, MIT licence
- Restoration, art and music: Asciiverse

cgram.title: Cgram
cgram.description: A 17th-century duke's sharpest sayings, scrambled into code: crack the substitution cipher letter by letter, and one good guess lights up the whole line.
cgram.provenance: David A. Holland wrote cgram around 2004 and added it to NetBSD's games in 2013; Roland Illig reworked it in 2020 and 2021.
cgram.page:
**A DUKE'S SHARPEST LINES. IN CODE.**

Every letter has been swapped for another, and somewhere under the scramble is a line that has been stinging people for over three hundred years. Your job: find the key.

It's the cryptogram from the Sunday paper. Put the cursor on a letter and type what you think it really is, and every copy of that letter changes at once, so one good guess can light up the whole text. Short words are the way in. Is that lonely letter an A or an I? Does that little word spell THE?

Behind every cipher hides one of the maxims of François de La Rochefoucauld, the 17th century French moralist who saw straight through everybody. "Self-love is the greatest of flatterers." "Hypocrisy is the homage vice pays to virtue." There are 456 of them, in J. Hain Friswell's 1871 translation, with a fresh key every game.

- **Hint mode:** stuck? Press `*` and every letter you've got right turns bold.
- **Any text you like:** started from a shell, `cgram file` scrambles that file instead.
- **The finish line:** get every letter right and the game says it: *solved*.

**CRACK IT.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, or **Ctrl-B**, **Ctrl-F**, **Ctrl-P**, **Ctrl-N**: move
  the cursor
- **A letter**: decode the letter under the cursor as that letter
- **\***: hint mode, which shows correctly decoded letters in bold
- **~**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `cgram file` makes a cryptogram of that file's
text instead of a maxim.

## History

David A. Holland wrote cgram around 2004 "for my own amusement", as he
put it when he added it to NetBSD in 2013; Roland Illig reworked it in
2020 and 2021. It takes its text from the fortune program, which the
Asciiverse does not ship, so this edition brings its own collection of
maxims from Project Gutenberg. It is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse
catalog, under the BSD licence.

changes.title: Changes
changes.description: You wake in a crashed cockpit, staring at a dying face that turns out to be your own. Then you wake again, somewhere soft, and something's different.
changes.provenance: David Given wrote Changes for the 2012 Interactive Fiction Competition.
changes.page:
**YOU WAKE AND SEE BLOOD.**

"There's blood everywhere." Behind it, a face twisted with pain, and a hand that spasms as it paws at the thing projecting from where a chest should be. You reach out to help, and that is when you realise you are looking into the inside of the reflective cockpit canopy, and the face you can see is yours.

Then you wake again. Somewhere warm and soft.

*Something's different.*

You fight your way out of a cocoon into the Forest Cathedral: huge columnar trees holding up the leaf canopy, golden rays angling down, a river running along the east side, and more green cocoons at the bases of the trees. The air is full of peace. But you're not going anywhere just yet, because something's wrong.

What are you now? How does the life of this forest fit together? And how do you survive in it?

David Given wrote Changes for the 2012 Interactive Fiction Competition: a text adventure on a strange forest world, where the first puzzle is yourself.

**WAKE UP. FIND OUT WHAT YOU'VE BECOME.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/changes`.

## Credits

- Changes: David Given, 2012
- License: Creative Commons BY-ND (the author's terms); shipped unchanged
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

checkers.title: Checkers
checkers.description: Twelve men a side, forced jumps, chains of captures and kings: take on a friend, or a computer that lets you win once, then learns exactly how good you are.
checkers.provenance: abakh wrote Checkers for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018.
checkers.page:
**IT LETS YOU WIN. ONCE.**

The computer in this checkers starts out playing badly on purpose, so your first game is likely a win. Its author's plan, written into the code: the second game you're likely to lose, so you don't think the computer is stupid, and after that it works out how good you are and plays on par with you. Beat it and it promises: "I'd play better next time." Keep beating it at its strongest and it can only ask: "Are you human?"

Twelve men a side. Men step one square diagonally forward; reach the far side and you're crowned a king (**K**), free to move both ways. Capture by jumping over an enemy piece, and string jumps into a chain to take several in one turn. And if you can jump, you must. Win when your opponent cannot move; fifty turns without gain for either side is a draw.

- **You against the computer,** a friend on the same keyboard, or the computer against itself. By default you play black, shown in red, and black moves first.
- **Keyboard or mouse:** arrows, hjkl or wasd, or just click.
- **A fixed strength** if you'd rather: `-p` from 1 to 127.

**YOUR MOVE.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move
- **Enter**: on your piece, pick it up; on a free square, move it there.
  In a chain of jumps, pick the same piece up again for each jump
- **Mouse**: click instead of Enter
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: resign

## Options

- `-1 h` or `-1 c`: a human or the computer plays black
- `-2 h` or `-2 c`: the same for white; either one skips the questions
- `-p 3`: a fixed strength for the computer, from 1 to 127
- `-n`: quit after one game instead of offering a rematch

## History

Checkers is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

chess-tui.title: chess-tui
chess-tui.description: Real chess in your terminal: take on Stockfish at five strengths, a friend at the same keyboard or across your local network, or real opponents and rated puzzles on Lichess.
chess-tui.provenance: chess-tui is Thomas Mauran's terminal chess game in Rust and Ratatui, from 2023 and still maintained with many contributors.
chess-tui.page:
**IT IS STRONGER THAN ANY HUMAN WHO EVER PLAYED. YOUR MOVE.**

Stockfish comes in the box, ready the moment you start: no setup, no engine to hunt down. At full strength it is far stronger than any human player. Feeling less heroic? Turn it down to one of four easier levels and work your way up.

This is chess with a proper board. On a big terminal the pieces are drawn large in block characters; on a smaller one, in chess symbols. Move with the arrow keys or the mouse, or just type it: `e4`, `Nf3`, `O-O`. The move history and captured pieces sit beside the board, so you always know who's winning, and why.

- **Stockfish at five strengths,** from Easy to full power, or any other UCI engine you point it at.
- **Two players:** share one keyboard, or host and join across your local network.
- **Lichess, from the terminal:** sign in and seek a game, join a friend's by its code, pick up your ongoing games, or solve rated Lichess puzzles.
- **Clocks** from UltraBullet to Classical, or none at all.
- **Save, load and replay:** load a PGN file and step through any game, move by move.
- **Skins:** press `s` and the board changes its look.

**WHITE TO PLAY.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the cursor; **Enter** or **Space**: pick up a
  piece, then put it down
- **m**: type a move in chess notation (`e4`, `Nf3`, `O-O`)
- **Esc**: put the piece back; **s**: change the board's look
- **?**: help with every key; **q**: quit
- In the menus: **Up** and **Down** to choose, **Enter** to go on

## Options

- `--difficulty easy`, `medium`, `hard` or `magnus`: the computer's
  strength for Play Bot
- `-e <path>`: use another UCI chess engine instead of the bundled
  Stockfish
- `-l <token>`: a Lichess API token, for playing on Lichess
- `--no-sound`: no move sounds (macOS and Windows; this build has none on
  Linux)

## Credits

- chess-tui: Thomas Mauran and contributors
  ([github.com/thomas-mauran/chess-tui](https://github.com/thomas-mauran/chess-tui)),
  2023 on, written in Rust with Ratatui
- Stockfish 11: the Stockfish developers
  ([stockfishchess.org](https://stockfishchess.org)), GPL-3.0-or-later,
  shipped beside chess-tui with its licence and source
- Asciiverse edition: Stockfish included and found without any setting
- License: MIT (chess-tui), GPL-3.0-or-later (Stockfish)

christbashtree.title: Christmas Tree
christbashtree.description: A Christmas tree of green stars, coloured lights winking on and off, and a greeting that flashes CODE: ChristBASHTree as one small program.
christbashtree.provenance: Sergio Lepore wrote ChristBASHTree in bash and tput in 2014, with later contributions to 2018.
christbashtree.page:
**MERRY CHRISTMAS, AND LOTS OF CODE.**

"You know, a Christmas tree on Bash :)" That's how Sergio Lepore introduced it in 2014, and it is still one of the nicest things you can leave glowing in a terminal in December.

A tree of bold green stars stands on its little `mWm` trunk. Lights pop on all over it, one after another, colour after colour, and wink out again. Underneath, the greeting: "MERRY CHRISTMAS, And lots of CODE in" next year, with CODE flashing in the colour of the newest light.

- **Two languages:** English, or `christbashtree es` for "FELICES FIESTAS, Y mucho CODIGO en" next year.
- **Tiny:** happy in a terminal of 26 columns by 14 rows.
- **No bash needed:** the same tree, lights and pace, as one small program that runs on Windows too.

**HAPPY HOLIDAYS. NOW GO WRITE SOME CODE.**

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `christbashtree es` shows the Spanish tree: "FELICES
FIESTAS, Y mucho CODIGO en" next year.

## History

Sergio Lepore wrote ChristBASHTree for Christmas 2014 as a short bash
script that drew with `tput`, run straight from the web with curl, and
others added to it until 2018. Asciiverse ported it to one small C
program with the same tree, lights and pace, so it runs on Windows too
and needs no bash; any key quits.

## Credits

- ChristBASHTree: [Sergio Lepore](https://github.com/sergiolepore/ChristBASHTree) and contributors
- Asciiverse edition: the C port, any key quits, Windows
- License: public domain (the Unlicense)

chroma.title: Chroma
chroma.description: Fiendish traps of sliding arrows and bombs, two pieces to steer and every star to collect: twenty-one abstract puzzles that start easy and end fiendish, with unlimited undo.
chroma.provenance: Amf wrote Chroma in C (2010 to 2025), with a graphical version and this terminal one, chroma-curses.
chroma.page:
**HAVE YOU GOT WHAT IT TAKES TO SOLVE CHROMA?**

That's the question its author, Amf, asks. Thirty-three levels are waiting for your answer.

Each one is a pattern of colourful shapes forming, in Amf's words, "fiendish traps that must be disarmed and mysterious puzzles that must be manipulated in order to give up their subtle secrets." You have two octagonal player pieces. Collect every star, then leave through the door. That's all.

Nobody tells you the rules. Arrows slide the way they point whenever there is room, and a moving one will crush a player piece flat. Bombs, circles and dots have rules of their own, and they set each other off. Experiment. Watch what happens. Then use it. The first six levels of each set bring the pieces in one by one; by the end you'll need both player pieces working together, move by careful move.

- **Three sets, 33 levels:** Initiation, nine for beginners, from Invitation onward; Coronation, twelve for experts, all the way to Culmination; and Enigma, twelve more. Play them in any order.
- **Mistakes cost nothing:** undo as far back as you like, and redo plays it forward again.
- **Save, load and replay:** keep positions, and watch a saved solution replay move by move.
- **A level editor:** build your own, test it and verify it.
- **Enigma's twelve levels:** the original levels of Enigma, a puzzle game of falling blocks, exploding bombs and pushing things around, from Darkness Falls to Shrouded Glory, played by Enigma's own rules.

**THE DOOR IS RIGHT THERE. GETTING TO IT IS ANOTHER MATTER.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the active player piece
- **Space** or **Enter**: swap to the other player piece
- **Delete**, **Backspace** or **U**: undo a move
- **Insert** or **Y**: redo
- **F**: let everything moving come to rest at once
- **P**: pause
- **Escape**: the game menu (save, load, replay, revert, display
  options, leave the level)

Keys can be changed under Display Options. In the editor, Page Up and
Page Down choose a piece and Space places it.

## Files

Saved and solved positions, levels under construction and the display
options are kept in `~/.local/share/chroma` (`%APPDATA%\chroma` on
Windows). Exported levels and solutions go to your home folder.

## History

Amf released Chroma in 2010 with a graphical SDL version and this
terminal one, and kept it going until version 1.21 in November 2025;
there is also a browser version and a port to the BBC Micro. It is
packaged by Debian. The Asciiverse edition is the terminal version, with
the levels found beside the program and saved positions in the player's
data folder.

## Credits

Chroma is by Amf (level7.org.uk), under the GNU GPL version 2 or later.

clani.title: CLiAni
clani.description: Endless landscapes of plain characters scroll past: Voronoi cells, Perlin clouds and cellular shapes, in rain, zig-zag or static, from a new random seed every run.
clani.provenance: Ryan Huth (hury) wrote CLiAni in C++ on ncurses (2020 to 2024), with resize handling by Sergeant-Salz.
clani.page:
**AN ENDLESS LANDSCAPE OF NOISE. NEVER THE SAME TWICE.**

Patterns made of plain characters roll down the screen without end, a new row every tenth of a second. Faint dots and colons swell into dense banks of D, # and @ wherever the noise runs strongest, then thin out again. Every run starts from a new random seed, so the landscape you see has never been seen before.

Ryan Huth made CLiAni for "some cool scrolling patterns and other animation effects", and, in his words, "just something I work on by the side for fun". It shows.

- **Three flavours:** Voronoi (the one av starts), Perlin noise and cellular Voronoi.
- **Four effects:** scrolling, raining (the pattern shows only in falling streaks), zig-zag, and static.
- **Your own characters:** up to ten, from faint to dense.
- **Make your choice:** started from a terminal with no options, it opens a menu to pick from.

**SIT BACK AND WATCH IT ROLL.**

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

From a terminal: `clani -f cell -e raining` picks the flavour and effect,
`-s 42` a fixed seed, `-c " .oO@"` your own characters, and `clani` on its
own opens the menu (arrows, Enter, F1 to leave). `clani -h` lists the
options.

## Credits

- CLiAni: [Ryan Huth](https://github.com/hu-ry/CLiAni), resize handling by
  Sergeant-Salz
- Asciiverse edition: options that start an animation at once, any key to
  quit, current ncurses, and bug fixes
- License: GPL-3.0-only

clidle.title: clidle
clidle.description: Five letters, six tries, one hidden word: the colours flip one by one, the on-screen keyboard keeps track, and every game adds to your running score.
clidle.provenance: Ajeet D'Souza wrote clidle, a terminal word-guessing game, in Go in 2022 and still maintains it.
clidle.page:
**FIVE LETTERS. SIX TRIES. ONE WORD.**

Type a guess, press Enter, and watch the letters turn, one at a time. Green: right letter, right place. Yellow: it's in there, but somewhere else. Grey: not in the word at all. Only real words count, so no cheating your way through the vowels.

Below the board, an on-screen keyboard colours every letter as you learn about it, so you can see at a glance what's left to try. Got it in three? That's 80 points. In one? A hundred, and bragging rights. Six squeaks home with 50, and it all adds up into a running score.

And you don't have to wait until tomorrow: every game picks a new word at random from 2,315 answers, with 12,972 words it accepts as guesses. Press Ctrl+R and there's another one.

- **Letters revealed one by one,** for that moment of suspense.
- **A running score** that keeps adding up, game after game.
- **Play it over SSH:** `clidle -serve` turns it into a server other people can connect to and play.

clidle is Ajeet D'Souza's five-letter word-guessing game in the style of Wordle.

**WHAT'S YOUR OPENING WORD?**

## Controls

- **a** to **z**: type a letter
- **Backspace**: clear the last letter
- **Enter**: check the guess; after a game, start the next one
- **Ctrl+R**: start a new word at any time
- **Esc** or **Ctrl+C**: quit

The on-screen keyboard needs a terminal of at least 58 columns by 30
rows.

## Options

- `-serve 0.0.0.0:1337`: run clidle as an SSH server, so others can play
  it with `ssh -p 1337 your-host`

## Credits

- clidle: Ajeet D'Souza
  ([github.com/ajeetdsouza/clidle](https://github.com/ajeetdsouza/clidle)),
  2022 on, written in Go with Charm's Bubble Tea and Lip Gloss
- Asciiverse edition: letters revealed one by one, Esc to quit, the
  score kept in view in a 30-row terminal, long messages fitted to narrow
  windows; written to be offered back upstream
- License: MIT

clines.title: Console Lines
clines.description: Slide coloured chips across a 9x9 board and line up five of a kind before three new ones land every turn. Keep the board clear as long as you can.
clines.provenance: Pawel S. Veselov wrote Console Lines in C on curses (2002 to 2006), after the classic Color Lines.
clines.page:
**THREE NEW CHIPS EVERY TURN. HOW LONG CAN YOU HOLD THEM OFF?**

The board is 9x9 and it is filling up. Every turn you fail to score, three more chips land at random: red, green, blue, yellow and purple, crowding your paths and closing the gaps you were saving. Your one weapon is a single move. Pick up a chip and send it to any free cell it can reach, sliding up, down, left and right around the others.

Line up five or more of one colour, across, down or diagonally, and they vanish. Better still, nothing new arrives: the move is yours again. Let the board fill and it is over.

- **Big clears pay big**: n chips cleared at once score n + n x (n - 5), so a line of six is worth 12, and two lines crossing at the last chip you drop are worth far more than two fives.
- **Chains pay too**: clear on turn after turn without letting new chips in, and each one adds a growing bonus, b x b for the b-th in a row after the first.
- **Keys or mouse**: arrow keys or h j k l and Space, or click a chip and then the cell to send it to.
- **Your best score**: kept between games and shown under the board while you play.

Plays in black and white too, with letters for the colours.

**One move. Five in a row. Don't let it fill.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h**, **j**, **k**, **l**: move the cursor
- **Space**: pick up the chip under the cursor (it starts to jump), then
  put it down on a free cell
- **Mouse**: click a chip, then the cell to send it to
- **Ctrl+L**: redraw; **q**: quit (your score is saved)

## Options

- `-l`: list the high scores
- `-m b`: black and white, with letters for the colours
- `-w`, `-t`, `-c`, `-i`, `-n`, `-N`: board width and height, number of
  colours, line length, chips per turn and chips to start with (scores
  are only kept with the defaults)

## High scores

Your best score is kept in your own folder
(`~/.local/share/clines`), so it survives updates, and shows under the
board while you play.

## History

Pawel S. Veselov started Console Lines in 2002, after the classic Color
Lines, added mouse support (both the terminal's and GPM on the Linux
console) and scoring, and released 1.0.4 in October 2006 with resizing,
smaller terminals, black and white mode and saved high scores. His site
has since gone; ALT Linux and OpenBSD kept packaging it.

The Asciiverse edition keeps scores in your own folder, animates the
jumping chip without curses calls inside signal handlers, and makes sure the mouse keeps
working in terminal emulators.

clok.title: CLOK
clok.description: Fantasy frontier-west and gaslamp MUD set in the Northern Lost Lands

cmines.title: cmines
cmines.description: Every square hides a number or a mine, and one wrong step ends it. Clear Beginner, Intermediate and Expert fields against the clock, with flags, chording, and keys or mouse.
cmines.provenance: Brian Raiter wrote cmines in C for the Linux console and curses (2000, last updated 2020).
cmines.page:
**ONE WRONG STEP AND IT'S OVER.**

Somewhere under this grid are 99 mines. Every square you open tells you how many of its eight neighbours hide one, and from those numbers, and nothing else, you work out where it is safe to step. Flag the mines you are sure of. Open the rest. The clock is running.

The first square you open is never a mine, so the opening move is free. After that, it's all you.

- **Three classic fields**: Beginner (8x8, 10 mines), Intermediate (16x16, 40 mines) and Expert (16x30, 99 mines), each with its own best time. Write your own into the setup file, or start one by name: `cmines Expert`.
- **Chording**: when a number has all its mines flagged, Return (or the middle mouse button) opens all its other neighbours in one go. That is how the fast times are made.
- **A peek when you're truly stuck**: **p** looks under one square, but a game with a peek in it can't set a best time.
- **A face to keep you company**: with `-e`, a little emoticon shows the game's mood, from :-) to B-).
- **Keys or mouse**: arrow keys or h j k l, or click.

**Beginner is a warm-up. Expert is a war.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: move; **H J K L**: move by three
- **Space** or **left click**: open a square
- **.** (dot) or **right click**: flag a mine
- **Return** or **middle click**: open the neighbours of a number
- **p**: peek at a square
- **?**: help and the best times
- **n**: new game; **b**, **i**, **e**: Beginner, Intermediate, Expert
  (between games); **q**: give up the game; **Q**: quit

## Options

- `-t`: keep the timer running on screen
- `-e`: show the game's mood as an emoticon
- `-s FILE`: use another setup file

## Credits

- cmines: Brian Raiter ([muppetlabs.com/~breadbox](https://www.muppetlabs.com/~breadbox/software/cgames.html)),
  2000 to 2020, written in C with curses; part of his cgames
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

colossal-cave.title: Colossal Cave Adventure
colossal-cave.description: The cave that started it all: find the way in, get the treasures past dwarves, a pirate and a troll, and say the magic word. The original text adventure, in its authors' final 430-point version.
colossal-cave.provenance: Will Crowther wrote Adventure in 1976 and Don Woods expanded it in 1977. Eric S. Raymond ported their last version, Adventure 2.5 (1995, 430 points), to modern C as Open Adventure.

upstream.name: Eric S. Raymond, after Will Crowther (1976) and Don Woods (1977)

colossal-cave.page:
**SOMEWHERE NEARBY IS COLOSSAL CAVE.**

Others have found fortunes in treasure and gold down there, "though it is rumored that some who enter are never seen again." You are standing at the end of a road before a small brick building. Take the lamp. Find the way in. Bring the treasure back.

Then the light runs out. "It is now pitch dark. If you proceed you will likely fall into a pit." There is a threatening little dwarf in the room with you, and one sharp nasty knife is thrown at you. A bearded pirate pounces out of the shadows: "Har, har," he chortles, "I'll just take all this booty and hide it away with me chest deep in the maze!" A troll guards the bridge ("Stop! Pay troll!"), a dragon is sprawled out on a Persian rug, and on one wall someone has scrawled MAGIC WORD XYZZY.

- **The original**: Will Crowther's 1976 cave, expanded by Don Woods, the game that started the genre and gave the world "a maze of twisty little passages, all alike".
- **The final version**: Adventure 2.5, the 430-point edition its two authors finished together in 1995, with more cave than the classic 350.
- **Help at a price**: when you seem stuck, the game offers a hint, and charges you points for it.
- **Two words is all it takes**: GET LAMP, UNLOCK GRATE, XYZZY.

**Magic is said to work in the cave. Say the word.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in one or two words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **score**
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**), and **in**, **out**, **building**
- **take lamp**, **light lamp**, **unlock grate**, **drop bird**
- **help** and **info** explain more; the game offers hints when you seem stuck, at a cost in points
- **save** writes your game to a file you name, and quits; to continue, start a new game and say **resume**
- **quit** to stop

The up and down arrows recall earlier commands. Saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/colossal-cave` (on Windows, `%APPDATA%\colossal-cave`).

## History

Will Crowther wrote Adventure in 1976 in FORTRAN on a PDP-10 at Bolt, Beranek and Newman, modelled on the Colossal Cave complex in Kentucky. Don Woods expanded it at the Stanford AI Lab in 1977 into the 350-point game that spread across the world's computers. The two kept working on it until 1995 and Adventure 2.5, with more cave and 430 points. Eric S. Raymond ported that version to modern C as Open Adventure; it plays the same game, with a command line that remembers.

## Credits

- Adventure: Will Crowther, 1976; Don Woods, 1977; both, version 2.5, 1995
- Open Adventure: Eric S. Raymond and contributors, BSD-2-Clause
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

counterfeit-monkey.title: Counterfeit Monkey
counterfeit-monkey.description: Your cover is blown, your face is on file, and you have eight hours to get off an island where words are tools. Change a thing's name and you change the thing.
counterfeit-monkey.provenance: Emily Short's Counterfeit Monkey (2012) won Best Game and four more categories at the 2012 XYZZY Awards; its community now maintains it in an open-source repository.
counterfeit-monkey.page:
**YOUR COVER IS BLOWN. GOOD LUCK GETTING OFF THE ISLAND.**

"Can you hear me?"

You wake in a back alley at noon, and you are two people. Alex and Andra have just been synthesised into one body, Alexandra, the most inconvenient disguise either of you has ever worn. You smuggle and spy for a living, the Bureau of Orthography has your faces on record, and a national holiday has the police spread thin for about eight more hours.

Welcome to Anglophone Atlantis, an independent nation since the April day in 1822 when "a well-aimed shot from their depluralizing cannon reduced the British colonizing fleet to one ship." Here, words are tools. Change a thing's name and you change the thing, and in your pocket is the tool to do it: a full-alphabet letter remover. Point it at something, pick a letter, take it out, and see what you're left holding.

- **A world built on wordplay**: every puzzle turns on letters and the words they make, across a whole town of streets, shops and museums, from Sigil Street to Ampersand Bend.
- **Two minds, one body**: your other half talks you through it, and your memories of how you got here come back as you go.
- **Gentle on newcomers**: a tutorial walks you through the first steps; type TUTORIAL OFF if you know your way.
- **Big and generous**: a full-length game by Emily Short, one of the great names in interactive fiction.

**Find a way off the island. Spell it out.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/counterfeit-monkey`.

## Credits

- Counterfeit Monkey: Emily Short, 2012; maintained by the Counterfeit Monkey contributors
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 (the feelies are not included)
- Played with Glulxe and GlkTerm by Andrew Plotkin (MIT)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

crawl.title: Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup
crawl.description: Go down through the Dungeon, take three runes of Zot from the depths of its branches, and carry the Orb back into the sunlight. Twenty-seven species, twenty-six backgrounds, gods to serve, and one life.
crawl.provenance: Linley Henzell wrote Linley's Dungeon Crawl in 1997, and the Stone Soup team has developed it as Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup since 2006, in the open on GitHub.

upstream.name: Linley Henzell (1997) and the Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup team (since 2006)

crawl.page:
**THE ORB OF ZOT IS DOWN THERE. COME BACK WITH IT.**

Somewhere deep beneath the world's surface lies the Orb of Zot. "Some say it will grant immortality or even godhood to the one who carries it into the sunlight; many undead creatures seek it in the hope that it will restore them to life. But then, some people will believe anything."

Between you and it: the Dungeon, and every branch that leads off it. The Orcish Mines. The Elven Halls. The Lair of Beasts, where "there is something to be said about getting gored, mauled and eaten rather than sliced, burnt or stabbed." The Swamp, the Snake Pit, the Slime Pits, the Vaults, the Crypt and, for the brave, Hell itself. To reach the Realm of Zot at all you need at least three magical runes from the bottoms of those branches. And Zot? "No one knows who or what Zot is: demon, god, wizard, something else entirely?" Only that it hunts those who go after the Orb.

- **Twenty-seven species, twenty-six backgrounds**: a Felid Berserker, an Octopode Necromancer, a Mummy, a Troll; play whatever you dare.
- **Gods to serve**: "a number of gods, demons and other assorted powers" will take your worship and grant favours in return, though "most gods resent being scorned".
- **One life, no grinding**: turn-based and permanent, built by designers on a crusade against grinding and "no-brainers", so every choice counts. Autoexplore and autotravel skip the dull parts.
- **Still growing**: in active development for twenty years, carried on in the open by the Stone Soup team.
- **Pure text**: this is the console game, drawn in characters.

**Three runes to win. Fifteen to brag about. One life to do it.**

## Controls

- **h j k l y u b n**, the arrow keys or the number pad: move, and attack
  by moving into a monster; with **Shift**, run
- **o**: explore the level automatically
- **Tab**: fight the nearest monster
- **5** or **s**: rest or wait
- **g** or **,**: pick up; **i**: inventory
- **w**: wield; **W**: wear armour; **P**: put on jewellery
- **q**: drink; **r**: read; **z**: cast a spell; **a**: abilities
- **f**: fire or throw; **V**: evoke
- **<** and **>**: take the stairs; **G**: travel to a level; **X**: map
- **?**: every command
- **Ctrl-S**: save and quit; your game continues the next time you start

## History

Linley Henzell wrote Linley's Dungeon Crawl in 1997; Brent Ross
maintained it later and released its final alpha, 4.1, in 2005. Since
2006 the Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup team has carried it on, with new
versions ever since, in the open on GitHub. The Asciiverse edition is
the console game, without tiles, with saves, morgue files and init.txt
in your data folder (`~/.local/share/crawl`).

## Credits

- Game: Linley Henzell; Brent Ross and the Crawl 4.0 team; the Dungeon
  Crawl Stone Soup team and contributors (see CREDITS.txt in the game's
  docs)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

cribbage.title: Cribbage
cribbage.description: Fifteen-two, fifteen-four, and a pair is six: cribbage against a computer that counts every hand for you, first to 61, in a seven-game match where a skunk counts double.
cribbage.provenance: BSD's cribbage was written by Earl T. Cohen, with Ken Arnold's screen interface (UC Berkeley, 1980). Mike Sharov rewrote it from scratch for his bsd-games in 2016.

upstream.name: Mike Sharov, after Earl T. Cohen and Ken Arnold (1980)

cribbage.page:
**FIFTEEN-TWO, FIFTEEN-FOUR, AND A PAIR IS SIX.**

Pull up a chair. The computer has shuffled, the pegs are in the board, and it wants a game. Six cards each: lay two away into the crib, and remember whose crib it is before you throw, because it belongs to the dealer. Then the play: you take turns laying cards and calling the count, pegging for fifteens, pairs, runs and 31, and saying "go" when you can't. Then the show, where every hand is counted with the starter card and the dealer counts the crib as well. Turn up a jack, and the dealer gets one for "his heels".

- **A quick game**: once round the board, first to 61.
- **A seven-game match**: and a skunk, winning before your opponent reaches 31, counts as two games.
- **No arithmetic homework**: the computer counts both hands and the crib, shows the breakdown (fifteens, pairs, runs, flushes, nobs) and waits before the show so you can count yours first.
- **No fault points**: you can only make legal plays, and when one card is all you can play, it plays itself.
- **Real suits**: hearts, spades, diamonds and clubs as card symbols in a UTF-8 terminal.

**"I get one for his heels." Make it pay for that.**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**, or **j** and **k**: choose a card
- **Space** or **Enter**: discard or play the chosen card, and go on
  after a pause
- **q** or **F10**: quit

Cards that would take the count past 31 are skipped, and when only one
card can be played it is played for you.

## History

Cribbage was one of the early BSD games: Earl T. Cohen wrote the game
logic and Ken Arnold added the screen interface (UC Berkeley, 1980).
Mike Sharov replaced it with a rewrite of his own in 2016 for his
bsd-games, and has since fixed its scoring of pairs, runs and flushes
and taught the computer to avoid easy fifteens for its opponent. Suits
show as card symbols in a UTF-8 terminal.

csokoban.title: csokoban
csokoban.description: Push every box onto its goal: you can never pull, and a box in a corner stays there. 1,043 levels by David W. Skinner, from gentle Microban to fiendish Sasquatch, with undo, redo and saved solutions.
csokoban.provenance: Brian Raiter wrote csokoban in C for the Linux console and curses (2000, last updated 2020).
csokoban.page:
**PUSH. NEVER PULL. THINK FIRST.**

A warehouse, a handful of boxes, and just as many goal squares. Your job: get every box onto a goal. You can push a box, one at a time, but you can never pull it, so one careless shove into a corner and that box is stuck there for good. The rules take a minute. The levels take much, much longer.

Here are 1,043 of them, all by David W. Skinner, from his fifteen finished sets.

- **Start with Microban**: 155 small puzzles, each showing one idea, good for beginners and children. **Mas Microban**, **Microban III** and **IV** carry on in the same spirit.
- **Then the Sasquatch sets**, I to XI: 550 levels from medium to very hard. Some are huge, up to 49 by 44; when one doesn't fit, the game says how much room it needs and waits for a bigger window.
- **Mistakes are free**: undo and redo one move or eight at a time, save positions to come back to, and record a run of moves to replay from the same spot.
- **Your best, kept**: the game stores your best solution to every level, in fewest moves and in fewest pushes, and starts you at the first level you haven't solved.

**One more level. Then bed. Honest.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: walk and push; **H J K L**: walk as far
  as you can
- **x** / **z**: undo / redo a move; **X** / **Z**: undo / redo eight
- **R**: start the level again; **s** / **r**: save / restore a position
- **N** / **P**: next / previous level
- **m**, **p**: record moves, play them back
- **?**: help; **q**: quit

## Options

- `csokoban sasquatch-03`: start with a set by name; `csokoban -l` lists
  them
- `csokoban -12`: start at level 12

## Credits

- csokoban: Brian Raiter ([muppetlabs.com/~breadbox](https://www.muppetlabs.com/~breadbox/software/cgames.html)),
  2000 to 2020, written in C with curses; part of his cgames
- Levels: David W. Skinner <sasquatch@bentonrea.com>, Microban (2000),
  Mas Microban (2002), Microban III and IV, and Sasquatch I to XI (1999
  on), freely distributed with credit, as he asked
- Sokoban: Hiroyuki Imabayashi, Thinking Rabbit, 1982
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

csol.title: csol
csol.description: Eleven solitaires in one: Klondike, FreeCell, Spider in one, two or four suits, Yukon, Russian, Eight Off, Golf and more, played by keyboard or mouse.
csol.provenance: Niels Sonnich Poulsen wrote csol in C in 2017 as a small collection of solitaire games, each one a short file of rules, and later ported it to DOS and Windows.
csol.page:
**ELEVEN WAYS TO LAY OUT A DECK.**

A whole shelf of patience games in one small program. Deal a Klondike,
then a FreeCell, then lose an evening to Spider: every game is played the
same way, with the arrow keys or the mouse, on proper drawn cards with
their suits in colour.

- **Klondike**, the one everyone knows, and **Klondike FreeCell**
- **FreeCell** and **Eight Off**, every card in view from the start and
  free cells to juggle with
- **Spider** with one, two or four suits
- **Yukon**, **Yukon FreeCell** and **Russian**, where whole stacks move at
  once
- **Golf**, up or down by one to clear the table

Undo and redo as far back as you like, a smart cursor that always lands on
a card, scores and times for every game, and a victory dance when the last
card goes home. Eight themes, from big framed cards to compact ones for a
small terminal, or plain ASCII.

**PICK A GAME. DEAL.**

## Controls

- **Arrows** or **HJKL**: move the cursor; with **Shift**, to the far end
  or the top or bottom of a pile
- **Space**: pick up the card (and those on it); again to send it home or
  to a free cell
- **Enter** or **M**: put it down on the pile under the cursor
- **Mouse**: left click picks up, right click puts down
- **A**: send a card to a foundation; **S** and **W**: deal from the stock,
  play from the waste; **1** to **9**: play from a free cell
- **U** or **Ctrl+Z**: undo; **Shift+U** or **Ctrl+Y**: redo
- **R**: deal again; **Q**: quit; **F10** or **Alt** with a letter: the
  menu bar, for games, themes and settings; **?**: how to play

## Options

- `csol freecell`, `csol spider2`, ...: start a game; `-l` lists them
- `-t compact`, `-t ascii`, ...: a theme; `-T` lists them
- `-S`: your stats for every game; `-S klondike`: every score in one
- `-s 12345`: deal from a fixed seed; `-m`: no colours

## Credits

- csol: [Niels Sonnich Poulsen](https://github.com/nielssp/csol)
- License: MIT

curse-of-war.title: Curse of War
curse-of-war.description: Real-time war on a hex map where you never move a single soldier: plant flags, build cities and watch your people pour across the front. Four countries, one map, one ruler at the end.
curse-of-war.provenance: Alexey Nikolaev wrote Curse of War in C on ncurses in 2013.
curse-of-war.page:
**YOU DON'T COMMAND SOLDIERS. YOU COMMAND A NATION.**

Four countries start in the corners of a map of hexagons. You rule the green one. The other three want the whole map, and so do you.

There are no units to click on here. Your people are your army. They grow in your villages, towns and fortresses and spill out over the grassland, up to 499 to a tile, and where two countries' people meet, they fight. Plant a flag and your crowds drift toward it. Push a line of flags into enemy land and you have a front, fought over tile by tile. Surround a gold mine to take it, spend the gold on new cities, and outgrow them. Lose a city under siege and it burns down a size: fortress to town, town to village, and a village to nothing.

- **Real time, and fast**: speed it up, slow it down or pause while the fronts move.
- **Rivals with character**: every computer ruler fights in its own way.
- **Maps your way**: rectangles, rhombuses, or hexagons with room for six countries, any size, and a seed to replay the same map.
- **Friends on your local network**: one machine hosts, the others join.
- **Gentle to brutal**: five difficulty levels, and a choice of how fair the start is.

Start gently with `curseofwar -i4 -q1 -dee`: the strongest starting position against the easiest opponents.

**Plant your flag. Hold the line.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: move the cursor
- **Space**: add or remove a flag
- **r** or **v**: build a village, then grow it into a town and a fortress (160, 240 and 320 gold)
- **x**: remove all your flags
- **c**: remove half of your flags
- **f** and **s**: speed up and slow down
- **p**: pause
- **q**: quit, after confirming with **y**

Keys are lowercase; with Caps Lock on only **q** works.

Your flags show as a white **P** on the right of a tile, computer flags as
an **x** on the left. Dots and colons on grassland show how many people live
there.

## Options
