- `-W N`, `-H N`: map width and height (default 21)
- `-S rect`, `-S rhombus`, `-S hex`: map shape; hex maps hold six countries
- `-l N`: number of countries
- `-i 0` to `-i 4`: how unequal the starting positions are
- `-q N`: start in the best (1) or a worse position
- `-r`: completely random start
- `-d ee`, `e`, `n`, `h`, `hh`: computer difficulty, easiest to hardest
- `-s sss` to `-s fff`: game speed
- `-R N`: map seed, to replay the same map
- `-T`: show the population timeline
- `-E N`: host a game for N players over the network (UDP port 19140)
- `-C address`: join a hosted game

## History

Alexey Nikolaev released Curse of War in 2013 and developed it in the open
on GitHub, where others contributed fixes until 2021; Debian, Ubuntu and
other distributions have packaged it ever since. It also has an SDL
graphical version, which is not part of this edition.

## Credits

- Game: [Alexey Nikolaev](https://a-nikolaev.github.io/curseofwar/), with contributions from the [curseofwar](https://github.com/a-nikolaev/curseofwar) community
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

cursed-platformer.title: Cursed Pl@tformer
cursed-platformer.description: Rescue the princess from the pharaoh Tutankhascii: jump, ride moving platforms, flip switches and dodge munchers, bats and spikes down into his underground pyramid, then follow his map across the sea to a Maya jungle.
cursed-platformer.provenance: Samsai, Tuubi and Ysblokje made Cursed Pl@tformer in C with curses for the Linux Game Jam 2019, with levels that are plain text files.
cursed-platformer.page:
**THE PHARAOH HAS THE PRINCESS. YOU HAVE AN @.**

The evil pharaoh Tutankhascii has carried a princess off into his underground pyramid, and somebody has to go down after her. That somebody is you: one brave `@`, who enjoys jumping very much and will tell you so.

Cursed Pl@tformer is a classic side-on platformer drawn entirely in text. Run, jump twice your own height, climb, flip switches that open doors somewhere else, ride moving platforms across pits, and keep out of the way of munchers, bats and spikes on the way down.

- **The pharaoh's ten levels**, from Muncher Meadows and the Railway to the Pit of Bats and the Pyramid of Tuthanascii
- **Four more by Ian T. Jacobsen**, quiet and strange, behind EXTENDED on the title screen
- **Then across the sea**: after the pyramid, the pharaoh's map leads to a jungle, along a road in the treetops, down a sacred cenote, through a ball court and up the steps of a Maya pyramid, eight levels more
- **Music and sound**: Kevin MacLeod's "Midnight Tale" and a jump with real spring in it
- **Progress is saved** at every level exit; Continue picks up where you left off
- **Make your own levels**: they are plain text files, a map and its colours

## Controls

- **Left** / **Right**: walk; **Space** or **Up**: jump
- **R**: restart the level; **M**: music on or off; **C**: colours on or off; **Q**: quit
- Gamepad: d-pad or left stick to walk, **A** or d-pad up to jump, **Y** restarts, **Back** quits

Holding an arrow to walk works in a terminal with the kitty keyboard protocol, such as Ghostty, kitty, WezTerm or foot. In other terminals a tap starts walking and the next tap stops.

## Credits

- Cursed Pl@tformer: Samsai, Tuubi and Ysblokje, for the Linux Game Jam 2019
- Extended levels: Ian T. Jacobsen
- Jungle levels: made for the Asciiverse edition
- Music: "Midnight Tale" by Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), CC BY 3.0
- Sound effects: freesound.org users jorickhoofd and javapimp (CC BY), and CC0 sounds
- License: GPL-3.0-only

curses.title: Curses
curses.description: All you wanted was the old tourist map of Paris from the attic. Graham Nelson's long, witty and famously hard puzzle game turns a search of the family house into something much stranger.
curses.provenance: Graham Nelson's Curses (1993) is a landmark of the years after Infocom.
curses.page:
**THAT MAP OF PARIS MUST BE UP HERE SOMEWHERE.**

"It's become a matter of pride now not to give up." It has been five years since your last trip, and the tourist map is lost somewhere in the attics of Meldrew Hall, your family's old house, in among the tea chests and the junk of generations. By the look of it, your great-grandfather was the last person to tidy up. You have a chocolate biscuit, an electric torch with no switch, and a crumpled list of things to do. Number one: find map. Let's face it, it's more enticing than the rest put together.

Then the attic key slips off a glass demijohn and rattles away down a crack in the floorboards, and the search starts turning into something much larger. This family has a history, and a curse to go with it. Aunt Jemima is potting daisies. The house hides ways into other times and places. And you start to wonder whether you are cursed too.

- **Long, witty and famously hard**: a big puzzle game in the grand old style, with a sense of humour all the way through.
- **Literary from the first screen**: lines from Shakespeare and Dorothy Parker turn up as you play.
- **A classic of the form**: Graham Nelson's 1993 game, released as "An Interactive Diversion".

**Find the map. Mind the family curse.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/curses`.

## Credits

- Curses: Graham Nelson, 1993 to 1995
- License: The author's terms: free to distribute and use, provided no profit is involved and the file is unmodified
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

dab.title: Dots and Boxes
dab.description: Draw a line, close a box, go again: dots and boxes against the computer, where one careless line hands over a whole chain. Win and the next board grows, all the way to level 9.
dab.provenance: Christos Zoulas wrote dab, in C++, for NetBSD's games in 2003. Mike Sharov rewrote it in C for his bsd-games in 2016.
dab.page:
**ONE CARELESS LINE CAN COST YOU THE WHOLE BOARD.**

The pencil and paper game from the back of every school notebook, now against the computer. Take turns drawing one line between two neighbouring dots. Draw the fourth side of a box and it's yours, and you must draw again. That's the trap: sooner or later every line gives a box away, and one wrong line can hand your opponent a whole chain of them.

Beat the computer and the next board is one box bigger each way. Lose, and it's over.

- **Nine levels**: from a small board up to level 9. Start higher with `dab 5`.
- **Simple to play**: arrow keys or h j k l to pick a line, Space to draw.
- **Deeper than it looks**: the manual points to Elwyn Berlekamp's book The Dots and Boxes Game, subtitled "Sophisticated Child's Play".

**Count the chains. Draw the line.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **hjkl**: move to a line
- **Space** or **Enter**: draw it
- **q** or **F10**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `dab 5` starts at level 5; levels go from 1 to 9.

## History

Christos Zoulas wrote dab for NetBSD's games in 2003, in C++. Mike
Sharov rewrote it in C for his bsd-games in 2016. For the strategy, its
manual points to Elwyn Berlekamp's book The Dots and Boxes Game.

daggerdeep.title: Dagger Deep
daggerdeep.description: Ten levels down to the undying Lich: a fast, bump-to-fight roguelike for one player, or two in co-op on a local network.
daggerdeep.provenance: Chad Lung wrote Dagger Deep, Return to Dagger Deep on its title screen, in Rust and Ratatui in 2026.
daggerdeep.page:
**THE LICH IS WAITING AT THE BOTTOM.**

Ten levels of rooms and corridors lie between you and the undying Lich, and every one is deeper and meaner than the last. Walk into a monster to fight it. Every blow is a roll of the die, every kill makes you a little tougher for good, and your hit points never reset between floors, so whatever you carry down is all you have.

Goblins, Mages and Rats crowd the first floors. Skeletons guard the last room of the middle levels, Worms soak up blow after blow further down, and from level seven every hit lands harder. On the ninth and tenth the Lich itself may rise: it hits for up to twelve, and when it's nearly beaten it vanishes and turns up somewhere else.

- **Potions** restore you to full the moment you step on one.
- **Chests** hold food that heals the whole party, a trap, or nothing at all. Do you risk it?
- **The stairs** only appear once every monster on the floor is dead.
- **Two players in co-op** on a local network: one hosts, the other joins by address, and you fight through the same dungeon together. Monsters get tougher to match, and each of you gets two respawns.

Reach the stairs on level ten to win. **HOW DEEP CAN YOU GO?**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move; walk into a monster to attack it
- **Esc**: quit, then **Y** or **Enter** to confirm and **N** or **Esc** to keep playing
- **Main menu**: **S** single player, **H** host a co-op game, **J** join one, **Q** quit

## Co-op

Both players on the same local network. The host chooses **Host** and waits for the other player on **TCP port 4444**; the other player chooses **Join** and types in the host's address.

## Credits

- Game: Chad Lung
- Packaged for Asciiverse; licence GPL

darrt.title: Darrt
darrt.description: The whole alphabet is flying around a dartboard: hit a letter's key, judge the drift, and nail it to the bullseye. Dead centre pays a million.
darrt.provenance: abakh wrote Darrt for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018.
darrt.page:
**THE ALPHABET IS LOOSE. NAIL IT TO THE BULLSEYE.**

Twenty-six letters fly around the screen, bouncing off the edges, swooping
over a round target. Press a letter's key and that letter is yours: it
keeps going for a moment, slows, and stops dead wherever it lands. You get
ten shots. Make them count!

The trick is the drift. A letter doesn't stop when you press, it stops a
little later, so you are not aiming at where it is but at where it is
going. Every ring closer to the middle doubles the score, a letter that
misses the target costs you points, and one that stops exactly in the
centre is worth **a million**. Land close and the game says "Very
close..."; land perfect and it says "Bravo!"

- **Ten shots, twenty-six targets**: pick the letter in the best spot, or
  gamble on the one heading for the middle
- **Doubling rings**: every step inwards is worth twice the last
- **A high score list of eleven**: beat the record and the game names the
  champion you just knocked off

Needs an 80 by 24 terminal. **Steady hands. Ten darts. Go.**

## Controls

- **A** to **Z**: stop that letter
- **F1** or **?**: how to play
- **Esc**: end the round; at the end of a round, **n** quits and **y**
  plays again (pressing **Q** a second time in a round also ends it)
- **Ctrl-C**: quit at once

## History

Darrt is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

discworld.title: Discworld MUD
discworld.description: Terry Pratchett's Discworld, over a million rooms, run by volunteers

doctor-m.title: The Life (and Deaths) of Doctor M
doctor-m.description: "We're losing the patient!" A doctor falls through the storm into a windswept nowhere between life and death, where even the signpost cannot decide which way is out.
doctor-m.provenance: Michael D. Hilborn entered The Life (and Deaths) of Doctor M in the 2011 Interactive Fiction Competition, under the name Edmund Wells.
doctor-m.page:
**"WE'RE LOSING THE PATIENT!"**

"Is that such a bad thing?"

"You have an oath!"

"An oath this one never bothered to follow."

Those are the last voices you hear before the clouds take you. Somebody
shouts **"CLEAR!"**, lightning rakes across the sky, and you fall (or
rise?) into the eye of the storm.

You land in an endless meadow of loose shale and gray scrub, under a
funnel of storm clouds that churn in a slow circle overhead. The wind
moans. A wooden signpost leans at an absurd angle, two arrows nailed to
it: **TO HERE** and **TO THERE**. Then the wind howls, and the signpost
spins. Above you, the clouds part on a silent vision: a circle of
paramedics, working frantically over someone you can't quite see.

You are Doctor M. You don't know which way to go. Or, maybe, which way
you went.

- **A surreal afterlife** that bends direction, time and memory, from
  Michael D. Hilborn's entry to the 2011 Interactive Fiction Competition
- **Real conversations**: the people you meet are talked to through a
  conversation system of topics and replies, so type ABOUT and
  CONVERSATION when you start
- **Built-in hints** in the ABOUT menu, if the storm gets the better of
  you

**An Interactive Deliverance. Which way will you go?**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/doctor-m`.

## Credits

- The Life (and Deaths) of Doctor M: Michael D. Hilborn, 2011
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs 3.0
- Played with Glulxe and GlkTerm by Andrew Plotkin (MIT)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

dominos.title: Dominos
dominos.description: Clack! Ivory tiles on green baize: the Block game, the Draw game and All Fives, against a sly computer or your friends round the table on the local network.
dominos.provenance: Asciiverse made Dominos in Rust in 2026. Rules after pagat.com's Block, Draw and All Fives.
dominos.page:
**IVORY TILES. GREEN BAIZE. CLACK!**

Pull up a chair. Three games, two to four players, and nobody minds if you count on your fingers.

- **The Block game**: the purest one. Match an open end or pass; the first to go out, or the lowest hand when everyone is stuck, takes everyone else's pips.
- **The Draw game**: the same, with a boneyard to draw from whenever you like, even when you could play, until only two tiles are left there. More tiles, more choices, more pips to be caught holding.
- **All Fives**: the first double becomes the spinner and the line grows four arms. Every time the open ends add up to a multiple of five, you score on the spot. First to 200 wins, the moment it's reached.

Play the computer, or open a table on the local network: your friends find it by themselves, take the open seats, and the computer fills the rest. At four, play partners, sitting opposite and scoring as a side. Everyone only ever sees their own hand, so no peeking.

The computer comes in three strengths, and in All Fives the hard one is sly: it remembers which numbers you couldn't play, and leaves you ends you can't match. **SHUFFLE UP.**

## Controls

- **← →** or **h l**: choose a tile from your hand, or click it
- **Enter** or **Space**: play it; where it fits two ways, **← →** choose the end
- **D**: draw from the boneyard
- **?** or **F1**: the rules of the game you are playing
- **Q** or **Esc**: back to the menu

## Options

- `--rules block|draw|fives`: the game the menu starts on
- `--demo`: the computer plays every seat
- `--seed N`: the same deal again

news.notes:
- The Block game, the Draw game and All Fives, chosen on the menu
- Two to four players, partners at four (sitting opposite)
- The computer at three strengths
- Local network play: the host runs the game, tables found by LAN
  broadcast or a typed address, empty seats filled by the computer, the
  host moves players between seats
- Keys and mouse, help (F1 or ?), `--demo`

dopewars.title: dopewars
dopewars.description: You owe the Loan Shark $5,500 and it grows every day. Buy low, sell high, outrun Officer Hardass across New York, and get out rich in a month, alone or against other dealers online.
dopewars.provenance: Ben Webb has written and maintained dopewars since 1998, after John E. Dell's MS-DOS game Drug Wars.
dopewars.page:
**YOU OWE THE LOAN SHARK $5,500. YOU HAVE ONE MONTH.**

You start in the Bronx with $2,000 in your pocket, a coat with room
for 100 units, and a debt that gets bigger every single day. The streets
of New York are your stock exchange. Buy where it's cheap, take the subway
to Manhattan, Brooklyn, Coney Island or Staten Island, and sell where it's
dear. Then do it again. Faster.

The market never sits still. "The Marrakesh Express has arrived!" and
hashish is dirt cheap. "Cops made a big bust! Prices are outrageous!" and
you'd better be holding. Officer Hardass and his deputies are on your
tail, the bank, the gun shop and a bigger coat all cost money you haven't
made yet, and the lady next to you on the subway has opinions: "Does your
mother know you're a dope dealer?"

- **The classic trading game**: eight boroughs and neighbourhoods, a
  dozen goods, prices that crash and spike on the news from the street
- **Run or fight**: when the cops catch up, flee, or shoot it out if you
  bought a gun
- **Deal against real people**: connect to a dopewars server, pick one
  from the public server list, or run your own; trade with other dealers,
  page them, or tip off the cops about them
- **Antique mode**: play it as close to John E. Dell's original Drug Wars
  as it gets

**Pay off the shark. Get rich. Don't get caught.**

## Controls

Each screen tells you which keys it takes. In the market:

- **b**: buy, **s**: sell
- **j**: jet to another part of town
- **l**: list players or high scores
- **g**: give money or drugs to another player (online)
- **q**: quit

When the cops catch up with you, **r** runs and **f** fights, if you have a
gun.

## Options

- `-n`: single player, without the server menu
- `-o host`: connect to a dopewars server, `-p port` (default 7902)
- `-s`: run a public server, `-S` a private one
- `-c`: add a computer player to a server
- `-a`: "antique" mode, as close to the original Drug Wars as possible
- `-P name`: your dealer's name
- `-b`: no colours

High scores are kept in `~/.local/state/dopewars.sco`.

## History

John E. Dell's Drug Wars was an MS-DOS game; Ben Webb rewrote it as
dopewars for Unix and Windows from 1998, adding networked multiplayer, a
metaserver listing public servers, and a configurable everything.

The Asciiverse edition is the text-mode client and server only, with two
small changes: high scores
go in your own state folder, and the static build finds your system's
certificates to reach the metaserver.

## Credits

- Original game: John E. Dell (Drug Wars)
- dopewars: [Ben Webb](https://dopewars.sourceforge.io/) and contributors
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

drl.title: DRL
drl.description: A fast, tactical roguelike: fight your way from a Martian moon base down into hell with shotguns, chainsaws and rocket launchers, and build your marine from traits and master traits.
drl.provenance: Kornel Kisielewicz started DRL in 2002 as a fan roguelike, later developed by his studio ChaosForge, which still works on it.
drl.page:
**THE ONLY WAY OUT IS DOWN.**

Something has gone very wrong on the Phobos base. The comm is full of screams, then gunshots, then silence. You are the marine they send in, with a pistol and a bad feeling, and the only way out is down: through the moon bases, through the gates, and into hell itself.

DRL is a fast, tactical roguelike. Every level is new, every death is final, and every fight is a question of where you stand: behind a barrel, next to a door, or far out of reach of whatever is coming around the corner. Pick up shotguns, chainguns, plasma rifles and rocket launchers, and modify them. Grow your marine with traits as you gain levels, and work towards a master trait that changes how you play.

- **Three classes**: Marine, Scout and Technician
- **Five difficulty levels**, from *I'm Too Young To Die!* to *Nightmare!*
- **Challenge games** that change the rules, and seeded games
- **Assemblies**: combine mods into unique weapons and armour

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or the number pad: move (Home, End, PgUp, PgDn diagonally)
- **Esc**: menu, help and Save & Quit
- In menus: **Up**, **Down** and **Enter**

Your settings, saves and scores are kept in `~/.local/share/drl`.

## Credits

- DRL: Kornel Kisielewicz (ChaosForge)
- Additional coding: tehtmi, Game Hunter, shark20061, add and brisbang
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-only

drop4.title: Drop4
drop4.description: The shapes keep falling and the well keeps filling: turn them, slide them, pack every row tight before the stack hits the top.
drop4.provenance: Drop4 is BSD's tetris, which Chris Torek and Darren F. Provine adapted from a 1989 International Obfuscated C Code Contest winner (UC Berkeley, 1992). Mike Sharov renamed it and changed its look in 2016 for his bsd-games.

upstream.name: Chris Torek and Darren F. Provine (1992), Mike Sharov

drop4.page:
**THE SHAPES KEEP FALLING. DON'T LET THEM REACH THE TOP.**

Four squares at a time, the shapes drop into the well. Slide them, spin
them, slot them into the gaps: fill a row from wall to wall and it
vanishes, and everything above it crashes down a line. Leave a hole and
it haunts you. Let the stack reach the top and it's over.

It only gets faster. Every level the shapes fall harder, at level nine
they come down nine squares a second, and the bravest players drop each
shape the moment it's lined up, because every square it falls on your
command is a point in your pocket. Your final score is multiplied by the
level you reached.

- **The next shape, shown in advance**: plan two moves ahead
- **Drop early, score more**: points for every row a shape falls when you
  send it down
- **Start where you dare**: pick a level from 1 to 9, or press **>** to
  speed up mid-game
- **A high score table** ranking every player by points and level

**One more row. Just one more.**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**, or **j** and **l**: move
- **Up** or **k**: turn a quarter counterclockwise
- **Space** or **Down**: drop
- **>**: go faster
- **p**: pause
- **q**, **F10** or **End**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `drop4 5` starts at level 5. Levels go from 1 to
9; at level n the shapes fall n times a second.

## History

This is BSD's tetris, which Chris Torek and Darren F. Provine adapted
from a winning 1989 entry to the International Obfuscated C Code
Contest (UC Berkeley, 1992); Hubert Feyrer added the preview of the next shape in 1999. In
2016 Mike Sharov renamed it Drop4 for his bsd-games and changed its
look: a wider well, no animation when rows clear, and the score and
next shape on the right. The high score table is kept per player.

dunemud.title: Dune MUD
dunemud.description: LPMud set in Frank Herbert's Dune universe, with ten guilds and over 30,000 rooms

durismud.title: DurisMUD
durismud.description: Full-loot PvP fantasy MUD where good and evil races fight an endless racewar

durthang.title: Durthang
durthang.description: A MUD client named for an orc-hold in Mordor: your worlds and characters in one list, passwords in the system keyring, and an automap that draws itself as you explore.
durthang.provenance: Durthang is Raimo Geisel's MUD client in Rust.
durthang.page:
**THE MUDS ARE STILL OUT THERE. WALK BACK IN.**

*"...stood the old castle of Durthang, now one of the many orc-holds that
clustered about the dale of Udûn."* Raimo Geisel named his MUD client
after a fortress in Tolkien's Mordor, and built it to be one: a single
terminal program that keeps every world you play and every character you
play there in one list. Pick one, press Enter, and you are through the
gate.

Inside, it does the chores so you can play. The map draws itself as you
walk, from the server's room data or from the "Exits:" lines it reads.
Your passwords go into your system's keyring, never into a config file.
Notes for each character sit right beside the action.

- **Automap**: a live ASCII map with you at the **@**, saved per server
- **Aliases and triggers**: type `k orc` for `kill orc`; highlight a line
  or answer it automatically when a pattern matches
- **Safe logins**: passwords in the Keychain, Credential Manager or Secret
  Service, never on disk in plain text
- **Plain TCP or TLS**, 16 and 256 colours, a 5,000 line scrollback,
  command history and copy mode
- **Sidebar** with the automap and a notes panel, toggled with **F3**

**Your characters are waiting. Reconnect.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move through servers and characters
- **Space**: expand or collapse a server
- **N**: add a server; **n**: add a character
- **Enter**: connect with the selected character
- **Ctrl+Q**: disconnect, back to the list
- **q**: quit

## Credits

- Durthang: [Raimo Geisel](https://github.com/Pommersche92/durthang)
- Asciiverse edition: packaging, and keyring stores for macOS and Windows
- License: GPL-3.0-only

entity.title: Entity
entity.description: N-inspired precision platformer: momentum, wall jumps, gold, mines, instant death
entity.provenance: Asciiverse made Entity in Rust in 2026 inspired by N (Metanet Software). It ports N's physics and object types and has a campaign of 100 levels of its own.
entity.page:
**ONE NINJA. ONE HUNDRED ROOMS. ONE SECOND IS A LONG TIME.**

Run, jump and wall-jump through rooms full of mines, drones, lasers,
turrets, thwomps and homing rockets. Touch the switch, the door opens,
reach it. Gold buys you time, and every five levels share one clock.
Death is instant, and so is the next try.

## The campaign

- 100 levels in twenty episodes of five, each episode teaching one thing
  before it mixes them: jumps and slopes, doors and keys, mines, launch
  pads and bounce blocks, drones, thwomps, lasers, turrets, rockets and
  chainguns, one-way gates, then everything at once
- N's momentum, wall jumps and wall slides, and its rule that only a hard
  landing kills
- The whole room on one screen, filling the terminal, the ninja drawn in
  Braille dots
- A level editor and a route bot that finds a way through your own levels

## Controls

- Arrows, WASD or HJKL to run; Up, W, Space or Z to jump, held for height
- Down or S to stop, R to try again, N and P for the next and previous level
- Esc asks before you quit
- Gamepad: d-pad or stick to run, A or B to jump, Y to try again, A, B or
  Start for the next level

Best in a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, foot, Ghostty,
Alacritty), or with a gamepad.

evilhack.title: EvilHack
evilhack.description: A much harder NetHack: tougher, smarter monsters that use your tricks against you, new races, roles, items and artifacts, and the Amulet of Yendor at the bottom of it all.
evilhack.provenance: Keith Simpson (k21971) began EvilHack in October 2018 as a much harder NetHack 3.6 variant, drawing on GruntHack, SporkHack and others; it opened for public play on the Hardfought servers in April 2019, and he still develops it.
evilhack.page:
**NETHACK, BUT EVERYTHING IS OUT TO GET YOU.**

You know NetHack. You know about Elbereth, about praying when you are low, about the soldier ants. EvilHack knows you know. Its monsters have more hit points, fight in packs, wear the armour they find and zap the wands they pick up. Things that were safe are not safe any more.

EvilHack is a NetHack 3.6 variant built to be very hard and still fair. It borrows the best of GruntHack, SporkHack, UnNetHack, xNetHack and others, and adds plenty of its own: new races such as centaurs, giants, illithids and tortles, new roles, new artifacts and item properties, player-made forges and much more. Winning is possible. It is just a long way down.

- **Tougher, smarter monsters** that use items and fight together
- **New races and roles**, and a reworked balance for the old ones
- **New items, artifacts, materials and object properties**
- **The full NetHack dungeon**, with new branches and changes on the way down

## Controls

- **h j k l y u b n**: move (shift to run); **.** wait; **s** search
- **i** inventory; **,** pick up; **w** wield; **W** wear; **q** quaff; **r** read
- **<** / **>**: stairs; **#**: extended commands; **?**: help
- **S** saves and quits; **#quit** gives up (type the whole word *yes*)

Your saves, scores and dumplogs are kept in `~/.local/share/evilhack`; your options go in `~/.evilhackrc`.

## Credits

- EvilHack: Keith Simpson (k21971), with code from many NetHack variants
- NetHack: the NetHack DevTeam, Stichting Mathematisch Centrum and M. Stephenson
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: NetHack General Public License (NGPL)

fate.title: Fate
fate.description: Nine months pregnant, Queen in name only, you see your son's death in a crystal ball. You have until the waters break to change his fate, whatever it costs.
fate.provenance: Victor Gijsbers entered Fate in Spring Thing 2007.
fate.page:
**YOUR SON IS NOT YET BORN. YOU HAVE ALREADY SEEN HOW HE DIES.**

You are nine months pregnant, and the contractions have already begun.
You are Queen in name but not in influence, trapped in a castle with more
enemies than friends, and at last your spells have worked: the crystal
ball in your den shows what waits for your child. Writhing lines of black
and purple, and then an image. It is not good.

The crown prince, Harold, wants no rival. His knight Sir Charles has
moved onto the couch in your parlour. Old Mebeira keeps her tower room
full of skulls and powders, and real power. And in a golden cage hangs
Amalia, your pixie, whose wings are worth a great deal to a sorcerer. You
can WAIT in your den for fate to arrive. Or you can act, with speed and
determination, and do what is necessary before the waters break.

- **Every move changes the vision**: look into the ball again and the
  future has shifted, toward banishment, ruin, glory or a quiet life
  far from the power games of kings
- **How far will you go?** The game asks it of you, and keeps the score
  in what you are willing to do, not in points
- **Victor Gijsbers' dark little fable**, first released in 2007, short
  enough for one evening and built to be replayed

*"The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, but in ourselves."*

**The waters will break soon. What will you do?**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/fate`.

## Credits

- Fate: Victor Gijsbers, 2007
- License: GNU GPL version 2 or later; the source (Fate-source.zip) is in the archive
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

fifteen.title: Fifteen
fifteen.description: The fifteen puzzle, shuffled: slide whole rows and columns at once, watch the tiles turn green, and put it all back in order. Then try it on a seven by seven.
fifteen.provenance: abakh wrote Fifteen for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018.
fifteen.page:
**FIFTEEN TILES. ONE GAP. PUT IT BACK THE WAY IT WAS.**

The oldest sliding puzzle there is, and still the one that eats an
afternoon. Fifteen tiles sit in a four by four frame, shuffled, with a
single empty space. Slide them back into order, 1 to 9 and then a to f,
with the gap in the bottom right corner. Sounds easy. It's the last three
tiles that get you.

Every tile turns green the moment it is in its right place, so you can
see your progress, and watch it come undone as you move one out of the
way to get another in. Put the cursor on any tile in line with the gap
and press Enter, and the whole line shifts in one move. Or just click.

- **Whole lines at once**: slide a full row or column toward the gap in
  one go
- **Keyboard or mouse**: arrow keys, hjkl, wasd, or a click on the tile
- **Bigger boards**: from three by three up to seven by seven, for
  forty-eight tiles of misery

**"You solved it!" Can you get it to say so?**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move the cursor
- **Enter**: slide
- **Mouse**: click a tile to slide it
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, Fifteen takes the size of the board, from 3 to 7:

- `fifteen -s 5`: a five by five board; past 9 the tiles carry letters,
  lower case and then upper case
- `-n`: do not ask to play again after a solved board

## History

Fifteen is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

firework-rs.title: Fireworks
firework-rs.description: New Year's Eve, any night you like: an endless fireworks show in coloured ASCII, bursts blooming all over the window and sparks drooping as they fade.
firework-rs.provenance: Fireworks is the demo of firework-rs, a Rust crate for ASCII-art fireworks by Wayoung7, from 2024.
firework-rs.page:
**THE SHOW NEVER ENDS. TURN OUT THE LIGHTS.**

Bang. A burst of sparks blooms in the corner of your terminal, sparks
arcing out, slowing, drooping under their own weight and fading as they
fall. Then another, over there. Then three at once. It never stops, and
it never repeats: every firework picks its own spot, its own moment and
its own palette, and a bigger window gets a bigger show.

Wayoung7 built firework-rs as a little particle engine in Rust, with real
gravity and air resistance on every spark, and the colours are hand-picked:
reds and golds, deep sea greens, ice blues, pastel pinks and lilacs, eight
palettes in all.

- **Endless and random**: no two minutes alike, as long as you leave it
  running
- **Fills any window**: from a corner of the screen to a wall-sized
  terminal, the number of bursts grows with the space
- **Five designed shows** too, from the command line, and a colour fade
  for black backgrounds

**Pour a drink. Press any key when the party's over.**

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `firework -d 0` to `firework -d 4` play five designed
shows (add `-l` to loop one), `-g` fades the sparks through a colour
gradient (best on a black background), `--fps` sets the frame rate from 5
to 30, and `--cjk` suits fonts with wide characters.

## Credits

- firework-rs: [Wayoung7](https://github.com/Wayoung7/firework-rs), the
  crate and its `firework` demo
- Asciiverse edition: any key quits
- License: MIT

fisher.title: Fisher
fisher.description: Drop your line through ten rows of sea, past the plastic bags, down to the tuna worth 100 points, and don't let anything swim into your line on the way.
fisher.provenance: abakh wrote Fisher for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018, as a port of Deep Sea Fisher, a MikeOS game.
fisher.page:
**THE TUNA IS AT THE BOTTOM. SO IS EVERYTHING ELSE.**

Your boat bobs on the surface. Below it, ten rows of sea, and something
swims along every one of them. Drop
your hook to a row, wait for the swimmer to reach your line, and reel it
in. "A tuna!" Now we're talking.

The catch is the depth. Up top it's plastic bags and PVC bottles, worth a
point or so; then face masks, shrimp, algae, jellyfish, molluscs, "Actual
fish!", salmon, and right at the bottom, the tuna, worth a hundred. But
the deeper your hook goes, the more line hangs in the water, and anything
that swims into the line above your hook takes the hook with it. You
have ten. When they're gone, so are you.

- **Ten rows, ten catches**: every row deeper is worth more, from 1 point
  to 100
- **Ten hooks**: lose one to every swimmer that crosses your line
- **Two-key controls**: down to drop, up to reel in
- **A high score list**, and a big "CONGRATULATIONS!!" when you beat
  the record

**Cast off. How deep do you dare?**

## Controls

- **Down arrow** or **s**: lower the hook
- **Up arrow** or **w**: raise the hook, and reel in a catch
- **F1** or **?**: help
- **q** or **Esc**: end the game; it shows the high scores and asks whether to play again

## History

Fisher is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
It is a port of "Deep Sea Fisher", a MikeOS game. The collection is
packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and
pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

fortress-earth.title: Fortress Earth
fortress-earth.description: The sky opens over a great city, then another, then another. Ten armies, twelve cities, one world slowly turning red. Your move, Commander.
fortress-earth.provenance: Filip Hracek wrote Fortress Earth in Dart between 2019 and 2025 as a keyboard-only strategy tech demo for the browser: armies that spread over a map of the Earth like a cellular automaton.
fortress-earth.page:
The first one comes down twenty days in. Nobody knows what they are. HQ
calls them the Arrivals, which is the polite word for it.

They land near the great cities and spill out across the land, red and
hungry, tile by tile. You have ten armies (Marines, Infantry, a couple of
Squads, the Air Force and HQ itself) and a map of the whole planet that
breathes. Throw them at Cairo. Hold Paris tight. Turn the Air Force loose
and let it hunt.

Every patch of ground is fought over. Your units pour into the gaps like
water, the enemy shoves back wherever it is strong, and the world goes
white or red one tile at a time. Your armies can fly; the war on the
ground stops at the shoreline.

Ten landings are coming, each one sooner than the last. Smash a landing
site outright, or ring it in once it runs dry and let it starve. Lose six
cities at once, or every last army, and that's it: Earth has fallen.

Your generals will keep you posted. Mostly with bad news.

## Controls

- **0** to **9**: pick an army, then:
  - **G** and a city's letter: go there
  - **T**: hold tight around the city
  - **E**: spread out further
  - **D**: go after the enemy anywhere
- **Space**: pause
- **F1**, **?** or **H**: how to play
- **Q** or **Esc**: leave (it asks first), **Ctrl+C**: leave at once

Fortress Earth shows the whole world at once and needs a terminal of at
least 186 columns by 55 rows: a big window, or a smaller font.

## Options

- `--demo`: watch the computer fight the war

## Credits

- Fortress Earth: Filip Hracek
  ([github.com/filiph/fortress-earth](https://github.com/filiph/fortress-earth)),
  2019 to 2025, written in Dart with Bob Nystrom's malison and piecemeal;
  the armies' simulation is his
- Map: Natural Earth (public domain)
- Asciiverse edition: the war around his simulation (landings, cities,
  sieges, reports, victory and defeat), the help screen, the map redrawn
  for terminal cells, and the terminal build
- License: MIT

fox-and-geese.title: Fox and Geese
fox-and-geese.description: One fox, a whole gaggle of geese, and a cross-shaped board: the medieval hunt game, as R. C. Bell gives it
fox-and-geese.provenance: Asciiverse made Fox and Geese in Rust in 2026. The rules are R. C. Bell's (1960), with thirteen or seventeen geese.
fox-and-geese.page:
**ONE FOX. A WHOLE GAGGLE OF GEESE. SOMEBODY GETS EATEN.**

One fox, thirteen geese (or seventeen, if you like a crowd), and a board shaped like a plus sign.

The fox jumps geese like a draughts piece and takes them off the board, several in one move if they're careless. The geese can't take anything at all. All they can do is waddle, one step at a time, and close in until the fox has nowhere left to go.

Play the fox and it's a hunt: find the gap, wait for the slip, pick the gaggle apart. Play the geese and it's a siege: hold the line, never leave a goose with an empty point behind it, and squeeze. Thin the gaggle down to three and the fox wins, because three can never trap him. Hover a landing point and every goose the jump would eat turns red.

Hunt games like this are old in the north: a medieval saga mentions one, and an English king's household bought silver-gilt foxes and hounds for one in the 1460s.

- **Thirteen geese**: the older form; geese step any way along a line, and Bell swears that geese played right must win
- **Seventeen geese**: four more geese, but none may ever step back; wedge them in and the fox wins anyway

Play the computer at three strengths, as fox or geese, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Arrows**: move the cursor
- **Enter**: pick up a piece, then put it down on a lit point; **Esc**: drop it
- **Mouse**: click a piece, then a point
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same game every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

freedoom.title: Freedoom
freedoom.description: The 1993 first-person shooter's engine in your terminal, in full colour, with music and sound, playing Freedoom's two free games: fight through bases and hells with shotgun and chaingun.
freedoom.provenance: id Software released the source of its 1993 engine in 1997; Chocolate Doom and doomgeneric carried it on, and Wojciech Graj brought it to the terminal in 2022. The Freedoom project has made free levels, monsters, sounds and music for it since 2001.

developer.name: The Freedoom project and Wojciech Graj

freedoom.page:
**THE ENGINE THAT DEFINED THE FIRST-PERSON SHOOTER, IN YOUR TERMINAL.**

The engine of the 1993 first-person shooter runs in your terminal: the real thing, with its doors, lifts, secrets and monsters, drawn in full colour two pixels to a character, and with its music and sound effects. It plays **Freedoom**, a complete free replacement for the original game's levels, monsters, sounds and music, so there is nothing else to buy or find.

Two games come with it:

- **Freedoom: Phase 1**: four episodes in the style of the original
- **Freedoom: Phase 2**: one long campaign of 32 levels, with the double-barrelled shotgun

The bigger your terminal window, the sharper the picture. It plays best in a terminal that reports key releases, such as Ghostty, kitty, WezTerm or foot: movement is then exact, and Ctrl, Shift and Alt work as fire, run and strafe.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move and turn
- **,** and **.**: strafe left and right
- **Space**: fire; **E**: use doors and switches; **]**: run
- **1** to **7**: weapons; **Tab**: map
- **Esc**: menu, to load, save and quit
- Gamepad, on Linux: left stick to move and strafe, right stick to turn,
  **RT** fires, **LT** runs, **A** uses doors and switches, **LB** and
  **RB** change weapons, **Back** shows the map, **Start** opens the menu;
  in menus the d-pad or stick moves, **A** chooses and **B** goes back.
  A game saved from the pad is named after its level

## Options

- `-iwad freedoom2.wad`: play Phase 2
- `-skill 1` to `-skill 5`, `-warp E M` (or `-warp M` in Phase 2): start where you like
- `-nosound`, `-nomusic`: play quietly
- `-chars ascii`, `-chars block` or `-chars braille`: the engine's other looks

Settings and saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/freedoom`, where `.default.cfg` holds the key bindings.

## History

id Software released its engine's source in 1997. Chocolate Doom keeps it faithful to the original, doomgeneric made it easy to port, and Wojciech Graj brought it to the terminal. This edition adds the sound effects and the music, played through an emulated OPL synthesiser as a 1990s sound card would, exact key releases, gamepads, and the half-block picture.

## Credits

- Engine: Wojciech Graj, after id Software, Chocolate Doom (Simon Howard and contributors) and doomgeneric (ozkl)
- OPL3 emulation: Nuked OPL3, Alexey Khokholov
- Freedoom: the Freedoom project
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later (the engine), BSD-3-Clause (Freedoom)

frobtads.title: FrobTADS
frobtads.description: Plays TADS 2 and TADS 3 text adventures in your terminal, from the 1990s classics to I Am Prey. Give it a story file and go.
frobtads.provenance: FrobTADS is Nikos Chantziaras' terminal player for TADS, the adventure system by Michael J. Roberts.
frobtads.page:
**TADS STORIES, STRAIGHT FROM YOUR COMMAND LINE.**

FrobTADS plays text adventures written with TADS, Michael J. Roberts'
Text Adventure Development System. TADS 2 games (.gam) and TADS 3 games
(.t3) both run, from the 1990s classics to modern stories such as I Am
Prey, where something hungry is hunting you through a sealed facility.
Status line, colours and scroll-back come along. Give it a story file
and play.

## Use

- `frob <story file>`: play a story (.gam and .t3 files)
- `frob -d <story file>`: the same, keeping saved games in the current
  folder instead of the story's
- `save` and `restore` inside a story keep your place
- At `[More]`, Space shows the next page and Enter the next line

In Asciiverse, story titles such as I Am Prey come with FrobTADS built in,
so you only need this to play story files of your own.

## Credits

- FrobTADS: Nikos Chantziaras; TADS: Michael J. Roberts
- Asciiverse edition: static builds and packaging, two small fixes
  (builds without libcurl; `-d` keeps TADS 3 saves in the current folder)
- License: TADS Freeware Source Code License; free to share, never sold

frotz.title: Frotz
frotz.description: Plays the Z-machine, Infocom's imaginary computer: Zork and the rest of Infocom's catalogue, and the Inform stories written for it since.
frotz.provenance: Stefan Jokisch wrote Frotz, a player for Infocom's Z-machine games; David Griffith and contributors maintain it.
frotz.page:
**THE COMPUTER THAT NEVER EXISTED, STILL RUNNING.**

Infocom wrote its games for "an imaginary computer of their own design
called the Z-Machine", so they could run anywhere a small interpreter
could. Frotz is that interpreter. It plays Infocom's own catalogue, Zork
among them, and the stories written for the Z-machine since in Inform.
Give it a story file and play.

## Use

- `frotz <story file>`: play a story (.z3, .z5, .z8 and Blorb files)
- `save` and `restore` inside a story keep your place

In Asciiverse, story titles such as Zork come with Frotz built in, so you
only need this to play story files of your own.

## Credits

- Frotz: David Griffith and contributors, after Stefan Jokisch's original
- Asciiverse edition: static builds and packaging, and one fix (a heap overread when guessing a story's Blorb file name)
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

froxcomposband.title: FroxComposband
froxcomposband.description: The great kitchen-sink Angband variant: dozens of races and classes, monster races you can play as, a wilderness above the dungeons and a deep descent to Serpent, carried on with fixes and loads of polish.
froxcomposband.provenance: sulkasormi made FrogComposband in 2018 from PosChengband, itself grown from Hengband, Zangband and Angband; in 2026 Gliktch forked it as FroxComposband to keep it going.
froxcomposband.page:
**EVERY RACE. EVERY CLASS. EVERY MONSTER. ONE DUNGEON TOO FEW.**

FroxComposband is the Angband family's great everything-included variant. Pick from dozens of races, among them monster races you play as a dragon, a vampire or a beholder would, and from classes from warrior and mage to necromancer, mystic and possessor. Walk out of town across a wilderness, take on the dungeons and the guardians at their bottoms, and go as deep as you dare.

It plays like Angband: turn-based, a single life, a level made new every time you take the stairs, and more items, spells and monsters than you will ever see in one game. FroxComposband carries FrogComposband on with many fixes and quality-of-life improvements, and loads Frog saves.

- **Dozens of races and classes**, including playable monster races
- **A wilderness and many dungeons**, each with its own boss
- **Beginner mode** for a gentler start
- **Huge variety**: artifacts, egos, spells, pets and more

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or the number pad: move and attack; **`**: travel
- **g**: pick up; **i**: inventory; **w**: wield; **q**: quaff; **r**: read
- **<** / **>**: stairs; **?**: help, with every command
- **Ctrl-X**: save and quit

Your saves and scores are kept in `~/.local/share/FroxComposband`.

## Credits

- FroxComposband: Gliktch
- FrogComposband: sulkasormi; before it PosChengband, Hengband, Zangband, Angband, and Moria by Robert Alan Koeneke
- License: the Moria/Angband licence, free to share, not for profit

galaxis.title: Galaxis
galaxis.description: Four lifeboats adrift, the passengers' air running out, and nothing to find them with but probes that count what they can see. Find all four in as few tries as you can.
galaxis.provenance: Eric S. Raymond began Galaxis in 1994 as a curses clone of Christian Franz's Macintosh freeware game, and still maintains it.
galaxis.page:
**FOUR LIFEBOATS. ONE STARFIELD. THE AIR IS RUNNING OUT.**

A crippled interstellar liner has cast four lifeboats adrift in a
starfield of 20 by 9 squares, and you can't see a single one of them.
What you can do is drop probes. Each probe looks out along all eight
compass directions and tells you in how many of them it sees a lifeboat
(only the nearest boat in each direction counts). Land a probe right on
a boat and the screen says it plainly: "You found a lifeboat!"

Your orders, straight from the rules: find them "as quickly as possible,
before the stranded passengers run out of oxygen!" Every probe is a try,
and the tries are counted.

- **Pure deduction**: once the boats are placed there is no luck left,
  only counts, crossing rays and the squares they rule out.
- **See where it looks**: the eight rays from the cursor are highlighted,
  so you know exactly which squares a probe would search.
- **It does the bookkeeping**: mark the squares you've ruled out, and once
  every boat a probe counted has turned up, the rest of its rays are
  marked for you. Asking an old probe again can mark more, and costs no
  try.
- **Keys or mouse**: arrows, vi keys or the number pad, or click to mark
  and double-click to probe.

Christian Franz made Galaxis as Macintosh freeware; Eric S. Raymond
cloned it for curses in 1994 and still maintains it. His version, he
says, "compensates by automating away some of the game's simpler
deductions."

**Drop a probe. Read the count. Bring them home.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **h j k l y u b n** or the **number pad**: move (the
  field wraps round)
- **p**: drop a probe, or ask an old probe again
- **Space**: mark a square as empty, or unmark it
- **o**: turn the ray highlighting off or on
- **Mouse**: click to mark, double-click to drop a probe
- **?**: the rules; **q**: give up and see where the boats were

## Credits

- Galaxis: Eric S. Raymond ([gitlab.com/esr/galaxis](https://gitlab.com/esr/galaxis)),
  1994 on, written in C with curses
- After Christian Franz's freeware Galaxis for the Macintosh
- License: BSD-2-Clause

gearhead-2.title: GearHead 2
gearhead-2.description: A roguelike mecha RPG: make a pilot, take jobs among the space colonies, buy and build giant robots, and follow a story the game writes for your character as you go.
gearhead-2.provenance: Joseph Hewitt made GearHead 2, the sequel to his GearHead: Arena, in Free Pascal; it was first released in 2005, and 0.701 came out in 2017.
gearhead-2.page:
**PILOT. MERCENARY. HERO, IF YOU LIVE THAT LONG.**

You start with a pilot, a little money and a home in the space colonies, where spinning habitats each have their own laws, factions and feuds. Talk to people, take jobs at the clubhouse, buy a mecha and go out to fight in it. Every character gets a story of their own, built by the game from your choices and the people you meet, so no two campaigns run the same way.

GearHead 2 is the sequel to GearHead: Arena, and the more ambitious game: more mecha, more factions, a world map to cross between cities, romance, lancemates who fight beside you, and quests that grow into a campaign-long plot.

- **Mecha by the dozen**: buy, repair and customise giant robots, part by part
- **On foot or in the cockpit**: fight hand to hand in town or in mecha out in the field
- **A story every time**: plots and quests generated for your character
- **Deep characters**: stats, skills, talents, relationships and reputations

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **1 to 9** on the number keys: move, diagonals with **Home**, **PgUp**, **End**, **PgDn** or **7 9 1 3**
- **t**: talk; **a**: attack; **A**: the attack menu; **l**: look
- **i**: inventory; **e**: equipment; **,**: pick up
- **u**: use something nearby; **s**: use a skill; **S**: search
- **>** or **<**: go through an entrance
- **M**: choose your mecha; **H**: field HQ; **C**: character info
- **m**: memos, email and news; **V**: past messages; **Z**: rest an hour
- **h**: help; **X**: save; **Q**: save and return to the title menu

## Options

- `SCREENWIDTH` and `SCREENHEIGHT` in `~/.config/gearhead2/gearhead2.cfg`: a larger screen

## History

Joseph Hewitt released the first GearHead 2 in 2005, a few years after GearHead: Arena, and kept building it into the 2010s; 0.701 came out in 2017. It runs in a graphical window or as ASCII in a terminal. This edition is the ASCII version, with one fix so a first start always finds a place for its settings and saves.

## Credits

- GearHead 2: [Joseph Hewitt](https://github.com/jwvhewitt/gearhead-2)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: LGPL-2.1-or-later

gearhead-arena.title: GearHead: Arena
gearhead-arena.description: The first roguelike mecha RPG. Make a pilot, wander a world of random adventures, talk your way into jobs and fight on foot or in giant robots you build and repair yourself.
gearhead-arena.provenance: Joseph Hewitt released GearHead: Arena in Free Pascal in 2002 and kept developing it for years; it moved to GitHub, where contributors still send fixes.
gearhead-arena.page:
**GIANT ROBOTS. A WHOLE WORLD. NO TWO STORIES THE SAME.**

You are a pilot in the GearHead universe. Make a character, pick a background, and set out from a small town with some money in your pocket. Talk to people: they have jobs, rumours and grudges. Buy a mecha, fit it out, and take it into the arena or out into the wilderness. Every campaign strings together randomly generated plots, so the story is yours alone.

It was the first roguelike mecha RPG, and it is deep: eight stats, thirty skills, mecha built part by part, called shots, and fighting on foot or in a mecha.

- **A world of random adventures**: towns, jobs, rivals and plots that change every campaign
- **Build your mecha**: frames, armour, weapons and systems, repaired and refitted in the field
- **Talk your way through**: every NPC has a job, a rumour or a reason to like or hate you
- **Arena mode**: run a mecha team and fight battle after battle

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or the **number pad**: walk in eight directions; **5** waits
- **t**: talk to someone; **a**: attack; **A**: the attack menu
- **i** / **e**: inventory and equipment; **,**: pick up
- **u**: use a door, computer or other scenery; **>** or **<**: stairs and portals
- **l**: look around; **C**: your character; **L**: spend experience
- **m**: memos, email and news; **X**: save; **h**: help
- **[** and **]** turn, **=** walks and **+** runs, for mecha; **.** changes movement mode
- **Esc**: leave a conversation or a menu; **Q**: quit

## History

Joseph Hewitt released the first version of GearHead in 2002, written in Free Pascal, and kept extending it for years before going on to GearHead 2. The game later moved to GitHub, where it still gets fixes. This edition is the ASCII version, built for the terminal.

## Credits

- GearHead: Arena: [Joseph Hewitt](https://github.com/jwvhewitt/gearhead-1) and contributors
- License: LGPL-3.0-or-later

genesis.title: Genesis
genesis.description: The original LPMud, founded in 1989 by students at Chalmers in Gothenburg

glider.title: Glider
glider.description: John Calhoun's Glider 4.0 in the terminal: fly a paper glider through a house, riding the air from the floor vents past candles, toasters, darts and sparking outlets
glider.provenance: John Calhoun wrote Glider 4.0 for the Macintosh in THINK Pascal, published by Casady & Greene in 1991, and released its source, art, sounds and houses in 2016.
glider.page:
**A PAPER GLIDER. A WHOLE HOUSE. NOTHING HOLDING YOU UP BUT THE AIR.**

You are at the controls of a paper glider loose in a big old house, and
the way out is through every room of it. A glider only falls; what keeps
it up is the air from the floor vents, so you drift from vent to vent,
steering left and right and climbing to the ceiling, while the room does
its best to bring you down. "Foresight and daring are rewarded," as John
Calhoun put it in 1991.

He also confessed he had no intention of telling you what everything in
the rooms does: the floor, tables, shelves and books are most certainly
bad, the clocks most certainly good ("points, points, what's a game
without points?"), and you'll enjoy figuring out the rest. A few
freebies: candles lift you too, "but not too close!"; toast leaps from
the toaster, fish from their bowls; outlets spark, grease spills,
shredders wait. And through the air come the balloons ("slow and
harmless looking, but not party invitations!"), paper 'copters ("of
mysterious origin, but of dire design!") and the darts: "Fast and
unforgiving... Out of way!" Folded paper is an extra glider, a battery a
burst of speed, rubber bands your only defense. Ducts and stairs lead on,
switches bring back the lights, the air or a fan, and the faster you
cross a room, the bigger its time bonus.

Twelve houses come with it, from The House and Calhoun's own Mad House to
the fans' houses of the day: the 120 rooms of the House of the Rising
Sun, the Glass House with a window in every room, and Hands-off House,
which plays itself. Any Glider 4 house file plays too.

It is Calhoun's game, translated from his Pascal, with his art, sounds
and houses read from his own files. The silhouette view is made for the
terminal: the room softened behind box-drawn furniture, and everything
that moves or hurts drawn sharp in solid colour. Or press **V** for his
art itself, in half blocks.

**Catch the air. Mind the darts.**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right** (or **,** and **.**): fly; let go and the glider
  just falls
- **Up** or **Enter**: burn the battery; **Space** or **Down**: fire a
  rubber band
- Mouse: point left or right of the room's middle to fly that way, as on
  the Mac; the button burns the battery
- Gamepad: d-pad or stick to fly, **A** fires, **B** or the right
  trigger boosts, **Start** pauses
- **Tab**: pause; **V**: the other view; **M**: sound; **B**: music;
  **Q**: end the game
- Type **Ozma** on the title screen for fifty gliders, as in the original

Best in a terminal that reports key releases (kitty, foot, WezTerm,
Ghostty and others). Elsewhere a tap sets the glider going that way, as
Glider's own tap control did; the mouse and a gamepad don't depend on it.

## Options

- `glider "Mad House"`: start in a built-in house; `--houses` lists them
- `glider path/to/house`: play a Glider 4 house file from disk
- `--watch`: no controls, for Hands-off House
- `--silhouette`, `--original`: which view to start in
- `--mute`: no sound

## History

Calhoun wrote Glider 4.0 for the Macintosh in THINK Pascal, and Casady &
Greene published it in 1991, "a wistful flight of fancy for those rainy
days". It came with a Room Editor, and players built houses of their own
and passed them around on America Online. Steve Sullivan offered $10 to
the first player to send him a screenshot of his House of the Rising Sun
finished, and soon after, Calhoun wrote asking to include it in a
collection of houses to be sold. Calhoun followed Glider 4 with Glider
PRO in 1994, and released Glider 4's source, art, sounds and houses
under the MIT licence in 2016.

This edition keeps his rules and his house files as they were. Three
timers in Hands-off House are moved, as it was tuned on a slower Mac, so
it still plays itself to the end.

## Credits

- **Glider 4.0**: John Calhoun, 1991, published by Casady & Greene;
  sound code by Patrick Buckland, electric bass by John Gnaegy
- **Houses**: John Calhoun (The House, Mad House), Ward Hartenstein
  (Hands-off House, Glass House), Steve Sullivan (House of the Rising
  Sun), JeffrC (House Full of Stuff and the one Next Door, House of
  Doom), Tony Korlath (Lumpy's Home), Brian Eaton (Usher House); Combo
  House joins The House to Mad House
- **Terminal edition**: Asciiverse
- License: MIT

- Gamepads work on Windows: gilrs reads them through XInput, since its
