glulxe.title: Glulxe
glulxe.description: Plays Glulx, the machine most Inform 7 stories run on: Counterfeit Monkey, Kerkerkruip and many more, right in your terminal.
glulxe.provenance: Glulxe is Andrew Plotkin's player for Glulx, the virtual machine he designed in 1999 when Inform games outgrew the Z-machine.
glulxe.page:
**WHEN INFORM OUTGREW THE Z-MACHINE, GLULX WAS WAITING.**

Glulxe plays stories written for Glulx, the virtual machine Andrew
Plotkin designed in 1999 when Inform games outgrew the Z-machine. Most
Inform 7 games are Glulx stories: Counterfeit Monkey, Kerkerkruip, Rover's
Day Out and many more. Here they run in the terminal with GlkTerm, so
status lines, side panels and Unicode text all work. Give it a story file
and play.

## Use

- `glulxe <story file>`: play a story (.ulx and .gblorb files)
- `save` and `restore` inside a story keep your place; saves go in the
  current folder
- Page Up and Page Down scroll back through the story

In Asciiverse, Glulx story titles come with Glulxe built in, so you only
need this to play story files of your own.

## Credits

- Glulxe and GlkTerm: Andrew Plotkin
- Asciiverse edition: static builds and packaging, four GlkTerm fixes
- License: MIT

gnuski.title: GNUSki
gnuski.description: Point your skis downhill and weave between trees and rocks as the slope rushes up at you. One trunk is all it takes. How far can you get?
gnuski.provenance: Rudolf Olah wrote GNUSki in 2007 as a small curses game in the spirit of SkiFree and released it on SourceForge.
gnuski.page:
**RACE DOWNHILL. MIND THE TREES.**

The slope rushes up the screen at you: pine trees, rocks and snowy hills, scattered as thick as a forest. You lean left, you lean right, you straighten out again, and you look for the gap. Hit a trunk or a rock and the run is over. All that counts is how far you got.

GNUSki is a little game in the spirit of SkiFree, the skiing game many of us played on Windows in the 1990s, drawn in plain characters for the terminal.

- **Three speeds**: take it slow through the trees, or put on speed in open snow
- **An endless slope**: new obstacles keep coming from below
- **Your distance and time** at the top of the screen

## Controls

- **Left** / **h**: lean left; from a right lean, back to straight down
- **Right** / **l**: lean right; from a left lean, back to straight down
- **Down** / **j**: faster
- **Up** / **k**: slower
- **q**: stop the run

## Credits

- GNUSki: Rudolf Olah
- Patch: Thierry Moisan
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

gofish.title: Go Fish
gofish.description: The children's card game against a computer that remembers what you asked for: ask for ranks, go fish, and collect the most books of four.
gofish.provenance: Muffy Barkocy wrote fish for BSD Unix. Mike Sharov gave it a curses display and one-key play in 2016 and renamed it Go Fish in 2020.
gofish.page:
**GOT ANY SEVENS? NO? GO FISH!**

The traditional children's card game, with the computer across the
table. You each get seven cards and the rest of the deck waits face
down. On your turn, ask for a rank you already hold. If the computer has
any, it hands over every one of them and you ask again. If not: "GO
FISH!" Draw from the deck, and if you draw the very rank you asked for,
you keep going.

Four of a rank make a book. When either of you runs out of cards, the
most books wins. And don't think the computer isn't paying attention: it
remembers what you've asked for, and it comes asking for it.

- **One key per ask**: a, 2 to 9, 1 for the ten, j, q or k.
- **Everything on show**: your hand, the cards left in the deck and both
  sets of books, in the panel at the bottom.
- **A sore loser, now and then**: beat it and it may mutter "Cheater,
  cheater, pumpkin eater!"; lose and it may crow "Hah! Stupid peasant!"

**Seven cards. One deck. Make your books.**

## Controls

- **a**, **2** to **9**, **1** (for 10), **j**, **q**, **k**: ask for that rank
- **?** or **F1**: the rules
- **x** or **F10**: quit

## History

Fish was written by Muffy Barkocy for BSD Unix (copyright 1990, with the
University of California). In Mike Sharov's bsd-games, the modern Linux
port of the BSD games, it got a curses display and one-key play in 2016,
and in 2020 its name became Go Fish, so the program no longer collides
with the fish shell. Go Fish is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse
catalog, under the BSD licence.

gomoku.title: Gomoku
gomoku.description: Five in a row on a 19 by 19 board against a computer that builds threats and blocks yours. Beat it to the fifth stone.
gomoku.provenance: Ralph Campbell wrote Gomoku for BSD in 1994, with a board display based on Peter Langston's goref. Mike Sharov reworked it in 2016 for modern curses, with cursor keys for moves.
gomoku.page:
**FIVE IN A ROW. IT'S WATCHING EVERY LINE.**

Gomoku is five in a row, the game played with stones on a Go board, and
here the board is 19 by 19 and your opponent is the computer. Take turns
placing stones. The first to get five in an unbroken line, across, down
or diagonally, wins.

Sounds simple. Then the computer starts building. It weighs every line of
five on the board for both sides, making threats of its own and blocking
yours, and an open three you leave alone soon becomes a line nobody can
stop. Win and it grumbles "Rats! you won". Lose and you'll read "Ha ha, I
won".

- **Cursor play**: steer with the arrows or hjkl, place with Space or
  Enter.
- **A coin toss to start**: the computer picks at random who goes first,
  and X always moves first.
- **Nothing slips past you**: each side in its own colour, and the last
  move of each side highlighted.

**Five stones. One line. Get there first.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **hjkl**: move the cursor
- **Space** or **Enter**: place your stone
- **q** or **F10**: end the game

## History

Ralph Campbell wrote Gomoku for BSD Unix in 1994, building the board
display on goref, a program by Peter Langston. Its computer player looks
for combinations of threats in every direction.

Mike Sharov reworked Gomoku in 2016 for his bsd-games, the modern Linux
port of the BSD games: a boxed board centred in
the terminal, moves chosen with the cursor instead of typed coordinates,
and colour for each side. Gomoku is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse
catalog, under the BSD licence.

gorched.title: Gorched
gorched.description: Two tanks, a range of hills, one shell at a time: find the angle, charge the shot and blow your rival off the hill. Artillery duels for two on one keyboard.
gorched.provenance: Ján Čabala (zladovan) wrote Gorched in Go on termloop in 2020, as a homage to Wendell Hicken's 1991 DOS game Scorched Earth.
gorched.page:
**TWO TANKS. ONE RANGE OF HILLS. FIRE!**

Two tanks face each other across procedurally generated hills, trees and
clouds. Turn your cannon, press Space to start charging, press it again
to fire, and watch the shell arc over the hills. Wherever it lands, the
ground blows out into a crater. Near misses chip away at the other
tank's armour; a direct hit can finish it. Land one and your tank says
so: "Yeeha !", "Take that !", "Rest in pieces !"

The last tank standing scores, the hills are swept away and the next
round starts on new ground. Between rounds, each player spends the
points they earned on Attack (bigger explosions, more shooting power) or
Defense (more armour).

- **Two players, one keyboard**: turn by turn, one shot each.
- **New terrain every round**: or replay the same rounds with `--seed`.
- **Fills your terminal**: with `--ascii-only` and `--low-color` for
  terminals that need them.

**Find the angle. Feel the power. Fire.**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**: turn the cannon
- **Space**: start charging; press again to fire at the power shown
- **s**: score board
- **a**: player attributes
- **h**: help
- **Ctrl+R**: restart the round
- **Ctrl+N**: skip to the next round
- **Ctrl+C**: quit

In the score and attributes windows, **Tab** moves between buttons and
**Enter** presses one.

## Options

- `--seed N`: replay the same sequence of rounds
- `--width N`, `--height N`: set the world size instead of filling the terminal
- `--ascii-only`: draw the tanks with plain ASCII, if you see question marks
- `--low-color`: use only the 8 basic colors, if the colors look wrong
- `--fps N`: lower the frame rate to save CPU

## History

Ján Čabala wrote Gorched in Go in 2020 as a homage to Scorched Earth,
Wendell Hicken's 1991 DOS artillery game, and has kept releasing it since.

## Credits

- Game: [Ján Čabala (zladovan)](https://github.com/zladovan/gorched)
- Engine: [termloop](https://github.com/JoelOtter/termloop) by Joel Auterson, terrain from [opensimplex-go](https://github.com/ojrac/opensimplex-go)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: MIT

greed.title: Greed
greed.description: Munch through a screen full of numbers, where every number you land on decides how far you move next. Eat as much as you can before you box yourself in.
greed.provenance: Matt Day wrote Greed in C (to 3.0a, 1990); Eric S. Raymond has maintained it since and ported it to Rust in 2026.

upstream.name: Eric S. Raymond, after Matt Day

greed.page:
**EAT THE SCREEN. EVERY NUMBER DECIDES HOW FAR.**

You are the @, standing in a field of numbers that fills the screen. Pick
any of eight directions and you munch your way along it: as many squares
as the first number you meet. Wherever you stop, the next number is
already waiting. As the game's own readme warns: "Beware! the length of
your next move is forced by the number you land on."

You can't leave the board, and you can't cross a square you've already
eaten. Paint yourself into a corner and that's it: when no move is left,
the game is over. Your score is every square you ate, shown beside it as
a share of the whole board.

- **One rule, eight directions**: learn it in a minute, then try to stop.
- **See your options**: press p and every move you can make lights up.
- **The whole window**: av starts Greed fitted to your terminal, so a
  big window means a big feast.
- **High scores**: `greed -s` shows the best games.

**Greedy? Good. Now don't get stuck.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **h j k l y u b n** or the **numeric keypad**: move in any of eight directions
- **p**: show or hide the moves you can make
- **Ctrl+L**: redraw the screen
- **q**: quit

Moving eats as many squares in that direction as the first number you
meet. You cannot leave the board or cross a square you have already eaten;
when no move is left, the game ends. Your score is the number of squares
eaten.

## Options

- `-f`: fit the board to the terminal (av starts Greed this way)
- `-w N`, `-h N`: set the board's width and height
- `-p`: start with possible moves highlighted
- `-r N`: fixed random seed, for replaying the same board
- `-s`: show the high scores

## History

Matt Day wrote the C version and released it up to 3.0a in 1990; it
probably goes back to a DOS game of the 1980s. Eric S. Raymond took over
maintenance and has kept it going since, porting it to Rust in 2026.

## Credits

- C version: Matt Day
- Maintainer and Rust port: [Eric S. Raymond](https://gitlab.com/esr/greed)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: BSD-2-Clause

gtypist.title: GNU Typist
gtypist.description: The GNU typing tutor: learn to touch-type from the home row up, with QWERTY, Dvorak and Colemak courses, number-pad and speed drills, and lessons in several languages.
gtypist.provenance: Simon Baldwin wrote typist in 1998; it became GNU Typist, part of the GNU project, and is still maintained there.

developer.name: Simon Baldwin, Mihai Gătejescu and the GNU Typist developers

gtypist.page:
**STOP LOOKING AT YOUR FINGERS.**

GNU Typist is the patient teacher you never had in school. It starts with your fingers on the home row, introduces each key one at a time, and gives you a line to copy. Hit the wrong key and it marks it, quietly. Make too many mistakes and you do the line again. Before long you are typing the whole alphabet, numbers and punctuation without looking down.

It has been teaching people to type since 1998, and it still works the same: short drills, honest speed tests, and a personal best to beat.

- **Courses for QWERTY, Dvorak and Colemak**, short and long
- **Drills and speed tests**, including passages from Shakespeare
- **Number pad, symbols and programming** lessons
- **Lessons in other languages**: `gtypist esp.typ` for Spanish, plus Czech, Romanian, Russian and many KTouch keyboard courses

## Controls

- In menus: **arrow keys** and **Enter**; **Esc** goes back
- In a drill: type the line you see, then **Enter**
- After an exercise: **R** to repeat, **N** for the next one, **E** to leave the lesson

Your personal bests are kept in `~/.gtypist-bestlog`.

## Credits

- GNU Typist: Simon Baldwin (original author), Mihai Gătejescu (maintainer) and the GNU Typist developers
- Lessons: many contributors; see the lesson files
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

hack.title: Hack
hack.description: The 1985 dungeon crawl that NetHack grew from: down through the Dungeons of Doom for the Amulet of Yendor, with your little dog at your side.
hack.provenance: Jay Fenlason wrote Hack in 1982 with Kenny Woodland, Mike Thome and Jon Payne, after Rogue, and Andries Brouwer reworked it at the CWI in Amsterdam into the 1985 game, version 1.0.3, that NetHack grew from.
hack.page:
**NOBODY HAS EVER BROUGHT THE AMULET BACK.**

Somewhere below the 20th level of the Dungeons of Doom lies the Amulet of
Yendor. Go down, find it, and get it out. As Hack's own 1985 manual puts
it: "Nobody has achieved this yet and if somebody does, he will probably
go down in history as a hero among heroes."

Choose who goes down: a Tourist, Speleologist, Fighter, Knight, Cave-man
or Wizard. Your little dog comes too. Below wait floating eyes, nymphs
who steal, leprechauns after your gold, cockatrices, umber hulks, a long
worm and worse, along with armour, weapons, potions, scrolls, rings and
wands you only learn to know by trying them. Crack a fortune cookie for
some advice ("A truly wise man never plays leapfrog with a unicorn.").
Death is final, and your ghost may wait on that level, with your
belongings, for the next player who comes down.

- **Where NetHack began**: Andries Brouwer's Hack 1.0.3, as BSD shipped it.
- **Everything is a letter**: you are the `@`, `#` is a corridor, `>` the
  stairs down, and every monster has a letter of its own.
- **Shops and shopkeepers**: who expect to be paid.

**Take the stairs. Keep the dog close. Bring back the Amulet.**

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the vi way (diagonals on yubn); with **Shift**,
  run
- **s**: search, **.**: rest, **>** and **<**: stairs
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **w**: wield, **W**: wear, **q**: quaff, **r**: read, **e**: eat,
  **z**: zap a wand, **t**: throw
- **?**: help, **/**: what is that symbol
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit, **^R**: redraw

## History

Jay Fenlason wrote Hack in 1982, his first-semester programming
project, with Kenny Woodland, Mike Thome and Jon Payne, after the game
Rogue. Andries Brouwer then reworked it at the CWI in Amsterdam ("in fact an entirely
different game", says its manual), and that 1985 version, 1.0.3, was
shipped with BSD and became the base of NetHack.

NetBSD keeps the original game; Mike Sharov's bsd-games trimmed it in
2018 and later dropped it. The Asciiverse edition ports it to Linux and
macOS and keeps its record, saved games and bones in the player's own
data folder.
Hack is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD
licence.

hangman.title: Hangman
hangman.description: Guess the computer's word a letter at a time, from 61,494 words of six letters or more. Seven misses and the gallows is finished.
hangman.provenance: Ken Arnold wrote Hangman for BSD in 1983, and Mike Sharov cleaned it up for modern curses in 2016.
hangman.page:
**SEVEN WRONG GUESSES AND HE HANGS.**

The computer thinks of a word and shows you a dash for every letter.
Guess a letter. Right, and it fills in every place that letter appears.
Wrong, and another piece goes up on the gallows. Seven misses and the
figure is complete, and the screen tells you: "Sorry, the word was..."
Get there first and it's "You got it!"

Every word is at least six letters long, picked from 61,494 everyday
English and American words, and they keep coming, one after another.
Beside the gallows sits your average number of wrong guesses. Bring it
down.

- **One key per guess**: a to z; Space gives up on a word and moves on.
- **Its own dictionary**: no system word list needed.
- **Bring your own words**: from a shell, `-d` takes a word list and `-m`
  sets the shortest word length.

**Pick a letter. Any letter. Choose well.**

## Controls

- **a** to **z**: guess a letter
- **Space**: give up on this word and go to the next
- **Enter**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `-d` takes a different word list, one word per
line, and `-m` sets the shortest word length, as in `hangman -m 8`.

## History

Ken Arnold wrote Hangman for BSD Unix in 1983, and Mike Sharov cleaned
it up for modern curses in 2016 for his bsd-games, the modern Linux port
of the BSD games. Hangman is part of BSD Games in
the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD licence.

The original reads the system's dictionary, which many computers no
longer have, so this edition comes with its own: 61,494 everyday English
and American words from SCOWL 2020.12.07, Kevin Atkinson's Spell Checker
Oriented Word Lists, used under SCOWL's permissive licence.

hauberk.title: Hauberk
hauberk.description: A hundred floors of dungeon, rebuilt every time you take the stairs. Light a candle, grip your stick, and go find out what happened to the last adventurer.
hauberk.provenance: Bob Nystrom has written Hauberk in Dart since 2012 as a roguelike for the web browser, and still works on it.
hauberk.page:
There's a little town at the top of a very long staircase. It has a home
for your loot, six shops with names like Dirk's Death Emporium and
Skullduggery and Bamboozelry, and not much else. Everything interesting is
downstairs.

A hundred levels down, to be exact, and none of them hold still: every
time you take the stairs, the dungeon builds itself anew. Rooms and halls,
dark water and narrow bridges, pools of candlelight and long stretches of
nothing at all. Bring a light. Seriously, bring a light.

Down there: sewer rats, giant cockroaches, scurrilous imps, frosty slimes,
a murderous eye or two and, if you make it that far, The Rat King. Also
the odd hapless adventurer, who got here before you and is not doing well.

Make yourself a dwarf, an elf, a gnome, a human or one of the fae, then an
adventurer, a barbarian or a sorceror. Then decide how much death should
hurt. Gentle: you lose what you found since the last stairs or shop.
Honest: you lose the hero, for good.

Fight, loot, haul it home, sell it, buy something sharper, go deeper.
Repeat until legendary, or dead.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, the **number keys**, or **i o p k ; , . /**: move;
  walk into a monster to attack it
- **Shift** with a direction: run
- **L**: rest, **g**: pick up, **e**: equip, **u**: use, **d**: drop,
  **t**: throw, **x**: swap weapons, **c**: operate doors and chests
- **a**: use an ability, **Shift+E**: spend experience, **Shift+A**: about
  your hero
- In item lists, a **capital letter** shows the item's details
- **h**: help, with every key
- **q** or **Esc** on the main menu, or **Ctrl+C**: quit

Hauberk needs a terminal of at least 80 columns by 40 rows.

## Saving

Heroes are saved in your data folder (`~/.local/share/hauberk`, or
`%APPDATA%\hauberk` on Windows) whenever you take the stairs or leave a
shop.

## Options

- `--hero NAME`: start in the town with your hero NAME
- `--demo`: watch the computer play a new hero

## Credits

- Hauberk: Bob Nystrom
  ([github.com/munificent/hauberk](https://github.com/munificent/hauberk)),
  2012 on, written in Dart with his malison and piecemeal libraries
- Asciiverse edition: Hauberk's own code, unchanged, with a terminal
  screen and keyboard layer in place of the browser, and a demo mode
- License: MIT

hnefatafl.title: Hnefatafl
hnefatafl.description: The Viking game of the king: twenty-four attackers, one king and his guard, and five rule sets from Copenhagen to Lapland
hnefatafl.provenance: Asciiverse made Hnefatafl in Rust in 2026. No Norse rules survive; it plays today's reconstructions as the World Tafl Federation and Aage Nielsen give them, and R. C. Bell's Tablut of 1960.
hnefatafl.page:
**ONE KING. TWENTY-FOUR VIKINGS WHO WANT A WORD WITH HIM.**

Before chess reached the north, the Vikings played tafl. In the middle of the board sits a king with his small guard. All round the edges wait twice as many attackers, and they would very much like a word with him.

The king wants out. His guards want to get him out. The attackers want to box him in. Every piece slides like a rook, so walls go up and come crashing down fast. Sandwich an enemy between two of yours to take it; the throne and the corners bite too. Get the king to safety and the defenders win. Surround him, and it's over.

The Norse rules are lost, so choose your reconstruction:

- **Copenhagen 11x11**: the tournament game, with shield walls along the edge and the exit fort
- **Fetlar 11x11**: the Shetland rules, no shield wall and no fort
- **Brandubh 7x7**: the quick Irish game, a king and four princes against eight Viking invaders
- **Tablut 9x9, Linnaeus**: written down by Linnaeus in Lapland in 1732, the only tafl game anyone recorded while it was still played
- **Tablut 9x9, Bell 1960**: the same game as an 1811 mistranslation left it, where the king can only be taken from all four sides, and the game shouts Raichi! when he sees one way out, Tuichi! when he sees two. It is not fair, and it is fun

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Arrows**: move the cursor
- **Enter**: pick up a piece, then put it down on a lit square; **Esc**: drop it
- **Mouse**: click a piece, then a square
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same game every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

hoosegow.title: Hoosegow
hoosegow.description: Locked in a frontier jail with Muddy Charlie and a hanging set for eight in the morning: put your heads together and bust out of the hoosegow.
hoosegow.provenance: Ben Collins-Sussman and Jack Welch's comic Western Hoosegow (2010) won the Casual Gameplay Design Competition #7.
hoosegow.page:
**THERE'S GOING TO BE A HANGING. YOURS.**

You blew up that railroad tunnel just the way Muddy Charlie planned it.
He just didn't plan on the sheriff getting word ahead of time. Now the
silver dollars of the Missouri, Kansas & Texas Line are evidence, you
and Muddy are locked in Sheriff Cheney's sturdy brick jail, and a
federal marshal is coming for you at eight o'clock tomorrow morning. The
sheriff's news for his deputy: "There's going to be a hanging!" And on
his way out the door: "Jimbo, don't screw up."

"Why are you not surprised to have landed right back in the hoosegow
after another one of Muddy's dubious plans? Will you ever learn?" Look
around. A broken stool. A small window above your head. A stranger in a
black suit, snoring on the bench. Muddy, tapping his harmonica on his
arm. And Deputy Jimbo, on the other side of the bars. Somewhere in all
that is a way out before eight.

Ben Collins-Sussman and Jack Welch's comic Western, "A Wild West Wreck",
won the Casual Gameplay Design Competition #7. Type "hints" when you're
stuck, "or just roll into town guns a-blazin'."

**Bust out by eight. Or hang.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/hoosegow`.

## Credits

- Hoosegow: Ben Collins-Sussman and Jack Welch, 2010
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-Noncommercial-Share Alike 3.0
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

huarongdao.title: HuaRongDao
huarongdao.description: The ancient Chinese sliding-block puzzle: ten pieces, two empty cells, and one big square that has to escape through the gap at the bottom. Easy rules, hard solution.
huarongdao.provenance: Qingning Huo wrote hrd, a curses HuaRongDao in C++, in 2004 and packaged it for Debian.
huarongdao.page:
**ONE BIG SQUARE. ONE NARROW GAP. NINE PIECES IN THE WAY.**

HuaRongDao is an ancient Chinese sliding-block puzzle, and its author
put it best: "The rules are very easy to understand, but the game is not
so easy to solve."

Ten pieces fill a box four cells wide and five high, leaving just two
cells empty: a big square, four tall rectangles, one wide one and four
small squares. Slide them, one at a time and never over each other,
until the big square escapes through the gap in the middle of the bottom
edge.

- **Every step counts**: moving one piece, even round a corner, is one
  step, and the counter shows how few you can manage.
- **Undo and redo**: back out of dead ends step by step.
- **Bookmarks**: keep a position in a slot and come back to it later.
- **More layouts**: the classic one is built in; give others as a
  pattern on the command line.

**Free the big square. Then do it in fewer steps.**

## Controls

- **0** to **9**: select the piece with that number, then
  **arrow keys** (or **l r u d**) to move it one or two cells
- **u**: undo a step, **r**: redo it
- **b**: save a bookmark in a slot (a letter or digit), **l**: load one
- **Enter**: clear the prompt, **Ctrl-L**: redraw
- **q**: quit (asks first)

## Options

- `hrd <pattern>`: play another layout, one letter a cell and a dot
  after each row: Q the big square, T and B the top and bottom of a tall
  piece, L and R the left and right of the wide one, P a small square,
  `_` empty. The classic layout is `TQQT.BQQB.TLRT.BPPB.P__P.`

## Files

Bookmarks are kept in `~/.local/share/hrd`.

## History

Qingning Huo wrote hrd in 2004 and maintained it in Debian until 2005.
The Asciiverse edition has his Debian build fix, bookmarks in the
player's data folder, and fixes for a crash without a home folder and
for unchecked memory mapping.

## Credits

hrd is by Qingning Huo, under the GNU GPL version 2 or later.

hunt.title: Hunt
hunt.description: Deathmatch in a maze over your local network: no rooms, no treasure, no monsters, just the other hunters, your gun and a very, very big bomb.
hunt.provenance: Conrad Huang, Ken Arnold and Greg Couch wrote Hunt at the University of California, San Francisco's Computer Graphics Lab, and Berkeley shipped it with 4BSD.

upstream.name: Conrad Huang, Ken Arnold and Greg Couch, UCSF Computer Graphics Lab

hunt.page:
**NO ROOMS. NO TREASURE. NO MONSTERS. JUST EACH OTHER.**

"The object of the game hunt is to kill off the other players." That's
the manual's whole pitch, and it's enough. Everyone on your network
drops into the same maze. Wander it, find the others, and shoot. Throw
grenades. Throw bombs: satchel charges, big bombs, even bigger bombs, all
the way up to the "very, very big bomb" and the biggest of all, if
you've saved the ammunition. Throw slime that oozes round the walls. Trip
mines, or defuse them for charges. Shoot down walls, and watch them grow
back.

You can only fire the way you're facing, and you can't see behind you.
Shots glance off diagonal walls and scatter through doors. Scan to see
where everyone is; cloak to hide from their scans. Every kill raises your
score, and when you die you can come straight back in.

Start Hunt and it looks for a game on your local network. If it finds
one, you join it (if it finds several, you pick); if there is none, it
starts a game on your machine for the others to find.

A word of warning from the original README: "hunt may be dangerous to
your health. "Arthritic pain" and "lack of circulation" in fingers have
been reported by hunt abusers."

**Find them. Face them. Fire.**

## Controls

- **hjkl**: move left, down, up, right; **HJKL**: turn to face that way
- **f** or **1**: fire a bullet; **g** or **2**: throw a grenade; **F**,
  **G** and **3** to **0** and **@**: ever bigger bombs, each costing more
  ammunition
- **o**, **O**, **p**, **P**: throw slime
- **s**: scan for the other players, **c**: cloak against their scans
- **Ctrl-L**: redraw, **q**: quit

You can only fire the way you are facing.

## Options

Started from a shell: `hunt host` joins the game on that machine, `hunt
-q` lists the games on the network, `-m` joins as a spectator who
watches the whole maze, `-n name` sets your name and `-t digit` puts you
on a team.

## Network

Hunt finds games with a broadcast on UDP port 26740, and the game itself
runs over two TCP ports the server picks when it starts. If your
firewall asks, allow Hunt and its server, huntd, rather than a single
port.

## History

Conrad Huang, Ken Arnold and Greg Couch wrote Hunt at the University of
California, San Francisco's Computer Graphics Lab, and Berkeley
distributed it with 4BSD. The Asciiverse edition ports it to Linux and
macOS with its network play intact. It is part of BSD Games in the
Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD licence.

i-am-prey.title: I Am Prey
i-am-prey.description: Your name is Prey, and the Predator is starving. Find all seven pieces of an environment suit and escape through the airlock before he finds you.
i-am-prey.provenance: Joey Cramsey wrote I Am Prey, a TADS 3 game, in 2023.
i-am-prey.page:
**YOUR NAME IS PREY. HE IS STARVING.**

You wake in the delivery room of a sealed facility, half drowned, and a
voice is already talking. It belongs to Skashek, the Predator: pale as
death, two rows of sharp teeth, long arms ending in clawed hands. He is
kind enough to explain the rules. "I'm starving, Prey. So run. Avoid
becoming my next meal. I've scattered pieces of an environment suit
around the place. If you collect all seven pieces, you will be able to
survive the poison gas, and escape."

So run. Climb, leap and crawl through the facility, sneak, hide, and set
tricks for him to fall for, while you gather the helmet, the torso and
the rest before he gathers you. Then out through the emergency airlock.
"I may not be the first, but I will be the most elusive."

- **A hunter who learns**: each kind of trick only fools him so many
  times.
- **Six difficulties**: from Cat Mode, where you play the Predator's pet
  cat and he won't chase you, to Nightmare Mode: "What the heck?!
  Something has really gotten into the Predator today! His cruelty is
  insatiable!"
- **Parkour**: climb, jump and slide your way around, and learn the
  routes.
- **Different every time**: built for replaying, and UNDO won't change
  what the dice decided.

The game warns of violence, frequent crude language and rare mentions of
suicide.

**Run, Prey. Run.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/i-am-prey`.

## Credits

- I Am Prey: Joey Cramsey, 2023
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0
- Played with FrobTADS by Nikos Chantziaras, on Michael J. Roberts' TADS (TADS Freeware License)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

ioccc-chaos.title: Chaos
ioccc-chaos.description: A cube, a pyramid, a desk, an X-wing and the IOCCC's own name tumble in 3D wireframe, drawn by a prize-winning C program written to be unreadable.
ioccc-chaos.provenance: Alan De Smet wrote chaos, a curses 3D wireframe viewer, for the International Obfuscated C Code Contest in 1998, where it won "Best object orientation".
ioccc-chaos.page:
**A 3D ENGINE YOU'RE NOT MEANT TO READ.**

Five objects turn in 3D in your terminal: a cube, a pyramid, a desk, an
X-wing fighter and the letters IOCCC, which sway back and forth so they
can be read. They're drawn as wireframes in dots, colons and backticks
that pack two lines of the picture into every row of text, and each one
tumbles about one axis after another before the next takes its place.

All of it comes from one small C program written to be impossible to
follow, the International Obfuscated C Code Contest's "Best object
orientation" of 1998. The judges asked: "Can you figure out why, in some
cases, it wants to read itself?" (Run it with no data file and it
searches its own program file for a cube hidden behind the word
"AlWuzEre".) Alan De Smet's own advice: "So just don't fly through
objects. You'll be happier."

**Sit back. Watch it spin. Don't read the source.**

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `ioccc-chaos -t 20` gives every object 20 seconds, `-l`
lists them, and naming objects shows only those (`ioccc-chaos xwing`). A
data file of your own in the entry's format works too.

## History

Alan De Smet wrote chaos for the International Obfuscated C Code Contest
in 1998, his first entry, and won "Best object orientation". Left alone,
the original turns its object about one axis; its keys turn and zoom it
by hand. Asciiverse runs the entry as the IOCCC publishes it, inside a
small launcher that sends it those keys to tumble each object, shows the
five in turn and quits on any key.

## Credits

- 1998/chaos by [Alan De Smet](http://www.highprogrammer.com/alan/), from the [IOCCC](https://www.ioccc.org/1998/chaos/index.html)
- Copyright Landon Curt Noll, licensed under [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/) ([the IOCCC's summary](https://www.ioccc.org/license.html))
- Asciiverse edition: the launcher, objects in turn, tumbling, any key quits; changes listed in PATCHES.md

jewels.title: Jewels
jewels.description: Falling pairs of jewels: line up four of a kind to blow them away, chain the explosions for bigger scores, and keep the pile from reaching the top.
jewels.provenance: abakh wrote Jewels for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018.
jewels.page:
**FOUR IN A ROW, AND THEY BLOW.**

Pairs of jewels drop into the well. Slide each pair left or right, turn
it, drop it. Line up four or more of the same jewel in a row or a column
and they explode for points. Whatever was resting on them falls, and if
that sets off another explosion, it scores more than the last. Chain
them and watch the numbers climb.

The catch: when one jewel of a pair lands, the other keeps falling on
its own, and the pile keeps rising. When the jewels reach the middle of
the top row, it's over.

- **Plan ahead**: the next pair waits at the top left.
- **Chains pay**: every explosion in a chain is multiplied by its place
  in it.
- **Beat the record**: top the high score and a trophy says so:
  "CONGRATULATIONS! You beat the previous record".

**Stack them. Line them up. Blow them away.**

## Controls

- **j** and **l**, **a** and **d**, or the **left** and **right arrows**: move the pair
- **k**, **w** or the **up arrow**: turn the pair
- **Space**: drop it
- **p**: pause
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Jewels is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

kaiku.title: Kaiku: Echoes Home
kaiku.description: A savage blast hurls you deep into enemy territory, where no human has ever flown! Fight through two hostile fleets, decode the lost voices of Earth, and find the one gate that leads home. Can you make it back alive?!
kaiku.provenance: Asciiverse made Kaiku in Rust in 2026. The echoes are NASA mission audio and John F. Kennedy's speeches; Gates of Zendocon (Epyx, 1989), ZType and Typespeed inspired it.
kaiku.page:
**THE WAR IS RAGING. AND YOU'RE ON THE WRONG SIDE OF IT.**

An intergalactic war burns across the stars, and you're right in the thick of it. Then, out of nowhere, a savage blast rips through your ship and hurls you off course, far beyond the front line, deep into enemy territory where no human has ever been!

No charts. No backup. No way back. Just the Amber and Jade fleets closing in from every side, and a receiver crackling in the dark...

*...the eagle has landed... houston, we've had a problem... godspeed, john glenn...*

Earth's old transmissions, bouncing through space for decades! Broken, garbled, half lost in the static, and they're your only map home. The clearer the echo, the nearer home!

Interceptors flash out of nowhere! Lancers charge down their deadly lines! Jammers scramble the very voices you need to hear! Every sector is a gauntlet, and at the end of every one wait three gates. Only one leads closer to Earth.

- **Fight with your guns, decode with your fingers!** Type each echo clear, letter by letter, with enemy fire all around you.
- **Choose your gate!** Pick wrong and you're thrown off the path. Pick right and Earth gets closer.
- **Snatch power-ups by typing their words:** spread shot, rapid fire, shields, smart bombs, an escort drone, even slow time!
- **The real words of Apollo, Mercury, Gemini and President Kennedy**, waiting to be pulled out of the static.
- **Two players, one ship!** Plug in a gamepad: one flies, one decodes.

You're alone, outgunned and light-years from home. **CAN YOU MAKE IT BACK?!**

## Controls

- **Arrows** or **Ctrl+h/j/k/l**: fly
- **Space** (hold): fire
- **a-z**: lock onto an echo or a power-up's word, and decode it
- **Backspace**: drop the lock (progress is kept)
- **Tab**: dash, a burst of speed you can't be hit in
- **Enter**: smart bomb; on the map, fly on
- **Esc**: pause; **F1**: the controls; **F8**: sound and music on or off
- **Gamepad**: stick or d-pad to fly, bottom face button to fire, right face button to bomb, left face button to dash

Terminals with the kitty keyboard protocol (kitty, foot, WezTerm, Ghostty) give exact key presses and releases.

## Options

- `--skip-intro`: straight into sector 1
- `--sector N`: start in a later sector
- `--demo`: the game plays itself; any key quits
- `--credits`: the credits on their own
- `--mute`, `--no-music`: no sound, or effects only

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Echoes: NASA mission audio (Mercury, Gemini, Apollo) and John F. Kennedy's speeches
- Inspired by Gates of Zendocon (Epyx, 1989), ZType and Typespeed
- Sound and music synthesised in the game

kerkerkruip.title: Kerkerkruip
kerkerkruip.description: One drunken boast, one portal, no way back: fight through a random dungeon, absorb the souls of what you kill, and finish Malygris, the Wizard of Kerkerkruip. A roguelike told in words.
kerkerkruip.provenance: Victor Gijsbers and contributors first entered Kerkerkruip in the 2011 Interactive Fiction Competition and worked on it until 2014.
kerkerkruip.page:
**YOU SAID YOU COULD TAKE HIM. NOW PROVE IT.**

When you claimed you were tough enough to take on Malygris
single-handedly, everyone knew you had been drinking much more than was
good for you. And the prince is not one to let an opportunity pass.
Before you could so much as protest, his court mage opened a portal and
you were shoved through. Predictably, the portal immediately
disappeared.

So here you are in the dungeon of Kerkerkruip, with a weapon or two,
three packages of ment (a powerful and highly addictive drug) and a
boast to make good on: kill Malygris, the Wizard of Kerkerkruip!

The dungeon is built new every game ("Placing epic treasures (well, you
hope)..."). Kill a monster with a level and you absorb its soul: it
heals you, makes you stronger and grants you its power. But a new soul
drives out every soul of the same level or lower, so the order you kill
in matters. Fights are tactical, with attacks, parries, dodges, blocks
and rolls, and a tension that rises the longer a fight drags on.

- **Permanent death**: no undo ("it would take all tension out of the
  game"); the game saves itself every turn.
- **A coffee-break roguelike**: short games, in Victor Gijsbers' own
  words.
- **Temples and gods**: sacrifice your powers for a god's favour.

**Absorb their souls. Find the wizard. Keep your boast.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- the game saves itself every turn and picks up where you left off; **quit** to stop

Your game in progress is kept in `~/.local/share/kerkerkruip`.

## Credits

- Kerkerkruip: Victor Gijsbers and contributors, 2011 to 2014
- License: GNU GPL version 3 or later; the source is kept in theasciiverse/stories
- Played with Glulxe and GlkTerm by Andrew Plotkin (MIT)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

klondike.title: Klondike
klondike.description: The best known patience, played entirely from the keyboard: build the four suits from Ace to King, with every move the selected card can make marked by a letter.
klondike.provenance: Mike Sharov wrote this Klondike in 2016 for his bsd-games, the modern Linux port of the BSD games, to replace canfield.
klondike.page:
**THE PATIENCE EVERYONE KNOWS, TURNED ON ITS SIDE.**

Seven sorting stacks, dealt from one card to seven, only the top card of
each face up. Move cards between the stacks, each one on a card one rank
higher and of the other colour, and build four final piles, one per
suit, from Ace up to King. The deck deals one card at a time, and when
it runs out the dealt cards turn over and go round again. Complete all
four suits and the screen says it in capitals: "*** YOU WON! ***"

The table is laid on its side: the sorting stacks run across the screen,
one per row, with the deck and the final piles down the right. There is
no cursor to drag. You step through the cards that can move, the game
marks with a letter each place the selected card can go, and you press
the letter.

- **All keyboard**: j and k to choose a card, a letter to place it, d to
  deal.
- **A new deal any time**: R starts over.

**Deal. Build. Bring them home to the King.**

## Controls

- **j** and **k**: select the next or previous card that can move
- **s**, **a**: move the selected card (and the cards on it) to the stack
  marked with that letter
- **f**: move the selected card to the final pile marked **f**
- **d**: deal a card from the deck
- **R**: start a new deal
- **q** or **F10**: quit

In a terminal with UTF-8 the suits are shown as symbols, otherwise as
the letters S, H, D and C.

## History

BSD Unix shipped Canfield as its solitaire. When Mike Sharov modernised
the BSD games for Linux in 2016, he replaced it with this Klondike,
written new, judging Canfield too rarely winnable to be fun. Klondike is
part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD licence.

konane.title: Kōnane
konane.description: Black and white stones, every hollow full, and every move a jump: the Hawaiian game Cook's expedition saw in 1779
konane.provenance: Asciiverse made Kōnane in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow Michael Ernst (1995), after Kenneth Emory (1924) and Peter Buck (1957), and the National Park Service at Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau; its largest board is the one James King described in 1779.
konane.page:
**EVERY MOVE IS A JUMP. RUN OUT OF JUMPS AND YOU LOSE.**

Every hollow of the board starts full, black and white in turn. Two stones are lifted out, and from then on every move is a jump: leap one of your opponent's stones into the empty hollow beyond and take it, and keep jumping along the same line if you dare. The first player who can't jump has lost.

Kōnane was played all across Hawaiʻi on boards cut into lava stone, with pebbles of coral and lava for stones. An officer on Captain Cook's third voyage saw it in 1779 on a board of 238 squares and thought it "much more intricate" than draughts. King Kamehameha, the story goes, sometimes beat his opponent in a single move.

- **Kōnane after Ernst**: the classic, 8 by 8, with jumps that may run on in a straight line
- **Modern Kōnane**: the same, but one jump a move
- **Puʻuhonua o Hōnaunau**: 9 by 11, like the old stone board there
- **King's papamū**: the great board of 238 squares, 14 by 17

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Arrows**: move the cursor; **Enter** or **Space**: lift a stone at the start, or pick one up and land it on a lit hollow; **Esc**: let go
- **Mouse**: click
- The stones a jump would take turn red when the cursor is on its landing
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same game every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

lambdamoo.title: LambdaMOO
lambdamoo.description: Social MOO founded by Pavel Curtis at Xerox PARC, where users build the world

larn.title: Larn
larn.description: Your daughter is dying of dianthroritis, and the only cure is somewhere in the caverns of Larn or the volcano below. Noah Morgan's 1986 roguelike, against the clock.
larn.provenance: Noah Morgan wrote Larn in 1986 and posted it to the net, and it was soon part of the BSD games.
larn.page:
**YOUR DAUGHTER IS DYING. THE CURE IS SOMEWHERE IN THE CAVERNS OF LARN.**

"At this moment, you face a great problem." Your daughter has contracted
a strange disease, and none of your home remedies seem to have any
effect. The doctor confirms it: dianthroritis, and he can tell you how
many mobuls she has left in this world. Her only hope is the very rare
potion of cure dianthroritis, rumoured to lie deep in the caverns of
Larn, the old haunt of the magician Polinneaus, or in the volcano
beneath them. "Good Luck! You're going to need it!"

Larn is a roguelike against the clock. Time runs in mobuls, and
everything costs some, even school. The town at the top has the College
of Larn (Fighters Training I: ten mobuls), the Bank of Larn, the Larn
Thrift Shoppe, the local trading post and the Larn Revenue Service,
which has ordered the shops not to do business with tax evaders. Go
down, come back rich, spend it, go deeper. The levels stay as you left
them, and the deeper you go, the more gold, magic and danger you find.

- **A deadline that matters**: every turn spends your daughter's time.
- **A town to come home to**: bank, college, shop, trading post, and a
  tax office.
- **Spells, potions and scrolls**: cast, quaff and read your way down.

**Find the potion. Beat the clock. Pay your taxes.**

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move (diagonals on yubn); with **Shift**, run
- **.**: stay, **i**: inventory, **d**: drop, **g**: pack weight
- **c**: cast a spell, **r**: read, **q**: quaff, **e**: eat
- **w**: wield, **W**: wear, **T**: take off armour
- **^**: identify a trap, **D**: list everything found so far
- **?**: help, **S**: save, **Q**: quit, **^L**: redraw

## History

Noah Morgan wrote Larn in 1986 and posted it to the net "for the
enjoyment of all"; it was soon part of the BSD games. With Larn 12.0 he
let anyone use, modify and port the sources as long as no profit is
made from them.

The Asciiverse edition ports it to Linux and macOS and keeps its
scoreboard and saved games in the player's own data folder.
Larn is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog.

legends-of-the-jedi.title: Legends of the Jedi
legends-of-the-jedi.description: Star Wars roleplay across iconic locations, approachable for new players

lera.title: Lera
lera.description: The Asciiverse MUD client: pick a world from the list and you are in the game in seconds, with colour, scrollback that keeps the live text in view, and your health and mana in the status line.
lera.provenance: Asciiverse made Lera to give every MUD in the catalog a home in your terminal; the name is Swedish for clay, which is to say mud.
lera.page:
**MULTI-USER CLAY.**

Lera is Swedish for clay, and for mud. Pick a world from the list, press Enter, and you are standing in it: no config language to learn, no host and port to look up. Every MUD in the Asciiverse catalog is already there, with what kind of world it is and how long it has been running, and you can add any other world in a few keystrokes.

Once you are in, the screen takes care of itself. Colour comes through as the MUD intended it, in 16, 256 or millions of colours. Scroll back through the fight you just had and the screen splits, so the live text keeps running underneath. Your health and mana sit in the status line when the MUD sends them, and your password never shows on screen.

- **Every catalog MUD in one list**, filtered as you type, plus worlds of your own
- **Scrollback that splits**, with PageUp or the mouse wheel, so you never miss what is happening now
- **Command history** on Up and Down, and the usual line keys
- **Vitals in the status line** from GMCP, on the MUDs that send them
- **TLS** where the world offers it, and compression to keep things quick
- **A log of every session**, kept per world as plain text
- **Reconnect** with one key when the line drops

## Keys

- **Enter**: connect to the world, then send each line
- **Up**, **Down**: earlier commands
- **PageUp**, **PageDown** or the **mouse wheel**: scroll back; **Esc** returns to the live end
- **Shift+drag**: select text to copy
- **Ctrl+R**: reconnect; **Ctrl+D**: disconnect
- **Ctrl+N** in the list: add a world of your own
- **F1**: all the keys; **Ctrl+Q**: quit

From the command line: `lera <world-id>`, or `lera <host> <port> --tls` for anywhere at all.

## Credits

- Lera: Asciiverse
- License: MIT

lexter.title: Lexter
lexter.description: Letters fall into a pit: steer them into words across or up and down, forwards or backwards, before the pit fills up. Palindromes count twice.
lexter.provenance: Mark Pulford wrote Lexter in C on curses from 1998 to 2001.
lexter.page:
**THE LETTERS ARE FALLING. SPELL FAST.**

Letters drop one at a time into a pit ten columns wide. Steer each one
left or right and let it land so that it spells words with the letters
around it: across or up and down, forwards or backwards, never
diagonally. A word of four letters or more scores and vanishes, and the
letters above fall into the gap. Palindromes count twice. The letters
fall faster as you find more words, and the game ends when the pit is
full.

- **Rare letters pay**: letter scores and how often each letter turns up
  come from the dictionary itself.
- **Blanks**: now and then a blank falls; press the letter you want it to
  be before it lands, or the game picks one for you.
- **Pit empty bonus!**: clear the whole pit and it pays extra.
- **English or French**: Lexter picks its dictionary from your language;
  `lexter -d fr` or `lexter -d en` chooses for yourself.

**Catch a letter. Make a word. Make room.**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**: move the letter
- **Down**: lower it a row; **Space**: drop it
- a letter key: what a falling blank should be
- **P**: pause; **H**: help; **L**: letter scores and chances;
  **W**: the words found so far
- **S**: save a screenshot as text; **Q**: quit

The keys are capital letters: **P**, **H**, **L**, **W**, **S** and **Q**
with Shift, so lowercase letters stay free for blanks.

## High scores

The table keeps the best 20 games, with each dictionary getting an equal
share. It lives in your own folder (`~/.local/share/lexter/scores`), so it
survives updates; `lexter -s` prints it.

## History

Mark Pulford started Lexter in 1998 and released it in February 2001, with
1.0.3 that March as the last version. It came with an English and a
French dictionary and was built to take others: any plain list of words
makes a new game.

The Asciiverse edition keeps scores and screenshots in your own folder,
stops a spurious
dictionary error at start, and shows the French dictionary's accented
letters properly on today's UTF-8 terminals.

lost-pig.title: Lost Pig
lost-pig.description: Grunk the orc lost the farm's pig, and boss say if Grunk not bring back pig, not bring back Grunk either. Into the dark woods, and under ground.
lost-pig.provenance: Admiral Jota's Lost Pig won the 2007 Interactive Fiction Competition and Best Game at the 2007 XYZZY Awards.
lost-pig.page:
**PIG LOST! BOSS SAY IT GRUNK FAULT.**

"Boss say Grunk go find pig, bring it back. Him say, if Grunk not bring
back pig, not bring back Grunk either." So Grunk, an orc with a torch
and a pair of pants, sets off after the pig into the dark woods, and
before long under the ground, where a gnome and a lot of old things are
waiting.

Every word of it is Grunk's own, and Grunk has thoughts. On the pig: "Pig
pink and chubby. Look tasty. Pig maybe smart, but Grunk catch pig. So
that mean Grunk more smart." On temptation: "Pig maybe tasty, but Grunk
have job. That job: not eat pig."

Admiral Jota's Lost Pig (And Place Under Ground) won the 2007
Interactive Fiction Competition and Best Game at the 2007 XYZZY Awards.

**Find pig. Bring pig back. Not eat pig.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/lost-pig`.

## Credits

- Lost Pig: Admiral Jota, 2007
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivs 3.0
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

lusternia.title: Lusternia
lusternia.description: Iron Realms fantasy MUD of rival city-states and nature communes

mahjongg.title: Mahjongg
mahjongg.description: Mahjong solitaire in the terminal: all ten of GNOME Mahjongg's layouts, from the Turtle to the Red Dragon, every deal solvable, by mouse or keys.
mahjongg.provenance: radha wrote this terminal Mahjongg in Rust in 2026, with layouts and game logic from GNOME Mahjongg.
mahjongg.page:
**CLEAR THE BOARD, ONE MATCHING PAIR AT A TIME.**

Mahjong solitaire, the tile-matching kind. The tiles are piled into a
shape (a Turtle, a Ziggurat, a Red Dragon) and you take away matching
pairs of free tiles until none are left. A tile is free when nothing
lies on top of it and its left or right side is open, and that's where
the thinking starts: take the wrong pair and the tile you need stays
buried. Seasons match any season, flowers any flower.

It's a faithful terminal clone of GNOME Mahjongg, with the same deal
generator, so every board can be cleared. Stuck? Ask for a hint, for 30
seconds on the clock, or reshuffle, for 60.

- **Ten layouts**: Turtle, The Ziggurat, Four Bridges, Cloud,
  Tic-Tac-Toe, Red Dragon, Overpass, Pyramid's Walls, Confounding Cross
  and Taipei.
- **Mouse or keys**: click two tiles, or move a cursor and jump between
  free tiles with Tab.
- **Never lose a game in progress**: it's saved after every move and
  waits, paused, for next time.
- **Best times**: kept for every layout.
- **Fits your window**: the board is drawn at the largest size that fits.

**Find the pair. Free the tile. Clear the board.**

## Controls

The whole game plays with the mouse: click two matching tiles, or the
buttons along the top. Double-click the background to finish once every
tile is free.

- **Arrow keys** or **H J K L**: move the tile cursor
- **Tab** and **Shift+Tab**: jump between free tiles
- **Enter** or **Space**: select or match
- **U** or **Ctrl+Z**: undo; **Shift+U** or **Ctrl+Y**: redo
- **Ctrl+H**: hint (adds 30 seconds; reshuffling adds 60)
- **P** or **Esc**: pause
- **Ctrl+N**: new game; **Ctrl+R**: restart
- **S**: best times; **M** or **F10**: menu, with layouts and tile themes
- **F1**: rules; **?**: all keys
- **Q**: quit (the game is saved)

## Credits

- Mahjongg for the terminal: [radha](https://github.com/radha/mahjongg)
- Layouts and game logic: [GNOME Mahjongg](https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gnome-mahjongg), Mahjongg Contributors
- Asciiverse edition: settings, scores and saves work on Windows
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

mancala.title: Mancala
mancala.description: Seeds, pits and a lot of counting: the sowing games of Africa, Asia and Europe, from Ghana's Oware to Toguz Kumalak of the steppe, each with its own rules
mancala.provenance: Asciiverse made Mancala in Rust in 2026. Each of its nine games follows a source: the Oware Society's tournament rules, R. C. Bell (1960), E. W. Lane's account of Cairo (1836), W. J. Champion's Kalah patent (1955), M. Hellier on Malay congkak (1907), Mrs H. G. Durai on Pallanguli (1928), the Kazakh competition rules of 2013 and Fritz Jahn (1917).
mancala.page:
**SEEDS, PITS, AND A LOT OF COUNTING.**

Two rows of pits, a pile of seeds, and one move: lift every seed from a pit and sow them one at a time into the pits that follow. Where the last one lands decides everything.

That's mancala, and it isn't one game but hundreds, played from West Africa to the Philippines. They all sow; after that they argue about nearly everything. Here are nine of them:

- **Oware (Abapa)**: the Ghanaian tournament game; capture twos and threes on the other side, but never take every last seed
- **Wari**: the same family, where taking everything is simply not allowed
- **Mankal'ah, the game of the ignorant** and **the game of the wise**: the coffee-house game of 1830s Cairo, played with 72 pebbles set out by hand. Don't like how they were set out? Turn the board round, and give up the first move
- **Kalah**: the American game most people call Mancala
- **Congkak**: the Malay game on a boat-shaped board, where the sowing runs on and on from every loaded hole
- **Pallanguli**: the Tamil game, where four seeds in a hole make a cow for its owner
- **Toguz Kumalak**: nine holes of nine stones from the Kazakh steppe, where three stones in an enemy hole make it yours for good
- **Bohnenspiel**: the bean game Fritz Jahn found on a Baltic baron's estate in 1908

Some games run over several boards: Kalah to 40 points, Lane's Cairo games to 60, Pallanguli round after round until someone is cleaned out.

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Left, Right**: choose a pit; **Enter**: sow it
- **Mouse**: click a pit
- **Any key or click** while seeds are moving: finish the move
- **Lane's games**: **Up** and **Down** drop a pebble in or take one out, **Tab** jumps to the other row, **R** scatters the rest, **Enter** when your hand is empty; then **T** turns the board round, **Enter** keeps it
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides, going through the games in turn
- `--seed N`: the same game every time

mandelbrot.title: Mandelbrot
mandelbrot.description: Dive into the Mandelbrot set in coloured characters: pan with the arrows and zoom a hundred levels deep into its spirals and seahorses.
mandelbrot.provenance: David Ulrich wrote mandelbrot viewer in C on ncurses (2015 to 2016), built on Ken Perlin's one-line Mandelbrot.
mandelbrot.page:
**ZOOM IN. THEN ZOOM IN AGAIN. A HUNDRED TIMES.**

The Mandelbrot set, drawn in characters and colour bands. It opens on
the whole set, fitted to your terminal. Steer anywhere along its edge
and zoom, and the spirals, seahorses and tiny copies of the set keep
coming, a hundred levels deep, until the view is magnified about five
billion times. In a 256-colour terminal the bands run from black through
red, orange and yellow to white.

Every point is worked out live as you move, from Ken Perlin's famous
one-line Mandelbrot, with more detail the deeper you go.

**Pick a spot on the edge. Dive.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the view
- **+** or **=**: zoom in
- **-**: zoom out
- **q**, **x** or **Ctrl+C**: quit

The most detail lives along the boundary of the black shape: try the
valley between the two big bulbs, or the tips of the small buds around them.

## Credits

- mandelbrot viewer: [David Ulrich](https://github.com/dulrich/mandelbrot-viewer),
  after Ken Perlin's one-line Mandelbrot
- Asciiverse edition: a view that fits your terminal, colour
  that works, more detail as you zoom, and a zoom limit instead of a hang
- License: AGPL-3.0-only

marble-recovery.title: Marble Recovery
marble-recovery.description: They say you've lost your marbles. They're right: twelve of them, rolled off into places that should not exist. Roll, tilt and tumble through strange worlds to bring every one of them home!
marble-recovery.provenance: Asciiverse made Marble Recovery in Rust in 2026, after Marble Madness (Mark Cerny, Atari, 1984), with twelve levels of its own.
marble-recovery.page:
**THEY SAY YOU'VE LOST YOUR MARBLES.**

They're right. Twelve of them, rolled off into places that should not exist. Time to go and get them back, one at a time.

No jump button. No fire button. Just a marble, gravity and your nerve. Ease it down the slopes, coax it along the ledges and keep it rolling, because one hard landing and it shatters.

The first worlds are almost reasonable: grey checkered terraces and blue cliffs, and a little slime that doesn't chase you, it just waits for you to stop. Then come the Gulpers, who mean no harm; they simply can't tell a marble from a snack. A tide that keeps its own time. Iron bully marbles, heavy, proud and not very bright, who come straight at you without looking where they're going.

And then the madness sets in. Ice where nothing holds you back. Floors with opinions, rising and falling beneath you. Springs that throw you somewhere higher. A world where falling takes its time. Physics that shouldn't work, does!

- **Twelve hand-built levels in three acts:** Losing It, The Madness, and Recovery.
- **Race your own ghost:** your best run on every level rolls right beside you.
- **Grab a gamepad** and the stick feels like an arcade trackball. Keyboard and mouse work too.

Twelve marbles, every one of them out there somewhere. **GO AND GET THEM BACK!**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **W A S D** or **H J K L**: roll
- **Mouse**: hold a button and push toward the pointer, like a trackball
- **Gamepad**: the stick rolls
- **Enter** or **Space**: go on, **R**: restart the level, **Esc**: back, **Q**: quit
- **N** and **P**: next or previous level, **+** and **-**: zoom

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- After Marble Madness (Mark Cerny, Atari, 1984); every level here is a new design

materiamagica.title: Materia Magica
materiamagica.description: Fantasy MUD set in the world of Alyria, first opened in 1996 as Moongate

maze-tui.title: Maze TUI
maze-tui.description: Mazes carved and solved before your eyes: ten building algorithms, fourteen solvers racing on several threads in colour, and eight wall styles, all on a timeline you can pause, slow down and step back through
maze-tui.provenance: Maze TUI is by Alex G. Lopez, written in Rust from 2023 as a way to explore maze algorithms by watching them, and grown into his "Rosetta Stones and Mazes" articles.
maze-tui.page:
**EVERY MAZE TELLS YOU HOW IT WAS MADE.**

Watch a maze being carved, wall by wall, and then watch it being solved.
Maze TUI animates the classic maze algorithms in your terminal: a
randomized depth-first search tunnelling ahead and backing out of dead
ends, Prim's maze spreading like frost, Kruskal's joining scattered
pieces, Eller's sweeping row by row, Wilson's loop-erased random walks,
recursive division splitting open floor into rooms. Then the solvers move
in, several threads at once, each painting its own colour as it races for
the finish, gathers every prize or hunts for the corners.

Every animation is a timeline. Pause it, slow it to a crawl or speed it
up, step forward and back one change at a time, or run the whole thing in
reverse and watch the maze unbuild itself. Press **i** while it plays and
a page explains the algorithm on screen.

Leave it at the home screen and a new random maze builds and solves itself
behind the menu, over and over.

**Pick an algorithm and watch it think.**

## Controls

- **Enter**: a random maze, or the one your flags describe
- **Space**: pause and play
- **<** and **>**: slower and faster
- **Left** and **Right**: step back or forward, and set the direction
- **i**: about the algorithm on screen
- **Up** and **Down**: scroll the help or the algorithm page
- **Esc**: back to the home screen, and quit from there; **Ctrl+C** quits
  from anywhere

## Flags

Type them on the home screen, in any order, then press Enter. Anything
left out is chosen for you.

- `-b`: the builder: `rdfs`, `hunt-kill`, `kruskal`, `prim`, `eller`,
  `wilson`, `wilson-walls`, `fractal`, `grid` or `arena`
- `-s`: the solver: depth-first, randomized depth-first, flood fill or
  breadth-first, each as `-hunt`, `-gather` or `-corner` (for example
  `bfs-gather`), or `distance` and `runs` to paint the maze by path
  length
- `-m`: shortcuts through the middle: `cross` or `x`
- `-w`: the walls: `mini`, `sharp`, `round`, `doubles`, `bold`,
  `contrast`, `half` or `spikes`

For example `-b wilson -s bfs-hunt -w round`, or `-b fractal -s distance`.

## Credits

- Maze TUI: [Alex G. Lopez](https://github.com/agl-alexglopez/maze-tui);
  his [wiki](https://github.com/agl-alexglopez/maze-tui/wiki) covers every
  algorithm
- License: MIT

medievia.description: Long-running medieval fantasy MUD with dragons, ships, wagon trading, clans and castles

mehen.title: Mehen
mehen.description: Race your pharaohs up the coiled snake by guessing marbles in a fist, and set lions on the other team: one of Egypt's oldest games, reconstructed in 2024
mehen.provenance: Asciiverse made Mehen in Rust in 2026. No ancient rules survive; it plays James F. R. Masters' 2024 reconstruction.
mehen.page:
**RACE YOUR PHARAOHS UP THE COILED SNAKE. MIND THE LIONS.**

Five thousand years ago, Egyptians played a game on a snake: a serpent coiled round its own head, its body cut into squares, with little lions, lionesses and marbles. Then everyone stopped playing it, and the rules went with them. This is a 2024 reconstruction, built from the old boards, pieces and tomb pictures of clenched fists and open hands.

Your pharaoh is a marble at the snake's tail. Hide one to five marbles in your fist; your opponent guesses how many. They guess wrong: your pharaoh slithers forward that far. They guess right: theirs moves instead, and they may set a lion on yours!

A pharaoh held by a lion goes nowhere until the lion is dead, and killing a lion is a guessing game of its own: they hide one to three marbles, and one right guess kills it. Land on an enemy and you swap places. Two right guesses in a row bring a dead lion back. The first team to get every pharaoh to the head is reborn, and wins.

Play one against one, or teams of two or three. The computer bluffs with the mix game theory says is safest, and on hard it notices that you always hide five. Two people at one keyboard get a look-away screen while the other hides.

## Controls

- **1** to **5**, or **arrows** and **Enter**: hide or guess
- **Arrows** and **Enter**: choose a pharaoh
- **Y** (or **Enter**) or **N**: set a lion loose
- **Mouse**: click numbers, pharaohs and answers
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and what is known; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both teams
- `--seed N`: the same choices every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

memoblocks.title: Memoblocks
memoblocks.description: Memory on a board of 128 hidden tiles where only the last tile you turned stays face up: find all 64 pairs, as fast as you can.
memoblocks.provenance: abakh wrote Memoblocks for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
memoblocks.page:
**128 TILES. 64 PAIRS. ONE GOOD MEMORY.**

Every tile on a board 16 wide and 8 high hides a glyph: a digit, a letter
or a punctuation mark, in one of six colours. Every glyph is on exactly
two tiles. Turn a tile, see its glyph, find its twin.

Here's the twist: only the tile you turned last stays visible. A pair
counts only when you turn a tile directly after its match; turn anything
else and the first one hides again. So remember where everything was,
because the board won't. Find all 64 pairs and it tells you how long it
took you: "You solved it!"

- **Keys or mouse**: arrows, hjkl or wasd and Enter, or just click.
- **Against the clock**: your time is shown when the last pair is found.
- **Help at hand**: F1 for the controls, F2 for how to play.

**Turn. Remember. Match.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move the cursor
- **Enter**: turn the tile
- **Mouse**: click a tile to turn it
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Memoblocks is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

merentha.title: Merentha
merentha.description: Free fantasy LPMud set in the lands of Cardania, with guilds, spells and quests

miketron.title: Miketron
miketron.description: Steer a vehicle that never stops and can't cross its own trail, and grab pick-ups for flight, immunity and bombs to keep it running.
miketron.provenance: abakh wrote Miketron for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C; its manual page says it was copied from MikeOS.
miketron.page:
**NEVER STOP. NEVER CROSS YOUR OWN TRAIL.**

You are driving "a strange vehicle which can survive explosions but
cannot cross the trail it has left behind": the **+**. It never stops.
It leaves a trail wherever it goes. It can slip off one edge of the
board and come out on the other. Run into your own trail and it's over.
Keep it running as long as you can; the score counts up as you go.

The pick-ups are how you live:

- **?**: flight for a few moves, over the trail
- **&**: no trail for a while
- **%**: immunity for a while; trail you run over is wiped away
- **8**: a bomb that clears the board around it and sets off any bombs nearby
- **B**: five more pick-ups
- **S**: a stop; the vehicle waits until you press a key

Every hundred points, five more pick-ups and twenty pieces of loose trail
appear. The vehicle moves at half speed up and down. The board fits the
terminal, from 40 by 10 up to 80 by 24, and your best scores go on a
top-ten list. If the flashing gets to you, the game has thought of that:
"Suffering PSE? Press e."

**Turn early. Turn often. Never stop.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: change direction
- **e**: turn off the colors (for the flashing effects)
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Miketron is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. Its manual page says it was copied from MikeOS. The collection is
packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and
pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

minesweeper-4d.title: 4D Minesweeper
minesweeper-4d.description: Minesweeper on a 4x4x4x4 field: every cell touches up to 80 others across four dimensions, and the cursor lights up every one of them.
minesweeper-4d.provenance: 4D Minesweeper is itabesamesa's minesweeper_4d in Rust and Ratatui (2025), their eighth Minesweeper variant and second in four dimensions, after an earlier one in C.
minesweeper-4d.page:
**FOUR DIMENSIONS. TWENTY MINES. EIGHTY NEIGHBOURS PER CELL.**

You know Minesweeper: a number says how many mines touch a cell. Here the
field runs along x, y, z and w, drawn as a grid of grids, and a cell
touches everything one step away in any of the four directions at once:
up to 80 neighbours. Move the cursor and every cell it reaches lights up,
so you can see the shape of a 4D neighbourhood before you trust a number.

- **Delta mode** (on by default): each number counts only the mines not
  yet flagged around it, so solved areas fall to zero.
- **Sweep mode**: a flagged mine is swept away. Flag wrong and the game is
  over.
- **Marks**: tag a group of cells and see how the mines in their reach
  overlap; a way to learn 4D tactics, not a way around them.
- **Any size you like**: `-d 6 6 3 3 -m 40`, or `-d 16 16 1 1 -m 40` for
  the classic flat game.

**SWEEP SIDEWAYS.**

## Controls

- **Arrows** or **H J K L**: move in x and y; **A D**: move in z;
  **W S**: move in w. Hold **Shift** to jump to the edge
- **Space**: uncover; **M** or **E**: flag; **Shift+M**: flag every
  covered cell around the cursor; **F**: find a zero and open it
- **X**: mark; **Shift+X**: uncover the obvious marked cells;
  **Alt+X**: flag them; **Ctrl+X**: clear the marks
- **U**: delta mode; **Shift+U**: sweep mode; **I**: info box
- **N**: new game; **R**: retry; **G**: give up; **P**: pause
- **C**: controls; **O**: settings; **Q** or **Esc**: quit

## Options

- `-d X Y Z W`: field size; `-m N`: mines; `-s N -r f`: a fixed seed
- `-cm t`: play with the mouse (left uncovers, right flags)
- Ctrl+O saves the game; start with the file's name to load it

## Credits

- minesweeper_4d: [itabesamesa](https://github.com/itabesamesa/minesweeper_4d_rs)
- Asciiverse edition: starts without a config file of your own
- License: MIT

miscom.title: Miscom
miscom.description: Defend six cities from falling missiles: aim, fire, and catch the warheads in chains of explosions before they land. There are no bonus cities.
miscom.provenance: Graham Richards wrote Miscom in C on curses (1995 to 1996), a terminal take on Missile Command; Russell Marks, who wrote Ztrack, added colour and sound and released it in 1998.
miscom.page:
**SIX CITIES. THE MISSILES ARE FALLING. THERE ARE NO BONUS CITIES.**

Warheads are streaking down on your six cities. Move the sight and fire:
the nearest of your three bases with ammunition left launches a missile
that bursts into a fireball where you aimed, and any warhead that flies
into it is gone. Catch several in one blast, or let one explosion set off
the next. As the manual says, "chaining explosions together like this is
the key to not running out of ammo. Tricky to do under pressure though."

And the pressure comes. Smart missiles swerve round your explosions. A
bomber crosses low over the cities, dropping missiles of its own; it
shows as the terminal's cursor ("it's a bit weird, but you'll know it
when you see it"). Some missiles split into several warheads on the way
down, which "is extremely nasty, so watch out for it." Your bases can be
hit too, but they're rebuilt for the next level. Lost cities are not.
Lose the last one and the game is over when the level ends.

**Aim. Fire. Chain it. Save the cities.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: move the sight
- **Space**: fire
- **p**: pause
- **Ctrl+C**: quit

On the title screen, **Return** starts a game and **Esc** quits.

## Credits

- Miscom: Graham Richards, 1995 to 1996, written in C with curses
- Colour, sound, the manual and the 1998 release: Russell Marks
- After Atari's Missile Command (1980)
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

moon-buggy.title: Moon-Buggy
moon-buggy.description: Craters ahead! Time your jumps, laser the meteors rolling at you, and keep your buggy on the moon for as long as you can.
moon-buggy.provenance: Jochen Voss wrote Moon-Buggy in C on curses in 1998 and still maintains it.
moon-buggy.page:
**THE MOON IS FULL OF HOLES. YOU ARE DRIVING ACROSS IT.**

"Drive some kind of car across the moon's surface," Jochen Voss wrote. "Unfortunately there are dangerous craters there. Fortunately your car can jump over them!"

The ground rolls towards your buggy and you time every jump. Too early or too late and a wheel drops into the crater. The game eases you in with "good luck (or use `<SPC>` to jump)", warns you that "some craters are wider than others", hands you a mining laser for the meteors rolling along the ground, and then lets a whole shower of them loose with a cheerful "... but what is that?" Survive all of that and it tells you: "You may start your journey, now."

- **Jump the craters**, narrow and wide, coming faster with each level.
- **Laser the meteors**: three hits break one up, and every shot costs you a point, so make them count.
- **Three buggies** to get as far as you can.
- **A hundred places on the high score table.** The top three stay for good; the rest fade after two weeks to six months, depending on the rank, and Thorin's company of dwarves moves into the empty places.

**GOOD LUCK, DRIVER.**

## Controls

- **Space** or **j**: jump
- **a** or **l**: fire the laser
- **q** or **n**: abort the game
- **r** or **Ctrl+L**: redraw the screen

On the title screen, **Space**, **Return** or **y** starts a game,
**s** shows the scores and **q** quits.

## Options

- `-r`: drive to the right instead of the left (the whole surface is
  drawn mirrored)
- `-n`: skip the title screen
- `-s`: print the high score table and exit

## Credits

- Moon-Buggy: Jochen Voss ([github.com/seehuhn/moon-buggy](https://github.com/seehuhn/moon-buggy)),
  1998 to 2025, written in C with curses; animations for version 1.0 by
  Piotr Grzybowski
- License: GNU GPL (no version named, so any version applies)

moraen.title: Moraen
moraen.description: The ice is gone, and the dwarves' treasure lies buried in the rubble it left behind. Dig in, gather the gems and bring the clan's treasure home, before the stone trolls awake!
moraen.provenance: Asciiverse made Moraen in Rust in 2026, a love letter to the 1984 cave-digging classic.
moraen.page:
**THE ICE IS GONE. THE TROLLS ARE STIRRING.**

When the great ice came down from the north, the dwarves sealed their treasure halls and fled. For ten thousand years the glacier lay over the mountain, and the stone trolls who guard its depths froze where they stood.

Now the ice has gone. All that's left is the moraine: rock, rubble, and somewhere underneath, the gems of the old halls. You're the youngest of the clan, sent back to bring the treasure home. And deep in the mountain, the trolls are starting to thaw...

Dig through the rubble and gather the gems. Collect enough and the old hall doors swing open. Mind the boulders: the moraine is still settling, and one careless dig brings a hillside down on your head. Drop a stone on a firefly and it bursts into flames; crush a butterfly and it scatters into gems. The old dwarf rune-stone still works after ten thousand years, turning every boulder that falls through it into treasure. And something green is creeping through the halls, filling every gap: trap it and it turns to gems, let it grow and it turns to stone.

But watch the boulders closely. Some of them blink.
