A sleeping stone troll looks like any other rock, until you get close and it starts to blink. Come any closer, or let the thaw reach it, and it wakes: too heavy to climb, it stomps along the ground hurling stones at you, down from above or straight across the cave. Its touch is death. But drop a boulder on a troll and... OOF! Just another rock. And when the hall doors open, daylight floods in, and every troll turns back to stone.

- **Twenty caves and five bonus intermissions** across the land the ice left behind, from First Thaw to the troll-haunted Bergschrund.
- **Five levels of difficulty,** every cave reshuffled for each.
- **Faithful to the 1984 cave-digging classic,** down to the tick, plus trolls of our own.
- **Chunky pixel art or crisp character graphics,** keyboard or gamepad.

The clock is the thaw, and the trolls are waking. **DIG FAST!**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **W A S D**: move and dig
- **Shift** with a direction, or **Space** / **Enter** held: grab or dig the next cell without moving
- **P**: pause, **Esc**: back
- **G**: pixel art or character graphics, **+** and **-**: zoom, **0**: automatic zoom
- **Gamepad**: stick or d-pad moves, any face button grabs, Start pauses

## Options

- `--cave N`: start at cave N (1 to 25)
- `--level N`: difficulty 1 to 5
- `--glyphs` or `--pixels`: the look to start in

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- A love letter to the 1984 cave-digging classic: a faithful engine for its rules, with our own caves, hero and creatures

news.notes:
- Gamepads work on Windows: gilrs reads them through XInput, since its
  default (Windows Gaming Input) only reports to a program with a focused
  window of its own, which a terminal game never has

morgengrauen.title: MorgenGrauen
morgengrauen.description: German-language LPMud, founded by students at the University of Münster

morris.title: Morris
morris.description: Three in a row takes a man: Nine Men's Morris and its family, from the Roman game boards to Morabaraba of South Africa
morris.provenance: Asciiverse made Morris in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow R. C. Bell (1960), the World Mill Association's rules, Ralph Gasser (1996) and Mind Sports South Africa's Morabaraba rules.
morris.page:
**THREE IN A ROW TAKES A MAN.**

Place your men one at a time on the points of the board, then slide them along the lines. Three of yours in a row is a mill, and a mill takes one of your opponent's men. Every move either builds a mill, blocks one, or sets up the next. Bring your opponent down to two men, or leave them no move, and you've won.

It's been scratched into Roman bricks, cut into an oak board buried with a Viking ship, written down by a Spanish king in 1283, and it's still played the world over as the mill, merels and morris. Six forms of it:

- **Nine Men's Morris, today's rules**: the tournament game; down to three men, yours fly to any empty point
- **Nine Men's Morris after Bell**: the older game, no flying
- **Morabaraba**: South Africa's game of twelve men, with diagonals at the corners
- **Six Men's Morris**: two squares and six men each
- **Three Men's Morris**: three men each on a small square, where a mill wins outright
- **Three Men's Morris, placing only**: four counters each and no moving

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Arrows**: move the cursor; **Enter** or **Space**: enter a man, or pick one up and put it down on a lit point; **Esc**: let go, or take back a mill before it bites
- **O**: the carved ornament on or off
- **Mouse**: click a point
- After a mill, the men you may take are lit red: choose one
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same game every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

mu-torere.title: Mū tōrere
mu-torere.description: Four men each on an eight-pointed star and one empty point: the Māori blocking game of New Zealand's East Coast
mu-torere.provenance: Asciiverse made Mū tōrere in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow Elsdon Best's Games and Pastimes of the Maori (1925), as Tuta Nihoniho of Ngāti Porou explained the game to him, and the rule most often played today.
mu-torere.page:
**FOUR MEN EACH. ONE EMPTY POINT. NOWHERE TO HIDE.**

An eight-pointed star drawn round a centre, like an octopus. You have four men, your opponent has four, and there's always exactly one empty point. Move a man into it, if it's joined. Nothing is ever taken: the side that can't move has lost. It sounds simple, and it's a knife-edge.

Mū tōrere was played on the East Coast of New Zealand's North Island, on a star marked in charcoal on a plank or on bark, sometimes just scratched in the earth, and written down in 1925 from Tuta Nihoniho of Ngāti Porou.

- **The pūtahi beside an enemy**: today's common rule; a man may step into the centre only from beside an enemy man
- **Mū tōrere after Best**: the rule as first written, where it holds only for the opening move, and the side that moves second can win at once; the game shows you how

The game is small enough to be solved, and the program solves it when it starts: on hard, the computer plays perfectly.

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Arrows**: move the cursor; **Enter** or **Space**: move the man under it; the men that may move are lit
- **Mouse**: click a man
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same game every time

muncher.title: Muncher
muncher.description: Eat the food, avoid the traps, and never stop moving: every bite brings more traps onto the board.
muncher.provenance: abakh wrote Muncher for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
muncher.page:
**EAT THE FOOD. AVOID THE TRAPS. NEVER STOP MOVING.**

You are the muncher, the **r**, and you do not stop. You keep going in the direction you last gave, so every turn counts. Eat the food, the **%**, and new food appears somewhere else on the board, often with new traps, the **^**, beside it. The higher your score, the more traps there are. Touch one, or a wall, and it's over.

- **A board that fills up**: the better you do, the more traps you have to weave between.
- **Flashing food past 2000 points** makes you immune for a while. Run into traps then and they just vanish.
- **Small board, big points**: the board fits your terminal, from 40 by 10 up to 80 by 24, and a smaller board scores more for each food.
- **Up and down is slower**: the muncher moves at half speed vertically, so plan your turns.
- **A top-ten list** for your best runs.

Flashing too much? The game has thought of that: "Suffering PSE? Press e."

**HOW LONG CAN YOU KEEP EATING?**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: change direction
- **p**: pause
- **e**: stop the flashing effects
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Muncher is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

myman.title: MyMan
myman.description: Those scary ghosts are back, and this time they've spotted you! Eat every dot, dodge four ghosts and turn the tables with a power pellet, in a maze chase with several hundred mazes built in.
myman.provenance: Benjamin C. Wiley Sittler wrote MyMan from 1998 to 2017.
myman.page:
**THOSE SCARY GHOSTS ARE BACK, AND THIS TIME THEY'VE SPOTTED YOU!**

That's how Benjamin C. Wiley Sittler sets the scene, and it gets worse: they have mistaken you for their old rival, "and they're out for (yellow) blood!"

Steer MyMan round the maze and eat every dot while four ghosts hunt you, each in its own way. Grab one of the big power pellets in the corners and the tables turn: for a few seconds the ghosts run, and you eat them for points. Fruit turns up now and then for a bonus. Clear the maze, and the next one is faster.

- **Several hundred mazes built in**, from the classic layout to ones after old home-computer versions for the ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64. Pick one with `-v`.
- **Any terminal, any size**: the maze scrolls to follow you.
- **Small tiles or big ones**, and more, with `-z`.
- **Written on a dare** on a Sunday in 1998, and grown for twenty years since.

**EAT EVERY DOT. TRUST NO GHOST.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or the number pad (**4 2 8 6**): move; a turn
  pressed early is taken at the next opening
- **P** or **Esc**: pause
- **S**: sound on or off
- **C**: colour on or off
- **T**: save a screenshot, as HTML and text, in the myman folder of your
  data folder
- **?**: help, with the credits for every maze
- **Q**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, MyMan takes options; `myman -h` lists them all.

- `-v VARIANT`: one of several hundred mazes, every one built in, among
  them `pacman`, `quackman`, and ones after old home-computer versions
  such as `paczx` (ZX Spectrum) and `pac64` (Commodore 64)
- `-z SIZE`: tile size, `small` (the default) or `big`, `huge` and more
- `-l NUM`: start with NUM lives

## History

Benjamin C. Wiley Sittler wrote MyMan on a dare on 28 June 1998, as 742
lines of C; colour and the small tiles came that December, and it grew
over the next twenty years into a game with hundreds of mazes that runs
on almost anything with a screen. Toru Iwatani's Pac-Man was the
inspiration.

This edition has the Termux and Fedora build fixes. Screenshots go to
your data folder rather than the game's own folder, and the attract
screen no longer leaves the ghosts' names behind on wide terminals.

## Credits

- Game: Benjamin C. Wiley Sittler
- Build fixes: Henrik Grimler (Termux), Jiri Vymazal (Fedora)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: MIT

nannymud.title: NannyMUD
nannymud.description: LPMud hosted by Lysator at Linköping University since 1990, with guests welcome

nard.title: Nard
nard.description: Fifteen men, two dice, and a neural-network opponent that doubles like it means it: backgammon on an inlaid bazaar board, the oldest game in the family.
nard.provenance: Asciiverse made Nard in Rust in 2026. The computer player is Mark Higgins' bgsage (Open Sage), and the board's look follows Pouya Hadidi's Backgammon TUI.
nard.page:
**THE OLDEST GAME IN THE BAZAAR. THE TOUGHEST OPPONENT IN TOWN.**

Fifteen men a side, two dice, and the oldest name the backgammon family still answers to: *nard*, as the game is called from Iran to Russia.

The board is dressed like an inlaid tavla set from a bazaar: a brass wall, ivory and crimson points, a rim of Braille inlay, and on a big terminal, a ground of eight-pointed stars all around it.

And across the table sits a real opponent: bgsage, a neural-network backgammon engine. On **easy** it's friendly, picks among the plays close to the best, and never doubles. On **normal** and **hard** it thinks one and two moves ahead, and it doubles, takes and passes like a player who means it. Push your luck too far and it will gammon you.

Money play with the doubling cube, gammons and backgammons, and the score kept across the session. Or hand the other side to a friend at the same keyboard. **YOUR ROLL.**

## Controls

- **Mouse**: click a man to pick it up, a lit point to put it down, anywhere to throw, the dice to finish the turn
- **Arrows** or **h j k l**: move the cursor; **Enter** or **Space**: throw, pick up, put down
- **Letters** and **1 to 9**: pick up a man listed under the board and put it on a listed point; a man can use both dice in one go
- **Esc**, **U** or **Backspace**: take back a move; **Enter**: finish the turn
- **D**: double before throwing; **Y** or **N**: take or pass
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off; **F1** or **?**: the rules; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays itself, game after game
- `--seed N`: the same dice again
- `--plain`: start without the ornament

nbsd-sos.title: SOS
nbsd-sos.description: Write S or O, complete S-O-S lines to score, and outwit a computer that plays better every time you beat it.
nbsd-sos.provenance: abakh wrote SOS for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
nbsd-sos.page:
**THREE LETTERS. TWO PLAYERS. ONE CRY FOR HELP.**

It looks like noughts and crosses, but here nobody owns a letter. Each turn you write an S or an O in an empty square of the 5x6 board. Complete S-O-S in a straight line, across, down or diagonally, and the point is yours, and the letters take your colour. One well-placed letter can finish more than one line at once. But every letter you write is one your opponent can use too...

When the board is full, the higher score wins.

- **Play the computer, a friend, or watch**: you play blue and move first, the computer plays yellow; two people can share one keyboard, and the computer can play itself.
- **A computer that learns from you**: it starts out playing at random, plays better after you win ("I'd play better next time.") and worse after it wins. Keep beating it and it asks: "Are you human?"
- **Mouse too**: left click writes S, right click writes O.

**SPELL IT OUT.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **hjkl**: move
- **S** or **O**: write that letter
- **Mouse**: left click writes S, right click writes O
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## Options

The command is `sos`.

- `-1 h` or `-1 c`: a human or the computer plays blue
- `-2 h` or `-2 c`: the same for yellow; either one skips the questions
- `-p 3`: a fixed strength for the computer, from 1 to 127
- `-n`: quit after one game instead of offering another

## History

SOS is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

ncmatrix.title: NCMatrix
ncmatrix.description: The Matrix's falling code, with your computer's network traffic falling in it: packets sent in red, received in magenta
ncmatrix.provenance: CMatrix is by Chris Allegretta from 1999 and Abishek V Ashok from 2017, with many contributors. In 2005 Thomas Bloedorn made NCMatrix from it, painting the packets the computer sends and receives into the rain.

developer.name: Chris Allegretta, Abishek V Ashok, Thomas Bloedorn and contributors

upstream.name: Chris Allegretta, Abishek V Ashok and contributors (CMatrix); Thomas Bloedorn (NCMatrix)

ncmatrix.page:
**THE CODE IS FALLING. SOME OF IT IS YOURS.**

The falling green code of The Matrix, as CMatrix has drawn it in terminals since 1999, with one thing more: your own computer's network traffic falls in it too. Every packet sent and received is painted into the rain as a bold run, red for what goes out and magenta for what comes in. Start a download and watch magenta pour down the screen; leave the machine idle and it rains plain green.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit (Asciiverse starts it in screensaver mode)

## Options

From a terminal, `ncmatrix` without `-s` takes keys while it runs: `N`
turns the network display off and on, `a` asynchronous scroll, `b` and
`B` bold, `0` to `9` the speed, `! @ # $ % ^ &` the colour, `p` pause,
`q` quit. `-I wlan0` (or `en0` on a Mac, `Wi-Fi` on Windows) shows one
interface only, `-T` and `-R` change the traffic colours, `-c` uses
Japanese characters. `ncmatrix -h` lists them all.

## Credits

- CMatrix: [Chris Allegretta, Abishek V Ashok and contributors](https://github.com/abishekvashok/cmatrix)
- Network display: Thomas Bloedorn, NCMatrix 1.0 (2005)
- Asciiverse edition: the network display carried over to CMatrix
  and fixed, traffic read on macOS and Windows too, quits cleanly
  on SIGTERM and SIGHUP
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

neon-rain.title: Neon Rain
neon-rain.description: A rainy city street at night seen from above: buzzing neon signs mirrored on the wet road, cars with headlight beams, people under umbrellas and the odd flash of lightning
neon-rain.provenance: Asciiverse made Neon Rain in Rust in 2026, after a GIF of Terminal Rain, a cyberpunk roguelike shown on the TIGSource forums from 2015 that was never released.
neon-rain.page:
**THE CITY NEVER SLEEPS. TONIGHT IT'S JUST GETTING WET.**

A city street at night in the rain, seen from straight above. NOODLES, KARAOKE, PACHINKO, 24H MART: neon signs hum over the shopfronts, buzz off now and then or lose a letter, and their colours run down the wet road in shimmering streaks. Cars, trucks and scooters swish past with their headlight beams sweeping the tarmac, and now and then a police car flashes red and blue. People under umbrellas walk the pavements, wait at the crossing while the traffic stops, or mill about in a lit lobby. Steam drifts from the manholes, rain streaks pick up the colour of whatever light they fall through, puddles ripple, and once in a while lightning flashes over the rooftops.

Every start lays out a new street to fit the window.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `neon-rain -s 7` lays out the same street every time.
It draws in full RGB colour, and in 256 colours on terminals that do not
report truecolor.

## Credits

- Neon Rain: Asciiverse, after a GIF of Terminal Rain, an unreleased
  cyberpunk roguelike shown on the TIGSource forums
- License: MIT

netgame.title: Net
netgame.description: Turn the tiles until every pipe joins one network at the centre, no loose ends and no loops: the classic net (netwalk) rotation puzzle.
netgame.provenance: Ben Falconer wrote Netgame in 2010, the net puzzle in a single C++ file that draws with ANSI escape codes.
netgame.page:
**ONE SOURCE. ONE NETWORK. NO LOOSE ENDS.**

A grid of scrambled pipe pieces: straights, corners, T junctions and dead ends. At the centre sits the source, and everything joined to it glows green. Turn the tiles one by one until every single piece is part of one network, with no loose ends and no loops. The count under the board tells you how close you are.

- **Turn either way**: clockwise or anticlockwise, one key each.
- **Lock what you're sure of**, so a stray key cannot turn it again.
- **Any size you like**, from 2 to 99 tiles a side, and a wrapping mode where pipes run off one edge and back in at the other.
- **A fresh puzzle on n**, the moment the whole board lights up.

**LIGHT IT ALL UP.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the cursor
- **Space** or **.**: turn the tile clockwise
- **,**: turn it anticlockwise
- **l** or **s**: lock or unlock the tile
- **n**: new puzzle
- **q** or **Ctrl+C**: quit

From a terminal, `netgame 15 20` plays on another size (2 to 99), and
`--wrapping` lets pipes run off one edge and back in at the other.

## Credits

- Netgame: [Ben Falconer](https://github.com/zed0/Netgame), under the MIT
  licence
- Asciiverse edition: wider tiles, n for a new puzzle, a clean exit on Ctrl+C, and a Windows build

nethack.title: NetHack
nethack.description: The great dungeon crawl: down through the Mazes of Menace and Gehennom for the Amulet of Yendor, with your pet at your side
nethack.provenance: Mike Stephenson merged the descendants of Andries Brouwer's Hack into NetHack 1.4 in 1987, and the NetHack DevTeam has developed it ever since.
nethack.page:
**DOWN THERE IS THE AMULET OF YENDOR. YOUR GOD WANTS IT.**

Go down through the Mazes of Menace, past the Gnomish Mines, Sokoban's boulder puzzles and the Oracle, all the way into Gehennom, and bring the Amulet back for your god. Choose one of thirteen roles, from Archeologist and Valkyrie to Wizard and Tourist, and take your kitten, little dog or pony along.

Everything is a character on the map, and almost anything you think of trying works: dip, engrave, pray, polymorph, kick, bargain with shopkeepers. Write Elbereth in the dust and many monsters will not dare step on it. Death is final, and when it comes the game asks, politely: "Do you want your possessions identified?"

- **Almost forty years in the making**, and still going: 5.0.0 came out in May 2026.
- **New to it?** Say yes to the tutorial at the start.

**THE DUNGEON IS WAITING.**

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift**, run
- **F** and a direction: fight; **t**: throw, **z**: zap a wand
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T**
  take off, **P** put on, **R** remove, **a** apply
- **o** and **c**: open and close doors; **s**: search; **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **#**: extended commands, such as `#pray`
- **?**: help, **;**: what is that symbol, **Ctrl-P**: earlier messages
- **S**: save and quit

## Saving and options

**S** saves the game to your data folder (`~/.local/share/nethack`), and
starting NetHack again carries on from there. Your options go in
`~/.nethackrc`, or in `nethackrc` in that folder. At the end of each game
a full account of it is written to its `dumplog` folder.
`OPTIONS=windowtype:curses` switches to the curses interface.

## History

NetHack grew from Hack, which Jay Fenlason wrote with Kenny Woodland,
Mike Thome and Jon Payne after Rogue and Andries Brouwer reworked at the
Mathematisch Centrum in Amsterdam (Hack 1.0.3, 1985, is also in the
catalog). Mike Stephenson merged its descendants into NetHack 1.4 in 1987,
and the NetHack DevTeam took it on from there. NetHack 3.6 came out in
2015; the next release, long known as 3.7, became 5.0.0 on 2 May 2026,
with over 3100 fixes and changes and its levels written in Lua.

This edition is built for Linux and macOS, keeping everything it writes
in your own data folder.

## Credits

- Game: the NetHack DevTeam and contributors, after Hack by Jay
  Fenlason, Kenny Woodland, Mike Thome, Jon Payne and Andries Brouwer
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: NetHack General Public License

nettoe.title: netToe
nettoe.description: Noughts and crosses against the computer at three levels, a friend at your keyboard, or a friend on another machine over the network.
nettoe.provenance: Gabriele Giorgetti wrote netToe in C in 2000 and 2001, and Mats Erik Andersson maintained it until 2014.

upstream.name: Gabriele Giorgetti and Mats Erik Andersson

nettoe.page:
**THREE IN A ROW. HOW HARD CAN IT BE?**

Noughts and crosses, the game everyone knows, with three ways to play it: against the computer at one of three levels, against a friend sharing your keyboard, or against a friend on another machine over the network. A running score is kept for as long as you both keep saying yes to one more game.

How hard can it be? That depends on the level. Weak is easily fooled. Normal goes for its own wins first. Better checks every winning and blocking move, and you will have to set a real trap to beat it.

- **Head to head over the network**: one of you hosts, the other types in the address, and you play direct, with no server in between.
- **Its own little history**: written in 2000 and 2001 by Gabriele Giorgetti, in Debian since 2001, and taken over in 2009 by Mats Erik Andersson, who added the hardest computer level.

**YOUR MOVE.**

## Controls

Moves and menus are typed and confirmed with **Enter**:

- **a1** to **c3**: your move, row (a, b, c) then column (1, 2, 3), as the
  coordinate grid beside the board shows
- the number of a menu item, or **q** to go back or quit
- **y** or **n** after a game: play again or not

## Playing over the network

One of you hosts: choose Two players over network, then Host the game,
and type a name. The screen lists this machine's addresses; tell your
friend one of them. Your friend chooses Connect to host and types that
address or the host's name. The game uses TCP port 7501, so the host's
firewall has to let it in; on a home network that usually means nothing
at all. Play is direct between the two machines, there is no server in
between.

## Options

- `-4`, `-6`: IPv4 or IPv6 only (both by default)
- `-nb`: no beeps; `-nc`: no colours

## History

Gabriele Giorgetti wrote netToe in 2000 and 2001, adding colours in 1.1.0
(July 2001); Debian has carried it since June 2001 (1.0.5). Mats Erik Andersson took it over in 2009 and added the
harder computer level, IPv6 and terminfo support, releasing 1.5.1 in March
2014, the last version.

The Asciiverse edition adds three fixes: the host screen now lists the
addresses a friend can actually connect to (it used to suggest 127.0.1.1
on many systems), colours no longer turn the screen bright red on
256-colour terminals when they reset, and prompts appear in the static
Linux build.

nflood.title: nFlood
nflood.description: One corner, six colours: flood the whole board with a single colour in as few moves as you can. The record to beat starts at 25.
nflood.provenance: Alexandre Dantas wrote nFlood, a Flood-It puzzle in C and ncurses, between 2011 and 2014, with help from Yu-Jie Lin.
nflood.page:
**ONE CORNER. SIX COLOURS. CAN YOU BEAT 25?**

A 14 by 14 board in six colours, and your patch starts in the top left corner. Pick a colour, and your patch turns that colour, swallowing every neighbouring cell that already had it. Pick again. And again. Keep going until the whole board is one colour. The fewer moves it takes, the better.

It sounds like there is nothing to it. Then you start counting. Grab the colour with the most cells along your edge, or the one that opens a road into the far corner?

- **One key per colour**, 1 to 6, or click a colour in the panel, or any cell on the board.
- **A best score to beat**, kept for the standard board. Before your first win, it stands at 25 moves.
- **Bigger or smaller boards** from a terminal, just for fun.

**DROWN THE BOARD.**

## Controls

- **1** to **6**: flood with that colour (the panel shows which is which)
- **Mouse**: click a colour in the panel, or any cell of the board, to
  flood with its colour
- **r**: a new board (or click "r: New Game")
- **c**: centre the board, or move it back to the corner
- **q**: quit

After "Congrats!", **r** plays another board and any other key quits.

## Options

- `-W <width>`, `-H <height>`: a board of another size (only the
  standard 14x14 counts for the best score)

## Files

The best score is kept in `~/.local/share/nflood` (`%APPDATA%\nflood` on
Windows). It starts at 25 before any game is won.

## History

Alexandre Dantas wrote nFlood, his terminal version of the Flood-It
puzzle, between 2011 and 2014, with Yu-Jie Lin adding mouse support,
custom board sizes and the best score. This edition has fixes so it
builds with current compilers and deals a different board each time it
starts, the best score in the player's data folder and shown as soon as
it is set, a working New Game click and a Windows build.

## Credits

nFlood is by Alexandre Dantas and Yu-Jie Lin, under the GNU GPL version
3 or later. Its option parser is TJ Holowaychuk's Commander (MIT).

nhfourk.title: NetHack Fourk
nhfourk.description: NetHack rebalanced, with NetHack 4's friendlier interface: autoexplore, travel, status bars, an inventory sidebar and levels you can look back on
nhfourk.provenance: Nathan Eady began NetHack Fourk in 2014 as a variant of NetHack 4, Alex Smith's reworking of NetHack 3.4.3 from AceHack and Daniel Thaler's NitroHack, and still maintains it for the Hardfought servers.

upstream.name: Nathan Eady, after NetHack 4 by Alex Smith and others

nhfourk.page:
**THE SAME DEADLY DUNGEON. A LESS HOSTILE INTERFACE.**

The Amulet of Yendor still lies at the bottom, past the Mazes of Menace, the Gnomish Mines, Sokoban and Gehennom, and the dungeon still wants you dead. What has changed is everything around it. NetHack 4 set out to give NetHack "a less hostile interface"; Nathan Eady's NetHack Fourk takes that and adds the balance changes NetHack 4 would not.

- **Autoexplore and travel**: **v** explores until something turns up, **_** walks you to any spot.
- **Status bars** for health and power, and **an inventory sidebar** on a wide terminal.
- **Every level remembered**: look back on any level you have seen.
- **Fewer ways to kill yourself with a typo.**
- **Rebalanced**: races matter for your limits and skills, Barbarians are the strongest fighters, ranged weapons and multishot reworked, amnesia gone. A new race, the sylph, and new levels and monster tricks.
- **Roles you earn**: you start as a human Barbarian or Wizard, and the rest unlock as you achieve things in play, and stay unlocked. The Archeologist? Win the game first.

It is the version played on the Hardfought public servers.

**ASCEND. THEN COME BACK AS AN ARCHEOLOGIST.**

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**, the cursor keys or the number pad: move, the last
  four letters diagonally; walking into a door opens it
- **F** and a direction: fight; **t**: throw, **f**: fire, **z**: zap
- **v**: explore automatically until something turns up
- **_**: travel to a spot (`<` or `>` there picks the stairs)
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **a** apply, **A** change your
  equipment (wield, wear, put on, take off, all in one)
- **s**: search, **.**: rest; a number first repeats, as in `20s`
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up; **Ctrl-O**: the levels you remember
- **#**: extended commands, such as `#pray`; **Ctrl-E**: write Elbereth
- **?**: help, **;**: what is that, **Ctrl-P**: earlier messages,
  **!**: the game menu
- **S**: save and quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder (`~/.local/share/nhfourk`);
pick it with **load game** in the main menu to carry on. Your options
(set from the main menu or with **O** in a game), the score list and a
full account of every finished game are kept there too.

## History

NetHack 4 began when Alex Smith merged his AceHack with Daniel Thaler's
NitroHack, two forks of NetHack 3.4.3, and rewrote much of the game's
insides and all of its interface while keeping the gameplay
conservative. Nathan Eady started NetHack Fourk from it in 2014 to try
out the balance changes NetHack 4 would not take, and still maintains
it; this edition is built for the terminal only, with its files in your
own data folder. NetHack itself is in the catalog too.

## Credits

- NetHack Fourk: Nathan Eady
- NetHack 4: Alex Smith and contributors, from AceHack and Daniel
  Thaler's NitroHack
- NetHack: the NetHack DevTeam, Stichting Mathematisch Centrum and
  M. Stephenson
- License: NetHack General Public License

ninuki.title: Ninuki
ninuki.description: Five in a row, with captures: flank two of your opponent's stones to take them, and win with five in a line or five pairs taken. Against the computer at six strengths, or a friend.
ninuki.provenance: William Shubert wrote this program between 1994 and 2001 as pente, and Debian has shipped it under that name since 1996. It plays five in a row with captures, known in Japan as Ninuki-renju.
ninuki.page:
**FIVE IN A ROW. TWO AT A TIME.**

Five in a row, with one twist that changes everything: captures. Put a
stone at each end of two of your opponent's, and both come off the
board. Five in a line wins, and so does taking five pairs, so every
attack leaves a weakness and every pair you build can be taken.

Play the computer at any of six strengths, or a friend at the same
keyboard. The opening rule: the first stone goes in the centre, and the
first player's second stone at least three points away from it.

## Controls

- **I J K M**, or **P B F N**: move the cursor up, left, right and down
- **Space** or **Enter**: place a stone
- **U**: undo; **R**: restart; **L**: redraw; **Q**: quit
- At the start, for each side: **0** for a person, **1** to **6** for
  the computer

## Credits

- William Shubert's pente 2.2.5 (2001), the program Debian ships as
  `pente`, with Debian's patches
- Ninuki-renju: the name in Japan for five in a row with captures
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

ninvaders.title: nInvaders
ninvaders.description: Mankind believes in you! Hold back the marching alien block from behind four crumbling bunkers, and pick off the UFO for 500 points.
ninvaders.provenance: Thomas Dettbarn wrote nInvaders in C on ncurses in 2002 and 2003 with Alexander Hollinger, Sebastian Gutsfeld and Matthias Thar, with code by Mike Saarna.
ninvaders.page:
**MANKIND BELIEVES IN YOU.**

"Right now you are earth's only hope to save it from alien invaders from space," says the README. "Make your job, and make it good, mankind believes in you..."

Rows of aliens march side to side and drop a step closer each time they reach the edge, bombing you as they come. Slide your gun along the bottom and shoot them down before they land. Four bunkers shelter you, and crumble with every hit. And now and then a UFO crosses the top of the screen, worth 500 points if you can lead your shot.

- **Points by the row**: 100, 150 and 200 points, more the higher they sit, and 500 for the UFO.
- **They get faster** as the block thins out and as the levels go by.
- **Ten skill levels**, from 0, which the game calls "NIGHTMARE", to 9, "May I play daddy?!"
- **A TOP 10 at last**: the high score table its authors wrote in 2003 and never released, finished, with a table for expert, normal and beginner play.

**DON'T LET THEM LAND.**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**, or **h** and **l**: move; hold the key down to
  move faster
- **Space** or **k**: fire
- **p**: pause, and again to go on
- **q**: quit
- **Space** on the title screen: start a game

## High scores

A score that makes the TOP 10 asks for your name after the game over
banner: type up to 8 letters and press **Enter**. The title screen shows
the table between its alien parades. Each skill level plays for its own
table: `-l 0` for the expert one, the default for the normal one, and
`-l 2` to `-l 9` for the beginner one. The table is kept in your own
folder (`~/.local/share/ninvaders/highscore`, or `%APPDATA%\ninvaders` on
Windows), so it survives updates.

## Options

- `-l 0` to `-l 9`: the skill level, from 0 (the game calls it "NIGHTMARE")
  to 9 ("May I play daddy?!"); 1 is the default
- `-gpl`: show the licence

## History

Thomas Dettbarn ("dettus") wrote nInvaders in 2002 with Alexander
Hollinger, Sebastian Gutsfeld and Matthias Thar, and code by Mike
Saarna; 0.1.1 (May 2003) added the title screen and a timer that made it
playable on more systems, and was the last release. Alexander Hollinger
and Sebastian Gutsfeld went on to add a high score table that summer,
which was never released; this edition has Debian's patches and brings
that table in, finished.

The Asciiverse runs the game in a loop instead of from a timer signal,
which makes it steadier and lets it run on Windows, and sends only what changes
to the terminal instead of repainting it 50 times a second. Each game now
plays out differently: the original never seeded its random numbers, so
every game was the same.

nsnake.title: nSnake
nsnake.description: The classic snake game in your terminal: eat the fruit, grow longer, don't bite yourself. Arcade mode, 31 levels and a pile of game modes.
nsnake.provenance: Alexandre Dantas wrote nSnake in C++ and ncurses from 2012 to 2014.
nsnake.page:
**EAT. GROW. DON'T BITE YOURSELF.**

The snake game everyone played on their phone, now in your terminal. Steer the snake to the fruit; every fruit makes it longer, and longer makes it harder. Run into a wall or your own tail and it's over.

Arcade Mode is the classic, on an open board. Or pick one of 31 levels in Level Select: arenas, spirals, three hearts ("Cute, right?"), the word NSNAKE spelled out in walls ("How meta. Watch out for the letter K!"), and Tricky, which its author signs off with: "Let's see you survive on this baby. While it scrolls."

- **31 levels**, each with its own high score, and your own levels from plain text files.
- **Make it your game**: starting speed 1 to 10, how many fruits at once, board size, teleporting through the edges, random walls, and a board that scrolls under you. Scores are kept for every combination.
- **Every key remappable**, and colours and borders to taste.

**HOW LONG CAN YOU GET?**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: steer the snake
- **p**: pause, **h**: help during a game
- **q**: quit at any time
- **Enter**: choose in the menus

Every key can be changed in the Controls menu, and colours and borders
in GUI Options.

## Levels

Levels are plain text files ending in `.nsnake`. Besides the 31 that
come with the game, nSnake reads your own from the `levels` folder in
its data folder (`~/.local/share/nsnake/levels`), where its settings
and scores are kept too.

## History

Alexandre Dantas wrote nSnake in C++ and ncurses from 2012 to 2014; it
is packaged by Debian, Fedora and others. This edition has a few fixes:
the bundled levels are found without copying them by hand, settings
follow `XDG_DATA_HOME`, and it builds for Windows.

nstars.title: nstars
nstars.description: Fly through a starfield: stars stream out from the centre and brighten as they rush past
nstars.provenance: nstars is the ncurses version of Philip J Freeman's stars, in C, from 2016 to 2020.
nstars.page:
**FULL SPEED AHEAD. MIND THE STARS.**

The classic starfield: you are flying forward through space, and stars stream out from the centre of the screen, faint and grey far away, brightening to white as they rush past the edges. Below the sky sits a small console with a frame counter and a command line, in the style of an IRC client: type `/sleep` to change your speed, or `/char` to draw the stars with any character you like.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit (while the command line is empty)
- **/**: start a command, then **Enter** to run it
- **Up** and **Down**: earlier commands
- **Esc** or **Ctrl+C**: quit at any time

## Commands

- `/sleep 10000`: the pause between frames in microseconds; higher is slower
- `/char *`: draw the stars with another character
- `/colormode mono` or `/colormode 256`: plain or shaded stars
- `/quit`: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `nstars -s '*'` sets the star character and `-c 256` (how
Asciiverse starts it) shades the stars; `-c mono` draws them plain.

## Credits

- stars and nstars: [Philip J Freeman](https://github.com/ph1l/stars)
- Asciiverse edition: any key quits, a memory fix and a Windows
  build
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

nudoku.title: nudoku
nudoku.description: Fresh sudoku every time, easy, normal or hard, with marks that show where a number can still go, hints, undo and a saved game.
nudoku.provenance: Michael Vetter (jubalh) has written nudoku in C and ncurses since 2014, with contributors adding translations.
nudoku.page:
**NINE ROWS. NINE COLUMNS. NINE BOXES. ONE OF EACH.**

Fill every row, column and 3x3 box with the numbers 1 to 9, each exactly once. nudoku deals you a fresh puzzle every time, easy, normal or hard, and then stays out of your way: move around the board, type numbers into the empty cells, and ask it to check your work whenever you like. "Correct so far"? Keep going.

- **Marks** light up every copy of the number under the cursor, so you can see at a glance where a 7 can still go.
- **Hints** when you are stuck: one cell filled in for you, and the count shown when you finish.
- **Undo, save and come back later**: a game in progress picks up where you left it.
- **Your own puzzles**: give one as a line of 81 characters.
- **Help in nine more languages**, from German and Japanese to Georgian and Vietnamese (Linux builds).

**JUST ONE MORE PUZZLE.**

## Controls

- **h j k l** or the **arrow keys**: move
- **1** to **9**: put a number in the cell, **x**, **Delete** or
  **Backspace** to clear it
- **u**: undo
- **c**: check the board so far
- **H**: a hint
- **m**: marks on or off
- **N**: a new puzzle
- **S**: show the solution
- **G**: save the game
- **r**: redraw
- **Q** or **Escape**: quit

## Options

- `-d easy`, `-d normal`, `-d hard`: the difficulty (easy unless given)
- `-r`: resume the saved game
- `-c`: no colours
- `-s <81 characters>`: play a puzzle of your own, given as one line of
  digits with `.` for the empty cells; `-o` prints a new one that way

The help text is translated into German, Spanish, French, Japanese,
Georgian, Russian, Turkish, Ukrainian and Vietnamese, chosen from your
language settings (Linux builds).

## Files

The saved game is kept in `~/.local/state/nudoku` (`%LOCALAPPDATA%\nudoku`
on Windows).

## History

Michael Vetter started nudoku in 2014 and has kept it going since, with
translations from contributors; it is packaged by Debian and many
others. This edition has the translations found beside the program,
saving that works in a fresh home folder, and a Windows build. The
optional export of puzzles to PDF and PNG is not included.

## Credits

nudoku is by Michael Vetter and contributors, under the GNU GPL version
3 or later.

nuzzle.title: Nuzzle
nuzzle.description: Three block-placing puzzles: drop the pieces, fill rows, columns, squares or colour groups to clear them, and keep going as long as anything still fits.
nuzzle.provenance: Dead End wrote nuzzle in C on ncurses (2019 to 2023), a collection of three block-placing puzzles.
nuzzle.page:
**THREE PIECES. ONE BOARD. WILL ANYTHING STILL FIT?**

Three pieces wait beside the grid. Pick one up, slide it into place, drop it. Fill a row or a column completely and it clears, one point for every block removed. Place all three and you get three new ones... right up to the moment none of them fits anywhere. Then it's over.

Nuzzle (an N-curses p-UZZLE, says its author) is three games in one:

- **Lines**: one colour on a 10x11 board; full rows and columns clear.
- **Squares-and-Lines**: a 9x9 board split into nine 3x3 squares; a full square clears as well as a full row or column.
- **Four-Colors**: one piece at a time, its blocks in four colours; four or more touching blocks of the same colour clear.

Each game keeps its own high score, and you can play with the keyboard or the mouse.

**MAKE ROOM.**

## Controls

- **Tab**: pick up a piece, or switch to the next one
- **Arrow keys**: move the piece onto the board, then around it
- **Enter**: drop the piece
- **Mouse**: click a piece to pick it up, move it without holding the
  button, click again to drop it; right click puts it back
- **Esc** or **m**: menu (continue, or start another game)
- **q** or **Ctrl+C**: quit

## Credits

- nuzzle: [Dead End](https://github.com/dead-end/nuzzle), under the MIT
  licence
- Asciiverse edition: scores in your data folder, colours for any
  256-colour terminal, and crash fixes

ohm.title: Ohm's Workshop
ohm.description: The old master's workshop is yours now. Fix the town's gadgets with real circuits and watch them glow, click and blink... or smoke, sizzle and pop!
ohm.provenance: Asciiverse made Ohm's Workshop in Rust in 2026, in the family of SHENZHEN I/O, Retro Gadgets and Turing Complete, with a real circuit solver at its heart.
ohm.page:
**THE OLD MASTER'S BENCH IS YOURS NOW.**

Welcome to Ohms Verkstad, the little electronics repair shop the whole town still calls Ohm's. It's the early eighties, you're the new apprentice, the old master's notebook is on the shelf, and the inbox is already filling up.

Mrs Berg's bike lamp keeps blowing its bulb. Elsa, who is eight, wants her doll's house lit upstairs and down. The last repairman's resistor in Café Ohlsson's van sign went up in smoke, the harbour club's model lighthouse has to flash like the real one, and on Mr Nilsson's model railway the barrier drops before the little cars are across.

Pull open the parts drawers, lay the copper, drop in a resistor... and watch. The circuit is alive while you build it: current ripples through the traces, LEDs glow, relays click and capacitors slowly fill. And get it wrong? That's a show too! Resistors glow red, then smoke. LEDs flare and die. A capacitor in backwards vents with a CRACK. One key puts the burnt parts back.

Then the test bench has its say: fresh batteries and tired ones, a bright day and a dark night. Pass, and the gadget goes home to its owner. Then see if you can match the old master himself: as cheap as his build, and lasting as long on a battery.

- **A real circuit solver underneath:** real volts, real milliamps, real parts, real kronor. What works here works on a breadboard.
- **From a bike lamp to your first chip:** 34 jobs in six chapters, through resistors, capacitors, relays, diodes, transistors and logic, one customer at a time.
- **The Master's Notebook:** a page for every idea, each with a live circuit you can switch and measure.
- **A multimeter and a scope** that read whatever you point at, and a sandbox to build anything you like.
- **Mouse, keyboard or gamepad,** whichever sits best in your hands.
- **No timer, no pressure.** Poke, measure, think, and try again.

The whole town is counting on you. **DON'T LET THE MAGIC SMOKE OUT!**

## Controls

Mouse and keyboard work together: point at a part with the mouse and press a key to act on it.

- **Arrow keys**: move the cursor; with **Shift**: lay copper behind it; **C**: lay copper with plain arrows
- **Mouse**: drag to lay copper, click to place a part, right click to erase, click a switch to flip it, the wheel turns a knob, a middle drag moves round the workbench
- **Space** or **Enter**: place the selected part, **R**: rotate, **X** or **Del**: erase
- **Tab** or **0** to **9**: pick a drawer (0 is copper), **D**: every drawer as cards
- **E**: operate the part under the cursor, **P**: clip the scope's probe on
- **T**: run the test bench, **F**: mend burnt parts
- **U** or **Ctrl+Z**: undo, **Ctrl+Y**: redo
- **N**: the Master's Notebook, **B**: the card binder, **PgUp** and **PgDn**: the previous or next job
- **M**: sound on or off, **Esc**: back, **Ctrl+Q**: quit
- **F1** or **?**: help, anywhere
- **Gamepad**: d-pad or left stick moves, **A** places (hold it and move to lay copper), **B** erases, **X** rotates, **Y** operates, the shoulders change drawer, the triggers undo and redo, **Start** runs the test bench; hold **Back** for the Notebook, the binder, help and the rest

## Options

- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Every electronics fact checked against a real datasheet or standard, listed on its Notebook page

omega.title: Omega
omega.description: The roguelike with a whole world: start in the city of Rampart, join its guilds and orders, then take on the countryside, its villages and its dungeons. Many ways to win.
omega.provenance: Laurence R. Brothers wrote Omega between 1987 and 1989; Erik Max Francis and others carried it on into the 1990s, and Lyle Tafoya has continued it in C++ as Omega Rebirth since 2019.
omega.page:
**A WHOLE WORLD, NOT JUST A DUNGEON.**

Most roguelikes give you a staircase and a long way down. Omega gives
you a world. You begin at the gates of Rampart, a city with a Duke,
guilds, temples, a college of magic, banks, shops and a few places you
would do well to stay out of. Beyond its walls lies a countryside of
villages, wilderness, special sites and dungeons, each with a master at
the bottom.

There are many ways to win. Rise to the head of the Legion, the
Thieves' Guild, the Collegium Magii, the Order of Paladins, the Circle of
Sorcerors or a priesthood of one of the gods; grow rich; or go after the
total winner's crown, with the Oracle to point the way. The hall of fame
remembers who holds every title.

## Controls

- **h j k l y u b n**: walk (or fight), the keypad too
- **H J K L Y U B N**: run until something is worth a stop
- **i**: inventory; **g**: pick up; **t**: talk; **x**: examine
- **m**: cast a spell; **M**: go straight to a place you know in the city
- **<** and **>**: up and down; **.**: rest a turn
- **?**: help, with every command; **S**: save and quit; **Q**: quit

## Credits

- Omega: Laurence R. Brothers (1987 to 1989), carried on by Erik Max
  Francis, Nathan Glasser, Robert Rendell, William Tanksley and others
- Omega Rebirth, the C++ continuation: [Lyle Tafoya](https://github.com/Lyle-Tafoya/Omega)
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

pachisi.title: Pachisi and Chaupar
pachisi.description: Four colours round a cross of four arms, thrown with six cowrie shells or three long dice: the game that became Ludo
pachisi.provenance: Asciiverse made Pachisi and Chaupar in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow Rajendralala Mitra's account printed by Edward Tylor (1879), Edward Falkener (1892, reprinted by R. C. Bell) and Abu'l-Fazl's Ain-i Akbari (about 1590).
pachisi.page:
**THE GAME THAT BECAME LUDO, AS EMPERORS PLAYED IT.**

A cross of four arms, four colours of four men, partners sitting opposite. Each man leaves the middle (in chaupar they start out on the board), runs right round the cross and comes home again: 84 steps. Land on an enemy and he goes back to the start, unless he sits on a castle. A pair holds its square; but play Falkener's rules and a pair is at its own peril, and one man takes them both! The partnership with all eight men home first wins.

At the emperor Akbar's court, around 1590, a sitting of sixteen games could last three months, and a player who lost patience had to drink a cup of wine. The name comes from the best throw of the cowrie shells, twenty-five: pachis. The English took it home in the 1880s, and called it Ludo.

- **Pachisi after Tylor**: six cowries, the rules as recorded from Calcutta in 1879
- **Pachisi after Falkener**: the rules of 1892, as Bell reprinted them
- **Chaupar after Abu'l-Fazl**: three long dice and no castles, the game of Akbar's court

Play the computer at three strengths, from either partnership, or a friend at the same keyboard; each side plays both colours of its partnership.

## Controls

- **Enter** or **Space**: throw; then arrows to a lit man, **Enter** to pick it up, a lit square to put it down; men sharing a square can march on together; **Esc**: let go; **P**: leave the rest of the throws unused
- **Mouse**: click
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same game every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

pacvim.title: PacVim
pacvim.description: Learn vim by playing it: steer the cursor over every letter in the maze with vim's motions, w, b, e, $, gg and the rest, while ghosts hunt you down. Ten levels.
pacvim.provenance: Jamal Moon wrote PacVim in C++ and ncurses in 2014 to make learning vim fun, with contributors adding to it until 2018.
pacvim.page:
**THE GHOSTS DON'T USE VIM. YOU DO.**

Every level is a maze of words. Your cursor has to pass over every letter until the whole maze turns green, while red ghosts close in. Walls can't be walked through, but vim's motions jump over them: **w** to the next word, **$** to the end of the line, **gg** to the top. Step on a **~** and you lose a life.

It's the friendliest way there is to get vim's motions into your fingers, and a tense little maze game besides.

- **Ten levels**, from a gentle first maze to word-filled labyrinths
- **Real vim motions**: words, WORDs, line ends, line numbers
- **A life back** after levels 0, 3, 6 and 9; after level 9 it starts again with faster ghosts
- **Two speeds**: hard by default, or `pacvim n` for slower ghosts

## Controls

- **h j k l**: left, down, up, right
- **w** / **W**: forward to the next word or WORD
- **e** / **E**: forward to the end of a word or WORD
- **b** / **B**: back to the start of a word or WORD
- **0** / **$**: start or end of the line; **^**: first word on the line
- **gg** or **1G**: first line; **G**: last line; a number then **G**: that line
- **Enter**: start a level; **q**: quit (**Esc** too, on the screen before each level)

## Options

- `pacvim N`: start at level N (0 to 9)
- `pacvim n` or `pacvim h`: normal or hard ghosts; `pacvim 4 n` combines them

## Credits

- PacVim: [Jamal Moon](https://github.com/jmoon018/PacVim) and contributors
- License: LGPL-3.0-or-later

panzer.title: Panzer
panzer.description: It is time to make a stand in toyland! Toy tanks - real ricochets! Bank your shells off the walls, plant your mines, and outfox nine enemy tanks with nine nasty tricks, all the way to the Last Stand!
panzer.provenance: Asciiverse made Panzer in Rust in 2026, after Wii Play's Tanks (Nintendo, 2006).
panzer.page:
**TOY TANKS. REAL RICOCHETS.**

Twenty missions. One little tank. And a whole toy box of enemy tanks that want you scorched off the map!

Every shell you fire bounces off the walls, and so does every shell they fire. Bank a shot round a corner! Shoot their shells clean out of the air! Drop a mine behind a crate and back away very, very slowly. You get five shells and two mines at a time, and one hit is all it takes. For them, and for you.

Meet the opposition:

- **Tinpot** can't move. It just sweeps its turret, waiting for the bounce.
- **Plodder** wanders about. Thump. Thump. Thump.
- **Hornet** hangs back and fires rockets twice as fast as your shells.
- **Skitter** dashes about in a nervous panic, sowing mines as it goes.
- **Rascal** comes straight for you, three shells at a time.
- **Sniper** never moves, and never misses the angle you forgot.
- **Viper** banks its shots, dodges yours and lays the odd mine.
- **Ghost** is invisible. Its tread marks are not. And it hums.
- And **Onyx**? The big black one. It will not stop coming.

Listen closely! Every enemy has its own engine voice, and the battle march picks up a new instrument for every kind of enemy on the field: a woodblock for the Tinpot, a tuba for the Plodder, a kazoo for the Hornet, timpani for the Onyx. Hear a theremin but see nobody? That's a Ghost. Lose a tank and you get a sad trombone.

- **Twenty missions,** from First Shot to Last Stand, with a spare tank every five.
- **Two-player co-op** on the local network, one machine each. The spare tanks are shared, and friendly fire is very much on.
- **Keyboard and mouse, or a twin-stick gamepad.**

**GOOD LUCK, COMMANDER.**

## Controls

- **W A S D** or the **arrow keys**: drive
- **Mouse**: aim (or **I J K L** for eight ways, **Q** and **E** to turn slowly)
- **Left click** or **Space**: fire (five shells at most)
- **Right click** or **F**: drop a mine (two at most)
- **P** or **Esc**: pause, **H**: help
- **M**: music on or off, **F8**: all sound on or off
- **Gamepad**: left stick drives, right stick aims, right trigger fires, left trigger or A drops a mine

Panzer needs a truecolour terminal. 160x50 is playable, 200x60 or more is comfortable: the arena scales to fit.

## Options

- `--mission N`: straight into mission N
- `--host`, `--join`: co-op on the local network
- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- After Wii Play Tanks (Nintendo, 2006), with original names, maps, art and music
- Music and sound synthesised in the game
- Networking: iroh

particles.title: Particle Fountain
particles.description: An emitter sprays particles that glow green, yellow and red as they age: steer it, add gravity and wind, and play
particles.provenance: Particle Fountain is particles.cpp by flarn2006, in C++ on curses, from 2013 to 2017, one of the programs in his MiscPrograms collection.
particles.page:
**A FOUNTAIN OF SPARKS AT YOUR FINGERTIPS.**

An emitter on the left of the screen sprays a fountain of particles that fly out, glow green, turn yellow, then red, and vanish. The keys change everything about them: how fast they leave, how long they live, which way gravity pulls and how hard the wind blows. Move the emitter around with the arrows and paint with it.

## Controls

- **Arrows**: move the emitter
- **-** and **+**: slower, faster
- **w** and **s**: pull up, pull down (gravity)
- **a** and **d**: wind to the left, to the right
- **[** and **]**: shorter life, longer life
- **x**: clear all particles
- **Backtick** (`` ` ``): change the display: help, emitter, both or neither
- **q**, **Q** or **Esc**: quit

## Credits

- particles.cpp: [flarn2006](https://github.com/flarn2006/MiscPrograms),
  2013 to 2017
- Asciiverse edition: just this program from his collection, Q and Esc
  quit too, and a Windows build
- License: MIT

patolli.title: Patolli
patolli.description: Five black beans, a cross painted on a mat, six stones each: the Aztec game that players staked themselves on
patolli.provenance: Asciiverse made Patolli in Rust in 2026. Its rules are R. C. Bell's suggested rules (1969), on the equipment Diego Durán describes (about 1579).
patolli.page:
**THE AZTEC GAME PLAYERS STAKED THEMSELVES ON.**

A cross painted on a mat, six stones each, and five black beans, each with a single white hole. Cast the beans: the holes showing count one to four, and all five count ten. Bring your stones in, take them once round the cross and off. The pinched squares cost you forfeits; the rounded ends give you another throw. The first with all six stones off wins the pool.

A Spanish friar in Mexico described patolli around 1579: the mat, the stones, the beans, the god of the beans, and the gamblers who, with nothing left, staked themselves, and became slaves for ever if they couldn't buy themselves back. The authorities tore up the mats and burned the beans, and nobody wrote the rules down. What you play here are the rules a games historian suggested in 1969, on the friar's equipment.

Your first throw picks the way round for every stone you own; one stone to a compartment, so nobody is ever taken.

Play the computer at three strengths, as Red or Blue, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Enter** or **Space**: cast the beans; then arrows to a lit compartment, **Enter** to send a stone there; **B**: bear a stone off
- **Mouse**: click
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same game every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

phantasia.title: Phantasia
phantasia.description: An old Unix fantasy role-playing game: make a character, roam an endless realm by its coordinates, fight what you meet, gather gold and gems, and climb the ranks towards king, valar and the Holy Grail.
phantasia.provenance: Edward Estes first wrote Phantasia in the late 1970s on a high school's HP 2000 and later rewrote it in C for Unix, where it shipped with the BSD games; it was made for many players sharing one machine.
phantasia.page:
**THE REALM IS ENDLESS. THE GRAIL IS OUT THERE.**

Phantasia drops you into a realm laid out on coordinates, with the Lord of the Realm's castle at its centre. Pick a character class, roll your strength, magic and luck, and set out. Every step may bring a monster: fight it, cast a spell, try your luck or run. Win, and you take its gold and grow stronger. Buy armour and weapons at the trading posts, and keep going.

Climb far enough and you can become a king, a council member, even one of the valar, and go in search of the Holy Grail. Phantasia was written for many players on one machine, who could meet, fight and rule over each other; alone, the whole realm and its monsters are yours.

## Controls

- **N**, **S**, **E**, **W** (or **K**, **J**, **L**, **H**): a step north, south, east or west
- The number keys pick from the menu on screen: **1** moves to a point, **4** shows your stats, **5** quits
- In a fight, the numbers on screen choose: fight, cast a spell, try your luck or flee
- Your character is kept with a password you choose

## History

Edward Estes wrote the first Phantasia in the late 1970s on a high school's HP 2000 and rewrote it in C for Unix by the mid-eighties, where it became one of the BSD games. Later bsd-games collections dropped it as unplayable on single-user systems. This edition keeps the realm's files in your own data folder, so it plays alone.

## Credits

- Phantasia: Edward (Ted) Estes, with many ideas from Chris Robertson
- License: public domain (its author put it out without copyright)

pipes.title: Pipes
pipes.description: The sewage starts flowing in 70 seconds: lay pipes from the queue and keep the pipeline one step ahead of it.
pipes.provenance: abakh wrote Pipes for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
pipes.page:
**THE SEWAGE IS COMING. YOU HAVE 70 SECONDS.**

Somewhere on the board is a source, and when the countdown ends, sewage starts pouring out of it. Your job: keep a pipeline ahead of the flow. Pipes come from a queue, the next five shown on the left, and you get no say in what comes next. Corners, straights, crossovers: lay them where they fit, and dump the ones that don't somewhere out of the way.

Once the flow starts it moves on one pipe every five seconds, and the moment it leaks out of your pipeline, the game is over. Its author warns you plainly: "This is a challenging game. Needs practice."

- **A point for every pipe** the sewage passes through.
- **Fast flow** (**f**) rushes it along for three extra points a pipe. Feeling brave?
- **Crossovers pay twice**: run the flow through one a second time for six more.
- **Can't wait?** **g** starts the flow now.
- **Second thoughts cost**: replacing a pipe costs a point, and pipes the sewage has reached are set for good.
- **A top-ten list** for the best plumbers.

**KEEP IT IN THE PIPES.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move the cursor
- **Enter**: lay the next pipe, or replace the one under the cursor
- **Mouse**: click a cell to lay a pipe there
- **g**: start the flow now, without waiting for the countdown
- **f**: fast flow on or off
- **p**: pause
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit, after offering the high scores

## History

Pipes is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

pokertui.title: pokertui
pokertui.description: Texas Hold'em at a six-seat table: read the bots, watch the odds rail, and take their chips one pot at a time
pokertui.provenance: pokertui is Aleksandr Babarika's terminal Texas Hold'em in Rust and Ratatui, from 2026.
pokertui.page:
**FIVE BOTS. TEN THOUSAND CHIPS EACH. ONE SEAT WITH YOUR NAME ON IT.**

Every hand you get two cards and a rail that does the arithmetic for you: your chance to win right now, the pot odds on the call, and a blunt verdict on whether calling is worth it.

The bots are not all alike. One is tight and aggressive, one calls anything, one bluffs more than it should, and one is a rock that only moves with a monster. They remember how often you fold, and they lean on you when you do. The game ends when one player has every chip on the table.

- **Four bot personalities** to read, and beat.
- **The odds rail**: equity, pot odds and a verdict, or switch it off and trust your gut.
- **Your table, your rules**: table size, blinds and bot speed in the settings.
- **Tired of bots?** `pokertui-server` comes in the box: start a table and your friends join it from their own machines on your local network.

**MAKE IT YOU.**

## Controls

- **F**: fold; **C**: check or call; **R**: raise; **A**: all-in
- **Up** and **Down**: change the bet size; **Enter**: confirm
- Any key after a hand: deal the next one
- **S**: settings (table size, blinds, bot speed, the odds rail);
  **Q**: quit

## Options

- `--join <host:port> --name <name>`: sit down at a network table
- `pokertui-server --seats 4`: host a table (port 4000; `--buy-in`,
  `--small-blind`, `--big-blind`, `--turn-secs` set the game)

## Credits

- pokertui: Aleksandr Babarika
  ([github.com/AlexAlexBabarika/pokertui](https://github.com/AlexAlexBabarika/pokertui)),
  2026, written in Rust with Ratatui
- Asciiverse edition: fits 100x30, smarter bots, no freeze on a short
  stack, Windows settings saved
- License: MIT or Apache-2.0

pq2.title: pq2
pq2.description: Nick Bollom's remake of Progress Quest, Eric Fredricksen's 2002 RPG parody that plays itself: roll up a hero, then watch the bars fill
pq2.provenance: Nick Bollom's remake in C++ and ncurses (2016 to 2025) of Progress Quest, the idle RPG parody Eric Fredricksen released in 2002.

upstream.name: Nick Bollom, after Eric Fredricksen's Progress Quest

pq2.page:
**THE ROLE-PLAYING GAME THAT PLAYS ITSELF.**

Roll up a hero. Pick a race (Half Halfling? Land Squid? Talking Pony?) and a class (Ur-Paladin, Voodoo Princess, Battle-Felon, Fighter/Organist), roll the stats until you like them, and press **Sold!**. Then sit back. Your work here is done.

Your hero takes it from there. "Experiencing an enigmatic and foreboding night vision." Off on a long and dangerous journey. "Heading to the killing fields." Slaying Cub Scouts and Bugboars, looting their parts, "Heading to market to sell loot", "Negotiating purchase of better equipment", learning spells like Cone of Annoyance and Holy Batpole, gaining levels and working through quests and the acts of an epic plot, all as progress bars filling on their own.

pq2 is Nick Bollom's remake of Progress Quest, the send-up of level-grinding RPGs that Eric Fredricksen released in 2002, rebuilt in C++ with the same races, classes, monsters, spells and items. It is not the original, which you can still play at [progressquest.com](http://progressquest.com). Leave it running in a spare terminal and check in on your hero now and then; it only advances while it is open.

**THERE IS MUCH TO BE DONE. YOU ARE CHOSEN!**

## Controls

- **Up**, **Down** and **Enter**: the main menu; **Esc** quits
- On the character sheet: **Tab** or the arrow keys move between the
  fields, **Enter** picks one (a random name, the race and class lists,
  Roll, Unroll), letters and digits type a name, **Backspace** deletes,
  and **Sold!** starts the game; **Esc** goes back
- **F1** equipment, **F2** spells, **F3** inventory, **F4** plot, **F5**
  quests; **Up** and **Down** scroll a list, **Esc** closes it
- **p**: show or hide the percentages on the bars
- **-** and **+**: redraw faster or slower
- **Esc** on the game screen: save and quit

## Saving

The game saves to your data folder when the character is created, at
every new level, act and finished quest, and when you quit. To carry
on, choose Load Game, which lists your saved heroes, or start it from a
shell as `pq2 <name>`.

## History

Eric Fredricksen wrote Progress Quest for Windows in 2002 as a send-up
of the online role-playing games of the day, and has kept it going for
over twenty years, with a web version and online realms (Windows
version 6.4.4 came out in 2022). He
released it under the MIT licence. Nick Bollom began his cross-platform
remake in 2016, with Qt, GTK and ncurses editions; this is the ncurses
edition, with saved games in your data folder
and a few bugs fixed.

## Credits

- Progress Quest: [Eric Fredricksen](http://progressquest.com), MIT
- pq2: [Nick Bollom](https://github.com/nbollom/pq2), GPL-3.0
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

prince-of-braille.title: Prince of Braille
prince-of-braille.description: Jordan Mechner's Prince of Persia, ported from his own Apple II source: sixty minutes, fourteen levels, traps and swordfights, the prince drawn in Braille dots.
prince-of-braille.provenance: Jordan Mechner made Prince of Persia on the Apple II between 1985 and 1989, its running and leaping rotoscoped from video of his brother. He released its source code in 2012, and Asciiverse ported it to the terminal routine by routine.
prince-of-braille.page:
**SIXTY MINUTES. FOURTEEN LEVELS. ONE PRINCESS.**

The Sultan is away at war, and the Grand Vizier Jaffar has seized the
palace. He has given the princess an hour: marry him, or die when the last
sand runs through the glass. You are in his dungeon, without a sword.

Run, leap and climb your way up through the dungeons and the palace. Test
each step for loose floor, time your run past the slicers, jump the spikes,
find the plate that opens the gate. Take a sword from the dungeon floor and
fight your way past the guards, each with a style of his own, and past the
skeleton that will not stay down. Drink the potions you find, if you dare,
and beware the stranger who steps out of the mirror.

The clock never stops. Every few minutes the time left goes up on the
screen, and in her room the princess waits as the sand falls.

## The original, in the terminal

Every routine is ported from Mechner's own 6502 source: the same moves,
traps, guards and levels, the same 12 frames a second. It is drawn with
the DOS version's art and fills the window at any size. The prince's
rotoscoped animation is drawn in Braille dots, so every frame of his run,
his leap and his careful step survives; the stone around him is drawn in
block glyphs. One key switches to the Apple II's own picture.

- All fourteen levels, the shadow, the skeleton, the vizier and the mouse
- The DOS title, story and credits, the princess's room between levels,
  and both endings
- The DOS sound effects and music
- `--demo` plays the original's attract demo

## Controls

- Arrow keys, WASD or hjkl to run, climb, crouch and jump; Home and PgUp
  (or `q` and `e`) jump up and to the side
- Shift or Space: grab a ledge, step carefully, drink, strike with the
  sword; Up blocks
- `r` restarts the level, `p` pauses, `m` turns the sound off, `v`
  switches between the DOS art and the Apple picture
- From level 3 on the game is saved on each new level, and Ctrl-G saves
  it on the spot; Ctrl-L continues a saved game from the title
- Esc twice quits
- A gamepad works too: d-pad or stick, Y up, A down, X or a trigger for
  the button, Start pauses

Held keys are read exactly in terminals with the kitty keyboard protocol;
elsewhere from the keyboard's repeat.

puzzletea.title: PuzzleTea
puzzletea.description: Fifteen logic puzzles in one: Nonogram, Sudoku, Netwalk, Hashiwokakero, Nurikabe, Takuzu and more, made to the difficulty you choose, with a daily puzzle, a weekly ladder and levels to earn.
puzzletea.provenance: D∆MI (FelineStateMachine) began PuzzleTea in Go in 2025, as a collection of puzzles for the Bubble Tea terminal toolkit.
puzzletea.page:
**FIFTEEN PUZZLES. ONE DAILY. NO TWO ALIKE.**

A whole shelf of logic puzzles in one place, every one of them generated
fresh: pick the puzzles you feel like, set how hard you want them, and
PuzzleTea makes one. Or share a seed, and a friend gets the very same
grid.

- **Nonogram**: fill cells to match the row and column clues
- **Sudoku** and **Sudoku RGB**, the second with three symbols instead of nine
- **Netwalk**: turn the tiles until every computer reaches the server
- **Hashiwokakero**: join the islands with bridges
- **Nurikabe**, **Hitori**, **Shikaku**, **Fillomino** and **Ripple Effect**
- **Takuzu** and **Takuzu+**, the second with `=` and `x` clues between cells
- **Lights Out**, **Word Search** and **Spell Puzzle**

Every day brings one puzzle that is the same for everyone, with a streak
to keep. Every week brings a ladder of 99, unlocked one rung at a time.
Solving earns XP and levels in each kind of puzzle, the stats screen
keeps score, and 365 colour themes let it look the way you like.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** and **Enter**: through the menus; **Esc**: back
- **Each puzzle shows its own keys** under the board: **z** and **x**
  fill and mark in Nonogram, **1** to **9** fill a Sudoku, **Space** turns
  a Netwalk tile and **Enter** locks it
- **Mouse**: drag in Nonogram, Nurikabe, Shikaku, Spell Puzzle and Word
  Search; click to pick a cell, turn a tile or toggle a light
- **Ctrl+C**: quit

## Options

From a terminal: `puzzletea new sudoku hard` or `puzzletea new nonogram
classic` starts a puzzle at once, `--difficulty 1200` asks for a
difficulty from 0 to 3000, `--with-seed myseed` makes the same puzzle every
time, and `puzzletea continue <name>` takes up a saved one.
`puzzletea --help` lists them all.

## Credits

- PuzzleTea: [D∆MI (FelineStateMachine)](https://github.com/FelineStateMachine/puzzletea)
- License: MIT

pwmangband.title: PWMAngband
pwmangband.description: Multiplayer Angband: go down a hundred levels to face Morgoth, Lord of Darkness, alone on your own server or with friends on your local network.
pwmangband.provenance: PWMAngband is a multiplayer Angband, based on Angband 4.2 and MAngband 1.5 and maintained by the MAngband and PWMAngband developers on GitHub.

upstream.name: MAngband and PWMAngband developers (draconisPW and others)

pwmangband.page:
**MORGOTH WAITS A HUNDRED LEVELS DOWN. BRING FRIENDS.**

"His figure is like a black mountain crowned with lightning." Morgoth, Lord of Darkness, Master of the Pits of Angband, waits at the bottom of the dungeon, a hundred levels deep, with Sauron one level above him. Create a character, set out from the town and go down, level after level, to face them.

PWMAngband is Angband for many players. Everything is a letter on the map: you are the `@`, monsters are letters of their own, and the numbers in town are the shops' doors.

- **Sixteen races**, from Hobbits and Ents to Dragons and Hydras.
- **Classes for every taste**, from Warriors and Mages to Necromancers, Telepaths and Shapechangers.
- **A whole wilderness** with more dungeons in it, from the Orc Cave to the Mines of Moria and Mount Doom.
- **Your own world**: started from Asciiverse, it runs a private server on your machine and connects you to it. The world and your characters are kept for next time, and friends on your local network can join the same world.
- **Chat** with the other players as you go.

The first time, you choose an account name and password; they protect your characters on that server.

**THE PITS OF ANGBAND ARE WAITING.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **1** to **9**: walk (diagonals on 1, 3, 7 and 9);
  walking into a shop's number goes inside, **Escape** leaves
- **<** and **>**: stairs, **R**: rest, **,**: stay still
- **i**: inventory, **e**: equipment, **g**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **w**: wear or wield, **q**: quaff, **r**: read, **E**: eat,
  **f**: fire, **m**: cast a spell
- **l**: look, **M**: map of the level
- **:**: chat with other players
- **?**: help, **Ctrl-X**: save and quit (**Q** and **Ctrl-C** retire the
  character for good)

## Playing online

`pwmangband-play <host> [port]` joins a server elsewhere (the default port
is 18346), and `pwmangband-play --list` shows the servers listed on the
mangband.org metaserver. A server must run the same version.
On 17 October 2026 none on the list did: it showed MAngband servers and one
older PWMAngband 1.4.0 server, which did not answer, and the servers named in
PWMAngband's own manual no longer exist.

## History

Angband goes back to 1990, to Umoria and to VMS Moria (1985). MAngband
made it a game for many players, and PWMAngband carries that on: it is
based on Angband 4.2 and MAngband 1.5, and the MAngband and PWMAngband
developers maintain it on GitHub. This edition has only its curses
client, with your files kept in your own data folder.

## Credits

- Game: the MAngband and PWMAngband developers (draconisPW and others), after
  Angband by Ben Harrison, Robert Alan Koeneke and James E. Wilson
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0 (or the Angband licence)

rabbithole.title: Rabbithole
rabbithole.description: You're a rabbit in a maze with walls you can't see: find every carrot before the clock runs out.
rabbithole.provenance: abakh wrote Rabbithole for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
rabbithole.page:
**THE CARROTS ARE OUT THERE. THE WALLS ARE INVISIBLE. THE CLOCK IS RUNNING.**

You are a rabbit, and somewhere in this maze are the carrots. Gather every one before time runs out. The catch: you cannot see the walls. The maze shows only the passages you have already walked, so it all comes down to, in its author's words, "your choice of paths and the speed of your fingers."

- **A maze made to fit your terminal**: a bigger maze has more carrots and more time, one carrot for every 50 cells and one second for every 5. In a 100x30 terminal that is 47 by 11 cells, 10 carrots and 103 seconds.
- **No pausing to read the help**: the timer keeps running while you do.
- **Scored in carrots**: when time is up, the game tells you what share you gathered.

**HOP TO IT.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
  (the timer keeps running while you read them)
- **q** or **Esc**: quit
- **y** or **n** at the end: play again, or stop

## History

Rabbithole is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

rain.title: Rain
rain.description: Raindrops land on a still pond and spread out in widening rings, one after another: the BSD screen piece from 1980
rain.provenance: Eric P. Scott wrote rain at Caltech High Energy Physics in November 1980, after the VAX/VMS program of the same name, and it shipped with BSD Unix from then on.
rain.page:
**IT HAS BEEN RAINING SINCE 1980.**

Drops of rain fall on a still pond. Each one lands as a dot, swells to a small o and then a big O, and spreads out in two widening rings before it fades and another drop lands somewhere else. Five ripples are on the water at any time, all in plain characters, and it never repeats the same pattern twice.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `rain -d 50` sets the pause between drops in
milliseconds (the default is 120).

## History

Eric P. Scott wrote rain at Caltech High Energy Physics in November
1980, modelled on the VAX/VMS program of the same name, and it has
shipped with BSD Unix ever since. This edition quits on any key and
makes a new pattern every run. It is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse
catalog.

## Credits

- rain: Eric P. Scott, from [NetBSD's source tree](https://github.com/NetBSD/src/tree/trunk/games/rain)
- License: BSD-3-Clause, copyright The Regents of the University of California

rantaiwarna.title: rantaiwarna
rantaiwarna.description: Clear groups of same-coloured elements from a packed board: the bigger the group, the bigger the score, and an empty board earns 1000 more.
rantaiwarna.provenance: Guido Berhoerster wrote rantaiwarna, a SameGame (Chain Shot!) for curses terminals, in C in 2014 and kept it in Mercurial until 2016.
rantaiwarna.page:
**BIG GROUPS. BIG SCORES. BE PATIENT.**

The board is packed with elements in four colours. Pick any group of two or more touching elements of the same colour and they vanish; everything above drops into the gap, and when a whole column empties, the columns to its right slide over. Keep going until no group of two is left.

Here's the trick. A group of n elements scores (n - 1) squared. Two at a time earns you a single point. Twenty at once earns 361. So leave the little groups alone, and let the colours run together into big ones. Clear the board completely and you get a bonus of 1000.

- **Two to five colours**, and any board from 5 by 5 up.
- **Keyboard or mouse**: aim and press Space, or just click.
- **The best ten scores** for every board size and number of colours.

**WAIT FOR IT...**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: move the cursor
- **Space** or **Enter**: remove the group under the cursor
- **Left mouse button**: remove the group you click
- **n**: a new game
- **i**: the high score table, **H**: help, **a**: back to the game
