- **Ctrl+L**: redraw
- **q**: quit

## Options

- `-c <colours>`: two to five colours (four unless given)
- `-w <width>`, `-h <height>`: the board's size, at least 5 by 5 (20 by
  10 unless given)

## Files

High scores are kept in `~/.local/share/rantaiwarna`.

## History

SameGame goes back to Chain Shot!, a 1985 game by Kuniaki Moribe. Guido
Berhoerster wrote rantaiwarna in 2014 for any curses that follows the
X/Open standard, from ncurses to the native curses of Solaris and
NetBSD, and kept it in a Mercurial repository until 2016. This edition
has its history rebuilt in git, the high scores moved to the player's
data folder, and a terminal that starts too small now waiting to grow
instead of quitting.

## Credits

rantaiwarna is by Guido Berhoerster, under the MIT licence.

rattys-cube.title: Ratty's Cube
rattys-cube.description: A 3x3 twisty cube in real 3D in your terminal: grab a sticker and drag to turn its layer, race the clock from a competition scramble, and when you are stuck, ask for a hint or watch it solve itself.
rattys-cube.provenance: Asciiverse made Ratty's Cube in Rust in 2026, starting from the cube example in Orhun Parmaksız's Ratty, a GPU terminal that draws 3D, and named it after that terminal.
rattys-cube.page:
**TWENTY-SIX CUBIES. FORTY-THREE QUINTILLION WAYS TO MIX THEM UP. ONE WAY HOME.**

A real 3D cube hangs in your terminal, shaded and turning in smooth animation. Grab any sticker with the mouse and drag it: the whole layer swings round with it. Drag the empty space around the cube to look at it from any side.

Then press Space. You get a scramble the way competitions make them, from a truly random position, and fifteen seconds of inspection while the judge calls eight and twelve. Your first turn starts the clock, the last one stops it, and every solve goes into your best time and your averages of five and twelve.

- **Turn it your way**: drag stickers with the mouse, or type the notation on the keyboard, faces, slices and whole-cube turns
- **A speedcubing timer** with inspection, +2 and DNF just like the real thing, best, ao5 and ao12
- **Stuck? Press h** for the moves that solve it from wherever you are
- **Or press Enter** and watch it solve itself, slowly enough to follow along
- **Its own solver**, Herbert Kociemba's two-phase algorithm, usually finds a way home in about twenty-one moves
- **A flat net** beside the cube shows every face at once
- **Clicks and calls**: every layer clicks into place, the judge calls the inspection, and a fanfare greets a new best

## Controls

- **Mouse**: drag a sticker to turn its layer; drag the background to look around; the wheel zooms
- **R L U D F B**: turn a face clockwise; with **Shift**, the other way
- **M E S**: a middle slice; **x y z**: the whole cube
- **Space**: scramble and start a timed solve; **Esc**: stop the solve
- **Backspace**: undo; **n**: a solved cube to practise on
- **h**: a hint; **Enter**: show me
- **Arrows**: look around; **0**: look home; **+ -**: zoom
- **Tab**: the net; **F8**: sound on or off; **?**: help; **q**: quit

## Options

- `--mute`: start with the sound off

## Credits

- Ratty's Cube: Asciiverse
- Started from the cube example in Ratty by Orhun Parmaksız (MIT), and named after it
- Solver: Herbert Kociemba's two-phase algorithm, written for this game from his description
- License: MIT

realmsofdespair.title: Realms of Despair
realmsofdespair.description: Medieval fantasy MUD, the original SMAUG game, with over 250 areas and prestige classes

rebels-in-the-sky.title: Rebels in the Sky
rebels-in-the-sky.description: Space pirates playing basketball: gather a crew, fly your ship between planets, trade, explore, and challenge other crews, local or online, to matches you watch play out on the court.
rebels-in-the-sky.provenance: Alessandro Ricottone started Rebels in the Sky in 2024, a terminal game written in Rust with Ratatui, with online play between players' own machines.
rebels-in-the-sky.page:
**SPACE PIRATES. BASKETBALL. WHY NOT.**

You are the captain of a crew of space pirates, and in this galaxy disputes are settled on the court. Recruit players from across the planets, each with their own skills and quirks, fit out your spaceship and fly it between worlds to trade, explore and go on space adventures. When you meet another crew, challenge them to a match and watch it play out, play by play, with your tactics deciding the game.

Other crews can be bots or other players: Rebels in the Sky finds other players online and lets you challenge their crews, or join tournaments.

- **Build a crew** of players with their own stats, skills and personalities
- **Fly between planets** to trade, explore and find new players
- **Basketball matches** played out on the court, with your tactics
- **Online play** against other players' crews, and tournaments

## Controls

- **Left** / **Right**: switch tabs
- **Up** / **Down**: choose in a list; **[** / **]**: change the selection
- **Tab**: cycle the view
- The keys for each action are shown on its button, and the mouse works too
- **?**: help; **Esc**: back or quit

## Options

- `-l`: play offline, without looking for other players
- `-a`: no audio
- `-f`: no local bot crews, only other players'

## Credits

- Rebels in the Sky: Alessandro Ricottone
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

redsquare.title: Redsquare
redsquare.description: Steer a red square through Conway's Game of Life: catch the X, or spread red until no white cell is left.
redsquare.provenance: abakh wrote Redsquare for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
redsquare.page:
**SEE ORDER IN THE CHAOS.**

"See order in the chaos and use the predictable to prepare for the unpredictable." That's Redsquare's advice, and you will need it. The board is Conway's Game of Life: white cells, **#**, live, die and are born by Life's rules, a generation every time you press a key, or by itself after a short wait. Into all that, you steer a red square of four cells.

Red cells live by the same rules, and a cell that is born or survives takes the colour of most of its neighbours. So when your square touches other cells, it sets off reactions that can spread red, **O**, across the board, or wipe it out. Once your square comes apart you cannot move it, until a new red square with nothing around it forms somewhere and you take control of that one.

- **Two ways to win a level**: catch the wandering X in your square for two turns in a row, or let red outnumber white until no white cell is left.
- **One way to lose**: no red cell left.
- **Set levels first, then random ones.** When the board settles down for long, the game stirs it up with new red and white cells.
- **A world with no edges**: 50 by 35, wrapping around at every side, scrolling to follow your square on a short terminal.

"Learn from your mistake and try again and again."

**TRY AGAIN. AND AGAIN.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move the square
- **p**: pause
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Redsquare is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

revenge.title: Revenge
revenge.description: You're the rat, and the cats have had it their way long enough: push rows of blocks to box them in, and trapped cats turn to cheese.
revenge.provenance: abakh wrote Revenge for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
revenge.page:
**THE CATS HAVE HAD IT THEIR WAY LONG ENOUGH.**

You are the rat, **r**, in the middle of a big square of blocks, **#**, and a cat, **f**, is coming for you. Run? No. Push. Moving into a block shoves it, together with every block lined up behind it, as long as there is a free cell at the end of the row. Wall the cats in. Once every cat is boxed in and cannot move, they all turn to cheese, **%**.

- **75 points a cat** turned to cheese, and 100 more for eating the cheese or pushing a block onto it.
- **Another wave** of two to eight cats comes in once a wave is trapped, and more cats turn up as time goes on.
- **Push diagonally** too, with **y**, **u**, **b** and **n**.

And if a cat reaches you? "You lost The Game."

**SWEET, CHEESY REVENGE.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move and push
- **y**, **u**, **b**, **n**: move and push diagonally
- **p**: pause
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit; after a lost game, **y** plays again and **n**
  or **q** quits

## Options

Started from a shell, `revenge -n` does not ask whether to play again
after a lost game.

## History

Revenge is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games.

reversi.title: Reversi
reversi.description: Outflank and flip: Reversi against a computer that plays better every time you beat it, or a friend at the same keyboard.
reversi.provenance: abakh wrote Reversi for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
reversi.page:
**TRAP THEM. FLIP THEM. TAKE THE BOARD.**

Black, **X**, and white, **O**, take turns putting a disc on the 8x8 board. Every disc you play must trap at least one line of the other side's discs between itself and another disc of yours, across, down or diagonally, and every trapped disc flips over to your side. One move can flip several lines at once, and the lead can change hands in a single turn. A side that cannot move is skipped; when neither can, the side with more discs wins.

- **Play the computer, a friend, or watch**: by default you play black and move first, the computer plays white; two people can share one keyboard, and the computer can play itself.
- **A computer that learns from you**: it starts out playing at random, plays better after you win ("I'd play better next time.") and worse after it wins. Keep beating it and it asks: "Are you human?"
- **Keyboard or mouse**: click a square to put your disc.

**YOUR MOVE.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move
- **Enter**: put your disc
- **Mouse**: click to put your disc
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: resign

## Options

- `-1 h` or `-1 c`: a human or the computer plays white
- `-2 h` or `-2 c`: the same for black; either one skips the questions
- `-p 3`: a fixed strength for the computer, from 1 to 127
- `-n`: quit after one game instead of offering another

## History

Reversi is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

risorgimento-represso.title: Risorgimento Represso
risorgimento-represso.description: Sneak out of the dullest lecture ever given, Celtic Elements in Early Teutonic Settlements, and stumble into a world of magic gone badly wrong.
risorgimento-represso.provenance: Michael J. Coyne wrote Risorgimento Represso in 2003 and revised it in 2006 and 2017.
risorgimento-represso.page:
**THIS CLASS TAKES THE BISCUIT.**

"You've heard about them from others. You've even had them yourself: classes that seem to last forever. But this one takes the biscuit."

Celtic Elements in Early Teutonic Settlements: "a field of study so narrow and boring, you'd wonder they would award doctorates in it." The professor drones on about the settling instincts of early German nomad tribes, your elevenses are finished, and the large and heavy double doors at the top of the hall are calling you. Surely there is something better to do with your time?

There is. Slip out, and you find a world of magic that has gone badly wrong. The title means "Renaissance Repressed": Michael J. Coyne wanted to capture a Wizards Guild suppressing a magical society on the verge of breaking through into the age of reason.

- **A long, good-humoured puzzle adventure**, written for the 2003 Interactive Fiction Competition and updated in 2006 and 2017.
- **British to the bone**: "carcase" is spelled correctly, the author assures you, and the ground floor is not the first floor.
- **Help built in**: type **HELP** if you are new to text adventures, or **ABOUT** for the author's notes.

**CLASS DISMISSED.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/risorgimento-represso`.

## Credits

- Risorgimento Represso: Michael J. Coyne, 2003, 2006 and 2017
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivs-NonCommercial 1.0
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

robotfindskitten.title: robotfindskitten
robotfindskitten.description: Yet another zen simulation: you are robot, and your job is to find kitten
robotfindskitten.provenance: Leonard Richardson wrote robotfindskitten in 1997 for the Nerth Pork magazine's contest of the same name, and contributors have kept it going since.
robotfindskitten.page:
**YOU ARE ROBOT. YOUR JOB IS TO FIND KITTEN.**

This task is complicated by the existence of various things which are not kitten. Every one of them looks like a random character on the screen, just as kitten does, so robot must touch each thing to find out what it is. Perhaps "A stack of 7 inch floppies wobbles precariously." Perhaps "Some coconut crabs are milling about here." Perhaps "A wireframe model of a hot dog rotates in space here." There are 726 of them to meet, and only one kitten.

There is no score, no timer and no way to lose. The game ends when robotfindskitten.

**"YOU FOUND KITTEN! WAY TO GO, ROBOT!"**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or the number pad: move robot; **yubn** (or
  **Home**, **PgUp**, **End**, **PgDn**) move diagonally
- **Ctrl-L**: redraw the screen
- **q** or **Ctrl-C**: give up

## Options

Started from a shell in its folder: `-n NUM` puts NUM things on the
screen (20 by default), `-s SEED` sets the layout, and `-f FILE` reads
the things from another list. Your own `.nki` files in
`~/.robotfindskitten` join the 726.

## History

In 1997 Peter A. Peterson II held a contest in his magazine Nerth Pork
for the best piece of art entitled "robotfindskitten". Leonard
Richardson submitted the winning (read: only) entry. This is the
canonical C version for terminals: Alexey Toptygin's 2004 to 2005 code,
merged by Eric S. Raymond in 2012 when he recovered the project's
history, and maintained since by Ryan Finnie, who moved it to Codeberg
in 2026. The game is upstream's, unchanged.

## Credits

- Game: Leonard Richardson and contributors
- C version: Alexey Toptygin, Eric S. Raymond, Ryan Finnie and contributors
- Windows console support: [PDCurses](https://pdcurses.org)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

robots.title: Robots
robots.description: Evil robots close in one step at a time, and all you have is a teleporter. Make them crash into each other before one of them reaches you.
robots.provenance: Robots was first written at the University of California in 1980, and Christos Zoulas contributed a new version to NetBSD in 1999. Mike Sharov rewrote it from scratch in 2016 for his bsd-games, keeping the play and the look of the field.

upstream.name: UC Berkeley (1980), Christos Zoulas (1999), Mike Sharov (2016)

robots.page:
**THEY ARE EVIL. THEY ARE NOT VERY BRIGHT.**

The field is full of robots, and every one of them wants you dead
("which is why they are evil", as the original manual puts it). Each
time you move, every robot takes one step straight toward you. You have
no gun and no blade, nothing to fight with at all. What you do have is
their stupidity: when two robots run into each other they crash into a
junk heap, and any robot that blunders into a heap is scrap too.

So you dance. Step aside, hold still for a turn, and watch them pile
into each other. Clear the field and the next one starts with sixteen
more of them, up to 64 at once. Cornered? Hit the teleporter. It drops
you on a random empty square, which might be safety and might be right
next to a robot.

- **One point for every robot wrecked**, and a bonus for each field you
  clear
- **One way out of a tight spot:** the teleporter, as often as you dare
- **A table of the top 16** to fight your way onto

When they finally get you, the game is honest about it:
"Congratulations! You have been eaten by the evil robots."

**How long can you keep them crashing?**

## Controls

- **h**, **j**, **k**, **l**: move left, down, up, right
- **y**, **u**, **b**, **n**: move diagonally up left, up right, down
  left, down right
- **.** or **Space**: stay where you are for a turn
- **t**: teleport
- **q** or **F10**: quit

The keys are also shown beside the field while you play. Robots are
`+`, junk heaps `*` and you are `@`.

## History

Robots is one of the oldest BSD games, first written at the University
of California in 1980. Mike Sharov rewrote it from scratch in 2016 for
his bsd-games, the modern Linux port of the BSD games, keeping the play
and the look of the field from Christos Zoulas's 1999 NetBSD version.
Robots is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog, under the BSD
licence.

rogue.title: Rogue
rogue.description: The game that named the roguelikes: the guild sends you into the Dungeons of Doom for the Amulet of Yendor, 26 levels down, and death is for good.
rogue.provenance: Timothy Stoehr's rewrite of Rogue 5.3, the game by Michael C. Toy, Kenneth C. R. C. Arnold and Glenn Wichman; he mailed Kirk McKusick at Berkeley about it in 1987, and it has been part of BSD since.

upstream.name: Timothy Stoehr, after Michael C. Toy, Kenneth C. R. C. Arnold and Glenn Wichman

rogue.page:
**THE GUILD SENDS YOU IN. THE DUNGEON DECIDES IF YOU COME BACK.**

Your years at the local fighters' guild are over, and the guildmasters
have one last test for you: go down into the Dungeons of Doom and bring
back the Amulet of Yendor. You get an enchanted mace, a bow, a quiver of
arrows, a suit of armour and enough food to reach the ruins at the
entrance. After that you are on your own.

Every level is a new map of rooms and corridors, drawn only as you
explore it. Down there wait twenty-six monsters, one for each letter:
bats and hobgoblins near the top, then the aquator that rusts your
armour, the leprechaun that steals your gold, the medusa, the xeroc that
is not what it looks like, the jabberwock and the dragon. Potions,
scrolls, wands and rings are unknown until you try them, and trying them
is half the danger.

- **The Amulet lies 26 levels down**, and the stairs back up stay shut
  until you hold it: "your way is magically blocked"
- **Death is final.** Your score is the gold you carry, less a tenth if
  you die down there
- **A new dungeon every game**, so no map and no walkthrough will save
  you

Make it out and the guild takes you in at last: "You return home, sell
all your treasures at great profit and retire into comfort." Most never
do.

**This is where the whole genre started. Go and see why.**

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way, with **Ctrl** run until something is next to you
- **f** or **F** and a direction: fight; **t**: throw, **z**: zap a wand
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off armour, **P** put on and **R** remove a ring
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest a turn
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start Rogue from
a shell as `rogue rogue.save`; a saved game is deleted once it is
restored, as in the original.

## History

Rogue's manual credits Michael C. Toy, Kenneth C. R. C. Arnold and Glenn
Wichman, the authors of the original, together with Timothy Stoehr,
whose rewrite of Rogue 5.3 this is: his November 1987 mail to Kirk
McKusick at Berkeley about this "public domain rogue" is still among its
sources, and it has been part of BSD's games since. Its notice lets
anyone change and share it but not sell it. This edition keeps saves and scores in
your own data folder. It is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog.

rogue36.title: Rogue 3.6
rogue36.description: Rogue as Berkeley shipped it in 1981: 26 monsters from giant ant to zombie, the Dungeons of Doom, and the Amulet of Yendor more than 25 levels down.
rogue36.provenance: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold's Rogue 3.6 of 1981, restored by Nicholas J. Kisseberth in the Roguelike Restoration Project.

upstream.name: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold (1981); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

rogue36.page:
**TWENTY-SIX LETTERS. EVERY ONE OF THEM WANTS YOU DEAD.**

This is Rogue as it was in 1981, the version that went out with BSD
Unix. The
guildmasters send you into the Dungeons of Doom with a mace and a bow;
your task is to find the Amulet of Yendor, somewhere below the 25th
level, and carry it back up into the light.

The alphabet is the monster manual. A is a giant ant, J a jackal, K a
kobold; further down wait the rust monster that eats your armour, the
floating eye you must never hit, the invisible stalker you cannot see,
the umber hulk, the xorn, the troll and, at the letter D, the dragon.
Potions, scrolls, rings and wands are unknown until you try them.

- **A new dungeon every game**, mapped only as you walk it
- **Death is final**, and your score is the gold you carry out
- **The headstone waits:** die and the game carves REST IN PEACE over
  your name; win and it tells you "Congratulations, you have made it to
  the light of day!"

**The original. Still merciless.**

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way
- **f** and a direction: move until something turns up; **t**: throw,
  **p**: zap a wand in a direction, **z**: zap
- **i**: inventory, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off armour, **P** put on and **R** remove a ring
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **space**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down, and up once you carry the Amulet
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start it from a
shell as `rogue36 -r`; a saved game is deleted once it is restored.

## History

Michael Toy and Glenn Wichman prototyped Rogue at UC Santa Cruz in
1980, and with Ken Arnold made the 1981 version 3.6, which reached BSD
Unix (it is in the reconstructed 4.1BSD release). Nicholas J. Kisseberth (Yendor) restored it for modern systems
in the Roguelike Restoration Project, releases 3.6.1 to 3.6.5, and keeps
it at rogueforge. This edition keeps its files in your data folder and
fixes a table overflow at
the start of every game and saved games that never restored. It is part
of the Roguelike Restoration Project in the Asciiverse catalog, next to
NetBSD's Rogue, a later clone of 5.3.

## Credits

Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold; restoration by Nicholas J.
Kisseberth. BSD licence.

rogue52.title: Rogue 5.2
rogue52.description: Rogue as Berkeley had it in 1982: the Dungeons of Doom and the Amulet of Yendor, now with a list of everything you have identified and a way to ask what a trap is.
rogue52.provenance: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold's Rogue 5.2 of 1982, restored by Nicholas J. Kisseberth in the Roguelike Restoration Project.

upstream.name: Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold (1982); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

rogue52.page:
**THE DUNGEONS OF DOOM, ONE YEAR DEEPER.**

A year after 3.6, the Berkeley team had another go at their dungeon. The
task has not changed: the local guildmasters send you down with an
enchanted mace, a bow and a quiver of arrows to fetch the Amulet of
Yendor from 26 levels below, and you only win if you carry it back up.
Neither have the monsters, twenty-six of them from the giant ant to the
zombie, with the rust monster, the nymph, the umber hulk and the dragon
on the way.

What changed is how much the game tells you. Press **D** and it lists
every potion, scroll, ring and wand you have identified so far. Point
**^** at a trap and it tells you what kind it is, before you step on it
twice.

- **A new map on every level**, drawn as you explore
- **Magic you learn by trying it**, and paying for it when it goes wrong
- **Death for good**, and a top ten for the gold you carry out
- **The same reward for the few who make it:** "Congratulations, you
  have made it to the light of day!"

**One more year of polish. The same appetite for adventurers.**

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way
- **f** and a direction: move until something turns up; **t**: throw,
  **z**: zap a wand in a direction, **^** and a direction: say what a trap is
- **i**: inventory, **d**: drop, **D**: what you have discovered
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off armour, **P** put on and **R** remove a ring
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down, and up once you carry the Amulet
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start it from a
shell as `rogue52 -r`; a saved game is deleted once it is restored.

## History

Rogue 5.2 is Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold's Berkeley
version of 1982, between the 3.6 of BSD and the 5.4 that most later
ports grew from. Nicholas J. Kisseberth (Yendor) restored it in the
Roguelike Restoration Project, releases 5.2.1 to 5.2.3, and keeps it at
rogueforge. This edition keeps its files in your data folder and fixes an overflow in the top
ten. It is part of the Roguelike Restoration Project in the Asciiverse
catalog.

## Credits

Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold; restoration by Nicholas J.
Kisseberth. BSD licence.

rovers-day-out.title: Rover's Day Out
rovers-day-out.description: Beep, beep, beep. Get out of bed, get through the morning, and work out why two engineers are watching you do it. Winner of the 2009 Interactive Fiction Competition.
rovers-day-out.provenance: Jack Welch and Ben Collins-Sussman's Rover's Day Out won the 2009 Interactive Fiction Competition.
rovers-day-out.page:
**BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.**

"Alarm clock. Next to bed. Make it stop." That is how your day begins,
on a futon, after a dream in which a dog called Rover puffed a stubby
cigar under a dealer's hat and played poker with Isaac Asimov and the
cleaning lady. Just an ordinary morning: get up, get dressed, get on
with things.

Except that before any of it starts, two voices are talking. Janet and
David are hooked in, testing a program called the ACU, and somewhere out
there a mission called MARSpace is waiting to launch. "A program is
never finished," says Janet, "but I think we're ready to go." Every
command you type comes back logged like a line of machine code.

- **A puzzle in the telling:** what you do in the morning and what is
  really happening are two different stories, and the game wants you
  to find the seam
- **Funny all the way through**, from the dream to the help menu, which
  explains adventure games to readers centuries from now
- **The winner of the 2009 Interactive Fiction Competition**, by Jack
  Welch and Ben Collins-Sussman

**Rise and shine. You have work to do.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/rovers-day-out`.

royal-ur.title: Royal Game of Ur
royal-ur.description: The oldest board game with known rules: race your pieces past the rosettes of a 4,500-year-old board, in four reconstructions
royal-ur.provenance: Asciiverse made Royal Game of Ur in Rust in 2026. The rules are Irving Finkel's reconstructions from a Babylonian tablet of 177 or 176 BC, and R. C. Bell's from 1960.
royal-ur.page:
**THE OLDEST BOARD GAME WE CAN STILL READ THE RULES OF.**

Somewhere around 2600 BC, someone in the city of Ur was buried with their favourite board game. It was dug up in the 1920s, all shell and lapis lazuli, and for most of a century nobody knew how to play it. Then a museum curator found the rules on a clay tablet that had been filed under bird omens.

Two players, seven pieces each, a path of fourteen squares. Throw the lots, move, and pray. Land on an enemy in the shared middle row and it goes all the way back to the start. Land on a rosette and you throw again. That middle rosette has been the most fought-over square on Earth for forty-five centuries.

Pick your rules:

- **Finkel 2017**: the one most people play today
- **British Museum 1990s**: five pieces and no safe rosette, a meaner race
- **R. C. Bell 1960**: a betting game; pieces enter only on a five, and a rosette makes your opponent pay
- **The Babylonian tablet**: five different birds, knucklebones you dare to throw, and every rosette a bet, won by landing and paid for by passing

In the two betting games your purse carries over from game to game. Lose it all and you'll know why the Babylonians kept their accounts in clay.

Play the computer at three strengths, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Space** or **Enter**: throw
- **Arrows** or **Tab**: choose a piece; **Enter**: move it
- **D**: dare the ox bone (tablet rules)
- **Mouse**: click to throw, then click a lit piece
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same throws every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

rusty-pinball.title: Rusty Pinball
rusty-pinball.description: Eight physics pinball tables drawn in Braille vector lines: orbiting bumpers, a spinning triangle round a pyramid, a real star map and multiball wherever the table has it. After Brian Nenninger's Vector Pinball.
rusty-pinball.provenance: Asciiverse ported Brian Nenninger's Vector Pinball for Android, written from its source code.
rusty-pinball.page:
**PULL THE PLUNGER. THE TABLE IS ALIVE.**

Real-time pinball physics, drawn in Braille vector lines right in your terminal. The ball rolls and ricochets off bumpers, slingshots and drop targets, the camera follows it up and down the table, and a dot-matrix display keeps the score.

Eight tables, each with its own rules. On Round and Round the bumpers orbit. On Eye of Horus a spinning triangle guards the pyramid at the centre. On Orbiters five planets circle a sun and tug at the ball as it passes. Ad Astra carries a map of the real night sky, 1,500 stars, and asks you to light up Orion, Leo or Ursa Major one star at a time. Pool Party racks them up and dares you to "Shoot the Eight Ball!" Ball locks, multiball and jackpots wait on every table that has them.

- **Eight tables**: Classic, Round and Round, Ringmaster, Compound Interest, Eye of Horus, Orbiters, Ad Astra and Pool Party
- **Real physics**: flippers, kickers, ramps, loops and layered mini tables
- **The original's sound**: score dings, rollover notes, and music that builds as you score
- **Faithful rules**: ball savers, halving multipliers and "Shoot Again", as Vector Pinball plays them
- **Your best five** on every table, and the last game's score
- **Settings** for music and effects apart, game speed, the whole table at once, and unlimited balls when you just want to play

## Controls

- **Space**: launch the ball; hold it to pull the plunger back for a softer or harder shot (on terminals with the kitty keyboard protocol)
- **Z**, **Left** or **Left Shift**: left flipper
- **X**, **Right** or **Right Shift**: right flipper (Shift works on terminals with the kitty keyboard protocol; elsewhere use the letters or arrows)
- **P**: pause
- **H**: help and the rules of the table in play
- **Esc**: back to the menu
- In the menu: **Up** or **k**, **Down** or **j**, **Enter** to choose, **Q** to quit; Settings, High scores and Help are below the tables

## Credits

- Tables 1 to 8: layouts and rules from [Vector Pinball](https://github.com/dozingcat/Vector-Pinball) by Brian Nenninger, GPL-3.0
- Star map on Ad Astra: from Vector Pinball, which credits Sky Map's catalog
- Terminal version: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-3.0

sail.title: Sail
sail.description: Command a man-of-war in the age of sail: work the wind, choose your shot and board the enemy in 31 sea battles against the computer.
sail.provenance: Dave Riggle wrote Sail at UC Berkeley from 1980, after Avalon Hill's Wooden Ships and Iron Men, with Ed Wang as co-author and Craig Leres making it portable; it shipped with BSD Unix. Mike Sharov rewrote it in 2016 as a single-player game with its own computer captains.

upstream.name: Dave Riggle and Ed Wang, UC Berkeley (1980)

sail.page:
**RUN OUT THE GUNS, CAPTAIN.**

You hold a commission in the Sail Navy and a wooden warship under your
feet. Every turn you give the orders: how far to sail and when to come
about, which sails to set, when to "let loose the terrible destruction"
of your broadsides (the manual's words) with round, double, chain or
grape shot, and when to throw out the grapples and board. The computer
captains everything else on the water.

The wind decides what is possible. Full sail makes you fast, until round
shot shreds it. A ship that stops moving drifts. And as every captain of
the day knew, whoever holds the weather gage usually wins.

- **31 battles** from the 1770s to the fall of Napoleon: Ranger against
  Drake, John Paul Jones boarding the Serapis at Flamborough Head,
  Constitution against Guerriere, and full fleet actions
- **A few that history forgot:** the Curse of the Flying Dutchman, the
  South Pacific aboard the USS Scurvy (crew rating: mutinous), and a
  Battle of Midway fought by Enterprise and Akagi under canvas
- **Every ship on one screen**, two letters for bow and stern: capitals
  under full sail, `!` when she has struck her colours, `~` sinking,
  `#` on fire

**Clear for action.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **j** and **k**: choose a scenario, ship and loads at the start; **Tab** or **Space** moves between the lists, **Enter** starts
- **m**: move, then a string of turns and moves such as `l3` (turn left, three ahead)
- **f**: fire broadsides, **l**: reload, **L**: unload to change shot
- **c**: change sails, **r**: repair
- **g**: grapple or let go, **u**: try to unfoul
- **b**: board an enemy ship, **B**: recall boarding parties
- **i**: the closest ship, **I**: all ships, **F**: find ships
- **C**: centre the view on your ship, **U**, **D**, **H**, **J**: move the view, **S**: follow your ship or not
- **Ctrl-L**: redraw, **q**: quit

The game's manual (`man sail`, also in the archive as `sail.6`) explains
movement, wind, shot types, boarding and every scenario in detail.

## History

Dave Riggle wrote the first Sail on a PDP-11/70 at Berkeley in the fall
of 1980, after Avalon Hill's board game Wooden Ships and Iron Men. Ed
Wang rewrote it almost from scratch in 1983, and Craig Leres made it
portable. It shipped with BSD Unix as a multi-player game for everyone
logged in to the same machine, with a separate driver program moving the
computer's ships.

In 2016 Mike Sharov rebuilt it for his bsd-games as a single-player
game: one program with its own computer captains, a new curses display
and the 31 scenarios built in. It is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse
catalog.

salvo.title: Salvo
salvo.description: Hide five ships on a 10x10 sea, then fire blind into the enemy's until one fleet is on the bottom: against the computer or a friend on the same keyboard.
salvo.provenance: abakh wrote it as Battleship for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C started in 2018. It plays here as Salvo, the name the pencil-and-paper game was sold under in the 1930s.
salvo.page:
**HIDE YOUR FLEET. FIND THEIRS. SINK THE LOT.**

A carrier, a battleship, a destroyer, a submarine and a patrol boat, on a
10x10 sea. Lay them out where nobody would think to look. Then take turns
firing blind into the other side's waters, one shot at a time: `*` is a
hit, `~` is a splash. Sink a ship and you hear about it ("You have destroyed
my destroyer!!"), and the first fleet on the bottom loses.

Take on the computer, which will crow "Hahaha! I won!" if it gets there
first, or a friend on the same keyboard. For two players there's even an
anti-cheater screen between turns: type the given letter three times before
you may look.

- **Single player or two on one keyboard**
- **Keys or mouse**: click to place and fire, right click to turn a ship
- **Help built in**: F1 for the controls, F2 for how to play

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move
- **Enter**: place a ship, or fire
- **R**: turn the ship while setting up
- **Mouse**: left click to place or fire, right click to turn
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## History

Salvo is one of the games abakh wrote, as Battleship, for New BSD Games, a
collection of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic
BSD games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR. Here it plays under the
pencil-and-paper game's old name: Salvo was what the paper game was sold as in
the 1930s, decades before plastic pegs and trays.

savoir-faire.title: Savoir-Faire
savoir-faire.description: Charming, well dressed and broke, you slip into an empty chateau with one gift: you can link two things so that what happens to one happens to the other. Four XYZZY Awards.
savoir-faire.provenance: Emily Short's Savoir-Faire (2002) is set in an alternate France where magic links like things to like.
savoir-faire.page:
**YOU ARE CHARMING, WELL DRESSED AND COMPLETELY BROKE.**

"The beautiful life is always damned, they say." Fifteen years of
champagne, carriage rides in the Tuileries and getting elegant ladies
out of elegant fixes, and now your creditors want paying. You came to
the Count's chateau to ask for an advance. But the Count has not been
home in months, Marie has vanished, and they have even turned off the
cook. So you slipped in through a gap in the kitchen garden wall, with
a dashing hat, a swordstick and a snuffbox. You will just have to find
what you can.

Emily Short calls it "an interactive search for loot", and you have a
rare talent for it. **LINK** two similar things, the
snuffbox to a small yellow box, say, and whatever you do to one happens
to the other. **REMEMBER** brings back your memories of what you find.
Put the two together, and the empty house starts to give up its
secrets.

- **Four XYZZY Awards** in 2002: Best Game, Best Story, Best Puzzles
  and Best Player Character
- **An old-fashioned puzzle game**, in the author's own words, set in
  an alternate France of the early 1780s
- **Cruel, and proud of it:** you can lock yourself out of winning, so
  save often

**Mind your manners. Help yourself to everything.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/savoir-faire`.

## Credits

- Savoir-Faire: Emily Short, 2002 to 2004
- License: Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivs-NonCommercial 1.0
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

scissor.title: Scissor
scissor.description: Rock, paper, scissors as a live action game: steer your scissor into the papers, dodge the rocks, and keep the scissors alive as long as you can.
scissor.provenance: abakh wrote Scissor for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
scissor.page:
**ROCK BLUNTS. PAPER WRAPS. YOU CUT.**

The playground game, "evolved to a super-hyper-great live action
strategy game", in its author's words. Rocks (**O**), papers (**#**) and
scissors (**>**) bounce around the screen, and whenever two meet, the
winner turns the loser into its own kind. Rock blunts scissors, scissors
cut paper, paper wraps rock. And somewhere in the crowd drifts a magic
piece (**?**) that turns whatever it touches into the thing it beats.

You steer the highlighted scissor. Hunt down the papers for 47 points a
hit, and stay well away from the rocks. Lose your scissor and another
one on the screen becomes yours: you have extra lives as long as there
are scissors left. So you are not just playing, you are farming: keep
enough papers alive to feed on and few enough rocks to survive.

- **Diagonal moves are faster**, and you will need them
- **Some of the other scissors follow your keys too**, now and then
- **"Patience and vigilance could lead to very high scores"**, says the
  help screen; lose the last scissor and it says "You have lost The
  Game"

**Snip, snip.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: steer up, down, left and right
- **y**, **u**, **b**, **n**: steer diagonally, which is faster
- **p**: pause
- **F1** or **?**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: end the game; at the end, **y** plays again and **n**
  or **q** quits

## History

Scissor is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games.

scrap.title: Scrap
scrap.description: You are a robot in a world of hostile robots: shoot them to wrecks, bolt their guns, tracks and scanners onto yourself, and fight your way twenty levels down.
scrap.provenance: Thijs van Ommen wrote Scrap in ten days for the Ten-Day Roguelike in 2005, extended it in 2006 and published it on GitHub in 2017.
scrap.page:
**YOU ARE WHAT YOU SALVAGE.**

You are a robot, the **@**, in a world full of robots that want you in
pieces. The only way out is down, twenty levels of it: open grass and
woods, rough ground, enemy buildings, caverns, chasms, flooded ruins
and, at the very bottom, a fortress of metal.

Every robot, you included, is built from up to eight systems: power
cells, weapons, propulsion, sensors and armour. Shots hit systems, not
hit points. A system knocked down to half stops working until your
power cell patches it up; one at zero is gone for good; and if a power
cell goes, it explodes and takes the robot with it.

So go for the power source. Knock it out and the enemy becomes a wreck,
and a wreck is a parts bin. Drive into it and take what survived: a buggy's
minigun, a tank's caterpillar tracks for the rough ground, a sentry's
X-ray scope to see through walls. Later come the juggernauts, the
destroyers, the dracos with their heavy flamethrowers, the steel elementals and
the mechalich, and all of them carry something you want.

- **Build your own robot**, one salvaged system at a time
- **Every system matters:** the wrong propulsion strands you, the wrong
  sensor leaves you blind
- **Written in ten days** for the Ten-Day Roguelike, and it shows only
  in how tight it is

Make it all the way down and the author has one last line for you:
"There's probably a great reward for you and your robot at the bottom
of the dungeon, but I'm afraid I haven't implemented it..."

**Pick your fights. Pick their bones.**

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**, the cursor keys or the numeric keypad: move, the last
  four diagonally; drive into a wreck to salvage it
- **1** to **8**: use a system; for a weapon, the nearest target is picked,
  **+** and **-** cycle through targets, **x** cancels and any other key
  fires; a power cell chooses which system it repairs, a sensor looks
  around
- **d**: details of your systems, or of the robot being looked at
- **r**: reorder your systems, **s**: switch a system on or off
- **.**: wait, `>`: take the exit to the next level
- **@**: which level you are on, **?**: the controls
- **S**: save and quit, **R**: restore the saved game, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder and quits. Start Scrap again
and press **R** to carry on; a saved game can be restored once, then it
is deleted, as in the original.

## History

Thijs van Ommen wrote Scrap in ten days, a Ten-Day Roguelike released
in March 2005. In October and November 2006 he released the Extended 10DRL
and its 1.1, which added saving and the other features the ten days had
left out while keeping the game itself as it was, and in 2017 he put it
on GitHub under the GPL. This edition keeps the savefile in your data
folder.

seega.title: Seega
seega.description: Fill a square of holes with your kelbs, then step and trap: the Egyptian game whose boards were cut into the top of the Great Pyramid
seega.provenance: Asciiverse made Seega in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow Edward William Lane's Manners and Customs of the Modern Egyptians (1836), the only early account of the game.
seega.page:
**FILL THE BOARD. THEN THE TRAPPING STARTS.**

A square of holes, every one filled but the centre, two kelbs at a time. Then someone steps into that empty centre, and the game cracks open. Move a kelb so that an enemy lies trapped between it and another of yours, and you take it; as long as you can take, you keep moving. Box your opponent in completely, and you must hand over a kelb of your own to open a way for them: even winning has its price.

In the 1830s, an Englishman living in Cairo wrote down the seega Egypt's farmers played in holes made in the ground, and noted boards cut into the stones on top of the Great Pyramid by the guides who took travellers up it.

- **Seega of five**: 5 by 5, twelve kelbs each
- **Seega of seven**: 7 by 7, twenty-four kelbs each
- **Seega of nine**: 9 by 9, forty kelbs each

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Arrows**: move the cursor; **Enter** or **Space**: set a kelb down, give one up, or pick one up and put it on a lit hole; **Esc**: let go
- **Mouse**: click a hole
- The kelbs a step would take are marked ✕ when the cursor is on where it goes
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same game every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

senet.title: Senet
senet.description: The Egyptian game of passing through the netherworld, played for three thousand years, with every honest reconstruction of its lost rules
senet.provenance: Asciiverse made Senet in Rust in 2026. No ancient rules survive; it plays Timothy Kendall's reconstruction in two forms and R. C. Bell's.
senet.page:
**PLAY YOUR WAY THROUGH THE NETHERWORLD.**

For three thousand years, Egypt played Senet. Pharaohs played it, scribes played it, and in time the dead played it too: the board became the soul's journey through the netherworld, and sets were buried with their owners, Tutankhamun among them.

Throw the four sticks, count the light sides, and race your pieces along the S-shaped track and off the board. Guard your pieces in pairs, block with three in a row, swap places with a lonely enemy. The House of Beauty must be landed on. The House of Water must not. And the last houses want just the right throw, and the gods are not in a hurry.

Nobody kept the rules, only thirty squares, a handful of sticks and a lot of tomb paintings of people having a great time. So choose your reconstruction:

- **Kendall, five pieces**: the rules on most sets sold today
- **Kendall, seven pieces**: the 1978 original, where falling into the House of Water stalls your whole side until you fish the piece out
- **R. C. Bell 1960**: ten men each, a long die, and capture by landing

Play the computer at three strengths, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Space** or **Enter**: throw
- **Arrows** or **Tab**: choose a move; **Enter**: make it
- **R**: rescue a piece from the water (Kendall, seven pieces)
- **Mouse**: click to throw, then click a lit piece
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and what is known; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same throws every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

shade.title: Shade
shade.description: Too late to sleep, too early to leave: your bags are packed for the desert and your ride comes in a few hours. Then your one small apartment starts to change.
shade.provenance: Andrew Plotkin wrote Shade for the 2000 Interactive Fiction Competition.
shade.page:
**TOO LATE TO SLEEP. TOO EARLY TO LEAVE.**

"Odd, how the light just makes your apartment gloomier." It is the dark
before dawn and you are sprawled on the futon with gritty eyes. Your
luggage is packed for a week in the deep desert at the Death Valley Om,
your ride arrives in a few hours, and there is nothing left to do but
wait. Water the hyacinth. Check the to-do list. Get a drink; your mouth
is dry wool.

One desk, one futon, one mirror trying to make the place look twice its
size. You know every inch of this room. So why does it keep looking
less familiar?

- **One room**, and everything in it matters
- **Short and best played cold:** the less you know going in, the better
  it works
- **By Andrew Plotkin** (credited on screen as "Ampe R. Sand"), coded in
  a race for the 2000 Interactive Fiction Competition, where it placed
  tenth

**Turn on the light. See what it shows you.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/shade`.

## Credits

- Shade: Andrew Plotkin, 2000
- License: The author's terms: may be distributed for free, but not sold
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

shatranj.title: Shatranj
shatranj.description: Chess before the queen and the bishop, as the masters of Baghdad played it, and the Indian chaturanga they wrote down
shatranj.provenance: Asciiverse made Shatranj in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow H. J. R. Murray's A History of Chess (1913), from the books of al-'Adli and as-Suli, and al-Biruni's account of India (about 1030).
shatranj.page:
**CHESS BEFORE THE QUEEN.**

This is chess as it was a thousand years ago. The king, knight and rook move as they do today. But the counsellor steps only one square diagonally, the elephant leaps exactly two, and a pawn that reaches the far row becomes a counsellor. No castling, no double step. Win by mate, by stripping away every enemy man but the king, or by leaving the enemy king without a move.

The masters of Baghdad played it at the caliph's court in the 9th and 10th centuries, and wrote it down, with over 1,600 problems that survive to this day. It came from India by way of Persia, and went on to Europe, where in time the counsellor and the elephant became the queen and the bishop.

- **Shatranj**: the Baghdad masters' game; stalemate the enemy shah and you win, and a shah stripped bare can still bare yours straight back for a draw
- **The Medinese victory**: whoever first strips the other's king bare wins at once
- **Chaturanga, the Indian rules**: where a stalemated shah wins
- **The elephant in the corner**: the Indian game, its elephant starting in the corner and leaping two squares straight along the ranks and files
- **Al-Biruni's elephant**: "the trunk and the four feet", one more old elephant

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Arrows**: move the cursor; **Enter** or **Space**: pick up a man, then put it on a lit square; **Esc**: let go
- **Mouse**: click
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same game every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

sigpipe.title: SIGPIPE
sigpipe.description: The data is already on its way! Lay pipe as fast as your fingers allow: loop it, split it, buffer it, and pray it never hits an open end. cat: write error: Broken pipe!
sigpipe.provenance: Asciiverse made SIGPIPE in Rust in 2026, after the pipe-laying puzzle games of the late 1980s.
sigpipe.page:
**THE DATA IS COMING. LAY PIPE. FAST.**

A process has started. Somewhere on the board, `cat` is about to start writing, and its data has nowhere to go. Yet.

You have seconds. Grab pieces from the queue and slam them down across the grid: straights, corners, crossovers, tees. Then the countdown hits zero, the modem chirps, and the green data starts creeping down your pipe, one segment at a time, each one a note higher than the last...

Keep laying. Stay ahead of it. Because the moment it reaches an open end, it's all over:

`cat: write error: Broken pipe`
`[exit 141]`

- **Loop it!** Send the stream back through a crossover for +500. Five loops in one level? That's a 5000 bonus.
- **Split it!** A tee sends the data down both arms at once, and suddenly you're racing two fronts.
- **Buffers** soak up the flow, **valves** let data through one way only, and the `nul` sink swallows whatever you feed it.
- **Press F when you're feeling brave:** fast flow, double points.
- **Endless levels,** each one longer, faster and more cramped than the last.
- **Versus on the local network:** race a rival on an identical board, and every three segments you pipe locks a cell on theirs.

Pause and you're `[1]+ Stopped`. Pass and it's `[exit 0]`. Fail and... well, you know the signal. **DON'T BREAK THE PIPE.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **W A S D** or **H J K L**: move the cursor
- **Enter** or **Space**: lay the next piece (or replace one, at a small cost)
- **Mouse**: point and click to lay
- **F**: fast flow (during the countdown, starts the data at once)
- **P**: pause, **M**: sound on or off, **Esc**: back, **Q**: quit
- On the title: **V** hosts a versus match, **C** joins one
- **Gamepad**: d-pad moves, bottom button lays, left or top button or right trigger for fast flow, Start pauses

SIGPIPE fits an 80x24 terminal. At 144 columns or wider, your rival's board shows live beside yours in versus.

## Options

- `--level N`: start at level N
- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Sound synthesised in the game
- Networking: iroh
