sil-q.title: Sil-Q
sil-q.description: Steal a Silmaril from Morgoth's iron crown and escape alive: a dungeon heist in the First Age, with no classes, no town and very few easy ways out.
sil-q.provenance: half and Scatha made Sil, a Tolkien roguelike grown from NPPAngband and Angband, from 2012 to 2016; Quirk continued it as Sil-Q from 2017 to version 1.5.0 (2022), and Michael G. Noll carries it on today.

upstream.name: Michael G. Noll and Quirk (Sil-Q), after Sil by half and Scatha

sil-q.page:
**STEAL A SILMARIL. GET OUT ALIVE.**

Its authors call it "a dungeon heist game", and that is exactly what it
is. You are an elf, a dwarf or a man of the First Age who has found a
way into Angband, the fortress of the Dark Lord Morgoth, unarmed and
with little food. A thousand feet below, in his throne room, Morgoth
wears the iron crown with the Silmarils set in it. You are going to
take one.

Between you and him are orcs and their captains, wolves and wargs,
wights, trolls, giant spiders, Balrogs and dragons. You will not beat
them all, and you are not meant to. Sil-Q stays close to Tolkien: no
classes, no wizards or priests, no magic scrolls and no town, but eight
skills to train, songs of power, smithing at the forges, stealth, and
careful, tactical combat with few easy escapes.

- **Sneak or fight:** experience comes from meeting new creatures,
  going deeper and learning what things are, as much as from killing,
  so slipping past a sleeping troll is a real choice; the game can be
  won without ever attacking
- **Always forward:** every level is made afresh, and as time passes
  you can no longer go back up past a minimum depth
- **Death is final**

**The crown is waiting. So is its owner.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or the **number keys** (1 to 9): move; walk into a
  monster to attack it
- **Z**: rest, **z**: stay in place, **.** and a direction: run
- **<** and **>**: take stairs up and down
- **g**: pick up, **i**: inventory, **e**: equipment, **w**: wear or
  wield, **r**: take off, **d**: drop
- **E** eat, **q** quaff a potion, **u** use an item, **a** use a staff,
  **f** and **F** fire from the first or second quiver, **t** throw
- **s**: sing a song, **S**: stealth mode, **Tab**: abilities,
  **0**: smithing at a forge
- **o** and **c**: open and close doors, **T**: tunnel, **D**: disarm
- **x**: examine an item, **l**: look around, **M**: map of the level,
  **@**: character sheet
- **?**: help, **Esc** or **m**: the menu, with options (a keyset with
  hjkl movement is there too)
- **Ctrl-S**: save, **Ctrl-X**: save and quit

## Saving

**Ctrl-X** saves your character and goes back to the title menu; choose
"Open saved character" and give the character's name to carry on.
Saved characters, the high scores, character dumps and options are kept
in your data folder (`~/.local/share/sil-q`).

## History

Sil was made by half and Scatha and released in 2012; its last version,
1.3, came out in 2016. It grew from NPPAngband, a variant of Angband,
but kept little of it. Quirk took up the Sil 1.3 code in 2017 as Sil-Q,
rebalancing abilities, smithing and the enemies with Scatha's feedback,
and released 1.5.0 in 2022 with tiles and a new manual by MicroChasm.
Michael G. Noll has carried it on since 2026, fixing the bugs reported
against 1.5.0 without changing the play.

This edition keeps your files in your own data folder and saves a new
character under its own name. Sil-Q is under the GNU GPL, version 2.

silent-night.title: Silent Night
silent-night.description: A snowy forest at night where the weather really moves: gusts bend the spruces and blow the snow into drifts around a lit cabin, and the wind you hear rises with the wind you see.
silent-night.provenance: Asciiverse made Silent Night in Rust in 2026 for Christmas, after finding no terminal snow with wind, drifting snow or depth.
silent-night.page:
**THE WIND PICKS UP. THE SNOW STARTS TO MOVE.**

Night in a snowy forest. Snow drifts down at three depths, near flakes
fast and large, far ones faint. Then a gust sweeps in from one side,
bends the spruces, shakes the snow off their branches in clumps and
lifts the snow off the open field in a low blizzard, laying it down
again behind the cabin and the trees. Watch long enough and the drifts
grow and creep downwind, and the snow on the roof builds until it
slides off.

A log cabin glows at its windows with smoke drifting from the chimney,
a spruce beside it is lit for Christmas, and above the mountains the
stars twinkle, the moon shines and a faint aurora moves. Every now and
then a sleigh crosses the sky.

The sound is made as it plays, nothing recorded: the wind in the trees
rises and falls with the gusts you see, whistles in the strongest, snow
thumps off the branches and the roof, an owl calls far off, and sleigh
bells ring while the sleigh is up.

**Turn the lights down and let it snow.**

## Controls

- **m**: sound off and on
- **Any other key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal: `silent-night --mute` starts quiet, `--no-sound` has no
sound at all, and `-s N` builds the same forest every time.

## Sound

On Linux the sound goes to PipeWire, PulseAudio or ALSA (through
`pw-cat`, `paplay` or `aplay`), or to `ffplay`, whichever is there; on
macOS and Windows to the default output. Without any of them it is a
silent night.

## Credits

- Silent Night: made by Asciiverse, 2026
- License: MIT

sjump.title: Square Jump
sjump.description: One key, one jump: send the O flying from square to square, land on an edge for a hundredfold bonus, and keep the combo climbing.
sjump.provenance: abakh wrote Square Jump for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
sjump.page:
**ONE KEY. ONE JUMP. DON'T MISS.**

An O runs round and round the border of a square. Press **Enter** and it
leaps off, in whatever direction it sits from the middle: from the
middle of the right-hand side it flies straight across, from higher up
or lower down it climbs or falls on the way. It has to land in the next
square. Overshoot, undershoot, fly off the screen, and the game is over.

Every landing scores your combo and raises it by one. Land right on the
top or bottom edge of the square and it scores the combo times 101. But
the combo drops back to 1 every time the O passes the bottom right
corner, so you cannot just sit and wait for the perfect moment.

- **One key to learn**, and a lifetime to get the timing right
- **Edge landings pay a hundredfold**, if you dare to aim for them
- **A high-score table** for when you finally get it right

**Time it. Jump. Again.**

## Controls

- **Enter**: jump
- **F1** or **?**: how to play
- **q**: end the game; at the end, **y** plays again and **n** or **q** quits

## History

Square Jump is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a
collection of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the
classic BSD games.

ski.title: Ski!
ski.description: You are skiing down an endless slope with your jet-powered skis on backwards, and the man-eating Yeti is gaining. Jump, teleport, launch ICBMs and summon the Fire Demon.
ski.provenance: Mark Stevans wrote Ski! for Roy's Games between 1983 and 1990, first in FORTRAN on DEC-10s and then in C for VT100 terminals; Eric S. Raymond took it up in 1993 and rewrote it in Python in 2003.
ski.page:
**THE YETI IS GAINING. YOUR SKIS ARE ON BACKWARDS.**

You are skiing down an infinite slope of trees, ice and bare ground, chased by the man-eating Yeti. Unfortunately, you have put your jet-powered skis on backwards, so you can't see where you are going, only where you have been. Each turn adds one line to the slope and asks for your next move.

Hazards grow in patches, so you can steer round them: trees are the worst, bare ground can throw you, ice can make you slip, and you cannot turn while you are on it. When the Yeti comes, jump over him, teleport away, fire an ICBM after him or call up the Fire Demon. Every one of them can go wrong.

- **Many ways to come to grief**: trees, ice, bare ground, the Yeti, a bad landing, your own nuclear backpack and a spell gone wrong
- **A score for every run**: meters skied, jumps made, Yetis melted, minus your injuries
- **Very silly**: in its maintainer's words, "a fun and very silly game that proves you don't need fancy graphical user interfaces to have a good time"

## Controls

Type a command and press **Enter**. Upper or lower case both work.

- **Enter**: keep skiing
- **l** / **r**: turn left or right (each press steers harder, up to five)
- **j**: jump, over trees and Yetis
- **h**: hop, a short jump
- **t**: teleport to somewhere random on the slope
- **i**: launch an ICBM at the Yeti
- **d**: summon the Fire Demon to melt the Yeti
- **?**: help and the map key
- a number in front repeats a command: **5** skis five turns, **3l** turns left three times

On the map, **I** is you, **A** the Yeti, **\*** an ICBM and **D** the Fire Demon; **Y** is a tree, **#** ice and **:** bare ground.

## History

Mark Stevans wrote Ski! for Roy's Games, first in FORTRAN on DEC-10s, then in C for VT100 terminals; version 6.0 is from 1990. Eric S. Raymond took it up in 1993 and rewrote it in Python in 2003, adding the online help and, soon after, repeat counts. This edition is that Python version ported to Rust, so it needs no Python, and asks whether to play again when a run ends.

## Credits

- Original game: Mark Stevans
- Python version and maintainer: [Eric S. Raymond](http://www.catb.org/~esr/ski/)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: BSD-2-Clause

sl.title: sl
sl.description: Typed sl instead of ls? A steam locomotive runs across your terminal, and Ctrl+C won't stop it. With an accident, a flying train, a little one and the C51.
sl.provenance: Toyoda Masashi wrote sl in 1993 as a joke punishment for typing sl instead of ls; it has been a Unix favourite ever since.
sl.page:
**YOU MEANT LS.**

Everyone mistypes `ls` sometimes. Since 1993, Toyoda Masashi's sl has made sure you remember it: a steam locomotive, smoke and all, rolls across your terminal from right to left, and nothing you type will hurry it along. Not even Ctrl+C.

It has become one of the best-known jokes in Unix, and it is still a pleasure to watch.

- **sl**: the D51 steam locomotive with its coal car and carriages
- **sl -a**: an accident, with people calling for help
- **sl -F**: the train flies
- **sl -l**: a little one
- **sl -c**: the C51 instead

## Controls

None. That is the point. Wait for the train to pass.

## Credits

- sl: Toyoda Masashi
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: SL (Toyoda Masashi's own: do anything with it, as long as you don't pretend you wrote it)

sleighride.title: Sleighride
sleighride.description: Second day of Christmas, Santa's asleep and the elves have found the keys! Grab a sleigh, a reindeer or a broomstick and race like mad, before Santa fires up the snowplough and comes for the ringleader!
sleighride.provenance: Asciiverse made Sleighride in Rust in 2026, out of the Christmas folklore of Julbocken, La Befana, the Yule Cat, the Yule Lads, Ded Moroz and Snegurochka.
sleighride.page:
**SECOND DAY OF CHRISTMAS. SANTA'S ASLEEP. THE ELVES HAVE FOUND THE KEYS.**

Every present is delivered. Santa is snoring in his armchair by the workshop fire. And every last one of his helpers has grabbed anything with runners and gone for a joyride!

Bob takes the big sleigh. Holly and Juniper saddle up the reindeer. Sprocket fires up the workshop snowmobile, Pip grabs a toboggan, Nutmeg straps on racing skis, Tomte rides Julbocken, the straw Yule goat, and Befana? Befana takes her broomstick. Pick your racer and floor it!

But come lap two... SANTA'S AWAKE! He's in the one thing they left behind: the snowplough. He's got a list, he's checking it twice, and whoever is out in front is clearly the ringleader. Take the lead and he's coming for YOU, a mitten the size of a sack swinging in for a good clip round the ear. YOU'RE ON THE NAUGHTY LIST!

Drift through the bends until your sparks burn frost blue, then gold, then aurora, and let them rip for a boost! Fly off the kickers and throw a barrel roll! Smash open present boxes for snowballs, homing tinsel and peppermint boosts, or hold out a sprig of mistletoe on a stick: any rival who gets too close gets kissed and stops dead in a cloud of hearts!

- **Ten courses!** A frozen lake, a lake of eggnog flecked with nutmeg, black ice full of holes (SPLASH!), a candy cane forest, a gingerbread village with a cottage right in the road (jump it!), Santa's own workshop with its conveyor belts, a glacier split by crevasses, a birch wood where Ded Moroz lays frost on the road, the clifftops of a fjord, and a Christmas night market where the crowd throws presents.
- **Hazards straight out of Christmas folklore:** the Icelandic Yule Cat, the prankster Yule Lads, snow tornadoes, blizzards, and a line of penguins waddling across the road with a polar bear lumbering after them, never quite fast enough. Plough into a penguin and it belly-slides away across the snow. Penguins like that.
- **Real hills and jumps,** carved in voxels, right in your terminal.
- **Up to eight players** on the local network, on keyboard or gamepad.

Ten courses, eight racers, one very cross Santa. **CAN YOU WIN WITHOUT GETTING CAUGHT?**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right** (or **A** and **D**): steer
- **Up** or **W**: gas; **Down** or **S**: brake and reverse
- **Space** or **Shift**, held while steering: drift
- **X**, **E** or **Ctrl**: use your item; with brake held, drop a present behind you as a trap
- **P**: pause, **R**: restart, **Esc**: back
- **F1** or **H**: help, with the drifting, items, Santa and the hazards
- **F8**: sound on or off, **M**: music on or off
- **Gamepad**: stick or d-pad to steer, A gas, B brake, right shoulder drift, X, Y or left shoulder item

On terminals without the kitty keyboard protocol, Up latches the gas on, Down turns it off, and Space toggles a drift.

## Options

- `--race`: straight into a race
- `--course N`: pick the course, 1 to 10
- `--as NAME`: race as Bob, Holly, Sprocket, Pip, Juniper, Nutmeg, Tomte or Befana
- `--host`, `--join`, `--name NAME`: races on the local network
- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Folklore: Julbocken, La Befana, the Yule Cat, the Yule Lads, Ded Moroz and Snegurochka, from Christmas traditions across Europe
- Networking: iroh

snake.title: Snake
snake.description: Grab the money, reach the exit, and don't get eaten: the 1980 BSD chase game where the snake gets hungrier the richer you get.
snake.provenance: Snake is a 1980 chase game from UC Berkeley that shipped with BSD Unix. Mike Sharov gave it a new chase algorithm and a longer, deadlier snake in 2016 for his bsd-games.
snake.page:
**GET RICH. GET OUT. DON'T GET EATEN.**

You are the red `@`. Somewhere on the field lies a `$`, and somewhere an
exit, `#`. And all the while a green snake is coming for you. Grab the
money and another `$` turns up; grab that one too. But as the manual
warns, "As you get richer, the snake gets hungrier."

You never stop moving: you keep going the way you last pointed, so every
turn is a plan. Walk out through the exit whenever your nerve gives out,
and the money is yours. Stay too long and it is the snake's: getting
eaten is worth nothing, and only players who escape make the high-score
table.

- **SPACE WARP!!!** throws you to a random spot when the snake has you
  cornered, at a price
- **A last chance:** if you are caught, a lucky match on the last digit
  of your winnings can still warp you free
- **Your choice of field:** the whole terminal, or a smaller one of the
  size you give it

**How greedy are you feeling?**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **hjkl**: change direction
- **w**: space warp, at a cost
- **q** or **F10**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `snake 40 20` plays on a field 40 wide and 20 high
instead of the whole terminal, and `snake -s` prints the high scores.

## History

Snake was written at UC Berkeley in 1980 and shipped with BSD Unix as one
of its "crt hack" games, made for the video terminals of the day. Mike Sharov
gave it a new chase algorithm and a longer, deadlier snake in 2016 for
his bsd-games, the modern Linux port. Only players who escape by the
exit make the high-score table.

snakeduel.title: Snakeduel
snakeduel.description: Your snake against the computer's, and both leave a wall wherever they go. Box it in before it boxes you: first to five rounds wins.
snakeduel.provenance: abakh wrote Snakeduel for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
snakeduel.page:
**TWO SNAKES. ONE ARENA. NO WAY BACK.**

Your snake against the computer's, side by side in the middle of the
board, and both of them leave a solid wall behind them wherever they
go. The help screen puts the rules in two sentences: "Don't hit the
walls, the other snake and yourself. Kill the other snake."

Every turn the arena gets smaller. The computer plays to cut you off and
keep room for itself, so you have to think a few moves ahead: lure it
into a corridor, swing across its path, and leave it nowhere to turn.

- **First to five rounds** takes the match; from four all it goes on
  until one side is two ahead
- **Any size of board**, fitted to your terminal or set from the command
  line

**Cut it off. Close it in. Win the duel.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: change direction (not straight back)
- **p**: pause
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, Snakeduel fits the board to the terminal, or takes
its size:

- `-w`: the width, from 40 to 127
- `-l`: the length (height), from 10 to 127
- `-h`: help on the options

## History

Snakeduel is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games. The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine,
Nix, Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

so-far.title: So Far
so-far.description: Hot, foul and dark: walk out of a stifling theatre, away from the woman who never came, into a chain of strange worlds. Andrew Plotkin's 'interactive catharsis'.
so-far.provenance: Andrew Plotkin's So Far (1996) was nominated in the 1996 XYZZY Awards.
so-far.page:
**HOT, FOUL, AND DARK.**

High summer, an indoor theatre, and you crammed in neck by neck with
your sweaty fellow citizens. On stage Rito has just found out about
Imita's affair, one of your favourite plays, and you cannot follow a
line of it. Aessa was supposed to meet you here. She has made excuses
before, and you are trying not to think about what that might mean. Was
that a flash of her copper hair by the aisle?

Get up. Push past the knees ("Sit down, horse-head"). Leave the play
behind, and the way out leads further than any theatre door should:
into world after world, each with its own logic and its own price.

- **"An Interactive Catharsis"**, as the title screen calls it, and a
  story about distance and what it takes to close it
- **Rated "cruel" by its own author:** you can make mistakes that stop
  you winning, so save often and keep your old saves
- **Andrew Plotkin's 1996 game**, nominated in that year's XYZZY Awards

**The play is in its final act. Yours is just starting.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/so-far`.

## Credits

- So Far: Andrew Plotkin, 1996
- License: The author's terms: it may be copied, distributed and played freely
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

solitty.title: Solitty
solitty.description: Klondike solitaire in your terminal, with proper card frames, coloured suits and the mouse: build the columns, clear the stock and send every card home.
solitty.provenance: Murilo Pereira wrote solitty, an ncurses Klondike, between 2010 and 2018.
solitty.page:
**FIFTY-TWO CARDS. SEVEN COLUMNS. ONE WAY HOME.**

The patience game everybody knows, laid out properly in your terminal:
real card frames drawn in Unicode, red and black suits (or four colours,
one for each suit, if you prefer), and a cursor you can drive with the
keyboard or the mouse.

Turn cards from the stock. Build down the seven columns in alternating
colours, uncovering the face-down cards as you go. Send every card up to
the four foundations, ace to king. Double-tap a card and, if there is a
place for it, it goes home by itself. Get them all up and solitty knows
you have won.

- **Keyboard or mouse**, click to pick up, click to put down
- **Pick up whole runs** or just the cards you want
- **Three passes through the stock** by default, or as many as you set
- **Your terminal's own background**, if you would rather keep it

**Deal. Build. Win.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: move the cursor
- **Space**: turn a card from the stock, flip a face-down card, or pick
  up a card and put it down where the cursor is
- **Space** twice on the same card: send it to a foundation if it fits
- **m** / **n**: while holding a column, take one more or one fewer card
- **M** / **N**: take every face-up card in the column, or only the top one
- **Esc**: put the held cards back
- **Left click**: pick up or put down; **right click**: cancel
- **q**: quit

## Options

- `--passes N`: how many times you may go through the stock (default 3)
- `--four-color-deck`: give each suit its own color
- `--no-background-color`: keep your terminal's own background

## History

solitty was written by Murilo Pereira, first released in 2017, and
developed through 2025. The Asciiverse edition adds a fairer
Fisher-Yates shuffle, a terminal that is restored properly when the
game is interrupted, and further fixes and tests.

## Credits

- Original game: [Murilo Pereira](http://murilopereira.com)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: MIT

spider-and-web.title: Spider and Web
spider-and-web.description: Caught at a door with no handle in a foreign capital, you tell the interrogator how you got in. He does not believe a word. Andrew Plotkin's spy story.
spider-and-web.provenance: Andrew Plotkin wrote Spider and Web in 1998.
spider-and-web.page:
**"DON'T BE ABSURD."**

You are a tourist. You have seen the grain-gold plains, the mountains,
the spires of the capital. And at the end of a bare brick alley you have
found a plain metal door with no handle, no keyhole and no sign, only a
dull black plate in the wall beside it.

Then the glaring light. You are strapped into a steel chair in a dim
metal room, and the man behind the desk of monitors is losing patience:
"You're no more a sightseer than the Old Tree in Capitol Square; and if
you'd had enough sense to walk away from that door, you wouldn't be
here." Now you are going to tell him how you got through it. You can
answer yes, no, or nothing at all. What you play is the story you tell
him, and he is listening very carefully.

- **A spy story told under interrogation**, where what you did and what
  you say you did are not always the same thing
- **"The strangest game I know"**, says its author, Andrew Plotkin, "and
  understanding what's happening is entirely your problem"
- **Play it straight through:** mistakes are part of the story, until
  the point where heartbeats count

**Start from the beginning. And this time, tell the truth.**

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/spider-and-web`.

## Credits

- Spider and Web: Andrew Plotkin, 1997 to 1998
- License: The author's terms: it may be copied, distributed and played freely
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

spirhunt.title: Space Pirate Hunt
spirhunt.description: The galaxy is overrun with space pirates and the clock is running: warp between sectors, fire plasers and torpedoes, take prisoners, and watch out for supernovas.
spirhunt.provenance: Eric Allman wrote trek at UC Berkeley in 1976, and it shipped with BSD Unix. Mike Sharov removed its Star Trek content and brought it back in 2020 as Space Pirate Hunt, then gave it a full-screen curses display and grid navigation.

upstream.name: Eric Allman, UC Berkeley (1976); Mike Sharov (2020)

spirhunt.page:
**THE GALAXY IS CRAWLING WITH PIRATES. THE CLOCK IS RUNNING.**

You command the one warship standing between the pirates and every
inhabited star system in the galaxy, and you do not have long. Warp from
sector to sector, charge the plaser banks, fire torpedoes three at a
time, and dock at starbases for fresh energy, shields and torpedoes
before the next fight.

Space itself is against you too. Stars go supernova. Black holes swallow
your torpedoes. A long-range tractor beam drags you off course, and a
time portal can throw you backwards or forwards in the calendar. Your
crew keeps you informed, after a fashion: "Captain, the pirates said...
uh, I don't think I can repeat that."

- **Fight or take them alive:** cloak, ram, or ask a pirate to surrender
  and hand your captives to a starbase for trial
- **Answer the distress calls** before starbases and inhabited systems
  fall
- **The whole galaxy on one screen:** your sector, the galaxy chart and
  the ship's condition side by side
- **Ways to lose that the manual never mentions:** among them, "Your
  ship was ticketed for speeding"

Clear every pirate in time and headquarters says it for you:
"Congratulations, you have saved the Galaxy."

**Plasers charged. Shields up. Go.**

## Controls

Each command is one key; the game then asks for what it needs.

- **m**: move, to a position such as `44` here or `3544` in another sector
- **I**: move under impulse, **w**: set the warp factor
- **p**: fire plasers, **t**: fire torpedoes, **R**: ram something
- **s**: shields up or down, **c**: cloak on or off
- **d**: dock or undock at a starbase, **H**: call a starbase for help
- **r**: rest, **i**: damage report
- **C**: ask a pirate to surrender
- **D**: self-destruct
- **?**: list the commands
- **S**: save and quit (the next start carries on), **Q**: quit at once

## History

Eric Allman wrote trek at UC Berkeley in 1976, and it shipped with BSD
Unix. Mike Sharov dropped it
from his bsd-games for its Star Trek content, then brought it back in
2020 as Space Pirate Hunt, with the same game and no Trek references.
Later that year he replaced its typed scan commands with a full-screen
curses display, moved navigation to a grid and simplified aiming.

The original teletype game, Klingons and all, is also in the catalog as
BSD Trek.

srogue.title: Super-Rogue
srogue.description: Bell Labs' bigger Rogue: 52 monsters, magic pools, mazes, Friendly Fiend's Flea Market, and the devil Asmodeus waiting below everything else.
srogue.provenance: Robert D. Kindelberger and co-workers at AT&T Bell Labs made Super-Rogue from Rogue 3.6 between 1982 and 1984; Kindelberger gave the 9.0 source to Nicholas J. Kisseberth in 2004, who restored it for the Roguelike Restoration Project.

upstream.name: Robert D. Kindelberger (1984); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

srogue.page:
**FIFTY-TWO MONSTERS. ONE DEVIL AT THE BOTTOM.**

At AT&T Bell Labs they took Rogue 3.6 and kept on building. You are still the young graduate of the fighters' guild, sent
into the Dungeons of Doom to bring back the Amulet of Yendor. But the
dungeon is deeper (the Amulet turns up no sooner than level 35), and
the alphabet now runs in both cases: after the giant ant and the zombie
come the cockatrice, the killer frog, the hell hound, the minotaur, the
titanothere and Yeenoghu. Go deeper than any of them
will follow and you meet the devil Asmodeus himself. (Hoping to
wipe him out with a scroll of genocide? "You cannot genocide Asmodeus !!")

- **Magic pools:** dip things in them and see what happens; just do not
  fall in ("Oh no!!! You drown in the pool!!!")
- **Whole maze levels** between the rooms and corridors
- **Friendly Fiend's Flea Market**, open for business in the dungeon
- **Four stats to keep up:** strength, dexterity, wisdom and
  constitution, all on two status lines with how much you are carrying

**The Rogue that kept growing. Go and find its floor.**

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way
- **f** and a direction: move until something turns up; **t**: throw,
  **p** and a direction: zap a wand that way, **z**: zap
- **i**: inventory, **d**: drop, **a**: your best stats so far
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off armour, **P** put on and **R** remove a ring, **D**: dip something
  in a pool
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down, and up once you carry the Amulet
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start it from a
shell as `srogue -r`; a saved game is deleted once it is restored.

## History

Super-Rogue was made at AT&T Bell Labs between 1982 and 1984 from Rogue
3.6, with Robert D. Kindelberger as the public face of the group; 9.0 is
its last version. Kindelberger gave its source to Nicholas J. Kisseberth
(Yendor) in 2004, and the Roguelike Restoration Project released 9.0-1
in 2005. This edition keeps your files in your data folder and fixes
it for 64-bit machines. It is part of the Roguelike Restoration Project
in the Asciiverse catalog.

## Credits

Robert D. Kindelberger and his co-workers at Bell Labs, after Rogue by
Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold; restoration by Nicholas J.
Kisseberth. BSD licence with clauses on the name Super-Rogue.

sshattrick.title: ssHattrick
sshattrick.description: One-on-one ice hockey at full tilt: skate, steal, wind up and shoot past a goalie who copies your opponent's every move. Against the computer, or a friend on your local network who joins with nothing but ssh.
sshattrick.provenance: ricott1 made ssHattrick in Rust in 2024, a hockey game anyone could play with nothing but ssh, after Bally Sente's arcade Hat Trick (1984).
sshattrick.page:
**ONE SKATER EACH. ONE PUCK. NINETY SECONDS.**

ssHattrick is one-on-one ice hockey, drawn in chunky pixels and played at full tilt. Your skater glides on real ice: lean on the arrows to build up speed, and lean the other way to stop. Skate into the puck to take it, skate into your opponent to steal it back, and hit space to wind up a shot you can still steer before it flies.

The twist comes straight from the arcade: **each goalie copies its own skater**, up and down the rink. Keep level with the puck and your goal is covered. Drift off to chase the play and your net lies wide open. Score while the other keeper is out of position, and don't leave yours stranded.

- **Play the computer** at easy, normal or hard. It skates, steals and aims for the empty side of the net.
- **Play a friend on your local network.** They don't need to install a thing: the lobby shows the one `ssh` line they type, and you're on the ice together.
- **Practice** against a wandering goalie, or **watch** two computers go at it.
- **Most goals in ninety seconds wins.** Forfeit with Esc if it's hopeless.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: skate
- **Space**: shoot; keep pressing the arrows during the wind-up to steer it
- **Esc**: forfeit and back to the lobby; in the lobby, leave
- **Lobby**: **c** play the computer, **l** change its level, **w** watch two computers, **p** practice, **a** play the next person who also presses a, **g** play a friend by code

## Options

- `--cpu easy|normal|hard`: straight into a match against the computer
- `--practice`: straight into practice
- `--watch`: two computers, one match after another
- `--offline`: play without opening the game to the network
- `--join HOST[:PORT]`: join a friend's game
- `--server`: run only the server, for people connecting with ssh
- `-p PORT`: the port friends connect to (default 3020)

## Credits

- Game: ricott1
- After Bally Sente's Hat Trick (1984)
- This edition's local play and computer player: Asciiverse

sshtron.title: SSHTron
sshtron.description: Keep moving, leave a wall of light behind you, and box the other riders in: the game you could always play with nothing but ssh, now against computer riders, friends on your network, or the public server.
sshtron.provenance: Zach Latta and Max Wofford built SSHTron in about twenty hours at BrickHack 2 in March 2016, a Tron game anyone could join with nothing but ssh, and its public server is still running.
sshtron.page:
**KEEP MOVING. LEAVE A WALL. BOX THEM IN.**

The grid is black. Your cycle is moving, and it is not going to stop.
Behind you it leaves a wall of light, and every other rider leaves one
too. Touch a wall, any wall, yours included, and you are gone: back at
once somewhere else on the grid with a score of zero and a fresh trail,
leaving a spot of your colour in the one you hit.

Your score climbs for every second you stay alive, and faster the more
riders there are. Box the others in, cut across their path, leave them
nowhere to turn. Seven colours fit in one arena: red, green, yellow,
blue, magenta, cyan and white.

SSHTron was built in about twenty hours at a hackathon, to be played
with nothing but `ssh`, and it still can be. Pick **Play** and you race
computer riders on a grid hosted on your own machine; anyone on your
network can ride in with `ssh -p 2022` and your address, or with
SSHTron's own **Join a friend**. **Play online** takes you to the
original public server at sshtron.zachlatta.com, where whoever else is
online that day shares the grid.

**Stay alive. Stay moving.**

## Controls

- **W A S D**, the **arrow keys** or **h j k l**: steer (also **z q s d**
  and **, a o e**)
- **Esc** or **Ctrl+C**: leave the game

In the menu, **Colour** asks for the colour you ride in; a computer rider
in it makes way for you.

## Options

- `-play`, `-online`, `-join host[:port]`: skip the menu
- `-color red`: ask for a colour
- `-bots N`: computer riders in each game (3, up to 6)
- `-demo`: watch the computer ride for you; any key ends it
- `-server`: run only the server, for others to join with `ssh -p 2022`

## Credits

- SSHTron: Zach Latta and Max Wofford, with Ali Yousuf and others
  ([github.com/zachlatta/sshtron](https://github.com/zachlatta/sshtron)),
  2016, written in Go at BrickHack 2
- Arrow keys and trail fixes: Yerlotic
  ([github.com/yerlotic/sshtron](https://github.com/yerlotic/sshtron))
- Asciiverse edition: the menu, the built-in SSH client, computer riders,
  games on the local network, and fixes for a server
  that could crash under load
- License: MIT

sssnake.title: sssnake
sssnake.description: Snake that can play itself: steer it, race it in arcade mode, or sit back while A* or BFS hunts the food, faster and faster, as a screensaver.
sssnake.provenance: AngelJumbo wrote sssnake in C in 2022 as an A* exercise on the snake game, then gave its autopilot a greedy solver after chuyangliu's snake AI; the name is for smart and sexy snake.
sssnake.page:
**SMART. FAST. HUNGRY. IT CAN PLAY WITHOUT YOU.**

The snake game you know, drawn in solid blocks instead of letters: eat the
food, grow longer, don't run into yourself or the walls. Steer it with the
arrows, WASD or Vim keys, or try arcade mode, where every bite makes it
faster.

Then hand over the controls. In autopilot the snake hunts the food on its
own with A* or breadth-first search, and with `--try-hard` it plans ahead
so it never traps itself, curling round the board until it nearly fills
it. Turn the speed up and leave it running as a screensaver.

- **Four modes**: normal, arcade, autopilot and screensaver
- **Four looks**: fancy, full, ASCII and dots
- **Your board**: any size, walls that teleport you across, and random
  junk to steer round

**LET IT EAT.**

## Controls

- **Arrows**, **WASD** or **HJKL**: steer
- **Space**: pause; **Q**: quit
- Autopilot and screensaver: **+** and **-** change the speed; in the
  screensaver any other key quits

## Options

- `-m arcade`, `-m autopilot`, `-m screensaver`: the mode
- `-l full`, `-l ascii`, `-l dots`: the look
- `-s 15`: the speed, 1 to 20; `-x 30 -y 20`: the board size
- `-j 3`: junk on the board, 1 to 5; `-t`: teleport through the walls;
  `-z`: show the snake's size
- `--try-hard 1` or `2`: an autopilot that keeps itself alive;
  `--short-path=bfs`: breadth-first search instead of A*

## Credits

- sssnake: [AngelJumbo](https://github.com/AngelJumbo/sssnake)
- Autopilot solvers after chuyangliu's greedy snake solver
- License: MIT

starlanes.title: Star Lanes
starlanes.description: Found shipping lines between the stars, buy their stock, force the mergers, and shove your rivals' companies into black holes: the classic trading game for one to four players.
starlanes.provenance: Brian "Beej" Hall wrote this curses Star Lanes in C (1995 to 1997, 1.2.2), after the Osborne version of Steven Faber's game, and modernised it himself in 2026 (1.4.0).
starlanes.page:
**BUY LOW. MERGE BIG. FEED YOUR RIVALS TO A BLACK HOLE.**

The star lanes are open and the money is out there for whoever moves
first. Each turn you claim one of five sectors on the star map. Land
beside a star and you can found a shipping company ("A new shipping
company has been formed!") with free shares for the founder; land
beside a company and it grows. Then the trading floor opens: buy into
the lines you believe in, and dump the ones that look doomed.

Altair Starways, Capella Freight Co., Eridani Expediters: every company
is worth more for each sector it holds and each star it touches. When
two companies meet, the bigger swallows the smaller, its shares turn
into half as many in the winner, and the shareholders get a cash bonus.
Push past $3,000 a share and the stock splits two for one.

And then there are the black holes, which the 1977 original never had.
Beej added them, he says, "to give players who have fallen behind a
chance to shaft the leaders." Push a company your rival owns more of
than you against one, and if its price drops to nothing, the whole line
"has been sucked into a black hole!" with everyone's shares in it.

- **One to four players** at one keyboard, taking turns
- **Mergers, splits and a 5% holdings bonus** every turn
- **The richest tycoon wins** when the companies fill 54% of the map

**Out-trade them. Out-merge them. Out-smart your friends and enemies.**

## Controls

- **1** to **5**: take one of the five sectors numbered on the map
- **Up** and **Down** (or **k** and **j**): choose a company while trading
- **Enter**: trade in that company; type a number of shares (negative to
  sell), **m** for as many as you can afford, **n** to sell them all
- **Esc**: end your trading and pass to the next player
- **s**: the standings; **c**: company details (size and total worth)
- **q** or **Ctrl+C**: quit, after showing the final standings
- **Ctrl+L**: redraw the screen

## Options

- `-c`: force colour; `-m`: force black and white

## History

Steven Faber's Star Lanes was printed as a BASIC listing in Interface Age
in June 1977 and went round many home computers from there (Brian "Beej"
Hall traced it in his starlanes-info notes). Beej played it from a
First Osborne Group disk in about 1982 and wrote this curses version in C
in 1995 to 1997, releasing 1.2.2 in 1997. His version has black holes,
which the original did not, "to give players who have fallen behind a
chance to shaft the leaders". In 2026 he took it up again, broke the one big source file
into modules and released 1.4.0.

starmourn.description: Space science fiction MUD by Iron Realms with over 50 alien races and hacking

sudoku.title: Sudoku
sudoku.description: Sudoku from a quick 4x4 to a monstrous 49x49 with letters for digits, with hints, the mouse and a generator that apologises for being slow.
sudoku.provenance: abakh wrote Sudoku for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
sudoku.page:
**FROM A 4x4 TO A 49x49. HOW BIG DARE YOU GO?**

You know the rules: fill the grid so that every row, every column and
every box holds each symbol exactly once. About half the cells start
filled in, in bold, and anything you write that clashes turns red. Fill
the last cell by the rules and the game cheers "Yay!! Wanna play
again?"

Then it gets interesting. Start it with a bigger box size and the
boards grow: 16x16, 25x25, all the way to 49x49, where the letters join
in as digits and a board will not fit on your screen without scrolling.
The generator does its honest best, though it warns you: "My algorithm
sucks, so you need to wait a bit."

- **Six sizes**, from 4x4 to 49x49
- **Hints** when you are stuck, a cell at a time
- **Mouse or keyboard**, whichever you like
- **Any valid filling wins**, even if it is not the one the generator
  had in mind

**Pick a size. Lose an evening.**

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move
- **1** to **9**: write a number; on boards bigger than 9x9 the letters
  from **a** on are symbols too
- **Enter**: step the number in the cell up by one
- **Space**: clear the cell
- **Mouse**: left click to step the number up, right click to clear
- **?**: hint, fills in the cell under the cursor (after showing the help)
- **r**: clear everything you wrote, **n**: a new board
- **F1**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **PgUp**, **PgDn**, **<** and **>**: scroll a board that does not fit
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

On the biggest boards some of these letters are symbols: **n** stops
working from 25x25, **q**, **r** and **Esc** from 36x36. **Q** always quits.

## Options

Started from a shell, Sudoku takes the size of the boxes:

- `-s 4` plays a 16x16 board; anything from `-s 2` (4x4) to `-s 7`
  (49x49) works, and the default is 3 (9x9)
- `-f` makes boards with a faster, cruder generator, which is always
  used from 25x25 up

## History

Sudoku is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection of
small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD games.
The collection is packaged by Debian, Ubuntu, openSUSE, Alpine, Nix,
Homebrew, FreeBSD and pkgsrc, and is in the AUR.

swarm.title: Swarm
swarm.description: Crash-landed on an alien planet with toxic air, you stay in your base and program robots to explore, gather and build, unlocking new language features as you go.
swarm.provenance: Swarm is by Brent Yorgey and contributors, in Haskell on Brick, since 2021.
swarm.page:
**CRASH-LANDED. TOXIC AIR. A BASE FULL OF ROBOT PARTS.**

"In a shockingly original turn of events, you have crash landed on an
alien planet!" The atmosphere will kill you, so you stay inside your
robotic base with its life support, and you send robots out instead.
And you program every one of them.

It starts small: move, turn, grab, build. Bring back a tree and you can
make a log; bring back enough and you can make better devices, which
give your robots new abilities and new parts of the language, which let
them gather more, which in turn will... as the tutorial says, you get
the idea. Before long you have loops, conditions, recursion and whole
fleets of robots running programs of their own.

- **A real little programming language** that grows as you craft
  devices for it
- **A tutorial that teaches it** one idea at a time, from your first
  `say "Ready!"`
- **Open worlds** in Classic and Creative modes, generated from a seed
- **Challenges:** mazes, the Towers of Hanoi, the wolf, the goat and the
  cabbage, lights out, ranching, bridge building and more

**Your robots are waiting for orders. Write them some.**

## Controls

- Type commands at the prompt and press **Enter** to run them, for example
  `move` or `build {move; grab}`; **Ctrl+C** or **Esc** stops a program
- **Alt+W**, **Alt+E**, **Alt+R**, **Alt+T**: focus the world, robot,
  prompt and info panels; the mouse works too
- **Arrow keys** or **h j k l**: scroll the world view
- **F1**: help, **F2**: robots, **F3**: recipes, **F4**: commands,
  **F5**: messages, **F6**: structures
- **Ctrl+G**: show the current goal
- **Ctrl+P**: pause, **Ctrl+X** and **Ctrl+Z**: double and halve the speed
- **Ctrl+Q**: quit

## Options

- `--scenario NAME`: start a scenario directly, e.g. `Tutorials/move`
- `--seed N`: world seed for generated worlds
- `--autoplay`: watch a scenario's built-in solution
- `--speed N`: starting game speed
- `swarm keybindings`: list every key binding

## History

Brent Yorgey started Swarm in 2021, written in Haskell with the Brick
terminal UI library, and it has grown into a community project with more
than thirty contributors. This edition has one small change: it
finds its data folder next to the program, so it runs straight
from the install folder.

## Credits

- Game: [Brent Yorgey and the Swarm contributors](https://swarm-game.github.io/)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: BSD-3-Clause

tabula.title: Tabula
tabula.description: The Roman ancestor of backgammon: fifteen men, three dice, and the one game position that survives from antiquity
tabula.provenance: Asciiverse made Tabula in Rust in 2026. Its rules follow the reconstructions of Louis Becq de Fouquières (1869), R. G. Austin (1934), R. C. Bell (1960) and H. J. R. Murray.
tabula.page:
**THE GAME THE EMPEROR LOST.**

Fifteen men each, three dice, and a race round the board and off it. Each die moves one man. Two of your men together close a point; a single man is hit when an enemy lands on him, and must start all over again. The first to bear off all fifteen wins. If that sounds like backgammon, it should: this is its Roman ancestor.

The Romans left boards by the hundred, dice towers, a tavern wall at Pompeii showing two players quarrelling over a throw, and exactly one recorded game: a poem tells how the emperor Zeno lost with a throw of 2, 5 and 6. Press F1 and see for yourself: the program sets up Zeno's board, and the poet was right. That throw leaves Zeno exactly one play, and it leaves eight of his men standing alone.

- **Tabula, the colours opposite**: the sides run against each other, as in backgammon
- **Tabula, the colours the same way**: both run the same way round, so every point is contested from the start
- **Ludus duodecim scriptorum**: the older game of three rows of twelve

Play the computer at three strengths, from either side, or a friend at the same keyboard.

## Controls

- **Enter** or **Space**: throw; then arrows to a lit man, **Enter** to pick it up, a lit point to put it down, one die at a time; **Esc**: let go, or take back the last step
- **Mouse**: click
- **F1** or **?**: the rules and where they come from; **M**: menu; **Q**: quit
- **O**: the braille ornament on or off

## Options

- `--demo`: the computer plays both sides
- `--seed N`: the same game every time
- `--plain`: start without the ornament, for fonts that draw braille thin

tarts.title: tarts
tarts.description: Twelve classic terminal effects on an endless tour: digital rain, the spinning donut, plasma, fire, flocking boids, the Game of Life and more, twenty seconds each.
tarts.provenance: tarts (Terminal Arts) is by oiwn and contributors, in Rust, since 2022.
tarts.page:
**TWELVE SCREENSAVERS. ONE ENDLESS SHOW.**

Leave your terminal running and walk away. tarts plays the classics of
terminal art one after another: falling digital rain, the spinning
ASCII donut, electric plasma, a crackling fire, flocking boids, pipes
that wind across the screen, Conway's Game of Life, a rotating cube,
drifting constellations, crabs and butterflies, and a maze that builds
itself. Each one fills your window for twenty seconds before the next
takes over, round and round for as long as you like.

Skip ahead when one catches your eye, go back to the one you missed, or
start any of them on its own from the command line, including
pocketworld, a little living planet with drifting continents, rivers
and weather that is not part of the tour.

**Lean back and watch.**

## Controls

- **n**, **Space** or **Right**: next effect
- **p** or **Left**: previous effect
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

To run one effect on its own, start it from a terminal by name, for
example `tarts donut`; `tarts pocketworld` grows a little world with
drifting continents, rivers and weather, and `tarts --help` lists them
all.

## Credits

- tarts: [oiwn and contributors](https://github.com/oiwn/tarts)
- Asciiverse edition: the tour
- License: MIT

terminal-orbit.title: Terminal Orbit
terminal-orbit.description: The aliens are already here! Fly real Newtonian orbits across the solar system in a starfighter drawn in Braille, from the Moon to the rings of Saturn and all the way out to Pluto.
terminal-orbit.provenance: Asciiverse ported Steve Belczyk's ORBIT, a 1999 OpenGL space combat simulator, from its original C source. The original campaign is all here, and the first part of Episode Two is new.
terminal-orbit.page:
**THE ALIENS ARE ALREADY HERE.**

It started with a message carried by hand from Titan Base: something alien is out in the Saturn system. Then the alien fighters came for Titan Base itself.

You fly a small starfighter, and out here nothing is faked: real Newtonian physics, real gravity, real planets at their real distances. Point your nose at a target and you'll sail straight past it! Learn to thrust, brake and coast, swing into orbit, match speeds and dock, and then do it all again with alien fighters on your tail.

Learn to fly out to the Moon and to Mars and back. Defend Titan Base. Hunt a hidden communications station in the Cassini Division of Saturn's rings. Pull the truth out of an alien data store: the whole alien presence at Saturn was a deception, and the real invasion is heading for Jupiter! Then chase the war out to Uranus and Neptune, back in to Mars, where a vast alien energy collector waits for a slow, mighty gun called Bertha, and finally to a strange portal orbiting Pluto.

- **Steve Belczyk's whole 1999 ORBIT campaign,** 28 missions from Earth orbit to Pluto, ported from his own C source.
- **Episode Two: Open Skies,** a new campaign: the aliens are gone and the science missions fly again, with salvager pirates and the breakaway Jovian Combine in the way. Its first part is here.
- **Space drawn in Braille:** ships, planets with real surface maps (press T), 2000 real stars from the Yale Bright Star Catalogue, and constellation lines (press B).
- **An orbit autopilot** (press G) that swings you into a perfect equatorial orbit, with the classic starship-in-orbit camera shots.

The solar system needs a pilot who understands orbits. **ARE YOU THAT PILOT?**

## Controls

- **W** / **S** or **Up** / **Down**: thrust forward and back
- **A** / **D** or **Left** / **Right**: yaw, **I** / **K**: pitch, **J** / **L**: roll
- **X**: warp engines, **H**: hold still (needed to dock)
- **Space**: fire, **U**: lock the nearest enemy, **Y**: next target, **F**: next weapon
- **G**: orbit autopilot, **C**: camera (in orbit: the two orbit shots and the cockpit)
- **T**: planet surfaces, **B**: constellation lines, **N**: names, **O**: the orrery, **Z**: dense star field
- **M**: recall the last mission message, **P**: pause, **Q** or **Esc**: back to the title (progress is saved)

## Credits

- ORBIT: Steve Belczyk, 1999, GPL
- Terminal port and Episode Two: Asciiverse
- Stars: the Yale Bright Star Catalogue, from ORBIT's own source

terminal-parrot.title: terminal-parrot
terminal-parrot.description: The party parrot, dancing in your terminal in every colour, for as long as you let it.
terminal-parrot.provenance: terminal-parrot is by John Hobbs and contributors, in Go, since 2016.
terminal-parrot.page:
**PARTY. PARROT. FOREVER.**

The party parrot, the dancing kakapo of a thousand chat rooms, in ASCII
art in your terminal. It bobs, it spins, it changes colour on every
frame, and it does not stop until you press a key. Speed it up, turn it
upside down for the Aussie edition, or give it a set number of dances.

**Every terminal deserves a parrot.**

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `-delay 25` makes it a fast parrot (the default is 75
milliseconds a frame), `-orientation aussie` turns it upside down, and
`-loops 5` stops after five dances. `-path` points at a folder of your own
`.animation` files, and `terminal-parrot <name>` plays one of them.

## Credits

- terminal-parrot: [John Hobbs and contributors](https://github.com/jmhobbs/terminal-parrot)
- The parrot: a jp2a rendering of the Party Parrot, after Sirocco the
  kakapo
- Asciiverse edition: the parrot only, any key quits, a clean exit on
  SIGTERM
- License: MIT

terminal-phase.title: Terminal Phase
terminal-phase.description: A side-scrolling space shooter in your terminal: fly through caverns of rock, dodge fire and shoot down squigglers, turrets, mines and kamikaze ships across a twinkling Braille starfield.
terminal-phase.provenance: Christine Lemmer-Webber wrote Terminal Phase in Racket in 2019 as a test program for Spritely Goblins and a reward for Patreon supporters, who are named in its credits. This is the Racket version as it stood before the move to Guile.
terminal-phase.page:
**A SPACE SHOOTER. IN YOUR TERMINAL. OF COURSE.**

Your little **>** ship drifts through a cavern of rock while the stars twinkle past in Braille dots. Then the enemies come: squiggling ships that weave toward you, turrets that fire across your path, mines, kamikazes that turn and aim themselves at you, and cannons firing up from the ground. Keep shooting, keep moving, and don't scrape the walls.

Two levels, three lives, and a credits roll of everyone who backed it.

- **Old-school shmup**: one ship, one gun, a lot of things that want you dead
- **Terrain that fights back**: the cavern narrows and widens as you fly
- **A starfield in Braille**: smooth, tiny stars in plain text
- **Time travel**: start it with `-t` and press **t** to step back through the last moments of play

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move
- **Space**: fire
- **q** or **Esc**: leave the level; **q** on the title menu quits
- In the menu: **Up** and **Down** to choose, **Enter** to pick

## Options

- `-t`: allow time travel with the **t** key
- `-f`: show frames per second
- `terminal-phase LEVEL-FILE ...`: play your own level files instead of the built-in ones

## History

Terminal Phase began in 2019 as a test program for Spritely Goblins, a library for programs built from communicating objects. Christine Lemmer-Webber later moved it to Guile; this is the Racket version, with the fixes and new enemies that came after its 1.1 release.

## Credits

- Terminal Phase: [Christine Lemmer-Webber](https://gitlab.com/dustyweb/terminal-phase), with thanks to the supporters named in its credits
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

terminal-pong.title: terminal.pong
terminal-pong.description: Ping pong in the terminal: beat the computer, take on a friend at one keyboard, or lean back and watch two AIs rally, with ten power shots a side.
terminal-pong.provenance: terminal.pong is IshmamR's Pong in Rust and Ratatui (2025).
terminal-pong.page:
**TWO PADDLES. ONE BALL. TEN POWER SHOTS EACH.**

The classic paddle game, in your terminal. Play against the
computer, take on a friend at the same keyboard, or pick "I like to
watch" and let two AIs rally for as long as you care to look. Each side
has ten power shots that send the ball flying; save them for the moment
the other side is out of position.

The court grows and shrinks with your window, even mid-game. Turn the
difficulty up or down from the pause menu, and dress the court in
Monokai, Solarized, Dracula, Gruvbox Dark, Nord, One Dark or High
Contrast.

**Serve.**

## Controls

- **Player 1**: **Up** and **Down** (or the mouse wheel), **/** for a power shot
- **Player 2**: **W** and **S**, **Space** for a power shot
- **P**: pause; in the pause menu, **D** cycles the colour themes
- **Esc**: back to the menu

Difficulty for each mode, and the default theme, are in Settings.

## Credits

- terminal.pong: [IshmamR](https://github.com/IshmamR/terminal.pong)
- Asciiverse edition: a court that follows the window size, and a frame-rate cap
- License: MIT

terminal-rain-lightning.title: Terminal Rain
terminal-rain-lightning.description: Rain streams down your terminal, and when the storm comes forked lightning cracks across it, with rain and thunder to listen to if you like.
terminal-rain-lightning.provenance: Terminal Rain is by rmaake1, in Python on curses, from 2025 to 2026, with slow motion by plasma and rain and thunder sounds contributed from Pixabay.
terminal-rain-lightning.page:
**RAIN ON THE SCREEN. THUNDER IN THE SPEAKERS.**

Rain streams down the terminal in cyan strokes and dots. Switch on the
thunderstorm and it pours harder and brighter, and now and then a bolt
of lightning forks down from the sky, flares and fades. With sound on,
the rain patters along and thunder rolls in a moment after each strike.

Slow it down, speed it up, turn the volume to taste, and pick your own
colours for the rain and the lightning.

**Stay in. It's pouring.**

## Controls

- **t**: thunderstorm on or off (Asciiverse starts in the storm)
- **s**: speed: fast, medium, slow
- **m**: sound on or off (needs `ffplay` from FFmpeg)
- **v**: volume: quiet, normal, loud
- **q** or **Esc**: quit

## Options

From a terminal: `terminal-rain --sound` starts with sound,
`--rain-color` and `--lightning-color` take black, red, green, yellow,
blue, magenta, cyan or white, and `--speed` and `--volume` set where they
start. `terminal-rain --help` lists them all.

## Credits

- Terminal Rain: [rmaake1](https://github.com/rmaake1/terminal-rain-lightning)
- Slow motion: plasma (xXBlackPlasmaXx)
- Rain and thunder sounds: Pixabay sound effects contributed to the
  project, cut and varied by rmaake1
- Asciiverse edition: the script ported to Rust, one program for Linux,

- License: MIT

terminal-space-program.title: Terminal Space Program
terminal-space-program.description: A real orbital-mechanics rocket simulator in braille: fly a Saturn V to orbit by hand, plan the transfer to the Moon, rendezvous, dock and come home under parachute.
terminal-space-program.provenance: jasonfen began Terminal Space Program in April 2026, in Go, to bring Kerbal Space Program to the terminal; its solar-system foundation comes from Francis' go-solar-system.
terminal-space-program.page:
**REAL ROCKETS. REAL ORBITS. ONE TERMINAL.**

Kerbal Space Program, in your terminal. Our own solar system at full
scale: low Earth orbit takes about 9.4 km/s, the Moon's orbit is tilted,
and the rockets on the pad are the real ones (Saturn V, SLS, Falcon 9)
with their real thrust and fuel.

Fly a launch off the pad by hand in the chase cam, drop your spent stages,
and watch the projected high point climb until ORBIT READY. Then plant a
burn and go: target the Moon, press **H**, and a transfer appears with
the orbit it will leave you in drawn on the map.

- **Five star systems**: Sol at full scale, Lumen at a tenth (the home
  planet Kern with its moons Cursor and Glyph, and the red planet Rust),
  Alpha Centauri, Kepler-452 and TRAPPIST-1.
- **Plan like a flight director**: burn nodes, one-key Hohmann transfers,
  Lambert and porkchop solvers for the planets.
- **Rendezvous and dock** port to port, with a true-scale Proximity view.
- **Build your own** in the Vehicle Assembly Building, with live
  delta-v, TWR and mass.
- **Flight School** walks you from the camera to orbit to your first
  docking; a Challenge ladder waits after it.
- **Play together**: host a session from your own game and friends on
  your local network join from their terminals, each with their own space
  program and their own clock.

**GO FOR LAUNCH.**

## Controls

- **F1**: every key, in the game
- **t** / **T**: set / clear the target; **H**: plan a transfer to it;
  **G**: warp to the next burn
- **z** / **x**: full throttle / cut; **b**: light the engine;
  **Space**: drop a stage
- **W**: point along your ground speed (the gravity turn);
  **→** / **←**: tip the nose toward / back from your heading
- **.** / **,**: warp faster / slower; **+** / **-**: zoom; **V**: launch
  view; **F2**: hide the instruments
- **M**: missions; **n**: new vessel; **Tab**: next star system
- **F5** / **F9**: quicksave / quickload; **Esc**: menu;
  **Ctrl+C**: quit

## Options

- `--launch-site KSC --loadout Saturn-V`: start on the pad
- `--orbit moon --altitude 100km`: start around the Moon
- `--system Lumen`: start in the Lumen system
- `--serve`: host a session for your local network

## Credits

- Terminal Space Program: [jasonfen](https://github.com/jasonfen/terminal-space-program)
- Solar-system foundation: Francis' go-solar-system
- License: MIT

termsuji.title: termsuji
termsuji.description: A real Go board in your terminal, wood and all, with GNU Go across the table: 9x9, 13x13 or 19x19, ten strengths, and handicap stones while you find your feet.
termsuji.provenance: termsuji is lvank's terminal client for online-go.com, in Go with tview (2022).
termsuji.page:
**BLACK MOVES FIRST. THE BOARD IS WAITING.**

Pull up a chair at a proper Go board: lines and star points on warm wood, black and white stones sitting right on the points, as big as your terminal can draw them. Across the table sits GNU Go, and it comes with the game. No account, no server, no waiting for an opponent to turn up. Just you, the stones and a patient adversary.

Pick your board: 9x9 for a quick, sharp fight, 19x19 for the full game. Pick your colour. Then pick how hard GNU Go should push back, from strength 1 to 10, and give Black up to nine handicap stones if you want a head start.

- **A board that looks like one**: wood, lines and star points; on a big terminal the points spread out and the stones become round discs
- **GNU Go built in**: it thinks while you study the board, marks the last stone played, and counts the game when both sides pass
- **Take it back**: **u** undoes your move and GNU Go's answer, as often as you like
- **Never lose a game in progress**: walk away mid-game and it is waiting under Continue, saved as an SGF file any Go program can open

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**: move the cursor; **Enter**: play a stone there
- **p**: pass; **u**: take back your move and GNU Go's answer
- **t**: change the board's look; **q**: back to the menu (the game is
  saved)
- **n**: a new game once the game is over
- In the menus: **Up**, **Down** or **Tab** to choose, **Enter** to go on

## Credits

- termsuji: lvank ([github.com/lvank/termsuji](https://github.com/lvank/termsuji)),
  2022, written in Go with tview and tcell
- GNU Go 3.9.1: the GNU Go authors
  ([gnu.org/software/gnugo](https://www.gnu.org/software/gnugo/)),
  GPL-3.0-or-later, shipped beside termsuji with its licence and source
- Asciiverse edition: play against GNU Go, saved games and the classic
  board
- License: MIT (termsuji), GPL-3.0-or-later (GNU Go)

ternimal.title: Ternimal
ternimal.description: A creature made of light crawls around your terminal on a path that never ends and never repeats. Its maker admits it is not very useful. Watch it anyway.
ternimal.provenance: Ternimal is by Philipp Emanuel Weidmann, one Rust file with no dependencies, from 2017.
ternimal.page:
**TERNIMAL. NOTE THE SPELLING.**

A lifeform made of light creeps around the window. Its body stretches and contracts as it crawls along a path of circular arcs that never ends and never repeats, glowing white along its spine and fading to blue and violet at its edges. Leave it running and watch it coil.

Its maker is honest about it: "From a practical perspective, the program is not very useful." What it does have is a glow renderer, a skeleton that bends along the path, and a body shaped by Fourier series, all in about a thousand lines of Rust with no dependencies at all.

- **Smooth as silk**: half blocks in 24-bit colour, so the body moves at twice the vertical resolution of the text
- **Never the same twice**: the path is generated as it goes
- **A shape-shifter**: one line of arguments turns it into an anaconda or a swarm (see Options)

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, everything about the creature can be changed with
`name=value` arguments: `length=100 thickness=1,4,1,0,0 radius=6,12` makes
a long snake, `length=200 thickness=0,4,19,0,0` a swarm, `speed=` and
`fps=` set the pace, `gradient=0:#666600,0.5:#00ff00,1:#003300` the
colours, and `true_color=false` falls back to 256 colours. Without
`fit=true` it draws a 60 by 20 arena below the prompt, as the original
does. The README lists the examples and the source lists every parameter.

## Credits

- Ternimal: [Philipp Emanuel Weidmann](https://github.com/p-e-w/ternimal)
- Asciiverse edition: quits on any key, and fills the window with `fit=true`
- License: GPL-3.0-only

tessera.title: Tessera
tessera.description: Mazes in four dimensions: every box on screen is one slice, and the way through runs between them. Twelve campaign mazes, a daily maze for everyone, and endless ones, in fog if you dare.
tessera.provenance: Asciiverse made Tessera in Rust in 2026, after bleuje's browser 4D maze, which draws a four-dimensional maze as a grid of flat ones.
tessera.page:
**FOUR DIMENSIONS. ONE WAY THROUGH.**

A maze with two more directions than you are used to. Tessera lays it
out as slices: every box on screen is one flat maze, the boxes beside it
are its neighbours in the third dimension, and the boxes above and below
are its neighbours in the fourth. Walk inside a slice, and where a cell
says so, step straight through into the slice beside it, or above, or
below, landing in the same spot.

The marks tell you where: cyan `◂ ▸ ↔` for a way through to the slices
left and right, amber `▴ ▾ ↕` for the slices above and below. Your place
shows faintly in every slice and lights up where a step through would
land, so you always know what the next jump does. Start in the top left
corner of the first slice; the pink `◆` waits in the far corner of the
last.

And when you are lost, turn the maze. Any two of its four directions can
be the slices, so every maze can be seen six ways, and a way that winds
through slice after slice in one view may run straight in another.

- **Campaign**: twelve mazes, the same for everyone, from two slices side
  by side to twelve slices of five by five; each one opens the next
- **Fog**: two campaign mazes, and any endless one you like, show only
  what you have already walked past
- **Daily maze**: one new maze a day, the same for every player; solve
  it on days in a row and Tessera counts the streak
- **Endless**: a fresh maze every time, in four sizes
- **Hints** when you are stuck, at ten seconds each, and your best time
  for every maze
- **Race yourself**: beat a campaign or daily maze, and next time your
  best run walks beside you as a grey `@`

**STEP THROUGH.**

## Controls

- **Arrows** or **WASD**: walk inside a slice
- **J** and **L**: step to the slice on the left or right
- **I** and **K**: step to the slice above or below
  (**Shift** with the arrows works too)
- **V** or **Tab**: turn the maze to its next view
- **H**: hint (+10 s); **P**: pause; **R**: start the maze over;
  **M**: sound off and on; **G**: show or hide your best run;
  **Esc**: back
- **Gamepad**: left stick or d-pad walk, right stick or the face buttons
  step between slices, the triggers turn the maze, LB hints, Start pauses

The first six campaign mazes play in 80×24, turned to a view that fits
when they need it; the largest mazes want about 95×39, and the game asks
for more room when a maze does not fit.

## Options

- `--daily`: straight into today's maze
- `--level N`: campaign maze N
- `--endless small`, `medium`, `large` or `huge`, with `--fog` for fog
- `--watch`: watch the way through being walked, the maze turning as it goes
- `--mute`: no sound

## Credits

- Tessera: Asciiverse
- After bleuje's 4D maze
- License: MIT

tetrix.title: Tetrix
tetrix.description: Six fields. Nine dirty tricks. One survivor! The late-90s LAN-party block buster legend is back: clear lines, grab specials, and Quake, Bomb and Switch your friends into oblivion!
tetrix.provenance: Asciiverse made Tetrix in Rust in 2026, after St0rmCat's TetriNET, the late-90s multiplayer falling-block game with attack blocks. Its rules follow TetriNET 1.13, and the rotation table and core rules are ported from Andrew Church's tetrinet 0.11.
tetrix.page:
**SIX FIELDS. NINE DIRTY TRICKS. ONE SURVIVOR.**

Remember the late 90s? Six friends, six fields, blocks falling faster and faster, and somebody across the room laughing a little too hard. That was TetriNET, and it's back in your terminal!

Clear lines and your field coughs up specials: lettered blocks that drop straight into your arsenal. Then pick a victim. Hit them with a Blockquake and watch every row in their field lurch sideways! Set off a Block Bomb and blow their O pieces to bits! Shove junk lines up from below until they're gasping at the ceiling! And when your own field is about to bury you? Switch Fields, and hand them the mess with a smile.

Clear two, three or four lines at once and everyone else eats one, two or four junk lines. Classic rules, classic cruelty.

- **Up to six players in one brawl!** Host a game and it simply appears on everyone's menu across the network. No addresses to type, no internet needed.
- **Nine specials**, from the sneaky Add Line to the life-saving Nuke Field.
- **Nobody else awake?** Ada, Blitz, Cobol, Dvorak and Emacs are always up for a game, from easy all the way up to brutal.
- **Bigger terminal, bigger boards.**

It's the one you play with five friends at a LAN party until somebody spills a drink. **WHO'S STILL STANDING?**

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**: move
- **Up** or **x**: rotate clockwise; **z**: counter-clockwise
- **Down**: soft drop; **Space**: hard drop
- **1** to **6**: fire your front special at that player (your own number for the ones meant for yourself)
- **d**: discard the front special
- **s**: the landing shadow on or off
- **?**: the keys, and what every special does

Tetrix needs a terminal of at least 92 columns by 28 rows.

## The specials

- **A** Add Line: a junk line pushed up from the bottom
- **C** Clear Line: removes your bottom row (use on yourself)
- **N** Nuke Field: empties your field (use on yourself)
- **R** Random Clear: knocks out ten random cells
- **S** Switch Fields: swap fields with the target
- **B** Clear Specials: the target's specials turn into plain blocks
- **G** Gravity: every column collapses, filling the holes (use on yourself)
- **Q** Blockquake: every row shifts sideways
- **O** Block Bomb: every O block in the target's field explodes

## Options

- `--solo`, `--host`, `--join`: straight to a way of playing
- `--bots N`, `--skill N`: how many bots, and how good
- `--name`, `--level N`, `--seed N`
- `--classic-delay`, `--slide`, `--no-classic`, `--noshadow`: rule and display tweaks; `tetrix --help` explains each

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- Rules after St0rmCat's TetriNET 1.13
- Piece rotation and core rules ported from Andrew Church's tetrinet 0.11
- Networking: iroh

news.notes:
- Title menu; solo play against up to five bots at four strengths
- LAN play for up to six: automatic discovery, a lobby, bots in empty seats
- The full TetriNET special set, classic lines, level averaging
- Win list across rounds
- Juice pass; a layout that scales with the terminal
- Direct join across networks (`tetrix --join <id>`)

tetro-tui.title: Tetro TUI
tetro-tui.description: A modern tetromino stacker for the terminal: seven game modes and two to unlock, every handling timing, ten palettes, fireworks on every line, and replays of your best runs.
tetro-tui.provenance: Strophox started Tetro TUI in June 2024 as a terminal stacker that could be tuned like the modern competitive ones, on a game engine of their own, falling-tetromino-engine.
tetro-tui.page:
**FOUR SQUARES. SEVEN SHAPES. AS MANY SETTINGS AS YOU LIKE.**

Pieces fall, you turn them and slot them in, full lines clear. The idea
is old; this is the modern way to play it, in your terminal, with the
handling a serious stacker expects: hold, previews, hard drops, and every
timing (DAS, ARR, soft drop, line clear and spawn delays) yours to set.

- **Seven modes and two to unlock**: Regular (160 lines as gravity
  climbs), Swift (40 lines against the clock), Puzzle (24 hand-made
  boards), Cheese, Survival, Combo and Custom; finish Regular for Classic
  and Master.
- **Your rules**: four rotation systems, piece randomizers from pure
  chance to bags, preview count, keys of your own.
- **Your look**: Unicode, ASCII, Braille or Elektronika 60 tiles, ten tile
  palettes, and line clears that burn, pop, sparkle or rain confetti.
- **Scores, replays and all-time stats**, kept in one save file.

**STACK CLEAN.**

## Controls

- **Left** / **Right**: move; **A** / **D**: rotate left / right
- **Down**: soft drop; **Up**: hard drop; **Space**: hold
- **Esc**: pause; **?**: every key, at any time
- Menus: arrows and **Enter**, or Vim keys

Keys, handling and graphics are all in Settings.

## Options

- `--seed N`: the piece sequence for a custom game
- `--board "..."`: a starting board for a custom game

## Credits

- Tetro TUI: [Strophox](https://github.com/Strophox/tetro-tui)
- License: MIT
