threshold.description: Roleplay-enforced high fantasy MUD with player-run politics, economy and guilds

tintin.title: TinTin++
tintin.description: The Kickin Tickin Dikumud Client: connect to any MUD and make it do your bidding with triggers, aliases, a mapper and a scripting language of its own.
tintin.provenance: TinTin++ grew from Peter Unold's TinTin III (1992); Bill Reis and then Igor van den Hoven continued it, and Igor maintains it today.

upstream.name: Peter Unold, Bill Reis and Igor van den Hoven

tintin.page:
**THE KICKIN TICKIN DIKUMUD CLIENT.**

That is what the name stands for: (T)he K(I)cki(N) (T)ickin D(I)kumud Clie(N)t. Since Peter Unold's TinTin III in 1992, it has been the client MUD players reach for when they want the game to work for them. Connect to any MUD on the internet with one command, then teach it your habits.

Hungry? `#action {You are hungry} {get bread bag;eat bread}` and you need never starve again. Tired of typing? One alias runs a dozen commands. Lost? The mapper draws every room you walk through, and walks you back.

Fair warning, from its own manual: "TinTin++ doesn't baby sit." You get the keys to everything.

- **Actions, aliases and substitutions**: react to anything the MUD sends, with up to 99 wildcards or full PCRE patterns
- **A scripting language**: variables, lists, loops and maths, all in its own `#` commands
- **The mapper**: rooms and exits drawn as you explore, and `#map run` to speedwalk across them
- **Several sessions at once**, a split screen for input and output, and TLS with `#ssl`

## Getting started

- `#session <name> <host> <port>`: connect, for example `#session bat batmud.bat.org 23`
- `#help`: the built-in manual
- `#end`: quit

## Credits

- TinTin++: Peter Unold, Bill Reis and Igor van den Hoven
- Asciiverse edition: static builds and packaging, no code changes
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

tinyfugue.title: TinyFugue
tinyfugue.description: The MUD client its players have called tf since the early 1990s: several worlds at once, and triggers, hilites, gags and macros to shape every line the MUD sends.
tinyfugue.provenance: TinyFugue is Ken Keys' MUD client; 5.0 beta 8 (2007) was its last release.
tinyfugue.page:
**SEVERAL WORLDS. ONE KEYBOARD. TOTAL CONTROL.**

TinyFugue, "tf" to its players, has been connecting people to MUDs since the early 1990s. Type `/connect` with a host and a port and you are in. Then make the game yours.

Tell tf what to watch for in the text the MUD sends, and it will light it up (a hilite), make it vanish (a gag), or fire off a macro of your own (a trigger). It keeps a history of every line, so you can `/recall` what scrolled past an hour ago or `/log` the whole session to a file. And it will hold several worlds open at once, switching between them as the action moves.

- **Macros**: from one-word abbreviations to whole programs in tf's own language; its library even solves the Towers of Hanoi, "not very useful except as an example of recursion"
- **Triggers, hilites and gags**: react to, highlight or silence any line
- **Many worlds at once**: name them with `/addworld` and connect with a word
- **A split screen**: output above, input below, and a status line between them
- **Debian's patches**: this edition carries the fixes that have kept it building

## Getting started

- `tinyfugue <host> <port>`: connect straight away
- `/connect <host> <port>`: connect from inside tf
- `/help`: the built-in manual
- `/quit`: quit

## Credits

- TinyFugue: Ken Keys
- Debian patches: Russ Allbery, Chris Lamb
- Asciiverse edition: static builds and packaging
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

tristam-island.title: Tristam Island
tristam-island.description: Stranded on an island in the Atlantic, you find a whole village with nobody in it, a white house behind a fence, and one very clever albatross. Get the radio working. Find out why everyone left.
tristam-island.provenance: Hugo Labrande wrote Tristam Island in 2020, in the style of a 1980s Infocom adventure and for the same Z-machine version 3.
tristam-island.page:
**A WHOLE VILLAGE. NOT A SOUL IN IT.**

After the accident, you find yourself on the south beach of a small island in the Atlantic. "The immensity of the Atlantic Ocean makes you feel minuscule, a needle in a haystack, with no chance of being rescued." So rescue yourself. Catch a fish. Light a fire with the last of your wet matches. Rig yourself a bed for the night.

Then climb the hill, and find what nobody should find on a deserted island: a dozen buildings, a pub, a storehouse, a radio tower, and a tall white house behind a fence, its metal door locked with a keypad. On the notice board, the community garden rota is filled in every day until February 18th. After that, nobody signs up at all. Strange.

You are not entirely alone, though. There is an albatross, and it seems to know exactly what it is doing.

- **An old-school adventure**: explore, map, puzzle and survive, written in 2020 in the style of the 1980s Infocom games and for the very same Z-machine they ran on
- **A mystery to unpick**: get the radio working, get past the keypad, and find out why everyone left
- **A friend with wings**: share your catch, and the albatross may return the favour

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something (or **x**)
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take**, **drop**, **open**, **push** things; **help** or **about** in most games
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/tristam-island`.

## Credits

- Tristam Island: Hugo Labrande, 2020
- License: Released as open source under CC0 1.0 by the author in 2023
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

trsr.title: Treasure
trsr.description: Minesweeper turned inside out, for two: take turns digging for treasure, and whoever finds more than half of it wins. Play the computer, a friend, or watch the computer play itself.
trsr.provenance: abakh wrote Treasure for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
trsr.page:
**THE TREASURE IS DOWN THERE. GET TO IT FIRST.**

Minesweeper, turned around, for two. Treasure lies hidden under the field, and two sides, Percent (**%**) and Square (**#**), take turns opening cells. A cell without treasure shows how many of its eight neighbours hold some, found or not, and a cell with none around opens its neighbours too. Strike treasure and you score it and dig again, a few times in a row at most. Find more than half of it and you win; there is always an odd number of treasures, so there is no draw.

In the game's own words: *Like Mines but you need to find stuff instead of avoiding them. Try to trick the AI into doing useless stuff.*

At the start it asks who plays each side. Press **Enter** twice to play Percent against the computer, which plays Square; you go first. Press **Enter** and then **h** for two players taking turns at one keyboard, or **c** and then **Enter** to watch the computer play both sides.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys**, **hjkl** or **wasd**: move
- **Enter**: dig the cell
- **Mouse**: click to dig
- **PgUp**, **PgDn**, **<**, **>**: scroll a field bigger than the
  terminal
- **F1** or **?**: help on the controls, **F2** or **!**: how to play
- **q** or **Esc**: quit; at the end, **y** plays again and **n** or
  **q** quits

## Field size

Started from a shell, Treasure takes the size and the amount of
treasure, for example `trsr -w 30 -l 20 -m 75`: `-w` is the width,
`-l` the length (height) and `-m` the number of treasures; without `-m`
an eighth of the cells hold one. The default field is 15 by 15, or 20
by 15 on a terminal narrower than 45 columns.

## History

Treasure is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a collection
of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the classic BSD
games.

tty-rex.title: tty-rex
tty-rex.description: No internet? No problem. The browser's offline T-Rex runs again in your terminal, rebuilt from Chromium's own source: jump the cacti, duck the pterodactyls, run through the night.
tty-rex.provenance: Asciiverse recreated Chrome's offline T-Rex runner, written from Chromium's own source: the same rules, timings, sprites and sounds.
tty-rex.page:
**NO INTERNET. NO PROBLEM. RUN.**

You know this dinosaur. It is the little T-Rex that waits on the browser's "No Internet" page, and now it runs in your terminal, drawn in Braille dots. Press Space and the road opens up. Jump the cacti. Past speed 8.5 the pterodactyls arrive, so duck. Every 700 points night falls. And it only ever gets faster.

Every rule, timing, sprite and sound comes from Chromium's own source, so it plays exactly the way you remember: hold jump for a higher leap, press down in mid-air to drop fast, and chase your own high score.

- **True to the pixel**: the original sprite art, every art pixel kept at the home scale
- **Fits anywhere**: from a 20x7 split pane to a big window; the dots get coarser or finer, the game doesn't change
- **Four looks**: Braille in your terminal's own colours, classic grey on white, coloured sprites, or colour blocks
- **Auto mode**: press **A** and he runs on his own, a strip of living scenery for the bottom of your tmux layout
- **Gamepad ready**: A jumps, B ducks, as in the original

## Controls

- **Space**, **Up**, **W** or **K**: jump (hold for a higher jump)
- **Down**, **S** or **J**: duck; in mid-air, drop fast
- **Enter**: run again after a crash (Space works too, after a moment)
- **P**: pause; **V**: next look; **A**: auto mode; **M**: mute
- **Q** or **Esc**: quit
- Gamepad: **A** jumps, **B** ducks, **Start** restarts after a crash and pauses otherwise, the D-pad's up and down jump and duck, **Select** toggles auto mode

Holding jump for a higher jump needs a terminal that reports key releases (the kitty keyboard protocol); elsewhere every jump is a full one.

## Credits

- The original game, its sprites and sounds: The Chromium Authors (BSD-3-Clause)
- Terminal version: Asciiverse

news.notes:
- Gamepads work on Windows: gilrs reads them through XInput, since its
  default (Windows Gaming Input) only reports to a program with a focused
  window of its own, which a terminal game never has

ttyper.title: ttyper
ttyper.description: A typing test for the terminal: type the words, then see your speed, your accuracy and the keys that tripped you up. English and a dozen other languages, or code in a dozen programming languages.
ttyper.provenance: Max Niederman started ttyper in Rust in 2021, and contributors have added languages and modes since.
ttyper.page:
**HOW FAST DO YOU REALLY TYPE?**

Fifty common words, one box to type them in. Each word lights up green or red as you go, and the moment you finish ttyper shows your words per minute, your accuracy, a chart of your speed through the test, and the keys you miss most.

Then press **r** for a fresh test, or **p** to practise the words you got wrong.

- **Many languages**: English (100, 200 or 1000 most common words, or advanced, or pirate), French, Galician, German, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Thai, Ukrainian
- **Or code**: C, C++, C#, Go, HTML, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Python, Ruby, Rust, SQL and Qt
- **Your own words**: any text file, line by line
- **Hard modes**: sudden death restarts on your first mistake; turn off backspace or going back

## Controls

- Type the words; **Space** moves to the next one, **Backspace** fixes the current one
- **Esc**: end the test
- On the results screen: **r** for a new test, **p** to practise your mistakes, **q** or **Esc** to quit

## Options

- `-w N`: number of words (default 50)
- `-l LANGUAGE`: word list, for example `-l english1000` or `-l rust`
- `--list-languages`: every list built in
- `--sudden-death`, `--no-backspace`, `--no-backtrack`: harder tests
- `ttyper FILE`: type the lines of a text file

## Credits

- ttyper: [Max Niederman](https://github.com/max-niederman/ttyper) and contributors
- License: MIT

tugow.title: Tug of War
tugow.description: Tug of war with your fingers: type the digits faster than the other side pulls and drag them over the line. Number row, numpad or home row.
tugow.provenance: abakh wrote Tug of War for New BSD Games, a collection of small curses games in C.
tugow.page:
**TYPE THOSE THINGS AND BEAT THE OTHER GUY.**

That is the game's whole instruction sheet, word for word, and it is all you need. Two figures pull on a rope. Under **Type!** is a row of digits: type the first one and the rope moves a step your way, while the other side keeps hauling it back at a steady pace. Drag them up to the line in the middle and you go up a level, where they pull faster and every digit is worth more. Get dragged to the line yourself and it is over: your score goes into the high score table, and beat the record and the game congratulates you in big letters.

The digits make it practice for the number row or the numpad. Press **h** during a game to switch to the home row instead: **a** to **l**, **;** and **'**.

## Controls

- **0** to **9**: type the next digit (in home-row mode, the next key)
- **h**: home-row mode, home-row keys instead of digits
- **F1** or **?**: how to play
- **q**: end the game; at the end, **y** plays again and **n** or **q** quits

## History

Tug of War is one of the games abakh wrote for New BSD Games, a
collection of small curses games started in 2018 and named after the
classic BSD games.

twistty.title: Twistty
twistty.description: A 3D twisty cube in your terminal: turn the faces, spin the whole cube, scramble it with a seed and solve it, in true colour, drawn in half blocks, sextants, real pixels or its creator's own coloured ASCII.
twistty.provenance: Benjamin Jones wrote this cube in C in December 2019, drawing it in 3D with his own small renderer and turning its pixels into coloured ASCII with CAM, a curses library he had written that summer.
twistty.page:
**TWENTY-SIX LITTLE CUBES. SIX COLOURS. ONE TERMINAL.**

A real 3D cube floats in your terminal, and every face of it turns. Spin the whole thing around with the arrow keys, twist any face a quarter turn with a single letter, and watch the layer swing round in smooth animation. Then scramble it thirty turns deep and try to bring it home.

Twistty draws its cube the way a 3D game would, triangle by triangle, with depth and perspective, and then decides how your terminal should show it:

- **Half blocks, sextants and octants** in full 24-bit colour, picked to suit your terminal
- **Real pixels** in terminals that do graphics, such as kitty and Ghostty
- **Classic**: Benjamin Jones' original look, every cell matched to the ASCII character that best fits its shape, so the cube is built from letters and punctuation
- **Scramble with a seed**: type any word and get the same scramble every time, or leave it empty for a random one
- **Save and load** a cube in the middle of a solve
- **Space squares it up**: the cube swings to the nearest straight-on view

## Controls

- **f b l r u d**: turn the front, back, left, right, up or down face counterclockwise; **F B L R U D** (with Shift) turn it clockwise
- **Arrows**: turn the whole cube; **z** / **Z**: roll it
- **Space**: square the cube up to the view
- **v**: the next look (classic, half blocks, quadrants, sextants, octants, pixels; only those your terminal can show)
- **m** or **Esc**: the menu: Resume, Scramble, Save, Load, Exit

Faces are named as the cube faces you now, so **f** is always the side looking at you.

## Options

- `--view NAME`: start in a look: `classic`, `half`, `quadrant`, `sextant`, `octant` or `pixel`

## History

Benjamin Jones built this cube in 2019 on CAM, his own library for drawing pixels as coloured ASCII in curses' eight colours. This edition moves it onto notcurses, which gives it true colour (the orange and white faces were magenta and cyan before), finer block and pixel graphics, and a cube that is square whatever your font.

## Credits

- Twistty: Benjamin Jones (the cube and CAM)
- Drawn with notcurses by Nick Black and its contributors
- License: MIT

typespeed.title: Typespeed
typespeed.description: Words fly across the screen and you have to type them before they escape. Let ten get away and it's over. Climb from Beginner to 3l33t and *(GOD)*, in Unix commands, code or nine languages.
typespeed.provenance: Typespeed is by Jani Ollikainen and Jaakko Manelius, later maintained by Tobias Stoeckmann; 0.6.5 (2008) was its last release.

upstream.name: Jani Ollikainen, Jaakko Manelius and Tobias Stoeckmann

typespeed.page:
**TYPE IT FAST, OR BE A LEWSER.**

That's the whole idea, straight from the game's own credits screen. Words drift across the screen from left to right. Type one and press Enter before it reaches the far edge. Let ten get away and the game is over. And the higher your score climbs, the faster they come.

Choose your words first: Unix or DOS commands, programming functions, C# keywords, or words in English, Finnish, French, German, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese, Spanish or Thai. Then type. At the bottom of the screen your rank rises every hundred points: Beginner, Learner, NoGood, Average, Good, VeryGood, Pro, 3l33t, *(GOD)*. Make it past *(GOD)* and the game simply calls you Computer.

- **Real numbers**: words per minute, characters per second, misses, and a rank for your typos as well
- **High scores** with your name on them
- **Word lists for everyone**: sysadmins, programmers, and nine languages

## Controls

- **Type** a word and press **Enter**
- **Esc**: end the game
- In menus: the numbers, **Up**, **Down** and **Enter**

Your high scores are kept in `~/.typespeed/score`.

## Credits

- Typespeed: Jani Ollikainen and Jaakko Manelius, with later work by
  Tobias Stoeckmann
- Debian patches: Dafydd Harries, Sudip Mukherjee, Helmut Grohne
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

typhon-accords.title: Star Trek: Typhon Accords
typhon-accords.description: Star Trek role-play after the Destiny and Typhon Pact novels, as the Federation rebuilds

typioca.title: typioca
typioca.description: A cozy typing speed test: race the clock or a word count, or type sentences from classic novels, then see your speed, accuracy and a chart of how you did.
typioca.provenance: Lukas Bloznelis started typioca in Go in 2022, built on Bubble Tea, and contributors have added word lists and layouts since.
typioca.page:
**TYPE FAST. TYPE COZY.**

Pick a test from the menu and start typing. The words wait in a few calm lines; what you've typed turns white, mistakes turn red. When you're done typioca shows your words per minute, your accuracy, your raw speed and a chart of your pace through the test, and keeps your results so you can see whether you're getting faster.

- **Three kinds of test**: against the clock (15, 30, 60 or 120 seconds), a word count (10 to 100 words) or a sentence count (1 to 30 sentences)
- **Classic books**: word and sentence lists from Frankenstein, Dracula, Pride and Prejudice, Sherlock Holmes, Treasure Island and more
- **Other keyboards**: Dvorak, Colemak DH and Gallium layouts
- **Your own words**: add word lists in the config file

## Controls

- **Up** and **Down**: choose a test in the menu; **Left** and **Right** move to its settings, where **Up** and **Down** change them
- **Enter**: start the test, or open Config
- Type the words; **Space** moves to the next one, **Backspace** fixes the current one, **Ctrl+W** deletes the last word
- **Ctrl+R**: restart the test; **Ctrl+Q**: back to the menu
- **Esc** or **Ctrl+C**: quit

## Options

- In the menu's Config screen, **e** turns a word list or layout on or off and **s** downloads or deletes it; lists beyond the two built in download from typioca's own repository
- `typioca serve`: run typioca as an SSH server on port 2229

## Credits

- typioca: [Lukas Bloznelis](https://github.com/bloznelis/typioca) and contributors
- License: MIT

umoria.title: Umoria
umoria.description: The original Moria. Below the town, the mines go down and down, and past the 49th level the Balrog is waiting. Roll a hero, buy what you can, go down. Death is final.
umoria.provenance: Robert A. Koeneke wrote Moria at the University of Oklahoma from 1981 to 1986, James E. Wilson made it Umoria for Unix from 1987 to 1994, and Michael R. Cook restored it as Umoria 5.7.

upstream.name: Robert A. Koeneke, James E. Wilson, Michael R. Cook

umoria.page:
**THE BALROG IS WAITING. IT HAS BEEN WAITING SINCE 1983.**

Below a small town of six shops, a mine goes down level after level, and every level is new each time you enter it. Somewhere past the 49th, 2450 feet beneath your boots, lurks the Balrog: "the biggest and baddest creature in the game." It cannot be slept, confused or polymorphed. Cast destruction at it and it simply teleports away to heal. To face it you will need to be the kind of hero who kills dragons "with but a mean glance and snap of the fingers."

You won't start out that way. Roll a character from eight races and six classes (halflings make excellent thieves, "but prefer to be called burglars"), buy what you can afford in town, and go down. Fight what you meet. Find gold, armour, weapons, potions, scrolls, wands and staves, most of which you will not know until you try them. Come back up, spend your gold, and go down deeper.

Death is final, and a tombstone marks it. But what your hero learned about the monsters can live on in the next one.

- **The original**: Robert A. Koeneke's Moria, the game Angband and a whole family of roguelikes grew from
- **A real town**: six shops to buy and sell in between descents
- **Monster memory**: what you learn about each creature stays with you, even past death
- **Number keys or roguelike keys**, on one classic 80x24 screen

## Controls

- **1 to 9** (the number keys or the keypad): move, 5 stays put; **.**
  and a direction runs
- Walk into a monster to fight it
- **o** and a direction: open a door, **c** close, **T** tunnel
- **i** inventory, **e** equipment, **w** wear or wield, **t** take off
- **E** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **a** aim a wand, **u** use a
  staff, **f** fire or throw
- **m** cast a spell, **p** pray, **G** learn new spells
- **R** rest, **s** search, **l** look, **C** your character
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up; walk onto a number in town to shop
- **?**: all the commands, **=**: options, among them the roguelike keys
- **Ctrl-X**: save and quit, **Ctrl-K**: quit for good

## Options

- `-r`: roguelike keys (hjkl to move)
- `-n`: start a new game even if one is saved
- `-d`: show the score table

## Saving

**Ctrl-X** saves your character to your data folder, and starting
Umoria again carries on where you left off. If the terminal is closed
mid-game, the game saves itself first.

## History

Robert A. Koeneke wrote Moria at the University of Oklahoma, after
playing Rogue there, and released it in 1983 for VAX/VMS. James E.
Wilson rewrote it in C for Unix as Umoria from 1987, and Umoria 5.x
became the Moria most people played; it was released under the GPL in
2008. Michael R. Cook restored and modernised it as Umoria 5.7. This
edition keeps saves and scores in your own data folder.

## Credits

Robert A. Koeneke (Moria), James E. Wilson (Umoria), David J. Grabiner
and many others (Umoria 5.x), Michael R. Cook (Umoria 5.7). GPL-3.0 or
later.

unitopia.title: UNItopia
unitopia.description: German LPMud with a fantasy realm, Magyra, and a replica of the Stuttgart campus

unnethack.title: UnNetHack
unnethack.description: NetHack as it might look if the releases had never stopped: more randomness, more levels, more challenges, and the Amulet of Yendor still waiting at the bottom.
unnethack.provenance: Patric Mueller started UnNetHack in 2009 as a fork of NetHack 3.4.3, the DevTeam's game, to be NetHack as it would look had its releases gone on; he and contributors still develop it.
unnethack.page:
**THE AMULET OF YENDOR IS STILL DOWN THERE. NOW THERE IS MORE IN THE WAY.**

Down through the Dungeons of Doom, into Gehennom, and back out with the Amulet of Yendor: the quest is NetHack's. The dungeon is bigger. Patric Mueller started UnNetHack in 2009 to show "how NetHack would look today if the DevTeam didn't stop releasing", and it promises "more randomness, more levels, more challenges and more fun than vanilla NetHack."

Step through the portal into the Advent Calendar. Find your way to One-eyed Sam's Market. Climb up into the Ruins of Moria, where "the dungeon here seems less persistent." Brave the Dragon Caves, then go down into Sheol, the icy branch of Gehennom, where crystal ice golems walk. Or start the game as a Convict, an escaped prisoner in a striped shirt with a heavy iron ball chained to you and a trusty sewer rat at your side.

New to all of this? The game asks you straight away: "New? Press T to enter a tutorial."

- **New branches and levels**: the Advent Calendar, One-eyed Sam's Market, the Ruins of Moria, the Dragon Caves, Sheol and more
- **A new role**: the Convict
- **Less predictable**: many smaller changes that make every game harder to read
- **A tutorial** for first-timers, right at the start

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift**, run
- **F** and a direction: fight; **t**: throw, **z**: zap a wand
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T**
  take off, **P** put on, **R** remove, **a** apply
- **o** and **c**: open and close doors; **s**: search; **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **#**: extended commands, such as `#pray`
- **?**: help, **;**: what is that symbol, **Ctrl-P**: earlier messages
- **S**: save and quit

## Saving and options

**S** saves the game to your data folder (`~/.local/share/unnethack`),
and starting UnNetHack again carries on from there. Your options go in
`~/.unnethackrc`, or in `unnethackrc` in that folder, as `OPTIONS=` lines;
`OPTIONS=windowtype:curses` switches to the curses interface, and
`OPTIONS=role:Valkyrie,name:Freya` skips the questions at the start.

## History

UnNetHack is Patric Mueller's fork of NetHack 3.4.3, started in January
2009, meant to show "how NetHack would look today if the DevTeam didn't
stop releasing". It gathered patches from the NetHack community and its
own new levels and branches, and it is played on public servers. This
edition is built for Linux and macOS, keeping
everything it writes in your own data folder. The succubus and incubus
seduction scene is left out, with upstream's own build option.

## Credits

- Game: Patric Mueller and the UnNetHack contributors, after NetHack by
  the NetHack DevTeam
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: NetHack General Public License

urogue.title: UltraRogue
urogue.description: Ten classes, Friendly Fiend's Flea Market, and eight unique artifacts deep in the Dungeons of Doom, from the Phial of Galadriel to the Wand of Yendor. Carry one home, if you can stand the side effects.
urogue.provenance: Herb Chong wrote UltraRogue in 1985 and 1986 from Rogue 3.6 and an early Advanced Rogue, gave its source to Nicholas J. Kisseberth in 1992 and worked on it with him to 1995.

upstream.name: Herb Chong (1985 to 1995); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

urogue.page:
**EIGHT ARTIFACTS. ONE DUNGEON. YOUR TOES MAY FALL OFF.**

"UltraRogue: The Ultimate Adventure in the Dungeons of Doom." Herb Chong grew it out of Rogue over ten years, and it shows. Pick one of ten classes, from fighter, paladin and ranger to druid, illusionist, assassin and ninja. Spend your gold at Friendly Fiend's Flea Market. Then go down, into a dungeon where the monsters come in both cases and many kinds.

Deep down lie eight unique artifacts: the Magic Purse of Yendor, the Phial of Galadriel, the Amulet of Yendor, the Palantir, Crown and Sceptre of Might, the Silmaril of Ea and, deepest of all, the Wand of Yendor. Only a hero carrying one can climb the stairs back up, and reaching daylight with it makes you a total winner. But power has its price, and the artifacts have side effects. "A wart grows on the end of your nose." "Your hair begins to turn white." "Your toes fall off."

- **Ten classes**, each with its own way to survive
- **Spells and prayers**, traps you can set yourself, pools to dip things in
- **Eight unique artifacts**, the first from level 15, the last from level 50, each with its own powers and curses
- **Rogue's family tree**: Rogue 3.6 and an early Advanced Rogue at its roots

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way, **m** and a direction to step without picking up
- **f** and a direction: fight; **t**: throw, **z**: zap a wand or
  staff
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off armour, **P** put on and **R** remove a ring, **A**: use an
  artifact
- **c**: cast a spell or say a prayer, **a**: affect the undead,
  **^**: set a trap, **D**: dip something in a pool
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up; up only while you carry an artifact
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder (press Return to take the name
offered). To carry on, start it from a shell as `urogue -r`; a saved
game is deleted once it is restored. Characters you choose to keep at
the start are stored there too.

## History

Herb Chong wrote UltraRogue in 1985 and 1986, from Rogue 3.6 and an
early Advanced Rogue. In 1992 he gave the source to Nicholas J.
Kisseberth (Yendor), its first restoration, and the two kept working on
it until 1995; the Roguelike Restoration Project released it as 1.0.7
in 2005. This edition keeps your files in your data folder and fixes
saving so that a saved game can be restored. It is part of the
Roguelike Restoration Project in the Asciiverse catalog.

## Credits

Herb Chong, after Rogue by Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold and
Advanced Rogue by Michael Morgan and Ken Dalka; restoration by Nicholas
J. Kisseberth. BSD licence with clauses on the names UltraRogue and
urogue.

uxo.title: uXo
uxo.description: 3:14 AM. One key pressed, and the machine pulled Dot in! A rogue program called purged has wired the whole system to blow. Defuse its charges, outwit its puzzles and blast your way out to the real world! Or grab three friends and blow each other sky-high in Battle!
uxo.provenance: Asciiverse made uXo in Rust in 2026, a love letter to the 90s bomb-arena games.
uxo.page:
**BLAST YOUR WAY OUT TO THE REAL WORLD!**

3:14 in the morning. One key pressed, and the machine pulled Dot in!

Every night at 3:14 a cleaning program called **purged** tidies the disk. Tonight it has decided the tidiest disk is an empty one. Its charges are planted all through the system, every last one set to wipe everything at four o'clock. Dot included!

Dot comes down in an old garden screensaver, where purged has rewritten every creature to guard its charges. Grubs, ladybeetles, hedgehogs that pretend to be hedges, frogs, rams, crows... and something big and prickly guarding the way out.

In here every bomb is a kill, and purged's creatures can't start one. So drop a bomb, run, and BOOM: the blast rips out in a cross and flattens everything in its path. Line them up right and one sets off the next, and the next, and the next... Set off purged's charges, and watch out, because they blow for real! Caught in your own blast? That one's on you.

But not every kill goes off. Some hang, and lie there grey and smoking, live... until a blast finds them, or you kick one, or it just decides it's time. Every bomb is unexploded ordnance. Every single one.

- **Bombs AND brains!** Push crates for cover, or onto switches to hold the gates open. Hunt down keys for locked doors, lost parts for the sealed sockets. Some stages are a race, some are a puzzle, most are both!
- **The surge!** Out in the open, your bombs flood outward every way at once, round corners. Mind where it spreads!
- **Ride your enemies!** Beat a Hopper or a Ram and it might leave an egg. Hatch it, climb on: hop clean over hedges, or charge. And when a blast catches you, your mount takes the hit.
- **Adventure, alone or with a friend:** twenty-seven stages for Dot alone, or Dot and Caret together. Through the Screensaver to the Bramblehog; into the Clock, where purged winds the time on toward four, the shutters open and shut on the beat and the Cuckoo waits to strike the hour; and down into the Buffer, where blocks come back as fast as you blow them away, and purged itself waits at the end.
- **Battle for up to four!** Six arenas, from the Ice Rink to the Catacombs. Blown up? Ride the edge and lob bombs back in for revenge. Let the clock run down and the walls close in.
- **Eighteen power-ups, and the dreaded skull.** Catch a disease and you might drop bombs nonstop, run backwards, turn invisible, or watch every bomb you drop fizzle. Bump into a rival and it's theirs instead!
- **Every gamepad is a player,** and two can share the keyboard.

Can you stop purged before four o'clock? **IF YOU SEE ME RUNNING, TRY TO KEEP UP!**

## Controls

- **Move**: stick, d-pad, **W A S D** or the **arrow keys**
- **Bomb**: A or X on a pad, **Space** (W A S D player) or **Enter** (arrows player); press again standing on your bomb with the line bomb to lay a row
- **Ride** (your mount's hop or charge): Y, **E** or **.**
- **Action**: B, **F** or **/**: throw what you carry, else punch the bomb ahead, else pick up the bomb underfoot, else set off your oldest remote bomb
- **Push a crate**: walk into it and lean on it a moment
- **Start** or **P**: pause (in the adventure, bomb then starts the stage over, for a life), **+** and **-**: zoom (**0**: automatic), **Esc** or Select: back to the title

## Credits

- Game: Asciiverse
- A love letter to the 90s bomb-arena games

news.notes:
- Gamepads work on Windows: gilrs reads them through XInput, since its
  default (Windows Gaming Input) only reports to a program with a focused
  window of its own, which a terminal game never has

vitetris.title: vitetris
vitetris.description: Falling blocks the way the early Nintendo versions played them, in your terminal: marathon or 25-line races, two players on one keyboard, on two terminals or over the network.
vitetris.provenance: Victor Geraldsson wrote vitetris in C from 2007, after Mike Taylor's 1989 Tetris for Terminals, and released it under a BSD licence; it is in most Linux distributions.
vitetris.page:
**SEVEN SHAPES. TEN COLUMNS. NO MERCY.**

The blocks fall, you turn them and slot them in, full rows vanish, and the speed creeps up. vitetris plays the way the early Nintendo versions did, with the same rotation, scoring, levels and speed, plus a short lock delay so the high levels stay playable.

Play a marathon for points, or a B-type game where you race to clear 25 lines, starting from a field already half full of junk if you like. Bring a friend: two players can share one keyboard, sit at two terminals on the same machine, or play over the network, each choosing their own level and height.

- **Two modes**: A-type marathon and B-type 25-line race
- **Head to head**: two players on one keyboard, on two terminals, or across the internet
- **Make it yours**: starting level and garbage height, rotation direction, soft-drop speed, block styles and colours, every key remappable
- **High scores** kept for you

## Controls

- **Left** and **Right**: move
- **Up**: rotate
- **Down**: soft drop; **Space**: hard drop
- **P** or **Enter**: pause
- In the menus: arrow keys and **Enter**, **Esc** or **Backspace** to go back, **Q** to quit at once

## Options

- `-level N`, `-height N`: start level (0–9) and garbage height (0–5)
- `-mode 1b`: B-type game; `-nomenu`: skip the menus
- `-listen PORT` / `-connect HOST:PORT`: network play
- `-hiscores`: print the high-score list
- `-help`: every option

Settings and high scores are saved in `~/.vitetris`.

## Credits

- vitetris: [Victor Geraldsson](https://github.com/vicgeralds/vitetris), after Mike Taylor's Tetris for Terminals (1989); the original game by Alexey Pajitnov (1985)
- License: BSD-2-Clause

vms-empire.title: VMS Empire
vms-empire.description: Two emperors, one world, and only room for one. Build armies, fleets and planes city by city and conquer a world against the computer, in the 1970s ancestor of Civilization.
vms-empire.provenance: Walter Bright wrote Empire in the early 1970s; Chuck Simmons wrote this C version in 1987, and Eric S. Raymond has maintained it since around 1990.
vms-empire.page:
**TWO EMPERORS. ONE WORLD. ONLY ROOM FOR ONE.**

A full-scale war between you and the computer, on a randomly generated world of continents and oceans. As the game's own README puts it: "Naturally, there is only room for one, so the object of the game is to destroy the other."

You start with a single city and a map you have never seen. Cities build armies, fighters, patrol boats, destroyers, submarines, troop transports, carriers, battleships and satellites. Explore. Take the unclaimed cities before the enemy does. Ship your armies across the sea and destroy the other side. The computer plays by exactly the same rules.

The game saves itself every 10 turns and picks up where you left off the next time you start it.

- **Every arm of war**: nine kinds of piece on land, at sea, in the air and in orbit
- **A new world every game**: choose how much of it is water, how smooth the coasts are and how big the map
- **A fair fight**: the computer gets no extra rules, only the ones you have
- **The ancestor**: in its maintainer's words, "the ancestor of all the multiplayer 4X simulations out there, including Civilization and Master of Orion"

## Controls

Keys work in upper or lower case. **h** shows help for the mode you are in,
and **Ctrl+L** redraws the screen.

In command mode, between rounds:

- **a**: automove, the normal way to play a round
- **z**: the whole world, zoomed out
- **s**: save the game
- **q**: quit

In move mode, when the cursor sits on one of your pieces:

- **q w e / a d / z x c** or the **arrow keys**: move one square
- **Space**: leave the piece where it is
- **y**: send an army to attack the nearest target by itself
- **g**: explore unknown territory
- **s**: sentry, park a piece until something comes near
- **b**: change what a city builds
- **o**: go back to command mode after this round

## Options

- `-w N`: percentage of the world that is water, 10 to 90 (default 70)
- `-s N`: how smooth the coastlines are (default 5)
- `-g WxH`: world size
- `-t`: wrap the map round at the edges
- `-d N`: how long, in milliseconds, each message stays at the top of the screen (default 2000)
- `-S N`: autosave every N turns (default 10)
- `-f file`: use another save file

## History

Walter Bright wrote Empire in the early 1970s as a student at Caltech. It
spread to DEC's VAX/VMS, which gave it the name VMS Empire; Craig Leres
added terminal support and Ed James converted parts to C with curses. In
1987 Chuck Simmons at Amdahl rewrote it completely in C with a new
computer strategy, pieces and map generator, and Eric S. Raymond has
maintained it since around 1990, adding colour in 1994. Its line leads
to Civilization (1990) and Master of Orion (1993).

This edition adds a small patch that lets it build and save games on
Windows.

## Credits

- Original game: Walter Bright
- C version: Chuck Simmons
- Maintainer: [Eric S. Raymond](http://www.catb.org/~esr/vms-empire/)
- Windows console support: [PDCurses](https://pdcurses.org)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-2.0-or-later

warp.title: Warp
warp.description: Larry Wall's real-time space war: fly an Enterprise and a Base at once against Klingons, Romulans and the Space Amoeba, in a universe where explosions chain-react. You're not likely to get far.
warp.provenance: Larry Wall wrote Warp from 1983 (version 7.0 is from 1986), before he wrote Perl; NetBSD added it to its games in 2020.
warp.page:
**THEY KEEP SHOOTING WHILE YOU THINK.**

Warp is a space war in real time: the enemies keep moving and firing whether you act or not. You command an Enterprise and a Base at the same time, in a universe that wraps around at every edge, against Klingons, Romulans, Gorns, Tholians, pirates, space amoebas, planet crushers and homing torpedoes. Harry Mudd turns up too. Anything that blows up damages what is near it, and a crowded universe can go up in a chain reaction.

Every wave is harder than the last, from difficulty 1 up to 99. In the words of its own manual: "You're not likely to get that far."

Besides phasers and photon torpedoes you have attractor and repulsor beams, a cloaking device, and a warp mode in which your keys change your speed, not your position. Phasers strike where a target is about to be, so phaser a Klingon that is about to ram you and you get phasered too. "This can be embarrassing, not to mention deadly."

- **Two ships, one captain**: switch between the Enterprise and the Base mid-fight
- **Chain reactions**: blasts spread, and a dense universe can go up all at once
- **Every universe different**: the shape of the star field changes how you fight
- **Before Perl, there was Warp**: Larry Wall wrote it from 1983

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: steer the current ship (diagonals on yubn)
- **Shift** with a direction: fire a photon torpedo that way
- **Ctrl** with a direction: fire phasers that way
- **%** or **Delete**: torpedoes in every direction
- **i** or **w**: Enterprise in impulse or warp mode, **p**: switch to
  the Base, **o**: the other vessel
- **c** and **v**: cloak and uncloak
- **s**: stop all torpedoes, **S** or **0**: stop the Enterprise
- **?**: command summary, **^R**: redraw, **q**: quit (it asks), **Q**:
  quit at once

## History

Larry Wall wrote Warp from 1983, years before he wrote Perl, and
version 7.0 came out in 1986. NetBSD added it to its games in November
2020, under the NetBSD Foundation's BSD licence.

The Asciiverse edition builds it for Linux and macOS, fixes three
overflows that crashed a second game in one run, and keeps its saved
games and scoreboards in the player's own data folder. Warp is part of
BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog.

westering.title: Westering
westering.description: Take a wagon party two thousand miles from Independence to the Willamette Valley in 1848: outfit, pace and rations, hunting, seven rivers and the forts between.
westering.provenance: A journey game in the line of The Oregon Trail (Don Rawitsch, Bill Heinemann and Paul Dillenberger, 1971), on the real road of 1848, written for Asciiverse in 2026.
westering.page:
**TWO THOUSAND MILES. FIVE OF YOU. ONE WAGON.**

Independence, Missouri, spring 1848. Between you and the Willamette Valley
lie the prairie, the Platte, the Rockies, the Snake River desert and the
Blue Mountains. Name your party, choose the month you leave, and spend your
$800 at the store: oxen, provisions, clothing, powder and shot, and spare
parts for a wagon that will break.

Then the road. Set the pace and the rations, rest when someone is failing,
hunt buffalo on the plains and elk in the mountains, trade with the trains
you meet. Every grave you leave behind gets the words you give it.

## The road

- Twenty-five landmarks of the 1848 road, from Chimney Rock and
  Independence Rock to South Pass, Fort Hall and the Blue Mountains, each
  with a note on what stood there that year
- Seven rivers to ford, float or ferry, high with snowmelt in May and June
- Two forks: the dry Sublette Cutoff or Fort Bridger; the Barlow Road over
  Mount Hood or a raft down the Columbia
- Forts with trade rooms, dearer the further west you go

## Controls

- Arrow keys to choose, Enter to do it, Esc to go back
- On the trail, the number keys pick from the menu at once, and Esc asks
  before you leave the journey
- In the store, Right or `+` buys and Left or `-` puts back

news.notes:
- The party and outfitting in Independence, spring 1848; the departure month
- The trail: pace, rations, health, weather by month and region
- The real route, landmark by landmark, with a note in our own words at
  each; forts with stores at rising prices
- Events and illness, river crossings, hunting as text
- The end: score and an epitaph for each who died; play again
- Balanced over 200 bot journeys
- Landmark scenes and a map of the road

wfc-worlds.title: WFC Worlds
wfc-worlds.description: Landscapes and cities grow out of a fog of question marks by Wave Function Collapse, one after the other, filling the whole window.
wfc-worlds.provenance: fezcode wrote the land and city generators in Go in March 2026 for Atlas Games, fezcode's collection of terminal games and generators.
wfc-worlds.page:
**EVERY CELL A QUESTION. EVERY WORLD AN ANSWER.**

The window fills with question marks, and a world settles out of them.
Wave Function Collapse picks the most certain cell, decides it, and lets
the decision ripple to its neighbours, until oceans, forests, mountain
ridges and lava flows have found their places. Then a city does the same:
roads that join up, blocks of houses, shops, parks and ponds. Then
another landscape, and so on, each one new.

## Controls

- **Space**: the next world now
- **Any other key**: quit

## Credits

- WFC Worlds: the land and city generators of [fezcode](https://github.com/fezcode/atlas.games)'s Atlas Games
- License: MIT

wilsons-revenge.title: Wilson's Revenge
wilsons-revenge.description: Wilson the chicken is back and it's personal: a three-lane runner where you dodge cars, jump barricades and blast through with a pick-up shotgun.
wilsons-revenge.provenance: fezcode wrote Wilson's Revenge in Go in February 2026; it grew into Atlas Games, fezcode's collection of terminal games and generators.
wilsons-revenge.page:
**THIS TIME IT'S PERSONAL.**

Wilson the chicken is back on the road. Three lanes, traffic coming the
other way, and it only gets faster: switch lanes, jump the barricades
and the people in your path, and grab a shotgun to blast through
whatever you can't get round.

The road is full of pick-ups, and not all of them are friends:

- **~-=**: a shotgun and five shells; **[A]**: three more shells
- **[P+]**: five seconds invincible, double points
- **[P-]**: lose a hundred points
- **[XJ]**: no more jumping, until you find **[OJ]**

Everything you get past is points; everything you shoot is more.

## Controls

- **↑** / **↓**: change lane
- **→**: jump
- **Space**: start, then shoot
- **P**: pause; **R**: run again after a crash; **Q**: quit

## Options

- `--demo`: watch Wilson play himself; any key quits

## Credits

- Wilson's Revenge: [fezcode](https://github.com/fezcode/atlas.games), part of Atlas Games
- License: MIT

wolfpack-empire.title: Wolfpack Empire
wolfpack-empire.description: Rule a country on a shared world against real people: farm, mine, build fleets and armies, make alliances and declare war. Empire has been played over the Internet since the 1980s, and the world keeps turning while you sleep.
wolfpack-empire.provenance: Empire is Peter Langston's game; this line of the code comes from Dave Pare (UCSD, 1986) through Chainsaw and Empire 3 to Wolfpack, who have kept it going as Empire 4 since 1996.
wolfpack-empire.page:
**YOUR NEIGHBOURS ARE REAL PEOPLE. SO ARE THEIR ARMIES.**

Empire is a war game played over the Internet since the 1980s. You rule a country on a shared world: explore the land around your capital, designate sectors as farms, mines, factories and harbours (the sector types run, in the manual's words, "from banks to nuclear fuel processing plants"), grow your population, research technology, and build ships, planes and armies. Then deal with your neighbours, who are real people, through trade, alliances, telegrams and war.

The world moves on whether you are logged in or not: updates happen on a schedule, and a game runs for weeks. No goal is set for you. Most players soon find their own, "ranging from the mundane desire to be the biggest, strongest country in the game" to the most efficient land use possible.

This is the Empire client. It connects straight to Wolfpack Fever, the game the Wolfpack team keeps running all year: no registration, grab a country and go.

- **A whole economy**: food, ore, oil and people feed the war machine
- **Real diplomacy**: telegrams, alliances, declarations of war, and a newspaper that reports it all
- **Real time where it counts**: the world updates on a schedule, but attacks happen the moment you order them

## Getting started

At the prompts, use one of the countries **1** to **8**, with the same
number as the password. Countries start in sanctuary, safe from attack;
the `break` command ends it, and breaking sanctuary counts as a promise to
play the game. Using more than one country is not allowed.

To look around first, log in as country `visitor` with any password and
read the message of the day (`motd`) and the newspaper (`newspaper`).

## Commands

Type commands at the `Command :` prompt. A few to start with:

- `nation`: your country at a glance
- `map #`: the map around you
- `census *`: your sectors
- `explore c 0,0 5 gh`: move 5 civilians from 0,0 west and claim land
  (directions `y u g j b n`, `h` to stop)
- `designate 2,0 m`: make a sector a mine
- `read`: your telegrams; `wire` for announcements, `newspaper` for the news
- `declare` and `relations`: alliances and war
- `info`: the built-in manual, and `info <command>` for any command
- `quit`: log out; your country stays in the game

## Options

- `empire COUNTRY PASSWORD`: log in without the prompts
- `-s host:port`: play on another Empire server
- `-u`: UTF-8 output
- `-2 file`: keep a log of the session

## History

Empire goes back to Peter Langston's game of the late 1970s and early
1980s. Dave Pare's reimplementation at UCSD in 1986 started the open line
of code, carried on through BSD Empire, KSU, Chainsaw and Empire 3 to
Wolfpack, who have developed it as Empire 4 since 1996. Wolfpack still hosts games and the code is still
developed.

This edition is the client, unchanged except that it connects to
Wolfpack Fever by default.

## Credits

- Empire: Peter Langston, Dave Pare, Jeff Bailey, Thomas Ruschak, Ken
  Stevens, Steve McClure, Markus Armbruster and [Wolfpack](http://www.wolfpackempire.com/)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

worm.title: Worm
worm.description: Steer a hungry worm to the numbers and watch it grow. It never stops moving, and the longer it gets, the harder it is not to run into something.
worm.provenance: Michael Toy wrote Worm at UC Santa Cruz around 1980, and it shipped with BSD Unix. Mike Sharov added colour and some grass for looks in 2016 for his bsd-games.
worm.page:
**IT NEVER STOPS MOVING. IT NEVER STOPS GROWING.**

The classic growing worm, from the BSD Unix games of 1980. Your worm is a line of `o`s with an `@` for a head, and it is always on the move. Somewhere on the field is a digit: eat it and the worm grows by that many segments, and a new digit appears somewhere else.

The longer the worm, the harder it is to find a way through, and every digit you eat adds to your score. Fill one eighth of the screen with worm and you have won. Run into the wall or into yourself, and the game puts it plainly: "Well, you ran into something and the game is over."

The blue grass is only there to look at; you can crawl straight over it.

## Controls

- **Arrow keys** or **hjkl**: turn
- **q**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, `worm 20` starts with a worm 20 segments long
instead of 7.

## History

Michael Toy wrote Worm at UC Santa Cruz around 1980, and it shipped with
BSD Unix among Berkeley's games for the video terminals of the day. Mike
Sharov's bsd-games, the modern Linux port, draws it in colour and added
the grass in 2016.

worms.title: Worms
worms.description: Eight coloured worms wander your screen, turning at random and crossing each other's paths: a BSD screen piece from 1980 that has never stopped crawling.
worms.provenance: Eric P. Scott wrote worms at Caltech High Energy Physics in October 1980, a Unix version of the DEC-2136 program of the same name, and it shipped with BSD Unix from then on.
worms.page:
**EIGHT WORMS. NO DESTINATION. NO HURRY.**

Eight worms crawl across the screen, each in its own colour and character, each with a head that looks different from its body. They turn at random, slide along the edges and cross each other's paths, and the ground behind them is wiped clean as they go. Nobody steers. Nobody wins. They just keep going, as they have on Unix screens since October 1980.

Leave them crawling on a spare terminal, or give them something to eat: from a terminal, `worms -f` covers the screen with WORM letters for them to graze on.

## Controls

- **Any key**: quit

## Options

From a terminal, `worms` takes more: `-n` sets the number of worms,
`-l 10` or `-l 5-40` their length, `-r` random lengths, `-t` a trail of
dots, `-f` a field of WORM letters for them to eat, `-d` the pause between
moves in milliseconds, and `-C` and `-H` colour and heads (Asciiverse
starts it with `-C -H -n 8`).

## History

Eric P. Scott wrote worms at Caltech High Energy Physics in October
1980, a Unix version of the DEC-2136 program of the same name, and it
has shipped with BSD Unix ever since. This edition quits on any key. It
is part of BSD Games in the Asciiverse catalog.

## Credits

- worms: Eric P. Scott, from [NetBSD's source tree](https://github.com/NetBSD/src/tree/trunk/games/worms)
- License: BSD-3-Clause, copyright The Regents of the University of California

wump.title: Hunt the Wumpus
wump.description: Somewhere in a cave of twenty rooms lives the evil Wumpus. Track it by smell, dodge bottomless pits and giant bats, and shoot it with a crooked arrow before it makes you dinner.
wump.provenance: Hunt the Wumpus was first presented in People's Computer Company in 1973; Dave Taylor of Intuitive Systems wrote this version for BSD Unix in 1989.

upstream.name: Dave Taylor, Intuitive Systems (1989), after Hunt the Wumpus (1973)

wump.page:
**SOMETHING IN THIS CAVE SMELLS TERRIBLE. AND IT'S HUNGRY.**

One of the oldest computer games there is. You are in a cave of twenty rooms, each joined to three others by tunnels, and somewhere in it lives the evil Wumpus. You cannot see it. But you can smell it: `*sniff* (I can smell the evil Wumpus nearby!)`. You can feel the draft from a bottomless pit next door: `*whoosh*`. And you can hear the bats that, if you blunder in, will carry you off to another part of the cave: `*rustle* *rustle*`.

Your quiver holds five "custom super anti-evil Wumpus arrows", and they are crooked: you tell each one which rooms to fly through, up to six. Hit the Wumpus and you win. Miss, and it may wake up and move, maybe right into your room. Give an arrow an impossible path and it flies off at random, maybe straight back into you. Some tunnels only go one way.

Walk into the wrong room and the game will tell you all about it: "Much to the delight of the Wumpus, you walked right into his mouth, making you one of the easiest dinners he's ever had!" Or you fall into a pit, and "have a lot of time to reflect on this error as you fall many miles to the core of the earth."

## Controls

The game is typed: enter a command and press **Enter**.

- **m** and a room number, such as `m6`: move to that room
- **s** and a list of rooms, such as `s8 4`: shoot an arrow along that path
- **?**: the instructions
- **q**: quit

## Options

Started from a shell, wump builds other caves: `-r` sets the number of
rooms (20), `-t` the tunnels from each room (3), `-p` the pits (3), `-b`
the bat rooms (3) and `-a` the arrows (5), as in `wump -r 30 -a 3`.

## History

Hunt the Wumpus was first presented in the pages of People's Computer
Company in 1973. This version was written for BSD Unix by Dave Taylor of
Intuitive Systems in 1989, and Mike Sharov's bsd-games, the modern Linux
port, prints its instructions directly and highlights the important
words in bold.

xaos.title: XaoS
xaos.description: Fly into the Mandelbrot set in real time, drawn in ASCII art: hold a button to zoom smoothly towards any point, watch Julia sets change under the pointer, cycle the colours or let the autopilot find the way.
xaos.provenance: Jan Hubicka and Thomas Marsh wrote XaoS in 1996, a fractal zoomer fast enough to fly through the set instead of waiting for each picture; Jan Hubicka's AAlib let it draw in plain text. The XaoS project has carried it on since.

developer.name: Jan Hubicka, Thomas Marsh and the XaoS project

xaos.page:
**THE FRACTAL ZOOMER. IN YOUR TERMINAL.**

Hold the mouse button and fly into the Mandelbrot set, smoothly and
without stopping, as fast as you dare. XaoS reuses the points it worked
out for the frames before, so the zoom never waits for a picture to be
drawn. Here it all comes out as ASCII art, each character standing for
four points of the picture.

Twenty-nine kinds of fractal, from the Mandelbrot set and its higher
powers to Newton, Barnsley, Phoenix, Magnet and the Sierpinski carpet,
with their Julia sets, plus a formula of your own. Watch a Julia set
change as you move the pointer, swap the colouring, run the colour
cycling, put on filters, or hand the controls to the autopilot and watch
it hunt for the interesting edges.
The built-in tutorials explain fractals as they play.

**Pick a spot on the edge. Hold the button.**

## Controls

- **Left mouse button**: hold to zoom in towards the pointer; drag to steer
- **Right mouse button**: hold to zoom out
- **Middle button** (or both): drag to move
- **Arrow keys**: up and down for zoom speed, left and right for detail
- **a**: autopilot
- **m**: from the Mandelbrot set to the Julia set under the pointer, and back
- **j**: fast Julia mode, a small Julia set for the point under the pointer
- **1** to **0**: fractal types
- **c** and **f**: outside and inside colouring; **p**: a random palette;
  **y**: colour cycling
- **e**: filters; **u**: undo
- **Enter**, or the pointer on the top row: the menu bar; **h**: help, with
  every key and menu explained
- **q**: quit

The Help menu's tutorials start with an introduction to fractals; try it
first.

## Credits

- XaoS: Jan Hubicka and Thomas Marsh, with Zoltan Kovacs, J.B. Langston
  and the [XaoS project](https://xaos-project.github.io) (CREDITS.md
  names everyone)
- AAlib: Jan Hubicka, Kamil Toman and others
- Asciiverse edition: dragging steers the zoom, the arrow keys, q and the
  full built-in help work in the terminal again
- License: GPL-3.0-or-later

xnethack.title: xNetHack
xnethack.description: NetHack with the tedium taken out and the balance put right: weapons and armour in many materials, crystal chests, reworked Gehennom mazes, new themed rooms, and the Amulet of Yendor still waiting at the bottom.
xnethack.provenance: copperwater began xNetHack in 2017 as a fork of NetHack, released it from 2018, and keeps it in step with the DevTeam's releases; version 10.0 is based on NetHack 5.0.0.
xnethack.page:
**THE SAME DUNGEON. FEWER CHORES. MORE SURPRISES.**

Down through the Dungeons of Doom, into Gehennom, and back out with the Amulet of Yendor: the quest is NetHack's. xNetHack sets out to "fix gameplay balance issues", "remove tedious and frustrating parts of the game" and "make uninteresting parts of the game more interesting", and it changes the game conservatively, deepening what is there rather than piling on more.

So that dagger might be silver, or glass. Armour comes in mithril, copper or bone. A crystal chest shows you what is inside and keeps it behind a lock no key can open. Gehennom's mazes are rebuilt around open caverns and themed rooms, and beneath Vlad's Tower there is a new level: a chasm of open air, home to vampires and a few demons.

Many of xNetHack's ideas have gone on to the official game. This is where they get tried first.

- **Object materials**: weapons, armour, boxes and amulets made of iron, silver, mithril, glass, bone and more, each with its own strengths
- **Crystal chests**: see-through, magically locked, with an extra item inside
- **A new Gehennom**: mazes rebuilt around open caverns and new special rooms
- **More themed rooms** throughout the dungeon
- **A tutorial** for first-timers, offered at the start

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift**, run
- **F** and a direction: fight; **t**: throw, **z**: zap a wand
- **i**: inventory, **,**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T**
  take off, **P** put on, **R** remove, **a** apply
- **o** and **c**: open and close doors; **s**: search; **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **#**: extended commands, such as `#pray`
- **?**: help, **;**: what is that symbol, **Ctrl-P**: earlier messages
- **S**: save and quit

## Saving and options

**S** saves the game to your data folder (`~/.local/share/xnethack`),
and starting xNetHack again carries on from there. Your options go in
`~/.xnethackrc`, or in `xnethackrc` in that folder, as `OPTIONS=` lines;
`OPTIONS=windowtype:curses` switches to the curses interface,
`OPTIONS=role:Valkyrie,name:Ada` skips the questions at the start, and
`OPTIONS=!tutorial` skips the tutorial offer. At the end of a game a
full account of it is written to `dumplog/` in the same folder.

## History

copperwater started xNetHack in 2017 as an "experimental" fork of
NetHack, a place to combine patches from the community and try new
ideas, and released it from 2018. It has followed the DevTeam ever
since: version 10.0, from May 2026, is built on NetHack 5.0.0. This
edition is built for Linux and macOS, keeping everything it writes in
your own data folder.

## Credits

- Game: copperwater and the xNetHack contributors, after NetHack by the
  NetHack DevTeam; object materials mostly from GruntHack
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: NetHack General Public License

xrogue.title: XRogue
xrogue.description: Nine classes, over 200 monsters, many of them clever, and a quest for one unique artifact deep in the Dungeons of Doom. In its own guide's words: very few players have won this game.
xrogue.provenance: Robert Pietkivitch wrote XRogue for the AT&T UNIX PC between 1989 and 1992 from Advanced Rogue 7.7, and restored it with Nicholas J. Kisseberth from 1996.

upstream.name: Robert Pietkivitch (1989 to 1992); Nicholas J. Kisseberth

xrogue.page:
**VERY FEW PLAYERS HAVE WON THIS GAME.**

That is XRogue's own player's guide talking, and it means it. "XRogue: Expeditions into the Dungeons of Doom" grew out of Advanced Rogue into a dungeon of more than 200 monsters, and many of them are intelligent: like you, they avoid traps and decide when it is better to fight or to run.

Share out your attribute points and choose one of nine classes: fighter, ranger, paladin, magician, cleric, thief, assassin, druid or monk. You begin on level 0 in Friendly Fiend's Equipage, a shop full of arms, armour and magic, with a quest: bring back one unique artifact. The Axe of Aklad, perhaps, or the Eye of Vecna, the Horn of Geryon, the Mandolin of Brian. Some of these items have minds of their own, and some "will kill you outright" if you pick them up while wielding another. Don't be too greedy with the artifacts!

Bring yours to the surface and great honour is yours. Or keep going down, "to match wits with an arch-devil, a demon-prince, or perhaps Charon the Boatman."

- **Nine classes**, from the spell-casting magician to the chanting druid and monk
- **Over 200 monsters**, many as cunning as you
- **A quest of your own**: choose your artifact in the shop at the start
- **Charon the Boatman**, and worse, for those who don't know when to stop

## Controls

- **hjkl yubn**: move, the last four diagonally; with **Shift** run that
  way
- **f** and a direction: move until something turns up; **t**: throw,
  **z**: zap a wand or staff
- **i**: inventory, **P**: pick up, **d**: drop
- **e** eat, **q** quaff, **r** read, **w** wield, **W** wear, **T** take
  off
- **C**: cast a spell, **p**: pray, **c**: chant, **a**: affect the
  undead, **D**: dip something in a pool
- In the shop: **$** price, **#** buy, **%** sell
- **s**: search for traps and secret doors, **.**: rest
- `>` and `<`: stairs down and up
- **?**: all the commands, **/**: what a symbol is
- **S**: save and quit, **Q**: quit (type yes)

## Saving

**S** saves the game to your data folder. To carry on, start it from a
shell as `xrogue -r`; a saved game is deleted once it is restored.

## History

Robert Pietkivitch wrote XRogue between 1989 and 1992 for the AT&T UNIX
PC, building on Advanced Rogue 7.7. He sent the source to Nicholas J.
Kisseberth (Yendor) in 1996 and worked with him to bring it back; he
died in 2002, before sending the enhancements he had made in 2000.
Kisseberth's Roguelike Restoration Project released 8.0.1 to 8.0.3, and
rogueforge carries it on. This edition keeps your files in your data
folder and fixes saved games that
would not restore and a score file that crashed on 64-bit machines. It
is part of the Roguelike Restoration Project in the Asciiverse catalog.

## Credits

Robert Pietkivitch, after Advanced Rogue by Michael Morgan and Ken Dalka
and Rogue by Michael Toy, Glenn Wichman and Ken Arnold; restoration by
Nicholas J. Kisseberth. BSD licence.

zoridor.title: Zoridor
zoridor.description: Quoridor against the machine: race your pawn across the board while the two of you wall each other in, ten fences each, and never quite shut the way.
zoridor.provenance: Toby Jaffey of Ringtail Software wrote Zoridor in Zig in 2024, for the terminal and the web, after Quoridor, the board game Mirko Marchesi designed for Gigamic in 1997.
zoridor.page:
**WALL THEM IN. NEVER SHUT THEM OUT.**

Quoridor, the board game of pawns and fences, at your keyboard against
the machine. Your pawn starts on one side of a 9 by 9 board, the
machine's on the other, and the first to reach the far side wins.

Each turn you either step your pawn one square or put down one of your
ten fences, two squares long, to lengthen the machine's road. It does the
same to you. A fence may cross nothing and must always leave both pawns a
way through, so the board turns into a maze you are building together,
and the shortest path is never where it was a turn ago.

- **One move or one fence**: every turn is a choice between racing and
  blocking
- **Pawns jump**: face to face, you can hop over the other pawn
- **The machine counts paths**: it weighs every move by how much it
  shortens its road and lengthens yours
- **Two at one keyboard**: hand the other side to a friend

**FIND THE WAY THROUGH.**

## Controls

- **Arrows**: pick the square for your pawn, or move the fence
- **Tab**: switch between pawn and fence; **Space**: turn the fence
- **Enter**: make the move (a green mark is legal, red is not)
- **Q**: quit

## Options

- `-2 human`: two players at one keyboard
- `-r 50`: shake up the machine's choices, 0 to 100 (the higher, the
  more it errs); `-s 12345`: fix its seed
- `-f`: play game after game, counting wins
- `-m`: a smaller board for 80x24

## Credits

- Zoridor: Toby Jaffey, [Ringtail Software](https://github.com/ringtailsoftware/zoridor)
- Quoridor designed by Mirko Marchesi, published by Gigamic
- License: MIT

zork1.title: Zork I: The Great Underground Empire
zork1.description: West of a white house there is a small mailbox. Below lies the Great Underground Empire: nineteen treasures, one thief, and a grue in every dark corner.
zork1.provenance: Infocom released Zork I in 1980; Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels and Tim Anderson wrote it.

developer.name: Infocom (Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels, Tim Anderson)

zork1.page:
**IT IS PITCH BLACK. YOU ARE LIKELY TO BE EATEN BY A GRUE.**

"You are standing in an open field west of a white house, with a boarded front door. There is a small mailbox here." Somewhere below lies the Great Underground Empire, and nineteen treasures for whoever is brave, clever and careful enough to bring them back.

Keep your lamp lit. Watch out for the thief, who would very much like your treasures too. And never, ever, go wandering in the dark.

This is where Infocom began: Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels and Tim Anderson's adventure of 1980, the original story file, now free under the MIT licence.

- **Type what you mean**: a parser that understands whole sentences, like `put sword in case`
- **Nineteen treasures** to find and carry home
- **The original story file**, unchanged, played in Frotz

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take lamp**, **open mailbox**, **put sword in case**
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/zork1`.

## Credits

- Zork I: Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels and Tim Anderson; Infocom, 1980
- Released under the MIT license by Microsoft, with Xbox and Activision, in 2025
- Played with Frotz by David Griffith and contributors (GPL-2.0-or-later)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse

zork2.title: Zork II: The Wizard of Frobozz
zork2.description: Deeper into the Great Underground Empire, where the Wizard of Frobozz whispers a word beginning with F and your day gets worse. A dragon, a unicorn, a robot and the Bank of Zork await.
zork2.provenance: Infocom released Zork II in 1981; Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels and Tim Anderson wrote it.

developer.name: Infocom (Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels, Tim Anderson)

zork2.page:
**HE WHISPERS A WORD BEGINNING WITH "F". THEN HE VANISHES, CHUCKLING NASTILY.**

You are inside an ancient barrow, hidden deep in a dark forest. A sword of Elvish workmanship lies on the ground, beside a strangely familiar brass lantern. Beyond the tunnel lies the next part of the Great Underground Empire, and the realm of the Wizard of Frobozz.

He has seen better days. He has a Doctor of Thaumaturgy degree from GUE Tech, a trophy room full of the "dull and nicked swords" of foolhardy adventurers, and a habit of turning up, "floating nonchalantly in the air beside you", to cast a spell. "Fear!" he cries, and you run. His words always begin with F, and they are rarely good news.

There are new treasures down here, and plenty in the way of them: a dragon in a flame-scarred lair, a dishevelled princess, a unicorn with a tiny key on a red satin ribbon, a robot who does what he is told, and a vandalised bank whose sign still reads "Thank You for Banking at the Zork!"

- **The middle of the trilogy**, with the Wizard of Frobozz at its heart
- **Puzzles with a sense of humour**: the Wizard, the robot and the Bank of Zork
- **The original story file**, unchanged, played in Frotz

## How to play

Type what you want to do, in plain words, and press Enter:

- **look**, **inventory** (or **i**), **examine** something
- **north**, **south**, **east**, **west**, **up**, **down** (or **n**, **s**, **e**, **w**, **u**, **d**)
- **take lamp**, **open mailbox**, **put sword in case**
- **save** and **restore**; **quit** to stop

Your saved games are kept in `~/.local/share/zork2`.

zork3.title: Zork III: The Dungeon Master
zork3.description: The end of the trilogy, at the foot of the Endless Stair. The Dungeon Master is waiting for an adventurer worthy to take his place. Is it you?
zork3.provenance: Infocom released Zork III in 1982; Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels and Tim Anderson wrote it.

developer.name: Infocom (Marc Blank, Dave Lebling, Bruce Daniels, Tim Anderson)

zork3.page:
**"YOU HAVE REACHED THE FINAL TEST, MY FRIEND!"**

As in a dream, you tumble down a great, dark staircase, past old struggles and diabolical traps, until an old yet oddly youthful man turns towards you, his long silver hair dancing in the breeze. "You are proved clever and powerful, but this is not yet enough! Seek me when you feel yourself worthy!"

The dream dissolves. You are at the bottom of the Endless Stair, your old friend the brass lantern at your feet. This is the deepest part of the Great Underground Empire, and here treasure matters less than worth. Ruined aqueducts. A royal museum that Lord Dimwit Flathead built "under two miles of mountain". A mirror that is not quite a mirror. A hooded figure who fights a little too much like you. And an exhibit from the Technological Museum that turned out not to be a nonworking model at all.

The Dungeon Master is watching. Only an adventurer who proves worthy will take his place.

- **The end of the trilogy**: the Empire's last secrets, and its master
- **Trials, not a treasure hunt**: a different kind of Zork
- **The original story file**, unchanged, played in Frotz

ztrack.title: Ztrack
ztrack.description: An endless three-lane road full of stupid but dangerous traffic, and you score most at 150 mph. Check your mirrors before you change lanes.
ztrack.provenance: Russell Marks wrote Ztrack in C on curses (1995, version 1.0 in 1996).
ztrack.page:
**150 MPH. THREE LANES. STUPID BUT DANGEROUS TRAFFIC.**

Get as far as you can down an endless three-lane road, and score the most by doing it flat out at 150 mph. You can go slower, of course, as its author put it, "if you enjoy doing pointless boring things." Run into the back of a car, or swerve into a lane that is already taken, and you lose one of your three cars.

You see the road from behind the wheel, over your bonnet. Cars level with you are out of sight, but your wing mirrors light up with a blob when a lane beside you is taken, so check them before you change lanes.

There is no pedal to hold: you set a mode. Accel keeps speeding up, decel keeps slowing down, and cruise holds your speed exactly.

## Controls

- **Up** or **q**: accel mode
- **Down** or **a**: decel mode
- **Space** or **Tab**: cruise at the current speed
- **Left** or **o**: move left a lane
- **Right** or **p**: move right a lane
- **Esc** or **X**: end the game

On the title screen, **Space** starts a game and **Esc** or **q** quits.
The high score lasts until you quit.

## History

Russell Marks wrote Ztrack 1.0 in October 1995, loosely after a Casio
LCD driving game he remembered as "Turbo Drive", and put it in the public
domain; it was uploaded to sunsite.unc.edu (now ibiblio) in 1996. FreeBSD still
carries it in its ports collection.

This edition reads the keyboard through curses rather than straight from
the terminal device. That makes the cursor keys steer (in the original they
ended the game) and lets the game run in the Windows console. It also fixes
an out-of-bounds read when drawing the title logo. The gameplay is
unchanged.

## Credits

- Game: Russell Marks
- Windows console support: [PDCurses](https://pdcurses.org)
- Asciiverse edition: Asciiverse
- License: public domain
